• Next Generation Mobile Networks Alliance (NGMN). Open RAN White Paper. NGMN – We make better connections

title: Space Domain Operational Environment Assessment
summary: The objective of this Phase I effort is to develop methods, including integration of intelligence information, predictive analytics, anomaly detection, threat prediction and environmental monitoring for timely space domain awareness, threat detection and operational environment assessment to support multi-domain operations.
description:
Objective:
The objective of this Phase I effort is to develop methods, including integration of intelligence information, predictive analytics, anomaly detection, threat prediction and environmental monitoring for timely space domain awareness, threat detection and operational environment assessment to support multi-domain operations. Traditional sensing alone cannot track or characterize emergent non-standard threats and current research neglects space-centric operational environment monitoring. To address these gaps, the U.S. Space Force (USSF) seeks novel sensing phenomenologies paired with real-time multi-INT data processing, predictive analytics, and anomaly detection concepts that demonstrate how new sensing and processing techniques can present a comprehensive space operating picture.

Description:
With the acknowledgement of space as a warfighting domain in 2019, the U.S. Space Command was established as a geographic combatant command. No orbital regime is entirely safe from intentional or unintentional threats. Adversary forces can track and target U.S. forces in all warfighting domains. The past two decades have witnessed rapidly maturing space based and counterspace capabilities of U.S. adversaries, as well as their attempts to interfere with U.S. military operations. U.S. operational space activities perform a continuous cycle of situational awareness, planning, execution, and assessment to support leadershipâ€™s decision-making process at all levels of command.

Space Domain Operational Environment Assessment is a prerequisite to achieving space superiority by

(a) understanding the situation in space, and (b) gaining insight into space-related activities in other domains. Even in peacetime, awareness and mission assessment in the space domain is difficult to maintain due to the scope and distances involved. Achieving timely awareness and assessment of space activities to support space superiority operations is a monumental, highly technical challenge that is only growing. The past 20 years has seen the number of objects in orbit grow from approximately 10,000 to over 50,000. As this number grows, so too does the need for timely space domain awareness and situation assessment.

Given the complexity and challenges of operations in space, this topic seeks to develop a proof-of-concept to leverage multi-INT, multi-domain data, intelligence, and information sources to monitor and assess space operations and their functionality in a timely manner in response to intentional and unintentional threats and situations of interest.

To accomplish this, the topic consists of two distinct Technical Areas (TAs). The first TA (TA1) focuses on the collection, processing and analysis of all data types and phenomenologies for advanced Space Domain Awareness and detection of non-standard threats. The second TA (TA2) focuses on analytics, data fusion, machine learning, dynamic command and control for understanding adversary capabilities, actions (offensive/defensive) and effects.

Technical Area 1 - Real-time Processing of Non-Traditional Phenomenologies for Non-Standard Threats

The space domain is becoming increasingly congested and contested as the population of satellites in the space domain is both increasing and expanding. The emergence of non-standard threats in the space domain poses a challenge for traditional phenomenologies, such as RADARs and electro-optical telescopes. Todayâ€™s non-standard threats are increasingly difficult to detect, track and characterize. The United States Space Force (USSF) must possess the capability to monitor the space domain for nonstandard threats in order to protect national assets. This topic seeks to identify new sensing phenomenologies and the processes necessary to detect, track, and characterize non-standard threats. Additionally, the USSF needs to understand how these new phenomenologies complement and improve information products generated by traditional phenomenologies.

Technical Area 2 - Real-Time Automated Data Fusion, Analysis & Exploitation

Joint space forces typically support multiple Combatant Commands, joint functions, and Operational Environments simultaneously to create effects during all military operations (strategic, operational, and tactical). Joint planners continually coordinate across internal and external equity holders to integrate intelligence and information for commander guidance and decisions on the development and refinement of space strategies, plans, and objectives. The timely assessment of space operations is critical for the iterative joint planning process, especially in a contested environment, and must keep pace with evolving conditions and considerations. This can be challenging in the space domain where operators often cannot directly observe the effects of an operation and resulting adversary behavior.

Space operations assessment measures the progress toward accomplishing a task, creating an effect, achieving an objective, or attaining an end state by comparing forecasted outcomes to actual events to determine the overall effectiveness of force employment. As planners identify specific space tasks, they also develop measures of performance and measures of effectiveness to assess each task and objective. Space operations assessment informs the decision-making process concerning the best way to employ and adapt limited resources in support of military operations.

Phase I:
TA1: Identify non-traditional phenomenologies that can be used to perform SDA collections. Investigate the technical challenges to exploiting the data from non-traditional phenomenologies for real-time SDA. Identify a collection strategy. Identify the benefits of leveraging the non-traditional phenomenology to complement and improve traditional phenomenologies. Define specific performance metrics and demonstrate how the approach enhances the defined metrics for tracking and characterizing targets. The offeror is expected to include a detailed plan outlining the development, testing, and integration of the proposed solution, including specific timelines and milestones. GFE will not be provided.

TA2: Design a concept for a workable and scalable prototype to address the basic capabilities and technical feasibility of the stated objective as well as data and information sources and the timeliness of their solution. Identify non-traditional phenomenology and data sources. Define a set of metrics and success criteria for a Phase 2 prototype. Include detailed findings in a Phase II plan in the final report. GFE will not be provided

Phase II:
TA1: Research and develop technical solutions to address the technical challenges of the non-traditional phenomenology identified in the Phase I effort. Develop and demonstrate a simulation capability to generate simulated data for the non-traditional phenomenology. Perform SDA collections with the nontraditional phenomenology and investigate the collected data. Develop a framework for processing of the non-traditional phenomenology. Develop a methodology to perform data fusion of the non-traditional phenomenology with traditional phenomenologies. Demonstrate an integrated prototype system or incorporation of new phenomenologies into an existing system. Demonstrate the ability to generate actionable information on relevant timelines through a simulation or deployment to a relevant environment. GFE will not be provided.

TA2: Develop, implement and test the proposed Phase 1 solution as prototype software to assess space operations using multi-INT multi-domain data and information in a timely manner in response events of interests and unintentional threats and their effects on space missions. Show the feasibility of the approach using modeling simulation and real-world data. GFE will not be provided.

For both Success criteria for Phase II include:

- Demonstrated software prototype capability. Demonstration will be measured against metrics and CONOPs use case.

- Ability to integrate outputs into operational workflows with minimal burden on users.

- Achievable path to Phase III transition, including identification of customers, funding mechanisms, and required approvals

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Further develop and deploy the prototype capabilities developed under Phase II. Develop a strategy to transition prototype residual capabilities and incremental proliferation based on operational USSF requirements. Mature prototype software into a commercial product for commercial SDA. Identify government and commercial organizations for transition. Generate the technical and training documentation required for third party integration. Provide services to the government to maximize the utility of the alerts to operations. Provide services to the government to update software prototype for different applications. This topic promotes dual-use opportunities to provide health and operational status of commercial satellites and their services in relation to adversariesâ€™ actions.

title: Counter Adversial GPS Jamming
summary: Developing a general, effective, and robust antijamming framework for GPS signals is a problem of critical importance. This topic seeks proposals that utilize exceptional-point stochastic resonance and modern machine learning to overcome the vulnerabilities of GPS signals to strong adversarial jamming and spoofing.
description:
Objective:
Developing a general, effective, and robust antijamming framework for GPS signals is a problem of critical importance. This topic seeks proposals that utilize exceptional-point stochastic resonance and modern machine learning to overcome the vulnerabilities of GPS signals to strong adversarial jamming and spoofing. This will ultimately enhance the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) for weak signals and maintain the operational readiness of the Air Force.

Description:
Military and commercial missions rely heavily on the Global Positioning System (GPS), but GPS signals, due to their weak intensity and their need to travel considerable distances, are vulnerable to external interference such as jamming and spoofing. Adversarial jamming can be strong in that its amplitude can be orders of magnitude larger than that of the GPS signal, and they share the same spectral band. Various methods based mostly on traditional signal-processing techniques, such as filtering or wavelet transform, were proposed to mitigate GPS jamming to a certain extent. Often, the effectiveness of a specific method depends on the type of jamming signals in terms of their waveform, amplitude, and frequency range.

GPS antijamming is essentially a nonlinear signal prediction and classification problem. For nonlinear signal prediction, a possible solution is exploiting modern machine learning, where a suitable neural-network architecture trained with features of the desired signals views the jamming as undesired and removes them. However, the inevitable noise represents a difficulty when employing machine learning to predict the GPS waveform and navigation signal, which can significantly degrade the antijamming capability. In nonlinear dynamical systems, the counterintuitive phenomenon of stochastic resonance (references 1 & 3) has been well established, where the signal-to-noise ratio for a weak signal can be enhanced by tuning the noise amplitude. This opens the possibility of enhancing the GPS signal through the stochastic-resonance mechanism.

Phase I:
This is a Direct to Phase 2 (D2P2) topic. Phase I proposals will not be evaluated and Phase I awards will not be made under this topic.. The offeror is required to provide detail and documentation in the Direct-to-Phase-II (D2P2) proposal which demonstrates accomplishment of a “Phase I-type” effort, including a feasibility study. For this D2P2 topic, the offeror should have accomplished the following in a Phase I-type effort via some other means. The offeror must have developed a concept for a workable prototype or design to address at a minimum the basic capabilities of the stated objective above. Proposal must show, as appropriate to the proposed effort, a demonstrated technical feasibility to meet the capabilities of the stated objective. Proposal may provide example cases of this new capability on a specific application. The documentation provided must demonstrate that the offeror has developed a preliminary understanding of the technology to be applied in their Phase II proposal to meet the objectives of this topic. Documentation should include all relevant information including, but not limited to, technical reports, test data, prototype designs/models, and performance goals/results. Feasibility documentation cannot be based solely upon or logically extend from any prior or ongoing federally funded SBIR or STTR work.

Phase II:
In an era of critical GPS technology, the security and safeguard of satellite navigation signals are at the forefront of national and military interest. And, as GPS signals become more integrated into essential infrastructure, the growing vulnerability of adversarial jamming prompts the need to bolster GPS resilience with innovative proposals and cutting-edge research. Stimulating and supporting basic research for GPS antijamming efforts holds the promise to advance the technological capabilities and operational readiness of the Department of Air Force.

Previous research explored the potential of higher-order exceptional points, uncovering a broad type of stochastic resonance where the system’s response to a signal is enhanced by the presence of noise. As the noise amplitude increases, the SNR reaches a global maximum, suggesting that higher order exceptional points can sustain high performance over a wide range of noise levels. The ability to achieve a high SNR with minimal performance decay paves the way for the development of robust and reliable signal processing and sensor technology.

Proposals in antijamming and counter measuring GPS technology would exploit the exceptional-point features design for the development of next generation sensors and communication systems both sensitive and resilient to GPS disruptions and jamming. In signal processing paradigms, robust systems that maintain high quality signal transmission, in the presence of adversarial interference, drives innovative solutions for the challenges and needs of the Department of Air Force’s operational readiness.

The technical merit of GPS antijamming research lies in the adaptability and efficiency of integrated sensing and cyber capabilities that remain robust under varying noise and interference levels. This would directly enhance the operational readiness and technological capabilities of the Department of Air Force, and the warfighter.

Offeror must develop and demonstrate a user-friendly computer program prototype that can be inserted into a GSP anti-jamming system.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
The integration of higher-order exceptional features into commercial technologies offers the promise of reliable, efficient, dynamical systems across a broad spectrum of industrial and military processes. In industrial sectors like manufacturing and logistics, efforts would improve the resilience of sensors, ensuring that they remain responsive and resilient to external interferences.

Potential research would also address the critical DoD areas in weak signal processing; a facet central to the GPS. Extracting weak signals in strong jamming/noise is a poised challenge to the GPS, magnetometer and numerous communication systems significant to commercial and DoD domains. Successful research in this domain promises the protection of aircraft and long-range vehicle capabilities, particularly in enhancing the accuracy of flight data, reduction of signal disruption risks and advancement of autonomous flight systems in the aerospace ecosystem.

As these advancements are realized, aircraft would adapt swiftly to changes in signal processing flight conditions, enhancing the overall readiness of flight operations: protection of commercial airline usage of GPS.

• S. Panahi, L.-L. Ye, and Y.-C. Lai, “Higher-order exceptional points and stochastic resonance in pseudo-Hermitian systems,” Phys. Rev. Appl. 22, 054063, 1-14 (2024).

title: Artificial Intelligence Performance Evaluation Tool
summary: The objective of this research effort is to design, develop, and demonstrate an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Performance Evaluation Tool that streamlines, standardizes, and enhances the evaluation of AI-enabled systems across various operational conditions.
description:
Objective:
The objective of this research effort is to design, develop, and demonstrate an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Performance Evaluation Tool that streamlines, standardizes, and enhances the evaluation of AI-enabled systems across various operational conditions. This Phase I STTR effort will focus on exploring innovative methodologies to quantify the performance, reliability, and robustness of AI models, particularly in applications related to sensors and information systems within the test and evaluation missions of the Air Force Test Center (AFTC). To demonstrate early-stage feasibility, the proposed tool must be capable of evaluating AI-enabled sensor suites (e.g., EO/IR, Radar, and Radio Frequency systems) and align with AFTC’s primary simulation and digital engineering environments, such as the Advanced Framework for Simulation, Integration, and Modeling (AFSIM), Ansys Test and Evaluation Tool Kit (TETK), or the Joint Simulation Environment (JSE).

By addressing critical gaps in assessing AI robustness under dynamic and contested conditions—including real-time inference latency, adversarial resilience, and data drift detection— the effort aims to establish early-stage feasibility for an adaptive framework capable of identifying key performance indicators (KPIs), assessing trustworthiness through explainability metrics, and ensuring compliance with evolving Department of Defense (DoD) AI standards, such as those delineated in the DoD Responsible AI Strategy and Implementation Pathway.

This tool will be designed to integrate seamlessly with the current test environment of the 412th Test Wing and support Operationally Focused Advanced Battle Management System (ABMS) initiatives by providing actionable insights that enable faster and more informed decision-making processes. Phase I will emphasize technical innovation, feasibility validation, and initial use-case alignment to ensure the framework’s scalability and adaptability for Phase II development and field-level implementation. The alignment of the initial use case must specifically demonstrate how the proposed evaluation tool will ingest AFTC-representative sensor data to ensure the framework’s scalability and adaptability for Phase II development. The overarching goal is to accelerate the operational utility and trusted deployment of autonomous and AI-driven systems in support of Air Force modernization priorities while improving mission readiness and capability sustainment.

Description:
The proposed research effort aims to address critical gaps in the evaluation and validation of Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems within the Air Force by developing an Artificial Intelligence Performance Evaluation Tool. The tool will provide a standardized, adaptive, and robust framework capable of assessing the performance, reliability, and explainability of AI models, with a targeted application in sensor and information systems used in test and evaluation missions under the 412th Test Wing (412TW) of the Air Force Test Center (AFTC). This effort aligns with the Department of Defense's (DoD) thrust toward advancing Trusted AI and Autonomy and operationally focused Advanced Battle Management System (ABMS) initiatives.

Problem/Unmet Need: Current AI evaluation processes lack standardization and reproducibility across varying operational environments, making it difficult for the AFTC to confidently assess AI models’ trustworthiness, reliability, and operational readiness. Furthermore, the escalation in complexity of AI-enabled systems has underscored the need for technologies that can quantitatively measure AI performance while adhering to DoD Responsible AI principles. These challenges prevent the Air Force from leveraging AI advancements at scale, impacting readiness and modernization goals.

Opportunity/Desired Outcome: By creating a modular AI evaluation tool, this effort provides an opportunity to establish a scalable and adaptable solution that aligns with emerging DoD AI standards. The desired outcome is a measurable enhancement in the fidelity, speed, and consistency of AI performance assessments, reducing decision-making cycles and increasing mission readiness. The tool will enable practical implementation of AI validation in secure environments, ensuring compliance with applicable standards and operational conditions. Successful deployment will support the broader modernization priorities tied to mission-critical AI deployment and advanced autonomy.

Approach

The project will begin in Phase I with baseline research and feasibility studies, advancing into a scalable prototype in Phase II for integration and testing in operationally relevant environments. A summary of planned efforts by phase follows:

Phase I: Feasibility and Concept Development (Initial TRL: 2; Target TRL: 4)

Research: Conduct an initial landscape analysis of AI performance metrics, methodologies, and tools with a focus on gaps and challenges specific to AFTC’s mission space. Identify and assess algorithms for measuring real-time inference latency, adversarial resilience, and data drift specifically for different sensor models. This research must establish and utilize open-source or synthetically generated surrogate sensor datasets that are representative of AFTC flight test scenarios.

Framework Design: Develop a software architecture for an adaptable AI performance evaluation framework designed to address reliability, robustness, and explainability metrics. Awardees will need to base their design on widely accepted DoD digital engineering and telemetry standards. The architecture must explicitly define the assumed data ingestion pipelines for surrogate sensor data and detail the computational methods that will be used to calculate reliability, robustness, and explainability metric.

Simulation: Perform initial simulation tests to explore early-stage integration of explainability metrics and KPI identification methodologies. This will consist of running dry-runs within a localized software sandbox. The objective of these tests is to demonstrate that the proposed mathematical models can successfully process these inputs, identify Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) such as data drift, and output quantifiable explainability scores.

Deliverables: A feasibility report describing how the tool can practically operate within the AFTC environment, a detailed framework design document, and initial simulation results demonstrating concept validity. This could include Surrogate Data Strategy and Baselining, algorithmic and mathematical validation, architectural alignment and computational overhead, and Phase II scalability and transition pathway.

Phase II: Prototype Development and Validation (Initial TRL: 4; Target TRL: 6)

Prototype Development: Build a functional prototype of the performance evaluation tool with a secure Python-based backend and a user-friendly Graphical User Interface (GUI).

Integration: Test and integrate the tool with existing sensor and information systems in a controlled 412TW test environment to assess real-world performance.

AI Metrics Library: Develop an expandable library of explainability metrics aligned with DoD Trusted AI standards to support diverse mission applications.

Validation: Conduct comprehensive testing in operationally relevant scenarios to ensure reliability, scalability, and compliance with DoD standards.

Deliverables: A fully functional prototype, test reports validating system performance, and a roadmap for field-level deployment.

Conclusion

This effort supports the Air Force’s operational imperatives by advancing capabilities for trustworthy AI deployment in mission-critical applications. Upon completion of Phase II, the AI Performance Evaluation Tool is expected to reach TRL 6, with a clearly defined transition pathway toward operational implementation across the 412TW and other DoD components. This innovation is anticipated to significantly enhance the Air Force's ability to validate AI systems, improve decision-making confidence, and maintain technological superiority in contested environments.

Phase I:
Phase I will establish the project's feasibility and lay the foundational groundwork. Key activities will include: Detailed Analysis: Conduct a comprehensive study of current flight test analysis workflows to identify specific bottlenecks, constraints, and user requirements. Architectural Design: Develop a detailed hardware and software architectural design that emphasizes modularity, security, and Python-based extensibility. Core Algorithm Prototyping: Develop and simulate proof-of-concept algorithms for automated metric generation and data processing. Feasibility Report: Deliver a final report summarizing findings, the complete system design, simulation results, and a detailed plan for the Phase II prototype development.

Phase II:
Phase II will focus on the creation and rigorous testing of a fully functional prototype in a controlled environment. Prototype Development: Build the integrated software application, including the graphical user interface (GUI), data analysis engine, and the AI-powered report generation module. Lab-Based Testing: Establish a reference system in a secure, closed-loop environment to conduct extensive testing. Performance Validation: Evaluate the prototype against a comprehensive set of metrics, including: Time Space Position Information (TSPI) processing accuracy. Comparative analysis against legacy methods. Integrity of automated report generation. System security and resilience against simulated threat/victim scenarios. Demonstration: Conclude with a successful end-to-end demonstration of the prototype's capabilities, proving its readiness for transition to a real-world operational testing environment.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
The 416th Test Squadron at Edwards Air Force Base, which specializes in F-16 flight testing and has a history of integrating advanced systems, will serve as the dedicated transition partner for this effort. Our commercialization strategy is multifaceted: Productization: Refine the successful Phase II prototype into a robust, user-friendly, and cost-effective commercial product. User-Centric Feedback: Conduct extensive operational testing with the 416th Test Squadron and other target users to gather feedback for iterative product improvements. Dual-Use Applications: While the primary customer is the DoW, we will explore dual-use applications for commercial aerospace, avionics testing, and other sectors that require complex data analysis. Infrastructure and Support: Establish comprehensive manufacturing, customer support, and training infrastructure to ensure a smooth and successful transition from a prototype to a fully supported operational tool that will revolutionize flight test analysis.

title: Automated Combat Assessment at the Edge
summary: Develop a real time automated combat assessment at the edge system.
description:
Objective:
Develop a real time automated combat assessment at the edge system.

Description:
Combat assessment (physical and functional) provides tactically relevant information for re-strike and re-planning. The state of practice for traditional targeting involves generating after-action reports including battle-damage assessment hours after mission execution relying on multiple imagery collects (EO). This analysis is performed as a sequence of independent tasks that are outdated, time consuming, and lack automation. This does not meet timeline requirements for prosecution of advanced enemy threat systems as critical missions require battle damage assessment immediately post-strike, to inform planning for restrike and to drive potential changes to operations.

Despite advancements in technology, challenges still remain for speeding processes such as time-consuming and often incomplete nature of traditional damage assessment methods, limitations in remote sensing technologies, hindering data collection especially in remote or difficult-to-access areas, the lack of real time pre- and post-event satellite imagery for model training. This topic seeks the development of a system for the automation of damage assessment following the below operational realities:

- Edge Processing Software. Software programs and data-sharing instructions designed to run directly on physical field equipment such as sensors and drones. For multi-sensor, multi-modal data collection and processing, damage classification and assessment at the edge in (near) real time, and information sharing protocols under low SWaP and contested environments constraints.

- AI/ML Software Model Development. AI/ML software designed to automatically classify military damaged. For damage classification (physical and functional) that is aligned to the CJCSI 3162.02 for DoD customers, confidence intervals aligned to the Intelligence Community Directive ICD 302, and performance metrics for accuracy, computation time, and sensors density & location.

- Robust Testing and Evaluation. To ensure the operational effectiveness, suitability, and survivability of the aforementioned technologies, testing and evaluation would be conducted in a phased approach. Beginning with laboratory-based testing to verify basic functionality and performance, followed by increasingly complex testing in simulated and field environments. The goal is to ensure that the technologies developed for combat assessment are operationally effective, suitable, and can be confidently deployed in operationally relevant environments.

Phase I:
Phase I will focus on the analysis and design of an automated combat assessment at the edge system for re-strike (a particularly targeted asset) and re-attack recommendations with preliminary laboratory model testing. Awardees must demonstrate an innovative approach to physical and functional combat assessment, and novel or under-utilized data modalities. The final report must detail feasibility study findings and a Phase II plan.

Phase II:
findings and a Phase II plan.

PHASE II: Develop, implement, test, evaluate, and demonstrate a distributed automated damage assessment system at the edge that follows the criteria on the Description and Phase I sections of this proposal. The final report must detail all criteria implementations and a Phase III plan.

Phase II performance will focus on the development, integration, and operational evaluation of a functional prototype software system for distributed, edge-based automated combat assessment. Awardees will transition Phase I designs into working software models running on representative edge hardware, culminating in a demonstration within a simulated or operationally relevant environment.

Required deliverables may include:

• Functional prototype software and compiled AI/ML model weights.
• Comprehensive system architecture and interface control documentation (ICD).
• Phase II final report detailing test results, performance metrics, criteria implementations, and a commercialization/transition plan for Phase III production and deployment.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
The awardee will identify and pursue commercial applications, including urban surveillance, disaster and humanitarian response, and other use cases.

title: Battle Damage Indications / Battle Damage Assessment Collection, Aggregation, and Analytics Improvement
summary: To accelerate decision-making and enhance space domain awareness across the joint force, the United States Space Force (USSF) requires an advanced data fusion and automated analytics platform.
description:
Objective:
To accelerate decision-making and enhance space domain awareness across the joint force, the United States Space Force (USSF) requires an advanced data fusion and automated analytics platform. This effort will deliver integrated collection, aggregation, and analytics software capabilities that automate multiple heterogeneous sensor and telemetry sources and telemetry sources into a unified Battle Damage Indication and Assessment (BDI/A) data store Ontology to optimize the Tasking, Collection, Processing, Exploitation, and Dissemination (TCPED) lifecycle. Targeted solution will execute automated cross-domain event correlation, implement a dynamic confidence scoring framework with user-adjustable thresholds, provide explainable Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning (AI/ML) diagnostics reaching >80% agreement with Government analysts, and supply a role-based user interface supporting tactical, operational, strategic, and Intelligence Community (IC) workflows.

Description:
To preserve decision advantage during contested-space operations, the United States Space Force (USSF) must rapidly correlate multi-source operational data to streamline Phase 5 (Mission Planning & Force Execution) and Phase 6 (Assessment) of the Space Tasking Cycle (STC) and Joint Targeting Cycle (JTC). The Space Systems Command (SSC) System Delta 85 (SYD 85) Program Management Office (PMO) and the Kronos Program of Record (PoR), in support of the Battle Management, Command, Control, Communications, and Space Intelligence Portfolio Acquisition Executive (BMC3I PAE), is seeking software-based solutions for the BMC3I TAP Lab (Tools, Applications, & Processing) to automate, aggregate, and score multi-phenomenology collection activities in a standardized, Unclassified environment designed for the eventual seamless scaling to classified operational networks. Within this request, there are 5 associated subtasks:

• Automated ingestion and schema mapping of multiple heterogeneous sensor and telemetry sources telemetry and sensor sources into a common BDI/A data store Ontology definition model while preserving metadata and timestamp traceability;
• Cross-domain synchronization and analytics of Electro-Optical/Infra-Red (EO/IR), Radio Frequency (RF), and Radar data products (such as resolved/unresolved observations, Doppler Residuals, and Area-to-Mass Ratio datasets) to detect pre-defined anomalous behaviors using configurable threat signatures;
• Execution of a dynamic, multi-phenomenology confidence scoring framework that evaluates collection source reliability and sensor quality metrics;
• Development of user-friendly, explainable AI/ML-assisted correlation diagnostics that expose the underlying analytical rationale to human operators to assist in target adjudication; and
• Delivery of a segmented user interface enabling Subject Matter Experts (SMEs) to isolate and execute workflows across the four distinct echelons of the BDI/A lifecycle (Tactical BDI, BDA Phase 1, BDA Phase 2, and BDA Phase 3).

Sample inputs include;

- Real-time or historical feeds;

- Ground- and space-based multi-phenomenology sensor data (commercial and government);

- Historical event repositories for change detection; and

- Simulated operational event logs.

Possible techniques may include but are not limited to;

- Automated schema mapping and metadata parsing;

- Change detection algorithms against historical patterns of life;

- Multi-hypothesis data association and Kalman filtering; and

- Explainable AI (XAI) natural language explanation generation.

The software product must be designed to integrate with existing and legacy Mission Unique Software (MUS) toolchains, publishing assessments back to source repositories via standardized application programming interfaces (APIs) and meeting all development requirements for future transition to secure operational networks.

Phase I:
: Phase I will focus on establishing the scientific, technical, and operational feasibility of the proposed automated, multi-phenomenology BDI/A collection, aggregation, and analytics capability. The primary objective is to validate the product-mission fit and construct a high-fidelity conceptual architecture for the unified BDI/A data store Ontology and cross-domain correlation engine. During the Phase I feasibility study, the small business concern (SBC) must:

• Identify and collaborate with specific United States Space Force (USSF) and U.S. Air Force stakeholders, operational end-users, and technical transition partners (aligning with Space Forces-Space (S4S), National Space Defense Center (NSDC), Combined Space Operations Center (CSpOC), Space Force Deltas, and the Intelligence Community) to map existing BDI/A workflows, data formats, and classification boundaries.
• Develop a comprehensive technical architecture and data schema for the proposed BDI/A Ontology, outlining how the system will ingest and normalize multiple heterogeneous sensor and telemetry sources and sensor sources (such as TT&C, RF, optical, and radar datasets) without losing source metadata or timestamp traceability.
• Define the algorithmic approach for multi-phenomenology sensor fusion, change detection, dynamic confidence scoring, and explainable AI/ML correlation models, detailing how the software will communicate its analytical reasoning to human operators to achieve >80% agreement with Government analysts.
• Create an integration and cybersecurity plan detailing how the proposed capability will interface with legacy and novel Mission Unique Software (MUS), comply with Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification (CMMC) frameworks, and transition from an Unclassified proof-of-concept environment to TS//SCI Classified networks.
• Formulate a commercialization strategy demonstrating how these decentralized analytics, multi-source fusion algorithms, and diagnostic user interfaces can be commercialized for private space operators, commercial satellite fleet managers, and space logistics providers.

The Phase I effort must culminate in a detailed feasibility study report and a low-fidelity mock-up or architectural software proof-of-concept validating user experience flows for the four distinct echelons of the BDI/A warfighting lifecycle.

Phase II:
Phase II will focus on developing, refining, and validating the software capabilities outlined in the Phase I feasibility study within the BMC3I TAP Lab testing environment. Specifically, Phase II aims to deliver the fully functional BDI/A data store Ontology, multi-phenomenology collection and aggregation engine, and dynamic confidence scoring framework, maturing the overall solution to a target technology readiness level (TRL) 7/8. The development process will require multiple heterogeneous sensor and telemetry sources, establishing automated schema mapping, and implementing real-time event correlation algorithms. The software must prove capable of detecting pre-defined anomalous signatures using configurable threat parameters, displaying event sequencing dependencies, and enabling deep-dive drill-down traceability to the originating raw data records. Evaluators will test the system's performance using realistic historical and simulated operational scenario runs, verifying that the AI/ML correlation recommendations and dynamic scoring outputs achieve >80% agreement with validated Government analyst assessments. The final operational assessment will require demonstrating thirty (30) days of continuous, high-availability operations on representative networks to ensure seamless integration with the Kronos PoR. The platform will undergo sustained operational assessments on representative networks, establishing a verified baseline of operational reliability and mission-essential resilience.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Potential Phase III efforts will focus on scaling and transitioning the matured BDI/A collection, aggregation, and scoring capabilities directly to operational joint targeting and space tasking systems under designated Programs of Record. Successful solutions will transition to TS//SCI Classified environments to automate target adjudication and operations assessment reporting for S4S, CSpOC, NSDC, USSC, and their IC partners. This ensures a rapid, automated flow from tactical BDI events to strategic and national-level BDA Phase 1, 2, and 3 intelligence outputs, significantly accelerating the targeting cycle loop.

Additionally, the technologies developed under this topic have dual-use potential within the commercial space sector. Commercial satellite fleet operators, mega-constellation managers, and space situational awareness (SSA) service providers require robust, automated systems to conduct vehicle health diagnostics and anomaly resolution. When commercial satellites experience sudden subsystem dropouts or structural degradation (due to orbital debris collisions, space weather events, or local RF interference), operators must quickly assess the damage, isolate the cause, and adjust operational risk postures. Applying this multi-source data fusion, change detection, and explainable AI-assisted scoring algorithms allows commercial operators to automate damage assessment pipelines, lower telemetry analysis overhead, and streamline insurance claim validations, directly increasing the safety and survivability of commercial orbital assets.

Develop a reusable illumination system for high-speed photo-optic data collection used at the Holloman High Speed Test Track (HHSTT) and other sled test tracks.

Description:
The PF300 flash bulbs, that provide high-intensity illumination for high-speed video acquisition, are no longer in production. The objective is to award a contract to a small business to engineer, design, and manufacture a modern, robust, reusable replacement for the legacy PF300 flash bulb. This new system must meet or surpass the existing illumination and performance requirements of the original flash bulbs to ensure seamless integration with current high-speed video systems. The ideal solution would leverage Commercial Off-The-Shelf (COTS) or near-COTS technologies to qualify this project as a direct-to-Phase-II effort. A successful reusable replacement would immediately solve the impending obsolescence issue, securing a reliable illumination source for future missions. Furthermore, transitioning to a reusable system would dramatically reduce consumable cost. This technological update could also pave the way for enhanced capabilities, such as adjustable light intensity and longer duration illumination, offering greater flexibility and improved data quality for high-speed video analysis across various applications

Phase I:

Prior “Phase I-type” work by other companies has produced similar illumination methods, but not to the requirements needed to operate in the Test Track Environment. The Phase II effort will culminate with the demonstration of an operational reusable illumination sled on the test track. The Phase III effort should further refine the illumination system design following lessons learned from the Phase II demonstration. title: Technical Data Package Modernization for Information Assurance and Secure Data Exchange
summary: The technology within this topic is restricted under the International Traffic in Arms Regulation (ITAR), 22 CFR Parts 120-130, which controls the export and import of defense-related material and services, including export of sensitive technical data, or the Export Administration Regulation (EAR), 15 CFR Parts 730-774, which controls dual use items.
description:
Objective:
The technology within this topic is restricted under the International Traffic in Arms Regulation (ITAR), 22 CFR Parts 120-130, which controls the export and import of defense-related material and services, including export of sensitive technical data, or the Export Administration Regulation (EAR), 15 CFR Parts 730-774, which controls dual use items. The objective of this Directed to Phase II (D2P2) SBIR effort is to develop an innovative, secure, and scalable solution for modernizing Technical Data Packages (TDPs) associated with complex Air and Space Force platforms. This initiative seeks to address challenges in managing large, diverse datasets by enhancing configuration control, ensuring data integrity, and strengthening Information Assurance (IA) in support of mission-critical operations. Specifically, the focus of this phase is to demonstrate the feasibility of advanced technologies that enable secure data lifecycle management and seamless data exchange within operational environments. Proposed solutions should align with Trusted AI and Autonomy modernization priorities by incorporating robust cybersecurity measures and leveraging cutting-edge advancements in autonomy, data management, and secure manufacturing capabilities. Outcomes of this phase are expected to validate technical concepts and establish a functional prototype that meets the operational imperative of readiness to deploy and fight, contributing to future scalability and transition opportunities in operational use cases.

Description:
Background and Problem Statement:

The modernization of Technical Data Packages (TDPs) is imperative to address the Air and Space Force’s operational challenges in securely managing large-scale, complex datasets associated with advanced platforms and their sustainment life cycles. Current TDP systems often lack robust Information Assurance (IA) capabilities, seamless integration with Product Lifecycle Management (PLM) environments, and effective mechanisms for secure data exchange across operational networks. This limitation not only hinders data integrity and configuration control but also increases vulnerabilities to cyber threats, jeopardizing mission-critical operations. The rapid pace of platform evolution and the increasing reliance on Model-Based Definition (MBD) and digital twin technologies further exacerbate the need for a comprehensive solution that ensures TDP security, scalability, and operational readiness.

Opportunity and Desired Outcome:

This Directed to Phase II (D2P2) SBIR effort aims to develop an innovative, scalable, and secure solution to modernize TDPs to support the lifecycle of highly complex Air and Space Force platforms. The envisioned solution will integrate advanced IA protocols, cryptographic protections, and tools for encrypted data exchange to facilitate the secure management of the "as-sustained" configuration state of critical assets. The outcome will be a functional prototype capable of enabling secure TDP lifecycle management while aligning with the Trusted AI and Autonomy modernization priorities and Zero Trust Architecture principles. The proposed solution will enhance operational efficiency, minimize cyber risks, and establish a foundation for scalable implementation across DoD platforms.

The project’s Technology Readiness Level (TRL) at the start is anticipated to be TRL 4, with the target of reaching a minimum TRL 6 by the conclusion of Phase II, including validation of core capabilities in a relevant operational environment.

Required Efforts and Phase Activities:

To achieve the stated objectives, the following efforts and activities are required for each phase of the project:

Phase II:

Develop a secure visualization tool for displaying large-scale MBD geometry and associated data through encrypted web-based interfaces.

Implement an encrypted configuration management system to maintain and update the "as-sustained" asset state while ensuring strict data integrity.

Create advanced tools for automated data quality checks, incorporating rules-based IA compliance validation to ensure all TDPs meet security and contractual requirements.

Design an end-to-end encrypted exchange framework for TDPs, incorporating user authentication, authorization, and audit trails while conforming to DoD Zero Trust Architecture guidelines.

Integrate AI/ML methodologies to enable secure damage detection, sustainment planning, and actionable insights into asset health.

Demonstrate the prototype in an operationally relevant environment, proving feasibility, security compliance, and system performance in handling large and diverse data streams.

Minimum Deliverables:

A secure web-based MBD visualization prototype capable of rendering large-scale geometry and TDP datasets with sub-second response times and role-based access controls.

Tools for encrypted configuration management and secure "as-sustained" state maintenance, integrated with PLM systems.

An automated framework for data quality checks and IA compliance validation of TDPs using defined security protocols and rules-based engines.

A cryptographic data transfer and exchange framework, with test results demonstrating alignment with DoD security policies and successful inter-organizational data exchange.

Technical documentation detailing methodologies, system architecture, and IA protocols implemented during the project, including recommendations for further scaling and operationalization.

A transition plan for integrating the developed TDP modernization technology into operational environments within the Air and Space Force platforms, supported by a detailed commercialization strategy aligned with mission needs.

Significance and Contribution to DoD Objectives:

The proposed solution directly addresses the Operational Imperative 7—Readiness to Deploy and Fight—by delivering secure and reliable tools for managing critical asset data. The project also supports the DoD’s Trusted AI and Autonomy priorities by incorporating advanced data protection mechanisms, secure autonomous processes, and scalable solutions for data management across platforms. Successful execution of this effort will enhance the DoD’s ability to maintain readiness, ensure data security, and streamline collaboration with stakeholders while safeguarding sensitive information in a rapidly evolving threat landscape.

Phase I:
As this is a Direct-to-Phase-II (D2P2) topic, no Phase I awards will be made. Offerors must demonstrate completion of Phase I feasibility research and development that is not based upon or logically extend from any prior or ongoing federally funded SBIR or STTR work, demonstrating clear technical merit, alignment with Trusted AI/Autonomy priorities, and DoD Zero Trust standards, such as validated data, performance metrics, technical reports, prototype success, or demonstrated capabilities in relevant operational environments.

Phase II:
The Phase II effort will deliver a secure, scalable prototype for modernizing Technical Data Packages (TDPs). Focus areas include encrypted configuration management, MBD visualization tools, automated IA compliance frameworks, and secure data exchange via Zero Trust Architecture. The solution will achieve TRL 6 with validated performance in operational environments, aiding readiness and alignment with Trusted AI and Autonomy priorities.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
The Phase III effort will advance the secure TDP modernization prototype to TRL 8, employing non-SBIR funds to integrate with Air and Space Force systems. Military applications include secure lifecycle management of technical data for advanced platforms, enhancing readiness and cybersecurity. Commercial use spans aerospace, manufacturing, and defense industries for data security and configuration management. Transition efforts target expanded adoption within DoD and allied partners.

title: US Production of Ultra-High Temperature Ceramic-Yielding Preceramic Polymers
summary: The Department of the Air Force seeks to establish the domestic production of ultra-high temperature ceramic (UHTC)-yielding preceramic polymers. UHTCs are used for demanding aerospace applications, including propulsion and aeroshell components.
description:
Objective:
The Department of the Air Force seeks to establish the domestic production of ultra-high temperature ceramic (UHTC)-yielding preceramic polymers. UHTCs are used for demanding aerospace applications, including propulsion and aeroshell components.

Description:
The scaled production of C/C-UHTCs composites (UHTCMCs) for defense applications requires the manufacturing of UHTC precursors in quantities sufficient to support acquisition programs. This SBIR will establish production of an AFRL-patented UHTC preceramic polymers so that the materials are available, at scale and affordable price point, to the high-temperature composite production community.

Phase I:
This topic is intended for technologies ready to move directly into a Phase II program. As this is a Direct-to-Phase-II (D2P2) topic, no Phase I awards will be made. Offerors must demonstrate completion of Phase I feasibility research and development that is not based upon or logically extend from any prior or ongoing federally funded SBIR or STTR work. Offerors must provide detailed documentation in their Direct to Phase II (D2P2) proposal that demonstrates the successful completion of a "Phase I-like" effort. This includes a feasibility study showing expertise in synthesizing and handling air/water-sensitive chemical compounds. Demonstrated experience in scaling chemical synthesis processes from the lab to pilot scale (e.g., 5-50 kg batches) is required. The feasibility study should clearly illustrate past successes in producing high-purity materials and a foundational understanding of the safety protocols necessary for handling the relevant precursors and reagents.

Phase II:
During the Phase II program, the awardee shall: 1) Establish and document a safe, robust, and scalable chemical process for the manufacturing of the AFRL-patented UHTC-bearing preceramic polymers that meets specified purity and production volume targets. 2) Conduct a thorough safety and handling analysis for all reagents, intermediates, and waste products. Production facilities must ensure safety and environmental compliance are permissible. 3) Deliver a 5x 1 kg samples of the UHTC preceramic polymer to AFRL for internal analysis, characterization, and quality verification. The offeror shall show i) for the produced polymer: NMR, elemental analysis, rheology, and ICP/MS of the produced polymer and ii) for the polymer-derived ceramic XRD, TEM/EDS, and SEM analysis, for each lot of material made. The offeror can assume a cost of $6300/kg in raw material cost if reagents, were to be purchased from commercial chemical suppliers, to produce UHTC preceramic polymers. 4) Establish and demonstrate a dedicated production capability yielding at least 50 kg per month (>600 kg per year). 5) Deliver a total of 75 kg of the qualified UHTC preceramic polymer, appropriately packaged, to the Government by the end of the Phase II effort. 6) Provide a comprehensive cost analysis and business plan for UHTC-bearing preceramic polymer production at the target scale of >1000 kg/year a target retail price of <$5000/kg, preferably <$4000/kg, identifying key supply-chain or processing factors to drive down per-kilogram costs.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
The awardee will be expected to transition the preceramic polymer production established during Phase II into a viable commercial business unit. This will involve supplying certified preceramic polymers to prime contractors and Tier 1/2 composite manufacturers supporting defense and commercial programs of record. Phase III efforts may include further scaling of chemical operations, qualifying the material across a broader vendor base (for high-speed aeroshells), and establishing long-term supply agreements to support critical national security missions.

title: Low SWaP, 2-micron Fiber Amplifiers
summary: Develop and demonstrate a rugged, kilowatt class 2-micron fiber amplifier module that matches size, weight, and power metrics of state-of-the-art 1-micron systems to accelerate the transition of laboratory technology to operational Department of the Air Force capabilities.
description:
Objective:
Develop and demonstrate a rugged, kilowatt class 2-micron fiber amplifier module that matches size, weight, and power metrics of state-of-the-art 1-micron systems to accelerate the transition of laboratory technology to operational Department of the Air Force capabilities.

Description:
High-power fiber lasers operating in the 2-micron regime offer critical advantages for defense, medical, and industrial applications, including eye-safer directed energy, advanced sensing, and precision materials processing. While kilowatt-class, narrow-linewidth thulium-doped fiber amplifiers have been demonstrated, the Department of the Air Force aims to reduce the size and weight of existing kilowatt-class 2-micron fiber amplifiers into a highly compact system with similar size, weight, and power metrics of existing 1-micron fiber amplifiers. This topic seeks to leverage existing Air Force laboratory architectures to prime industry for production of robust 2-micron fiber amplifiers, paving the way for transition into active directed energy programs.

Phase I:
This topic is intended for technologies ready to move directly into a Phase II program. As this is a Direct-to-Phase-II (D2P2) topic, no Phase I awards will be made. Offerors must demonstrate completion of Phase I feasibility research and development that is not based upon or logically extend from any prior or ongoing federally funded SBIR or STTR work. Applicant(s) should provide documentation demonstrating a clear understanding of high power, 2-micron fiber amplifier design, thermal management in constrained operating spaces, and package ruggedization for high-stress environments. Qualifying 'Phase I-type' efforts would include but not limited to the prior design, development, and demonstration of low SWaP, kilowatt-class, 1-micron fiber amplifier modules.

Phase II:
In Phase II, the USAF requires the execution, physical build, and delivery of a fully functional, low SWaP, 2-micron fiber amplifier prototype. This system must deliver kilowatt-class output while complying with the mandatory low-SWaP requirements of state-of-the-art 1-micron fiber amplifiers. The delivered hardware must undergo laboratory verification to validate output power (> 1 kW), beam quality (M2 < 1.2), spectral stability, narrow linewidth (< 5 GHz), and electro-optical efficiency (E-O > 25%). Final deliverables for this effort must include the physical prototype, complete electrical and optical schematics, and a comprehensive test and characterization report.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Phase III success will be driven by transitioning the 2-micron fiber amplifier design into full-rate production and securing commercial market pathways.Additionally, work on the system-level integration of the proven 2-micron fiber amplifier into a deployable, multi-kW laser defense system for real-world environmental validation.

title: Agile Wire Harness Manipulation and Installation for Unmanned Aerial Systems
summary: Develop and demonstrate a modular, agile robotic manufacturing workcell capable of autonomously routing, aligning, inserting, and verifying flexible, non-rigid wire harnesses and electrical connectors within the highly constrained physical geometries of Unmanned Aerial Systems (UAS) and advanced munitions.
description:
Objective:
Develop and demonstrate a modular, agile robotic manufacturing workcell capable of autonomously routing, aligning, inserting, and verifying flexible, non-rigid wire harnesses and electrical connectors within the highly constrained physical geometries of Unmanned Aerial Systems (UAS) and advanced munitions.

As a Direct-to-Phase-II (D2P2) topic, the immediate goal is to transition a validated proof-of-concept software and mechanical baseline (Technology Readiness Level 4) into fully integrated, operationally viable production workcells evaluated at defense prime contractor manufacturing sites. The system must eliminate the need for hard-tooled, single-product automation by delivering an agile platform that integrates deterministic planning models with real-time, adaptive online sensory feedback. This enables the robot to navigate the unpredictable, non-rigid deformation behaviors of flexible cabling, achieve sub-millimeter positioning tolerances, and safely execute intricate "blind-mate" connection sequences within tight bulkhead quarters without manual intervention.

To support a dynamic, high-mix/low-volume defense production environment, the workcell must be designed for rapid retaskability. Offerors must demonstrate a system architecture that allows shop-floor operators to completely retask the workcell to handle an entirely different munitions or UAS harness family within a single eight-hour shift. Furthermore, the platform must establish the first end-to-end digital thread for harness operations, generating machine-readable traceability records for every routing, tensioning, and insertion step to prevent latent defects and ensure 100% military standard compliance.

The ultimate phase outcome must demonstrate a two-to-four-times cycle time improvement over legacy manual wiring techniques and a reduction in skilled labor hours per unit by at least 50%. This will directly remove the primary assembly bottleneck constraining the scale-up, surge capacity, and high-rate production of critical defense systems.

Description:
Context & BackgroundModern Department of Defense (DoD) manufacturing and depot sustainment environments increasingly depend on agile automation to scale up production and maintain rapid operational readiness. While automated assembly technologies have matured substantially for rigid components with predictable geometries, the handling of flexible materials remains a persistent challenge. Specifically, wire harness routing, connector inspection, and insertion operations are ubiquitous across the production lines of Unmanned Aerial Systems (UAS), advanced munitions families, and autonomous collaborative platforms. Currently, these intricate electrical assembly processes represent a bottleneck in UAS assembly operations. Assembly technicians must manually route non-rigid cables through confined structural cavities and execute high-precision connection steps under high-mix, low-volume production conditions. Traditional industrial robotics break down when tasked with these operations because flexible wiring deforms unpredictably during manipulation, completely violating the rigid-part assumptions and fixed, hard-tooled rules of standard automation. Problem, Opportunity, & Unmet Need The complete reliance on manual wire harness installation creates a critical capability deficiency that severely penalizes DoD manufacturing agility and surge capacity. Manual operations are fundamentally non-scalable, meaning production lines cannot dynamically "ramp-to-rate" to meet sudden spikes in theater demand. Furthermore, manual wire routing and insertion introduce human-induced variability, resulting in unquantifiable defects such as partially seated connectors, overstressed wires, or compromised bend radii. These latent defects frequently slip past standard visual inspections and surface as catastrophic electrical or communication failures during critical mission times. Aerospace prime contractors and program offices have identified this manual chokepoint as the largest automation gap in UAS and munitions production. This deficiency creates a major opportunity to implement a flexible automation solution. Resolving this challenge requires a modular, adaptive robotic workcell that handles deformable materials, operates with high positional accuracy in restricted footprints, and can be rapidly retasked between completely different product designs within a single factory shift. Desired Outcome & Technological Improvement The desired outcome of this research and development effort is a fully integrated, single-arm modular robotic manufacturing workcell capable of autonomously handling the core manipulation and installation scenarios for flexible UAS and munitions wiring harnesses. Shifting the technology from manual assembly to adaptive, sensor-driven automation will fundamentally advance the DoD technological state of the art by achieving the following targeted improvements: Deformable Material Control: The platform will combine deterministic offline path planning with adaptive, real-time online sensory feedback (such as tactile, force-torque, and vision monitoring). This closed-loop configuration enables "search and settle" machine behaviors to dynamically correct for micro-misalignments and part variability on the fly. Sub-Millimeter Tolerances: The workcell will successfully execute precise connector insertion and blind-mate assembly steps within tightly constrained geometries to a targeted positioning tolerance of $\le$ 0.5 mm.Rapid Retaskability: The system will break the paradigm of dedicated single-product manufacturing by allowing shop-floor operators to ingest new geometric data and completely retask the workcell to a novel harness family in less than 8 hours.End-to-End Digital Thread: The workcell will generate machine-readable traceability records of every insertion force profile and routing path. This delivers a reliable data audit trail to eliminate quality escapes and predict latent field defects before they manifest in flight.Minimum Acceptable DeliverablesThe following deliverables must be successfully turned over to the government to satisfy the performance requirements of this solicitation:Integrated Single-Arm Robotic Workcell: One fully functional, operational modular automation cell comprising a COTS collaborative arm manipulator, reconfigurable mounting base, interchangeable end-effectors, integrated real-time compute block, and the complete multi-modal sensor stack (vision, tactile, and force-torque instrumentation). Autonomous Software Stack & Executables: Full, unencumbered delivery of the native software architecture, including the offline CAD data-ingestion pipeline, real-time adaptive control algorithms, and localized vision-tactile tracking scripts, along with complete integration documentation.Cross-Program Retasking Report: A documented technical package demonstrating the step-by-step procedures, software tools, and data workflows used to successfully transition the physical workcell between two distinct harness families in less than 8 hours.Comprehensive Technical Data Package (TDP): System layout schematics, wiring diagrams, universal end-effector interface control documents, operational manuals, and interface guides for MES/ERP factory network synchronization. Final Performance & Verification Report: A verified engineering data package from the live prime facility demonstration detailing empirical success metrics. This must validate insertion position accuracy ($\le$ 0.5 mm), insertion force variance curves, production cycle time gains ($\ge$ 2x throughput), labor hour compression ($\ge$ 50%), and a sample data pull of the machine-readable digital thread registry.

Phase I:
As this is a Direct-to-Phase-II (D2P2) topic, no Phase I awards will be made as a result of this topic. To qualify for this D2P2 topic, Offerors must demonstrate completion of Phase I feasibility research and development that is not based upon or logically extend from any prior or ongoing federally funded SBIR or STTR work. Applicant(s) should provide documentation demonstrating a clear understanding of the mechanical handling of flexible materials, single-arm robotic kinematics, deterministic offline tool-path planning, hybrid position/force control loops, multi-modal sensor fusion (vision, force-torque, and tactile feedback), and the implementation of a machine-readable digital thread within restricted weapon and unmanned system assembly architectures.

Phase I Feasibility Context & Technical Goals

For the context of this technology's lifecycle, a traditional Phase I feasibility study represents a focused research and development effort to demonstrate the scientific, technical, and commercial merit of an automated single-arm robotic solution for non-rigid material manipulation. A successful Phase I Period of Performance establishes a baseline across the following specified technical goals, operating parameters, and functional requirements:

Deformable Material Kinematics: Analytical and simulation validation proving that a single collaborative robotic manipulator arm can grasp, lift, and maneuver flexible wire harnesses without causing structural damage, violating minimum bend radii, or exceeding maximum cable strain limits. Confined Space Operating Parameters: System modeling showing the capacity for a robotic arm to navigate and thread cabling through tight apertures and restricted structural bulkheads typical of unmanned aerial systems and compact missile fuselages. Closed-Loop Alignment Logic: Verification of multi-modal tracking logic that utilizes localized computer vision and tactile feedback to continuously calculate micro-adjustments, allowing the arm to align electrical connectors under dynamic part deformation. Compliant Mating Force Boundaries: Formulation of hybrid position/force control profiles that maintain sub-millimeter insertion accuracy while monitoring force thresholds to detect pin engagement and prevent over-force structural damage. Traceable Digital Logging: Drafting a localized data logging schema capable of recording physical insertion forces, path coordinates, and connector seating confirmations to create an immutable digital thread registry.

Successful completion of these Phase I parameters provides a clear, quantitative understanding of the underlying physics and control logic governing non-rigid material manipulation, proving the system is ready for immediate physical hardware-in-the-loop integration.

Required Feasibility Documentation for D2P2 Qualification

To bypass a traditional Phase I award and qualify for this Direct-to-Phase-II pathway, applicants must submit robust, empirical Feasibility Documentation within their proposal. This package serves as the technical justification proving the small business's technology has already retired early-stage conceptual risk and rests at an acceptable maturity level (Minimum Technology Readiness Level 4).

The following documentation types are considered sufficient to substantiate proposal feasibility and must be explicitly provided:

• Empirical Performance Reports and Laboratory Data

Applicants must submit formal engineering reports, test logs, software execution records, or laboratory datasets detailing the execution of prior automated material insertion or routing. This documentation should highlight successful testing of collaborative robotic systems manipulating flexible parts. Data must explicitly demonstrate that the applicant has previously developed software or hardware-in-the-loop scripts capable of driving multi-axis trajectories to grip and move non-rigid items dynamically.

• Cross-Program Proof-of-Concept Benchmarks

Sufficient documentation includes technical summaries, contract performance reviews, or closeout reports from prior non-SBIR federal, academic, or internally funded manufacturing R&D efforts. Specifically, applicants can substantiate feasibility by detailing successful milestones from past automated flexible-assembly initiatives, such as:

Documented integration of robotic platforms optimized for compliant, multi-modal material tracking (e.g., past project outcomes managed under Advanced Robotics for Manufacturing Institute programs).Validated operational results from previous laboratory validation campaigns focused on flexible component manipulation, demonstrating early-stage handling of part deformation and configuration variability.

• Prototype Success Criteria and Interface Control Documents

Applicants must provide evidence of an existing physical or digital prototype. The documentation must exhibit a functional architecture of a single-arm cell, demonstrating how the software handles geometric inputs to calculate tool paths. Success criteria of the prior prototype must demonstrate that the hardware and software configuration can successfully manage flexible materials under variable lighting or workspace clutter, establishing a stable, cloud-independent edge-computing loop prepared for live factory scaling.

By compiling these specific reports, datasets, and mechanical baselines, the applicant provides the Air Force with clear evidence that the foundational technological risks have been thoroughly retired. This proves the single-arm architecture is mature, viable, and prepared to immediately enter the accelerated Phase II prototype integration, laboratory workcell validation, and live TRL 7 pilot production testing schedule.

Phase II:
The Phase II period of performance represents a substantial research, development, and hardware-software integration effort. It transitions the single-arm robotic technology from a validated laboratory concept into an operationally viable, modular manufacturing prototype ready for deployment on active aerospace production lines. To establish a clear, unambiguous standard for project success, the following functional requirements, operating parameters, testing regimens, and quantitative milestones are defined as the mandatory baseline for the Phase II effort.1. Functional Requirements & Technical GoalsThe Phase II effort must deliver a fully integrated, single-arm modular robotic manufacturing workcell that achieves the following technical benchmarks:Hardware-Agnostic Core Integration: Physical integration of a single collaborative manipulator arm mounted onto a reconfigurable or mobile mounting base. The control layer and sensory infrastructure must remain entirely program-agnostic, allowing the system to adapt to different vendor components without requiring a structural mechanical redesign.Autonomous Ingestion & Macro Planning: An offline planning engine capable of ingesting 3D CAD models, engineering metadata, and raw wire harness specifications. This engine must automatically produce verifiable, macro-approach robot trajectories and cable-routing path plans that strictly respect part geometry, cable bend radii, and strain limits.Adaptive Online Control Loop: A native, low-latency software control stack that runs in real-time on local hardware without cloud dependency. The system must utilize real-time tactile, force-torque, and vision feedback to dynamically adjust joint positions and execute compliant connector mating.Human-Like "Search and Settle" Behavior: Integration of hybrid position/force control mechanisms. The single arm must actively use force-torque feedback to perform search-and-settle sub-millimeter corrections during blind-mate insertion sequences where direct visual confirmation is obscured or impossible.Machine-Readable Traceability (Digital Thread): The workcell must implement the first end-to-end digital thread registry for harness assembly operations. The software must automatically log machine-readable records of every cable insertion force profile, routing coordinate, and connection seating confirmation to eliminate quality escapes and prevent latent field failures.2. Operating Parameters & Use CasesThe integrated single-arm automation system must operate reliably within the following boundaries:Physical Footprint & Access Clearance: The complete robotic tool head and manipulator assembly must be engineered to operate within the highly constrained physical envelopes and narrow clearance tracks of defensive aircraft and munitions architectures.Part Deformation Management: The system must dynamically adapt to non-rigid part behavior, actively compensating for the unpredictable bending, flexing, and micro-variability introduced during manual pre-assembly or technician handling.Primary Mission Use Case (Single-Arm Munitions Wiring): The primary operational use case involves deploying the modular workcell to automate the core wiring and electrical routing steps for complex defense systems—including the Franklin Affordable Mass Missile (FAMM) and Coyote Missile families. The system must execute aperture threading, vision/tactile-guided connector alignment, force-compliant insertion, and connection verification on representative aerospace hardware.Achieving the above should deliver a fully validated, production-ready manufacturing technology that drops labor constraints, provides comprehensive digital quality data, and dramatically scales the industrial surge capacity required for Great Power Competition.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
The contractor will pursue commercialization of the technology, targeting government program offices, commercial industrial base stakeholders. and dual use industrial customers.

title: Agile Autonomous Technical Data Package to Path Robotic Task Specification
summary: The technology within this topic is restricted under the International Traffic in Arms Regulation (ITAR), 22 CFR Parts 120-130, which controls the export and import of defense-related material and services, including export of sensitive technical data, or the Export Administration Regulation (EAR), 15 CFR Parts 730-774, which controls dual use items.
description:
Objective:
The technology within this topic is restricted under the International Traffic in Arms Regulation (ITAR), 22 CFR Parts 120-130, which controls the export and import of defense-related material and services, including export of sensitive technical data, or the Export Administration Regulation (EAR), 15 CFR Parts 730-774, which controls dual use items.
