title: Quantum Sensing Analyzer
summary: Investigate and validate the feasibility of developing a novel quantum-based sensing technology utilizing Rydberg atomic sensors as an ultra-wideband universal measurement standard for electromagnetic systems. Demonstrate the potential of these sensors in a calibrated and highly sensitive universal measurement standard to enhance radar, electronic warfare, and antenna characterization.
description:
Objective:
Investigate and validate the feasibility of developing a novel quantum-based sensing technology utilizing Rydberg atomic sensors as an ultra-wideband universal measurement standard for electromagnetic systems. Demonstrate the potential of these sensors in a calibrated and highly sensitive universal measurement standard to enhance radar, electronic warfare, and antenna characterization.

Description:
The “Quantum Sensing Analyzer” project aims to address critical limitations in existing electromagnetic measurement technologies by developing a novel quantum-based sensing capability utilizing Rydberg atomic sensors. These sensors, leveraging quantum properties, exhibit extraordinary sensitivity and accuracy over a widespread frequency spectrum ranging from DC to 1 THz, with potential scalability to even broader ranges. This initiative is designed to modernize and standardize test and evaluation processes within the Department of Defense (DoD), particularly benefiting the Benefield Anechoic Facility (BAF) and its mission to support advanced electromagnetic system testing.

Problem Statement and Opportunity:

Current electromagnetic measurement techniques rely on diverse and complex instruments, which introduce inefficiencies, inconsistencies, and increased costs for the acquisition, testing, and integration of modern radar systems, electronic warfare platforms, communication systems, and antennas. These existing systems also face challenges in maintaining accuracy and repeatability, particularly when evaluating performance across a wide range of radio frequencies or within controlled environments like anechoic chambers.

The introduction of Rydberg sensor technology represents a disruptive opportunity to establish a universal, high-precision, SI-traceable standard for electromagnetic measurements. By adopting a single, compact, and adaptable sensor for diverse measurement tasks—including spectrum analysis, field strength monitoring, and chamber characterization—this capability promises to significantly reduce infrastructure requirements, simplify operational workflows, and enhance confidence in test data accuracy.

Project Objectives:

● Develop and validate a proof-of-concept Rydberg-based quantum sensing system capable of performing highly accurate and repeatable electromagnetic measurements across 1.5 MHz to 40 GHz.

● Demonstrate the ability of the sensor to serve as a universal measurement standard for radar, electronic warfare, communication systems, and antenna evaluation.

● Establish enhanced chamber characterization capabilities, including electromagnetic leakage detection, direction finding, near-field measurement, reflection mitigation, and quiet zone mapping, to improve the testing environment quality.

● Progress the technology readiness level (TRL) from TRL 2 at project initiation to TRL 6 by the conclusion of Phase II.

Required Efforts and Phase Activities:

Phase I:

● Perform a comprehensive feasibility study to assess the applicability of Rydberg atomic sensors as a universal electromagnetic measurement standard.

● Evaluate the sensors’ technical attributes, including sensitivity (targeting sub-microvolt/meter thresholds), dynamic range, and bandwidth.

● Identify potential integration challenges with existing test facilities and systems, particularly those used in the BAF.

● Deliverables: Feasibility study report detailing technical analyses, identified challenges, and potential solutions; preliminary system design for a prototype quantum sensing analyzer.

Phase II:

● Develop, fabricate, and demonstrate a functional prototype of the Rydberg-based quantum sensing system, incorporating key findings from Phase I.

● Conduct extensive testing and validation of the prototype in operationally relevant environments, including the BAF, with emphasis on precision, SI-traceability, and repeatability of electromagnetic measurements.

● Integrate the system into existing DoD testing workflows, showcasing improvements in efficiency, reduced equipment requirements, and testing performance.

● Deliverables: Fully operational prototype, detailed test and evaluation report, system integration plan, and transition strategy for scaling and deployment within the DoD.

Desired Outcome:

The successful development of a Quantum Sensing Analyzer will revolutionize the DoD’s electromagnetic measurement and testing capabilities by delivering a single, universal, quantum-enabled sensing standard. This solution will eliminate the need for multiple specialized instruments, streamline developmental and operational testing, and significantly enhance test accuracy and repeatability. Furthermore, the technology will address critical modernization priorities, such as advancing quantum science and enabling operationally focused Advanced Battle Management Systems (ABMS). This effort aligns with the Air Force’s strategic goals to improve mission readiness, accelerate technology deployment to the warfighter, and invest in cutting-edge testing capabilities that sustain innovation and technical superiority in defense systems.

Phase I:
Phase I will assess the feasibility of Rydberg sensors for precise electromagnetic measurements (1.5 MHz–40 GHz). Goals include evaluating sensitivity, bandwidth, and range while addressing DoD test needs. Deliverables: technical feasibility analysis, preliminary design, and simulated performance data to validate the sensors’ potential as a scalable, SI-traceable measurement standard for advanced defense applications.

Phase II:
Phase II focuses on developing, integrating, and testing a Rydberg-based quantum sensing prototype for 1.5 MHz–40 GHz electromagnetic measurement. Deliverables include a tested SI-traceable system demonstrating dynamic range, ultra-wideband operation, noise-level performance, operational integration, and resilience to interference. Success is defined by achieving TRL 6, validating accuracy, scalability, and compatibility with DoD testing environments such as BAF, and enabling future operational deployment.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Phase III will advance the TRL 6 prototype Quantum Sensing Analyzer to TRL 8+ with non-SBIR funding, integrating it for operational assessments at BAF and other DoD labs. The system will support electromagnetic testing (1.5 MHz–40 GHz) for radar, EW, and communication systems. Commercial uses include electromagnetic compliance testing and telecommunications. Transition involves DAF partners, certifications, training, and infrastructure development for deployment.

title: Solid Propellant Environmental Effects Digital Twin
summary: The objective of the proposed effort is twofold: 1) Model and simulate the combined effects of thermal, temporal, chemical, and geometric changes to solid propellants that occur over time for in rocket motor grains, and 2) integrate predictive behavior tools into solid rocket motor design tools for decision-quality models and simulations.
description:
Objective:
The objective of the proposed effort is twofold: 1) Model and simulate the combined effects of thermal, temporal, chemical, and geometric changes to solid propellants that occur over time for in rocket motor grains, and 2) integrate predictive behavior tools into solid rocket motor design tools for decision-quality models and simulations. The intended result is a solid propellant aging and environmental process digital twin.

Description:
Solid Rocket Motors (SRMs) provide propulsion for many critical defense applications including surface launched, air launched, ballistic, and space vehicles. The propellant that creates acceleration through these SRMs is a complex active material that can be sensitive to environmental effects from thermal loads, exposure to air or humidity, chemical changes, pressure, or vibration loads due to time or ingredient changes. Both mechanical response characteristics and ballistic properties can be affected. This topic requests projects that will combine computational modeling and design capability from several sources to simulate aging responses due to environmental effects. The framework must follow Modular Open Systems Approach standards mandated in 10 U.S.C. § 4401 for compatibility with several commercially available computational tools such as ANSYS, ABAQUS, Python, MatLab, SysML, and others.

Phase I:
Define a ballistic or structural degradation mechanism in solid propellent that can be implemented in a damage tolerant design process for solid rocket motors. Develop the technical argument for transitioning non-continuum mechanisms to a continuum-based analysis techniques. Develop a Digital Engineering plan to create the desired capability to model Solid Rocket Propellant and predict behavior over extended periods of time and environmental conditions.

Phase II:
Phase 2 will build out the combined moderate fidelity predictive models of at least two environmental effects and anchor predictions to historical propellant aging data implemented through Cameo, OMG, or other SysML 2.0 platform. Performance predictions including both ballistic degradation and structural reactions should be included. Analytical techniques must be compatible with a MBSE enabled design threads.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Phase 3 is intended to create a “digital twin” of the solid propellant aging process that can be integrated into solid rocket motor design tools and SySML – based predictive and systems engineering tools. Models and tools have three opportunities for transition and commercialization: 1) transition to Government Refence Architectures for SRM design and vehicle integration, 2) incorporation into commercial SRM design capabilities through the SRM industry, or 3) transition or reuse into other commercially viable polymer-dependent industries such as rubber tires, automotive components, in-vivo medical devices, hazardous response Personal Protective Equipment (PPE), and sporting goods.

title: Next-generation Green Monopropellant Gas Generation
summary: Develop a low-power, real-time precision liquid-to-gas phase-change feed system featuring active molecular feedback control to enable the seamless integration of liquid propellants (including next-generation green liquid propellants such as ASCENT and LMP-103S) with high-efficiency in-space plasma propulsion systems.
description:
Objective:
Develop a low-power, real-time precision liquid-to-gas phase-change feed system featuring active molecular feedback control to enable the seamless integration of liquid propellants (including next-generation green liquid propellants such as ASCENT and LMP-103S) with high-efficiency in-space plasma propulsion systems. While legacy propellants like hydrazine vaporize with relative ease, next-generation green propellants possess near-zero vapor pressures that streamline ground operations but make efficient vaporization and stable gas-phase molecular composition extremely difficult to control. Proposed solutions must actively monitor and modulate the vaporization process in real time to deliver precise molecular species fractions under tight power constraints, ultimately establishing a versatile, fuel-agnostic propellant conditioning capability to support dynamic space operations and emerging in-space refueling architectures.

Description:
The USSF has a desire to use liquid monopropellants for high thrust propulsion (natively in chemical thrusters) and for low-thrust, very energetic missions (in electric propulsion thrusters) - so called Multimode Propulsion (MMP) capabilities - to support Dynamic Space Operations. Such MMP capabilities have a number of very favorable characteristics including high propellant density, reduced need for high pressure storage systems, continued need for chemical propulsion on DoW assets for high thrust prompt maneuver, and compatibility with future on-orbit liquid propellant refueling capabilities.

One critical capability gap is an energy efficient, precision propellant feed system which efficiently converts next-generation liquid monopropellant into non-reactive vapor phase products which can be fed into the electric propulsion (EP) thruster. Key challenges arise from the fact that next-generation monopropellants have negligible vapor pressure and are extremely difficult to combust at low temperature and pressure.

The desired technology should present a solution for a feed system capable of supporting sub-kW to 100 kW class EP systems:

- Operation at minimum on ASCENT propellant (T) or on ASCENT and other monopropellant formulations (O)

- Realtime telemetry, including mass flow rate, species composition, and temperature as inputs to the EP device

- Maintain consistently characterized molecular composition (T) and extremely stable molecular composition (O) of the output vapor and support both steady-state and pulsed operation at frequencies greater than 5 Hz

- Minimal SWaP with particular focus on low power consumption

- Incorporate fluid/vapor facing materials that can reliably withstand long-term exposure to green monopropellants and their breakdown products over the required lifespan. Potential issues also include condensation or freezing for long-duration propellant storage in ullage and plenums if these or similar components are used

- Demonstrate rapid warmup/gas generation in less than 10 minutes (T) or on-demand (O)

- Ensure lifetime design consideration for future multiple refueling opportunities

This work directly supports the Contested Logistics Technologies (LOG) Critical Technology Area with respect to space mobility operations.

Phase I:
As this is a Direct-to-Phase-II (D2)2) topic, no Phase I proposals will be accepted and no Phase I awards will be made under this topic. Offerors responding to this topic shall demonstrate “Phase I-type” technical feasibility through prior research, development, laboratory validation, commercial development, or operational demonstrations performed outside of the SBIR/STTR program. Phase I proposals will not be evaluated and will be rejected as nonresponsive.

For this D2P2 topic, the Government expects that the small business would have accomplished the following in a “Phase I-type” effort via some other means (e.g. IRAD, or other funded work). It must have developed a concept for a workable prototype or design to address at a minimum the basic capabilities of the stated objective above. Proposal must show, as appropriate to the proposed effort, a demonstrated technical feasibility or nascent capability to meet the capabilities of the stated objective. Proposal may provide example cases of this new capability on a specific application. The documentation provided must substantiate that the proposer has developed a preliminary understanding of the technology to be applied in their Phase II proposal to meet the objectives of this topic. Documentation should include all relevant information including, but not limited to, technical reports, test data, prototype designs/models, and performance goals/results.

Phase II:
The rapid advancement of plasma thruster operation on next-generation molecular propellants is currently bottlenecked by the lack of an energy-efficient, precise, real-time vaporization solution. While previous research has explored thermal and catalytic vaporization strategies, existing options suffer from high power consumption, ill-defined operational lifetimes, inconsistent vapor-phase molecular output, and a total lack of real-time compositional feedback to the thruster. To bridge this critical technology gap and enable commercial transition, Phase II efforts must focus on developing a robust, energy-efficient liquid-to-gas propellant conditioning system when operating on both legacy and next-generation green monopropellants.

Proposals must deliver a low Size, Weight, and Power (SWaP) vaporization solution capable of providing a well-quantified, repeatable vapor stream to high-efficiency plasma thrusters, such as Hall Effect Thrusters (HETs) or Magnetoplasmadynamic (MPD) thrusters. Key technical requirements include the ability to deliver real-time feedback on the actual molecular composition being provided, and the capacity to actively modulate operation to target and maintain specific molecular species fractions. While the target operational envelope spans plasma propulsion systems from <1 kW to 100 kW, a single hardware unit is not expected to cover the entire spectrum; rather, performers must demonstrate actual performance across a subset of this range alongside a credible, physics-based pathway for modular scalability.

To maximize commercial transition and support the emerging in-space refueling architecture, Phase II projects must focus on developing flight-like engineering development units (EDUs) designed for integration into existing and future plasma propulsion systems. While formal spaceflight qualification (e.g., strict shock, vibration, and radiation acceptance testing) is not required during this phase, performers are highly encouraged to team with established thruster manufacturers. This collaboration will ensure that relevant aerospace engineering best practices, interfaces, and integration protocols are incorporated into the design, positioning the technology for rapid transition.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
This technology is directly applicable to both defense and civil spacecraft, delivering a hybrid propulsion capability that enables both prompt, high-thrust maneuvers (e.g., threat and debris avoidance) and high-efficiency, low-thrust orbital transfers. In the near term, the primary market is centered on Department of War (DoW) applications to meet critical requirements for Dynamic Space Operations (DSO), enhanced space warfighting maneuverability, and the rapid emergence of tactical in-space refueling architectures. The primary Phase II deliverable-an Engineering Development Unit (EDU) gas generator-is optimized for direct integration into various molecular plasma thrusters currently under development by commercial space partners. Although final flight qualification must be accomplished on the integrated, combined propulsion system (thruster and gas generator), the Phase II EDU serves as the critical hardware stepping stone. Depending on future government and commercial funding profiles, this technology is well-positioned for independent maturation as a standalone, platform-agnostic product through a follow-on Phase III contract or Tactical Funding Increases (TACFI) effort.

title: AI-Enabled Computed Vision Air-to-Air Refueling Performance Assessment and Automated Pilot Debrief System
summary: Develop, integrate, and demonstrate an artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled computed vision and human-machine interface capability that transforms aerial refueling operations from subjective, observation-based evaluation into an objective, data-driven performance assessment and adaptive training environment.
description:
Objective:
Develop, integrate, and demonstrate an artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled computed vision and human-machine interface capability that transforms aerial refueling operations from subjective, observation-based evaluation into an objective, data-driven performance assessment and adaptive training environment. The system shall leverage advanced computer vision, machine learning, and aviation (flight dynamics) analytics techniques to automatically extract operationally relevant performance metrics from aerial refueling events, quantify deviations from desired flight profiles, and generate actionable post-flight feedback to improve aircrew proficiency, reduce human-factor-driven mishaps, and enhance mission readiness.The capability shall analyze video from cameras mounted on the tanker (esp. the KC-46) to provide near-real-time post-flight reconstruction of aerial refueling engagements by correlating aircraft position, motion dynamics, refueling geometry, pilot inputs, and operational context to identify performance trends and training opportunities. The developed system shall perform automated assessment of complex aerial refueling behaviors including aircraft stability, closure rate management, alignment accuracy, control surface position, other situational awareness indicators, and adherence to established refueling procedures.The objective is to mature existing advanced AI-enabled aviation analytics into an operationally relevant post-flight “hotwash” and training capability that increases the instructional value of each aerial refueling sortie, reduces reliance on subjective human assessment, accelerates pilot proficiency development, decreases equipment damage associated with refueling deviations, and establishes a scalable foundation for future intelligent aviation training systems across Department of the Air Force and joint aviation communities.The resulting prototype shall demonstrate the ability to ingest operational aerial refueling data, autonomously generate objective performance assessments, provide intuitive visualization and debrief products, and support transition into existing aviation training, evaluation, and modernization ecosystems. Importantly, the system will also include automated security management of the video so that implementation is seamless and complies with security classification guidance.

Description:
Air-to-air refueling (AAR) is a critical Department of the Air Force and Department of the Navy capability enabling global mobility, long-range strike, combat airpower projection, and sustained aviation operations. However, aerial refueling remains one of the most technically demanding and safety-critical aviation tasks performed by aircrews. Successful execution requires precise aircraft positioning, coordinated control inputs, accurate closure rate management, continuous situational awareness, and effective crew coordination between tanker and receiver aircraft.Current aerial refueling training and post-flight assessment processes rely heavily on instructor observation, pilot self-assessment, manual video review, and subjective evaluation of performance. These approaches provide limited ability to quantitatively assess the thousands of individual performance variables that influence successful refueling operations. Existing methods do not provide pilots with objective, moment-by-moment feedback on aircraft positioning, closure rates, control inputs, deviations from desired procedures, or trends in individual performance over time.This topic seeks to develop, demonstrate, and transition an artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled computed vision capability that (post-flight) automatically analyzes aerial refueling operations and provides objective, data-driven pilot performance feedback. The desired capability will mature existing advances in autonomous aerial refueling analytics and apply them toward training, readiness, and safety improvement by transforming aerial refueling video and available aircraft performance data into actionable post-flight debrief products.The developed system shall provide an automated “hot wash” which analyzes aerial refueling events, identifies performance deviations, and generates intuitive visualizations that allow pilots and instructors to better understand execution quality and areas for improvement. The system shall reduce reliance on subjective recollection and manual review by providing objective measurements of aircraft performance throughout the refueling profile.The capability shall focus on analysis of tanker-mounted video data, such as KC-46 aerial refueling camera systems, while maintaining an architecture capable of expanding across additional tanker and receiver platforms. The vendor may pick (with Government concurrence) the first 3-5 receiver platforms to use in developing this system. Future applicability includes KC-135, C-17, all fighter receiver aircraft, naval aviation communities, autonomous aerial refueling systems, and other aviation training environments requiring advanced performance analytics.The desired solution shall leverage artificial intelligence, machine learning, computer vision, and advanced human-machine interfaces to provide capabilities including:• Automated detection and tracking of tanker (boom and hose) and receiver aircraft during aerial refueling operations.• Measurement of relative aircraft position, movement, velocity, and alignment throughout the refueling engagement.• Assessment of aircraft position within the approved refueling envelope.• Analysis of closure rates, approach vectors, aircraft stability, and deviations from nominal procedures.• Ability to correlate video with other aircraft data if/as available (e.g. telemetry, fuel transfer rate, fuel state, and pilot inputs) to evaluate performance drivers.• Generation of objective performance scores and trend analysis across multiple training events.• Creation of visual performance assessment products for receiver pilot post-flight review of their performance during refueling, including graphical overlays, heat maps, event timelines, and immersive or interactive debrief environments.• Support for instructor review, adjudication, and refinement of automated assessments during initial deployment.The system should evaluate innovative approaches for integrating automated analytics with existing or future aviation training environments, including virtual reality (VR), augmented reality (AR), mission rehearsal systems, simulator environments, or other computer-based training tools.The solution must address operational challenges associated with military aviation data, including secure processing of controlled aviation video, automated data protection, and protection of sensitive operational information. The capability should consider approaches for minimizing processing burden on operational units while enabling rapid generation of post-flight assessments.The Government seeks solutions which provide an operationally relevant prototype supporting aerial refueling training organizations. Successful completion of this effort will provide Air Force and joint aviation communities with a next-generation training and assessment capability that improves pilot proficiency, increases the training value of each refueling event, reduces equipment damage and maintenance impacts, and enhances overall mission readiness.The desired end state is an operationally demonstrated capability ready to implement for at least one type of receiver aircraft and that can support transition into existing aviation training ecosystems and provide a scalable foundation for future AI-enabled aviation performance assessment across the Department of Defense.

Phase I:
As this is a Direct-to-Phase-II (D2)2) topic, no Phase I proposals will be accepted and no Phase I awards will be made under this topic. Offerors responding to this topic shall demonstrate “Phase I-type” technical feasibility through prior research, development, laboratory validation, commercial development, or operational demonstrations performed outside of the SBIR/STTR program. The purpose of this demonstration will be for the Government to determine the feasibility of the ideas that appear to have the potential to satisfy the objectives of this topic:

The Government is seeking offerors with demonstrated experience and technical maturity equivalent to a successful Phase I effort. Proposals shall demonstrate existing capabilities, relevant past performance, or validated technologies applicable to the development of an AI-enabled aerial refueling performance assessment and automated pilot debrief capability.

Qualified offerors shall demonstrate experience in at least half of following technical areas:

• Development and application of artificial intelligence, machine learning, and computer vision algorithms for analyzing dynamic objects in video imagery.
• Processing and interpretation of high-speed motion imagery to determine object position, movement, velocity, orientation, and spatial relationships.
• Development of algorithms capable of tracking aircraft, vehicles, or other dynamic platforms in complex operational environments.
• Aviation-focused data analytics, flight performance monitoring, flight simulation, or aircrew training systems.
• Development of human-machine interfaces, virtual reality (VR), augmented reality (AR), immersive training environments, or advanced visualization tools.
• Integration of sensor data, video analytics, telemetry, or flight performance information into automated assessment systems.
• Experience handling, processing, protecting, or analyzing controlled aviation or operational data.
• Automated video processing techniques including object recognition, classification, filtering, masking, or data protection methodologies.
• Development of secure software systems capable of operating within government aviation environments.

Offerors shall demonstrate prior technical maturity equivalent to a Technology Readiness Level (TRL) 4 or greater at contract award. Relevant experience may include laboratory demonstrations, commercial applications, government-sponsored research, operational prototypes, or other non-SBIR/STTR funded development activities.

The offeror shall demonstrate the ability to transition existing technical capabilities into an operational prototype supporting aerial refueling performance analysis. Successful offerors will demonstrate sufficient technical foundation to immediately begin Phase II activities including adaptation of computer vision algorithms, integration of aviation video data, development of automated performance metrics, and operational prototype demonstration.

Evaluation of Phase I-equivalent experience will consider:

• Relevance of previous computer vision, artificial intelligence, or machine learning development efforts.
• Demonstrated ability to analyze complex motion-based systems, especially aviation maneuvers.
• Experience applying technology within aviation, aerospace, defense, and related training environments.
• Demonstrated ability to mature existing technologies into operationally relevant prototypes.
• Ability to address cybersecurity, data protection, and integration challenges associated with military aviation applications.

Phase II:
Phase II will develop, integrate, and demonstrate an operational prototype of an AI-enabled computer vision air-to-air refueling (AAR) performance assessment and automated pilot debrief system. The effort will mature existing autonomous AAR analytics into a post-flight training and evaluation capability providing objective, data-driven feedback to tanker and receiver aircrews.The prototype shall ingest AAR video and available aircraft performance data, identify deviations from desired procedures, and generate automated post-flight hotwash products. The system shall reduce reliance on pilot memory and manual instructor video review through objective measurements, visualization, and historical trend analysis.Task 1: System Architecture, Data Acquisition, and Secure ProcessingEstablish the architecture to ingest, process, analyze, and protect AAR video and associated aircraft data.Activities shall include:Develop system architecture, data flows, and cybersecurity approach.Establish procedures for CUI and operational aviation data.Integrate available tanker-mounted cameras, aircraft video, and applicable flight-performance data.Evaluate local processing with transfer of lightweight outputs versus secure video transfer to approved computing environments.Develop data-management procedures supporting expansion across tanker/receiver platforms.Deliverables: System Architecture Design; Data Management and Security Plan; CUI Processing Workflow; Initial Prototype Data Ingestion Capability.Task 2: Computer Vision Model Adaptation and Performance AnalyticsAdapt and mature existing computer vision technologies for automated AAR analysis, including aircraft motion, relative positioning, and flight-performance assessment.The capability shall:Detect/track tanker boom or hose and receiver aircraft.Determine relative position, orientation, and movement.Measure closure rates and approach vectors.Assess position within the approved refueling envelope.Identify boom, probe, or hose/drogue alignment.Analyze stability and deviations from nominal procedures.Support multiple tanker and receiver configurations.Demonstrate performance equivalent to TRL 6+ through prototype demonstration in a relevant operational environment.Deliverables: Adapted Computer Vision Models; Aircraft Tracking Algorithms; Performance Assessment Algorithms; Technical Validation Report.Task 3: Automated Performance Assessment and Pilot FeedbackConvert AAR data into objective post-flight performance feedback, including:Moment-by-moment scoring against nominal profiles.Positioning heat maps relative to the refueling envelope.Closure-rate and approach-vector analysis.Timeline reconstruction of key events.Identification of deviations/improvement areas.Historical individual and crew trend analysis.Where available, correlate performance with pilot inputs/data including fuel state/transfer rate, control inputs, throttle response, aircraft corrections, response timing, crew coordination indicators, and situational-awareness factors.To support organizational change and adjudicate corner cases, provide an instructor/"master debriefer" capability for trained personnel to review, validate, and provide feedback on automated assessments during initial deployment.Stretch Goal: Recognize, or provide a growth path to recognize, bent/broken boom, probe, or hose conditions and associated FOD.Deliverables: Automated Performance Assessment Engine; Pilot Feedback Products; Instructor Review Interface; Performance Analytics Dashboard.Task 4: Automated Data Protection and Video ProcessingDevelop secure video-processing capabilities that minimize operational burden and protect sensitive information.The system shall:Detect when a receiver aircraft is present and activate analytics only during relevant events.Identify and prevent processing/retention of unauthorized aircraft or sensitive platforms.Remove/obscure sensitive geographic information, terrain, markings, and other operationally sensitive information.Support automated masking/filtering before distribution.Demonstrate an architecture supporting future cybersecurity certification.Deliverables: Automated Video Processing Capability; Data Protection/Filtering Methodology; Cybersecurity Assessment Documentation.Task 5: Pilot Debrief Visualization and Training IntegrationDevelop intuitive visualization methods translating analytics into actionable training feedback. Evaluate/demonstrate:Immersive VR/AR replay environments.Squadron-level 2D visualization.Graphical overlays depicting aircraft position, closure rates, desired flight paths, deviations, and refueling-envelope margins.Apply instructional-design principles to support pilot learning, instructor evaluation, and squadron training discussions.Deliverables: Visualization Trade Study; Pilot Debrief Interface Prototype; Training Integration Plan.Task 6: Operational Demonstration, Testing, and TransitionDemonstrate the prototype with operational military aviation users and validate:Accuracy of automated assessments.Correlation with experienced instructor evaluations.Negligible manual video-review workload.Usability within existing training/mission-debrief workflows.Ability to generate actionable post-AAR pilot feedback.Desired Technical Performance Objectives:Generate automated debrief products within 15 minutes of video ingestion.Accurately track aircraft position, movement, and refueling geometry.Identify significant deviations from nominal procedures.Achieve ≥95% agreement between experienced instructors and automated assessments during validation.Demonstrate integration with at least one operational AAR training organization.Deliverables: Operational Prototype Demonstration; Test and Evaluation Report; User Feedback Assessment; Phase III Transition Plan.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Phase III will support transition of the AI-enabled aerial refueling performance assessment capability into operational Air Force, Navy, USMC, and select foreign aviation communities through program office integration, operational funding pathways, and sustainment planning.Potential transition applications include:· KC-46 aerial refueling training and readiness improvement.· KC-135 and legacy tanker modernization efforts.· C-17 and other receiver aircraft training applications.· Fighter receiver aerial refueling proficiency improvement.· Navy and Marine Corps aerial refueling operations.· Autonomous aerial refueling development and validation.· Advanced aviation training and performance analytics.Commercialization opportunities may include adaptation of aviation analytics, pilot training analytics, flight performance monitoring, and simulation technologies for commercial aviation, allied aviation partners, and other safety-critical transportation environments.

title: Fusion of Cooperative Information Sharing for Uncrewed Air Systems (FOCISAUS)
summary: The Department of the Air Force seeks mature, innovative solutions ready for prototype development and demonstration in cooperative perception for uncrewed or autonomous air systems.
description:
Objective:
The Department of the Air Force seeks mature, innovative solutions ready for prototype development and demonstration in cooperative perception for uncrewed or autonomous air systems. The objective of this topic is to develop and demonstrate a scalable prototype that enables distributed sensing nodes to share, prioritize, and fuse mission-relevant information in near real time to improve object detection, tracking, navigation, and operator situational awareness in cluttered and bandwidth-constrained environments.

Solutions should support efficient information exchange, adaptive transmission under changing network conditions, and a credible data fusion design that converts distributed sensor observations into actionable fused products. Offerors should propose technologies with demonstrated Phase I-type maturity and a clear path to prototype integration, testing, and transition.

Description:
Distributed air operations increasingly depend on timely awareness of objects, hazards, and activities beyond the field of view of any individual platform. Cooperative perception offers a path to extend sensing coverage and reduce blind spots by allowing multiple platforms and supporting nodes to share sensor-derived information. Yet this benefit is limited by the large size of modern sensor data, the variability of wireless links, the need for rapid decision making, and the difficulty of combining observations from different platforms, geometries, and sensing modalities.

This topic seeks prototype-ready solutions that build on prior feasibility work in distributed information sharing, compression, adaptive transmission, and sensor data fusion. The government is interested in capabilities that can select and transmit the most relevant information, manage latency and bandwidth constraints, and fuse data from multiple sources into improved perception outputs for autonomy or operator use.

Offerors should address the data fusion aspect as a core requirement of the overall solution, whether through point cloud fusion, image or radar correlation, feature or object fusion, track association, or other mission-appropriate methods. Solutions should also describe how fused outputs are exposed to mission applications, edge processing nodes, or user interfaces. Approaches that can operate under degraded or intermittent communications and can scale across multiple sensing platforms are of particular interest.

Prototype capabilities may include, but are not limited to: Distributed organization, naming, publication, discovery, or retrieval of sensor information; Adaptive data selection, fidelity control, compression, and transmission policies; Real-time or near-real-time fusion and correlation of data from multiple platforms or sensor types; Delivery of fused perception products to autonomy software, edge analytics, or mobile mission applications; and Measurable improvements in latency, bandwidth efficiency, blind-spot reduction, and detection or tracking performance.

Phase I:
This topic is intended for technologies that are sufficiently mature to proceed directly into prototype development. Therefore, Phase I awards will not be made for this topic and Phase I proposals will not be accepted. Offerors must provide detail and documentation in the D2P2 proposal demonstrating completion of a Phase I-type effort. This should include evidence of scientific and technical feasibility, relevance to a Department of the Air Force need, and a clear basis for moving directly into integrated prototype development.

The "Phase As this is a Direct-to-Phase-II (D2)2) topic, no Phase I proposals will be accepted and no Phase I awards will be made under this topic. Offerors responding to this topic shall demonstrate “Phase I-type” technical capability through prior research, development, laboratory validation, commercial development, or operational demonstrations performed outside of the SBIR/STTR program. This should include evidence of scientific and technical feasibility, relevance to a Department of the Air Force need, and a clear basis for moving directly into integrated prototype development.

The “Phase I-type” effort should have:

• Identified representative operational needs and stakeholders for cooperative perception and distributed situational awareness;
• Demonstrated technical feasibility in distributed information exchange, sensor-data management, compression, or adaptive transmission;
• Established an initial and credible data fusion approach appropriate to the mission problem;
• Produced evidence of prototype-readiness through modeling, simulation, laboratory integration, or early demonstration; and5
• Described a clear path to Phase II integration, testing, and transition.I-type" effort should have:1. Identified representative operational needs and stakeholders for cooperative perception and distributed situational awareness;2. Demonstrated technical feasibility in distributed information exchange, sensor-data management, compression, or adaptive transmission;3. Established an initial and credible data fusion approach appropriate to the mission problem;4. Produced evidence of prototype-readiness through modeling, simulation, laboratory integration, or early demonstration; and 5. Described a clear path to Phase II integration, testing, and transition.

Phase II:
Phase II will focus on developing and demonstrating an integrated prototype for cooperative perception and sensor data fusion using distributed air and ground sensing nodes. The prototype should build on validated prior work and demonstrate how shared sensor information can be selectively transmitted, fused, and delivered to mission applications with measurable operational value.

Phase II efforts may include implementation of distributed data-sharing mechanisms; adaptive policies for what information to exchange and at what fidelity; integration of compression, decompression, or bandwidth-management functions; real-time or near-real-time fusion of representative sensor products; delivery of fused outputs to edge or user applications; and evaluation of performance under representative wireless and mission conditions.

Key deliverables may include: A functioning prototype demonstrating cooperative perception among multiple sensing nodes; Fusion-enabled outputs delivered to an autonomy, edge, or user-facing application; Performance results addressing latency, bandwidth efficiency, perception quality, and mission relevance; and System documentation and a transition plan for operational experimentation or integration.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Phase III efforts will focus on transition, operational deployment, and scaling of prototype cooperative perception capabilities. Defense applications include counter-UAS, tactical reconnaissance, base and perimeter security, special operations, disaster response, search and rescue, and other missions requiring distributed awareness from mobile sensors. Commercial applications include public safety, infrastructure monitoring, industrial inspection, autonomous delivery, emergency response, and remote operations where shared perception and efficient data fusion provide value.

title: B-52 Multi-Factor AI Performance Charts
summary: Develop and validate a capability that modernizes B-52 AI Performance Chart capability that automates approved performance calculations, supports disconnected EFB operations, and provides accurate, auditable outputs for aircrew decision-making.
description:
Objective:
Develop and validate a capability that modernizes B-52 AI Performance Chart capability that automates approved performance calculations, supports disconnected EFB operations, and provides accurate, auditable outputs for aircrew decision-making.

Description:
The B-52 Stratofortress has been the backbone of the United States Air Force's long-range strategic bomber capability for more than six decades. Despite multiple upgrades to its avionics and mission systems, aircrews continue to rely on labor-intensive, manually interpreted paper Technical Order performance charts and multi-step worksheets to calculate critical operational calculations such as takeoff and landing distances, brake energy limits, crosswind restrictions, runway condition impacts, directional control limits, and degraded-performance scenarios. These manual processes are time-consuming, increase cognitive workload and introduce opportunities for human error, and require aircrews to make high-stakes decisions under challenging time constraints, often during dynamic operational scenarios. Continued reliance on manual processes reduces operational efficiency, increases crew workload, and can negatively impact decision-making, especially in contested or degraded environments.

The current state of the art within commercial aviation utilizes Electronic Flight Bag (EFB)-based performance planning tools capable of rapidly calculating aircraft performance using approved aircraft data and validated calculation methodologies. While these solutions demonstrate the feasibility of digital performance-planning capabilities, they do not incorporate B-52-specific TO data, military performance procedures, cybersecurity requirements, airworthiness considerations, or Department of the Air Force EFB integration requirements. As a result, a capability gap exists between current B-52 performance-planning processes and modern digital aviation decision-support systems. The proposed effort will begin at approximately TRL 3-4, leveraging prior Phase-I-like work including operational requirements analysis, commercial market research, chart digitization methodologies, deterministic algorithm concepts, and successful demonstrations of related technologies in both government and commercial aviation sectors. Commercial aviation performance applications, technical-order digitization technologies, and deterministic calculation engines have demonstrated feasibility and provide a strong foundation for this effort. The objective of the Phase II effort is to advance the capability to TRL 6 through development, validation, and operational demonstration of a prototype capability suitable for transition into the Air Force EFB ecosystem. The Government is particularly interested in approaches that leverage secure research infrastructure, advanced computing resources, AI-assisted data extraction capabilities, and development of government-owned intellectual property to accelerate chart digitization, data validation, and long-term sustainment. Additionally, the Government seeks to leverage existing federally funded research investments such as those within U.S. National Laboratories or other Federally Funded Research & Development Centers (FFRDCs) to the maximum extent possible. Leveraging existing investments around AI security, vulnerability assessments, red teaming, model assurance, secure deployment of advanced models, and evaluation of AI systems supporting national security missions will help accelerate technology maturation and transition.

To meet this goal, the Phase II D2P2 effort is expected to include the following activities:

• Integration of the AI-driven solution for chart mining and digitization to extract data; Refinement of deterministic algorithms to calculate performance metrics (e.g., takeoff/landing distances, brake energy limits, crosswind tolerances) based on TO and other authoritative data sources.

• Development of intuitive user interface and operational workflows that align with aircrew feedback and mission requirements, ensuring a transparent and user-friendly application.

• Rigorous testing and validation of algorithm accuracy, decision-support reliability, and adherence to airworthiness and compliance standards, incorporating inputs from operational stakeholders and SMEs.

• Coordination with USG relevant Program Offices and certification authorities to support EFB system accreditation, operational testing, and fielding - this would translate into the existing U.S. Government EFB system with offline capabilities to ensure reliable operation in contested, degraded, or denied environments.

• Coordination with U.S. National Laboratories or FFRDCs already investing in similar capabilities to enable rapid technology advancement, alignment of development roadmaps towards broader national security priorities, and aid in the transition into operational systems.

This STTR effort stands to vastly improve the DoW's technological state by eliminating the inefficiencies of current manual performance calculations and transitioning the B-52 platform into a new era of data-driven, AI-enhanced operations that rapidly generate transparent and auditable aircraft performance assessments using approved source data. The capability shall not generate unvalidated performance estimates, extrapolated values, or inferred outputs when required data are unavailable or outside approved limits. The resulting solution will enable faster, more reliable decision-making, directly enhancing safety and mission outcomes while reducing aircrew workload. Moreover, the offline functionality ensures the tool's efficacy in a range of operational environments, including denied, degraded, and contested settings. Minimum acceptable deliverables include:

• A prototype closed loop EFB-compatible software capability suitable for operational evaluation.
• Digitized and validated performance datasets derived from approved B-52 source material.
• Verified and validated calculation methodologies demonstrating agreement with approved reference calculations.
• User workflows and interfaces suitable for operational aircrew use.
• Test and validation reports documenting accuracy, reliability, and operational suitability.
• Sustainment and transition documentation supporting future EFB integration, cybersecurity accreditation, airworthiness review, and operational fielding.

Through these efforts, the B-52 will evolve to keep pace with the Air Force’s operational imperatives, including enhanced readiness to deploy and fight (Operational Imperative 7) and modernization priorities such as trusted AI and autonomy. Success in Phase II will position this innovation for further development and transition under Phase III, facilitating its adoption as a fielded capability that aligns with the U.S. Air Force’s modernization goals and long-term sustainment strategy for the B-52 fleet.

Phase I:
As this is a STTR Direct-to-Phase-II (D2P2) topic, no Phase I awards will be made. To qualify, applicants must demonstrate feasibility via prior "Phase I-type" efforts, providing data validating deterministic algorithms. Documentation should include validated algorithm outputs, prototype results, proving accuracy and offline functionality.

Phase II:
Phase II will produce a validated, EFB-integrated AI Performance Chart prototype for the B-52, delivering automated, traceable outputs for critical performance metrics like takeoff/landing distances and brake energy limits. Achievements include TO-compliant algorithm validation, rigorous offline testing, and a prototype demonstration in an operationally relevant environment to enhance mission safety, efficiency, and readiness in contested environments. The prototype should be cyber-compliant for EFB use, and demonstrate feasibility of digitized, automated performance decision support—without attempting full-scale automation, certification, or fleet deployment.

Phase II Technical Efforts include:- Integration of the AI-driven solution for chart mining and digitization to extract data; software model optimization techniques and high performance computing desired.

- Must be closed loop in flight application without reliance on internet, cloud, AI inference, or other external sources

- Compatible with existing Government Hardware.- Approaches that leverage secure research environments, high-performance computing (HPC) resources, deep scientific expertise, cutting-edge research facilities, AI-assisted data extraction capabilities, and expertise in model optimization and reduction are highly desirable to accelerate chart digitization, improve validation processes, support handling of CUI data, and enable deployment on resource-constrained EFB platforms.

- Refinement of deterministic algorithms to calculate performance metrics (e.g., takeoff/landing distances, brake energy limits, crosswind tolerances) based on TO and other authoritative data sources.

- Development of intuitive user interface and operational workflows that align with aircrew feedback and mission requirements, ensuring a transparent and user-friendly application.

- Rigorous testing and validation of algorithm accuracy, decision-support reliability, and adherence to airworthiness and compliance standards, incorporating inputs from operational stakeholders and SMEs.

- Prevent generation of unvalidated performance data/estimates when inputs are unclear, outside performance parameters, or unknown.

- Coordination with USG relevant Program Offices and certification authorities to support EFB system accreditation, and operational test. This would translate into the existing U.S. Government EFB system with offline capabilities to ensure reliable operation in contested, degraded, or denied environments.

- Coordination with U.S. National Laboratories or FFRDCs already investing in similar capabilities to enable rapid technology advancement, alignment of development roadmaps towards broader national security priorities, and aid in the transition into operational systems.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Expected TRL at entry is approximately TRL 6. The Phase III effort will field a certified, TO-compliant AI-driven EFB system for B-52 performance calculations, enhancing mission readiness and safety. Expected activities in Phase 3 include: operational test and evaluation, USG certification activities, fielding, and training. In addition, a long term sustainment and funding model should be in place for continuous revisions and updates to the TOs. Commercial aviation is well advanced in this arena so will not benefit. Other industries that rely on legacy data, however, may benefit from chart digitization and software model reduction techniques. Transition strategies include collaboration with the B-52 SPO for deployment and aligning with broader Air Force AI modernization goals. Coordination is already in place with the B-52 and EFB program offices to include long term funding plans. Following successful fielding on the B-52 platform, the framework may be expanded to additional Air Force aircraft communities that continue to rely on manual TO performance-chart calculations, including mobility, tanker, ISR, training, and other legacy aircraft platforms. This could also be leveraged DoW wide for all organizations that continue to rely on legacy data.

• United States Air Force Operational Imperatives, with emphasis on Operational Imperative 7: "Readiness to Deploy and Fight," Air Force Modernization Priorities, 2023
