title: DIRECT TO PHASE II: Modular Software Reference Implementation for Waveforms
summary: Develop and demonstrate a modular software reference implementation of a government-specified tactical waveform on a Digital Transceiver to establish an open architecture that leverages novel processing to transition from legacy Field-Programmable Gate Array (FPGA)-based systems.
description:
Objective:
Develop and demonstrate a modular software reference implementation of a government-specified tactical waveform on a Digital Transceiver to establish an open architecture that leverages novel processing to transition from legacy Field-Programmable Gate Array (FPGA)-based systems.

Description:
The Multifunctional Information Distribution System (MIDS) Program Office (PMA/PMW-101) is driving a critical architectural pivot in tactical data link (TDL) communications. Historically, the defense sector has relied heavily on FPGAs to host complex tactical waveforms due to strict RF timing constraints. However, as noted in recent software-defined radio (SDR) surveys, this hardware-centric approach suffers from severe developmental friction [Ref 1]. Programming FPGAs via Hardware Description Languages (HDL) requires lengthy synthesis, complex place-and-route cycles, and difficult timing closures. Because software compilation bypasses these physical routing and synthesis barriers, transitioning from HDL to high-order software languages (C/C++) on general-purpose architectures typically reduces development timelines by 50% to 80%—compressing multi-year hardware upgrade cycles into a matter of months.

To overcome legacy constraints, this initiative mandates a transition toward a modular open systems architecture (MOSA). By decoupling the physical layer (PHY) from the underlying hardware, containerized Software-Defined Waveforms (SDWs) can be deployed across modern processing. Because standard Central Processing Units (CPUs) often lack the deterministic throughput required for heavy RF pipelines, modern SDR frameworks dynamically offload computationally intensive PHY tasks to coprocessors like GPUs, Neural Processing Units (NPUs), or adaptive System-on-Chips (SoCs).

This heterogeneous approach enables the execution of highly parallel mathematical pipelines via software Application Programming Interfaces (APIs), including:

Vectorized Signal Processing on GPUs or NPU cores:

• Executing Fast Fourier Transforms (FFTs)
• High-throughput Forward Error Correction (FEC)
• Matrix Multiplications

AI-Driven Cognitive Radio: As demonstrated by O'Shea and Hoydis [Ref 2], traditional heuristic PHY blocks can be replaced by "neural receivers" and deep learning autoencoders. By reusing embedded AI inference blocks, radios can perform real-time channel estimation, signal classification, and non-linear error correction at the tactical edge.

By migrating to this software-first model, the Navy ensures rapid portability across joint-force platforms to provide highly scalable parallelism, allowing waveforms and AI-enhanced microservices to execute, reconfigure, and recover dynamically, ensuring maximum resiliency in contested electronic warfare environments.

Work produced in Phase II may become classified. Note: The prospective contractor(s) must be U.S. owned and operated with no foreign influence as defined by 32 U.S.C. § 2004.20 et seq., National Industrial Security Program Executive Agent and Operating Manual, unless acceptable mitigating procedures can and have been implemented and approved by the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency (DCSA) formerly Defense Security Service (DSS). The selected contractor and/or subcontractor must be able to acquire and maintain a secret level facility and Personnel Security Clearances. This will allow contractor personnel to perform on advanced phases of this project as set forth by DCSA and NAVWAR in order to gain access to classified information pertaining to the national defense of the United States and its allies; this will be an inherent requirement. The selected company will be required to safeguard classified material during the advanced phases of this contract IAW the National Industrial Security Program Operating Manual (NISPOM), which can be found at Title 32, Part 2004.20 of the Code of Federal Regulations.

Phase I:
For a Direct to Phase II topic, the Government expects that the small business will have accomplished the following in a Phase I-type effort and developed a concept for a workable prototype or design to address, at a minimum, the basic requirements of the stated objective above. The following actions would be required to satisfy the requirements of Phase I:

Crucially, the evidence of this foundational research MUST NOT rely exclusively on previous or active federally funded SBIR/STTR contracts. Tangible proof of feasibility is an absolute prerequisite for award consideration.

To satisfy these Phase I prerequisites, the submitted documentation must substantiate that the offeror has successfully executed the following:

Validation of Feasibility: Comprehensive preliminary research into the development, integration, and demonstration of software-defined waveforms. This must be backed by empirical evidence, including theoretical modeling, simulation results, physical experimentation, and a clear mapping of anticipated technical risks.

Proven Engineering Capabilities: A documented track record in advanced digital signal processing (DSP) and the engineering of modular, hardware-agnostic software waveforms. Offerors must detail their practical experience in optimizing these waveforms for modern, heterogeneous compute environments—specifically multi-core CPUs, GPUs, and NPUs—and demonstrate scalability from enterprise server environments down to constrained tactical radio form factors.

Standardization and Interoperability: A deep, working knowledge of the governing interoperability standards for the specified military waveform family, ensuring the firm is fully equipped to engineer the required operational variants.

Phase II:
Design, develop, and integrate a real-time, software-defined physical layer implementation of the government-specified waveform utilizing a Digital Transceiver Software Development Kit (SDK). Validate that the Domain-Specific Architecture (DSA) processing core on the transceiver can natively host the specified waveform family, verifying the performance, agility, and modularity advantages of a software-defined physical layer.

• Architectural Integration: Port and optimize the modular waveform software to run directly on the transceiver's processing core, maximizing instruction-set efficiency and parallel execution.

• Spectral Verification: Conduct over-the-air or over-the-wire RF transmission testing of the waveform using the transceiver SDK test set.

• Performance Acceptance: Execute a comprehensive, multi-point validation campaign in accordance with a government-approved acceptance test plan to confirm functional communication limits, latency, and spectral compliance.

Work in Phase II may become classified. Please see note in the Description.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Complete operational testing, interoperability verification against the government reference waveform, and transition the waveform baseline for deployment on MIDS Joint Tactical Radio System (JTRS) and other approved tactical radio platforms via the government’s accredited integration and release pipeline.

Commercial organizations increasingly require the ability to rapidly deploy, update, and scale high-performance wireless communications without relying on inflexible, proprietary hardware. Technologies developed under this topic may have broad applicability in 5G/6G telecommunications (Virtualized Radio Access Networks), commercial satellite communications (SATCOM), Non-Terrestrial Networks (NTN), private enterprise networks, emergency responder communications, autonomous vehicle networks, and industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) infrastructure.

title: Mobile Vehicle Forensics
summary: Design, develop, and demonstrate a ruggedized, field-deployable vehicle forensics device capable of non-destructive, rapid data triage and extraction.
description:
Objective:
Design, develop, and demonstrate a ruggedized, field-deployable vehicle forensics device capable of non-destructive, rapid data triage and extraction.

Description:
Operational Need & Gap: During tactical site exploitation (TSE), Marine Corps and Joint operators require immediate, field-deployable hardware and software to recognize, preserve, and collect materials of forensic value. While multi-purpose forensic kits exist to process traditional materials, a critical intelligence gap remains regarding vehicle-derived data. Modern vehicles function as mobile data hubs featuring advanced navigation, localized track logs, and cached external device connections. Exploiting this telematics and informatics data is vital for generating actionable intelligence, mapping networks, and establishing identity dominance.

The Problem (Technological Fragmentation): The primary barrier to tactical vehicle exploitation is severe technological fragmentation. Current vehicle forensic solutions are often designed for controlled laboratory environments. Because In-Vehicle Infotainment (IVI) systems and Electronic Control Units (ECUs) rely on proprietary software architectures and inconsistent file structures, existing tools are often restricted to narrow manufacturer subsets. Consequently, field operators may be forced to perform invasive, time-consuming physical disassembly of the vehicle dashboard—a method that is untenable in many field environments.

Scope of Effort: This SBIR topic seeks innovative proposals to develop a low-SWaP (Size, Weight, and Power), ruggedized, all-in-one device that automates the forensic exploitation of vehicle data systems. The system must interface via standard external access points (e.g., On-Board Diagnostic [OBD-II] ports or Universal Serial Bus [USB]); automatically profile the vehicle’s make, model, year, and digital architecture; and execute an automated script to extract and structure data. Crucially, these features must be achieved through a non-invasive approach requiring no component disassembly, while maintaining strict forensic data integrity and verifiable accuracy.

The system must seamlessly interface with a broad registry of modern commercial and civilian vehicles across diverse model years, makes, and international manufacturers. Specifically, the device must extract and normalize data from disparate telematics systems (e.g., embedded GPS, localized track logs) and informatics modules (e.g., infotainment systems, paired Bluetooth logs, Wi-Fi cache, and cellular device pairings) without requiring laboratory-grade component disassembly.

Performance Goals:

• Threshold (Minimum): Demonstrate compatibility with representative samples of common vehicles; extract high-priority telematics (i.e., GPS, route history) and informatics (paired device logs) in under 15 minutes with verifiable accuracy (i.e., comparison with test data collected separately); packaged in a portable, field-ruggedized kit.
• Objective (Ideal): A pocket-sized, plug-and-play device that requires minimal operator training; demonstrates a modular path to broad vehicle compatibility; and extracts a comprehensive forensic data set in under 5 minutes via an intuitive, automated interface.

Phase I:
Develop a technical approach and assess the feasibility of a mobile, software-intelligent vehicle forensics capability that enables rapid data extraction from vehicle telematics (e.g., GPS, navigation logs) and infotainment systems (e.g., paired Bluetooth devices, call histories) and prioritizes universal applicability across diverse vehicle head units, makes, and models, avoiding dependencies on specific hardware teardowns.

Required Phase I deliverables include:

• A comprehensive feasibility study and initial system design architecture.
• An assessment of projected data extraction speeds, performance metrics, and technical limitations.
• A detailed Phase II development plan mapping out performance goals, key technical milestones, and risk mitigation strategies.

Phase II:
Develop, demonstrate, and validate a functional, field-ready prototype based on the feasibility concepts established in Phase I. Focus on expanding compatibility across a broader registry of vehicle makes, models, and head unit architectures, while increasing the depth and fidelity of extracted telematics and informatics data. Ensure that the prototype is ruggedized or packaged appropriately for expeditionary testing.

Required Phase II deliverables include:

• A fully functional prototype vehicle forensics tool (software, hardware, or hybrid) ready for Government evaluation.
• Demonstrations of the tool’s capability in an operationally relevant environment against representative vehicle targets.
• Complete technical documentation, including system architecture, user operating manuals, and finalized performance data metrics.
• A commercialization and transition plan detailing manufacturing viability and scaling strategies for military integration.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Upon successful completion of Phase II, support technology transition into a Phase III acquisition pathway for integration into the Forensics Dominance System – Marine Corps (FDS-MC) tactical site exploitation kits. Given the Joint requirement, position this rapid field-extraction capability for immediate transition to U.S. Special Operations Command (USSOCOM) exploitation programs and other Department of War service forensic intelligence elements.

In the commercial sector, this software-intelligent tool has direct dual-use applicability for federal, state, and local civilian law enforcement agencies by significantly modernizing digital forensics units through enabling roadside or scene-of-crime vehicle data extraction, thus bypassing extensive laboratory backlogs. Additionally, the capability will serve private sector markets, including automotive insurance fraud investigators, crash reconstruction experts, and corporate cybersecurity firms analyzing fleet vehicle telematics breaches.

title: Lightweight, Energy-Efficient Portable Nitrogen Generator for Expeditionary Operations
summary: Develop and demonstrate a man-portable, self-contained nitrogen generator capable of producing high-purity (equal to or less than 99.5%) nitrogen at 1,800 to 3,500 pounds per square inch (PSI), operating strictly within a 120-volt, 25-Amp single-phase electrical limit to support United States Marine Corps (USMC) expeditionary maintenance operations.
description:
Objective:
Develop and demonstrate a man-portable, self-contained nitrogen generator capable of producing high-purity (equal to or less than 99.5%) nitrogen at 1,800 to 3,500 pounds per square inch (PSI), operating strictly within a 120-volt, 25-Amp single-phase electrical limit to support United States Marine Corps (USMC) expeditionary maintenance operations. While utilizing common enabling gas-separation technologies similar to topic N244-P02, this effort is strictly distinguished by its unique requirement for a highly modular, lightweight, two-man portable form factor engineered specifically for point-of-need operations in austere, forward-deployed environments.

Description:
The United States Marine Corps (USMC) requires high-pressure nitrogen gas at forward operating locations to perform essential maintenance tasks, including aircraft and ground vehicle tire servicing, recoil mechanism servicing, recharging of gas suspension and accumulator components, and filling gas cylinders. Historically, the military relies on pre-filled, heavy steel gas cylinders resupplied through a vulnerable logistics chain. This process creates a severe logistical burden and hazardous material handling risk. Generating nitrogen at the point of need is essential to sustaining mission readiness in distributed, austere, and expeditionary environments consistent with USMC Force Design 2030 and Expeditionary Advanced Base Operations (EABO) concepts. The final product will be employed by USMC maintainers operating from forward tactical enclosures, specifically integrating with the JLTV Electronic Maintenance Shelter (JEMS). The system will provide point-of-need, high-purity nitrogen to service tactical vehicle and aircraft tires, hydraulic accumulators, recoil mechanisms, and suspension struts in support of distributed expeditionary operations.

While the USMC currently utilizes a legacy portable nitrogen generation system, it presents severe technical limitations that hinder expeditionary operations. First, the legacy system weighs 450 pounds, severely limiting mobility and requiring a four-person lift. Second, it requires 240-volt single-phase electrical power drawing 25 Amps. This exceeds the standard 120-volt, 25-Amp electrical limits of forward tactical enclosures, such as the Joint Expeditionary Maintenance Shelter (JEMS). Third, the current system only achieves 99.0% nitrogen purity (falling short of the required 99.5% for sensitive aviation and vehicle struts) and suffers from extremely slow flow rates, taking up to 6 hours to fill a standard 244-cubic-foot cylinder.

Commercial industry has introduced 120-volt single-phase configurations that achieve high purity. However, these state-of-the-art commercial units fall short of expeditionary physical requirements: they weigh in excess of 650 pounds, require separate external air compressors to operate, and maximize output at only 3,000 pounds per square inch (PSI). No known existing solution simultaneously achieves man-portable weight limits, 120-volt/25-Amp operation, self-contained air compression, high purity (Develop and demonstrate a man-portable, self-contained nitrogen generator capable of producing high-purity (equal to or less than 99.5%) nitrogen at 1,800 to 3,500 pounds per square inch (PSI), operating strictly within a 120-volt, 25-Amp single-phase electrical limit to support United States Marine Corps (USMC) expeditionary maintenance operations.

This SBIR topic seeks innovative small business proposals to design, develop, demonstrate, and deliver a prototype device for a man-portable, energy-efficient, self-contained nitrogen generator that overcomes the stated limitations. Proposed approaches may include advanced membrane separation, pressure swing adsorption (PSA) with novel sorbent materials, hybrid separation architectures, lightweight composite enclosures, advanced electric motor/compressor technologies, intelligent power management, or other innovative approaches that meaningfully advance the state of the art. The prototype device must address extreme environmental challenges, specifically maintaining gas separation efficiency in high heat and high humidity, and must physically fit within tactical maintenance shelters.

The prototype device shall target the following performance parameters to bound the scope of effort, while remaining open to innovative approaches that may refine specific parameters:

Performance Parameter Phase II Threshold (T = Minimum Acceptable) Phase II Objective (O = Desired)

Output Pressure (Selectable/Continuous): No less than 3,500 PSI (T); Greater than 3500 PSI (O)

Nitrogen Purity: =/- 99.5% (T); =/- 99.99% (O)

Continuous Output Flow Rate: =/- 60 Standard Cubic Feet per Hour (SCFH) (T); =/- 120 SCFH (O)

System Weight & Transportability: =/+ 250 lbs total. Must include two-wheeled cart configuration. System can break down into modular components where no single module exceeds the two-person lift limits defined in MIL-STD-1472 (T); =/+ 150 lbs total. System can break down into modular components where no single module exceeds the two-person lift limits defined in MIL-STD-1472 (O)

Form Factor/Size Limits: Must physically clear a 51.5 in (W) x 64.5 in (H) shelter door Modular, compact footprint (e.g., =/+ 30 in x 30 in base) (T = O)

Electrical Power Input: =/+ 3.4 kW, 120 VAC (single-phase, 50-60 Hz, max 25-Amp draw) (T): =/+ 3 kW, 120 VAC (single-phase) AND/OR 28V DC (Tactical Vehicle Integration) (O)

Operational Temperature: 40°F to +90°F (-32°C to +49°C) (T); -40°F to +140°F (-40°C to +60°C) (O)

Operational Humidity: Operable in 0% to 95% Relative Humidity (RH) (T); Operable in up to 100% RH (condensing) (O)

Proposals shall clearly identify the selected nitrogen generation approach, provide a credible technical basis for meeting the target performance parameters (particularly regarding thermal/moisture management and weight reduction), demonstrate awareness of the state of the art, and demonstrate that the effort is achievable within SBIR Phase I and Phase II timelines.

Phase I:
Define and develop a conceptual approach to portable high-pressure nitrogen generation that meaningfully advances beyond the current state of the art, with particular emphasis on achieving significant weight reduction (via modularity), self-contained air compression, and thermal/moisture management in expeditionary environments. Determine the technical feasibility of the conceptualized man-portable, self-contained nitrogen generator.

Perform modeling and simulation to predict prototype device performance against the parameters defined in the Description. Develop engineering approaches to address key technical challenges, including modular enclosure design to meet MIL-STD-1472 lift limits, high-efficiency nitrogen separation (e.g., advanced membranes or PSA sorbents) at reduced power input, and intelligent power management to ensure seamless integration with the Joint Light Tactical Vehicle (JLTV) Expeditionary Maintenance Shelter (JEMS) Power Entry Panel. Identify and assess critical technical risks associated with the proposed approach and define mitigation strategies.

Deliver the following required Phase I deliverables: a final technical report documenting the proposed conceptual design, modeling and simulation results, technology trade space analysis, technical risk assessment, and a recommended path forward for Phase II prototype device development.

Phase II:
Based on the conceptual design, modeling and simulation results, and technical feasibility findings from Phase I, design, fabricate, and validate a prototype man-portable, self-contained, energy-efficient portable nitrogen generator capable of producing high-purity nitrogen (=/- 99.5%) at up to 3,500 pounds per square inch (PSI) output pressure on 120-volt, 25-Amp single-phase electrical power in support of United States Marine Corps (USMC) expeditionary maintenance operations.

Demonstrate and validate the prototype device against the performance parameters defined in the Description, with particular emphasis on modularity to meet MIL-STD-1472 two-person lift limits, single-phase power consumption, output pressure range, nitrogen purity, and operational flow rate in high heat and high humidity environments. To guide prototype development and ensure suitability for long-duration expeditionary deployments, the prototype design should target a Mean Time Between Failure (MTBF) of no less than 1,000 operating hours, and scheduled preventive maintenance intervals (e.g., filter or seal replacements) of no less than 250 operating hours Fabricate and validate the prototype device through laboratory testing and, where feasible, demonstration in a tactically representative expeditionary environment in coordination with USMC end-user representatives.

Develop and validate the manufacturability process for the prototype device, identify critical components and supply chain considerations, and produce a Phase III transition plan identifying the target acquisition program, production pathway, and dual-use commercialization strategy.

Deliver the following required Phase II deliverables: a functional prototype device, a comprehensive test and evaluation report documenting measured performance against Threshold and Objective parameters defined in the Description, and a Phase III transition plan.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
The expected final state of this technology is a fully validated, production-ready, man-portable expeditionary nitrogen generator. Upon successful completion of Phase II, support Phase III transition of the prototype device to the Product Manager Maintenance Support Systems (PdM MSS), under Program Manager Combat Support Systems (PM CSS) at Marine Corps Systems Command (MCSC). Assist with formal integration of the nitrogen generator into the Tool Sets and Kits Program of Record as a direct replacement for the legacy High-Pressure Deployable (HPCD) system.

In addition to the primary military transition path, the new nitrogen generator has substantial commercialization potential. A lightweight, 120V single-phase, high-pressure (3,500 PSI) nitrogen generator that does not require heavy industrial power or external air compressors has direct applicability in several commercial sectors, including remote commercial aviation maintenance (e.g., servicing landing gear struts and tires at austere airstrips), the automotive and off-road racing industry for high-performance shock absorber tuning, and remote heavy industry such as mining, agriculture, and oil/gas exploration, where transporting heavy, pre-filled nitrogen cylinders is costly and logistically prohibitive.

References:
• “Commercial Item Description (CID) A-A-59503E: Nitrogen, Technical (4 June 2025).” https://everyspec.com/COMML_ITEM_DESC/A-A-59000_A-A-59999/A-A-59503_31795/
• “MIL-STD-1472H: Department of Defense Design Criteria Standard, Human Engineering (15 Sep 2020).” https://everyspec.com/MIL-STD/MIL-STD-1400-1499/MIL-STD-1472H_57041/
• “MIL-STD-810H: Department of Defense Test Method Standard, Environmental Engineering Considerations and Laboratory Tests (31 Jan 2019).” https://everyspec.com/MIL-STD/MIL-STD-0800-0899/MIL-STD-810H_5598/

title: Integrated Multi-Spectral Periscope for the Amphibious Combat Vehicle (ACV)
summary: Develop and demonstrate a ruggedized, multi-spectral imaging, 360-degree-capable camera system capable of integration into Amphibious Combat Vehicle (ACV) periscopes.
description:
Objective:
Develop and demonstrate a ruggedized, multi-spectral imaging, 360-degree-capable camera system capable of integration into Amphibious Combat Vehicle (ACV) periscopes.

Description:
Current periscopic vision systems on Marine Corps combat vehicles are limited to daylight optical performance, over a limited Field of View (FoV), and lack the ability to integrate modern digital imaging, thermal, and night vision technologies. The new system shall provide daylight, low-light/night vision, and thermal (IR) imaging capabilities through a single, compact, and modular unit; and enhance situational awareness, target detection, and crew safety for Marines during water, transition, and land operating environments.

This SBIR topic seeks to develop an integrated camera-based periscope module that:

• Provides visible (Electro-Optical [EO]), night vision (Near-Infrared Low-Level Laser (or Light) [NIR/LLL]), and long-wave infrared (LWIR) imaging in a compact unit.
• Is retrofit-compatible with existing periscope housings used in the USMC ACV FOV, or is capable of replacing optical viewports with an electronic display module.
• Includes onboard image fusion and low-latency video output for vehicle displays and augmented-reality systems.
• Meets ruggedization standards (MIL-STD-810H, MIL-STD-461D, and EC Standard 60529, rating IP66) for temperature, shock, vibration, EMI, dust and water resistance.
• Provides hardware resistance to seawater corrosion, as tested in accordance with GMW 14872, “Exterior, Exposure D” as stated in Table A3.
• Does not result in significant weight increase over that of the standard periscope.
• Supports integration with vehicle electronics architectures, including Vehicular Integration for C4ISR/EW Interoperability (VICTORY) and NATO STANAG 4609 standards.

title: Distributed Multispectral Event-Driven Integrated Sensing and Communications
summary: Develop a distributed multispectral event-driven integrated sensing and communications capability that can timely provide robust detection of a wide range of objects and integrate into existing onboard sensors to expand operational battlespace.
description:
Objective:
Develop a distributed multispectral event-driven integrated sensing and communications capability that can timely provide robust detection of a wide range of objects and integrate into existing onboard sensors to expand operational battlespace.

Description:
The Navy Aegis Program Office is interested in expanding battlespace awareness to support cross-domain operations through the integration of remote passive sensors. Currently, these sensors rely on real-time frame-based processing that generates large volumes of data, requiring significant processing power and energy and creating constraints for resource-limited hardware platforms with finite battery life, processing capabilities, and memory. In addition, transmitting large volumes of data over dynamic communication links can introduce delays and encounter bandwidth limitations that cannot meet time-critical operational needs. The complexity of the battlespace and electromagnetic environment further presents challenges for robust detection, classification, and identification. Advanced remote passive-sensor technologies that enable efficient and distributed sensing and processing will support multidomain operations by providing timely and resilient battlespace awareness. Successful technologies will be transitioned to the Aegis Combat System (ACS) to enhance distributed sensing, accelerate decision-making, and enable cross-domain operations.

The Navy is seeking to develop Multispectral Integrated Neuromorphic Sensing and Communications (MINSC) technology to support endurant remote sensing capability. MINSC is an event-driven sensor featuring low-probability-of-intercept (LPI) data transmission that can timely identify a wide range of objects and transmit the information to remote platforms to integrate into the existing decision-making process. Neuromorphic computing can provide energy efficient, parallel processing, and low-latency framework for passive sensing, edge computing, and remote inference.

Neuromorphic sensors deliver high temporal resolution, asynchronous, energy and bandwidth efficient data inspired by biological vision. The Navy seeks to build an Event-Driven Energy-Efficient Ecosystem to support Endurant Long-Range Sensing and Communications capability. Solutions can be software, neuromorphic hardware, and/or end-to-end neuromorphic system that can deliver robust information and fuse with existing sensors to provide improved tracking, detection, classification, and identification. The Navy is open to innovative ideas of novel system design that can make decisions locally and communicate sparingly or timely send out the event-driven information for remote inference. The intended capability is an integrated remote passive-sensing capability that performs event-driven local sensing and processing, communicating only the information necessary to enhance remote awareness, and fuses with existing sensors to improve tracking, detection, classification and identification.

Distributed MINSC will provide advantages in dynamic environment and resilience to noise and debris associated with military applications. Incorporating event-based multispectral remote sensors with onboard sensors will expand operational battlespace, contribute to robust Common Operational Picture (COP) and enhance situational awareness. It will integrate with the Aegis and permit realistic testing of all threat types and configurations in a dynamic testing environment. Track visualization will be delivered through the existing ACS console Graphical User Interfaces (GUIs). The solution will support current operator track management and decision-making and integrate with the AEGIS Test Bed (ATB) to facilitate system evaluation against more advanced threats. The solution will provide an enhanced capability to address targets in all configurations and optimal engagement options to the sailors, which will increase mission capability and effectiveness against the latest threats.

Work produced in Phase II may become classified. Note: The prospective contractor(s) must be U.S. owned and operated with no foreign influence as defined by 32 U.S.C. § 2004.20 et seq., National Industrial Security Program Executive Agent and Operating Manual, unless acceptable mitigating procedures can and have been implemented and approved by the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency (DCSA) formerly Defense Security Service (DSS). The selected contractor and/or subcontractor must be able to acquire and maintain a secret level facility and Personnel Security Clearances. This will allow contractor personnel to perform on advanced phases of this project as set forth by DCSA and PAE MS in order to gain access to classified information pertaining to the national defense of the United States and its allies; this will be an inherent requirement. The selected company will be required to safeguard classified material during the advanced phases of this contract IAW the National Industrial Security Program Operating Manual (NISPOM), which can be found at Title 32, Part 2004.20 of the Code of Federal Regulations.

Phase I:
Develop a design concept for MINSC technology for remote, instant, and robust reporting of objects of interest. Demonstrate the feasibility in meeting the requirements in the Description to support the tests and operational environments. Establish feasibility through analysis and modeling. Consider Design for Manufacturing (DFM) framework in the hardware design to simplify production processes throughout the design phase, ensuring design aligns with manufacturing standards. The Phase I Option, if exercised, will include the initial design specifications and capabilities description to build a prototype solution in Phase II.

Phase II:
Develop and deliver a MINSC prototype based on the results of Phase I. Ensure that the hardware prototype includes firmware and detailed interface specifications to support tests and evaluation in a Government Lab. Support evaluation of the prototype through lab testing, analytical methods, modeling, and simulation (if a simulation model is provided). For software prototype provide an emulator or hardware to demonstrate the technology to be evaluated by Government subject matter experts for validation. Deliver two prototypes at the end of Phase II. Provide a Phase III commercialization/transition plan.

It is probable that the work under this effort will be classified under Phase II (see the Description for details).

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Support the Navy in transitioning the prototype to allow for further experimentation and refinement for Navy uses. Incorporate the prototype into the AEGIS baseline testing modernization process and/or incorporated into Electronic Support Measures (ESM) in the SEWIP program to include integration into a baseline definition and incorporation of the baselines existing and new threat capabilities, validation, and combat system certification.

Integrated Neuromorphic Sensing and Communications will have applications in FutureG, Autonomous Vehicles, IoT, Surveillance, Robotics and Automation, Wearable Electronics, and Healthcare.

title: Automated Hardening for Cyber Secure Operating Systems
summary: Develop an automated tool to cyber harden various platform instantiations built on a Linux operating system.
description:
Objective:
Develop an automated tool to cyber harden various platform instantiations built on a Linux operating system.

Description:
Navy platforms have computing devices that drive their operational capabilities, especially autonomous or unmanned systems. Many platforms such as autonomous vehicles have some version and distribution of Linux as their operating system (OS) as well as an application running on it. Providing cybersecurity to these platforms is not only challenging due to their complexities but also very time consuming from a manpower perspective. This workload includes analyzing all levels of software (to include the OS) and configuring them to make them more secure as well as other cyber hardening operations such as software debloating to remove unnecessary functionality. The Navy has many platforms so each would require its own analysis and hardening. There are various means for improving the cybersecurity posture of the platform, each either manual or with its own tool, which creates undue burden on the developer of the platform for hardening without missing certain security features.

The focus of this SBIR effort is strictly on the OS, in this case Linux. The tool should determine the Linux OS functionality actually required by a specific platform instantiation, remove unnecessary OS components and functionality, and configure the remaining Linux OS to improve cybersecurity posture while preserving required system functionality. The goal is to create an automated tool that analyzes the various specifications, configurations, applications, etc. to harden the cybersecurity posture of the underlying Linux OS. The performer should propose their own platform, preferably either a commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) or open source platform that has a Linux OS and use this for design and experimentation on how to automate the cyber hardening of just the OS. It is preferred that the device be some type of autonomous vehicle. The performer will produce an overall software architecture for the automated OS hardening tool as well as a demonstration of the conceptual capability in Phase I while Phase II will involve development of a prototype in cooperation/guidance with Navy personnel. Metrics to demonstrate the improvements from the automated tool should be provided in the proposal.

Phase I:
Determine a conceptual software architecture for an automated cyber hardening tool for the Linux OS. Ensure that this tool will (1) leverage available runtime information for an existing system to identify the minimal set of OS functionality required for system functionality and (2) then recommend and/or configure the OS, removing unnecessary OS components and functionality and add/or configure recommended security features/functionality. At the conclusion of Phase I, present the proposed software architecture (i.e., the tool’s design and specification of functionality) and a demonstration on a representative platform (e.g., COTS or open-source autonomous platform) that shows improvement in cybersecurity posture (e.g., code analysis, pen testing, etc.). Tools will be compared on cybersecurity OS hardening completeness and approach (i.e., architecture) for ingesting various sources to automate the tool’s execution.

Phase II:
Develop a functional prototype of the automated tool. Interact with Navy personnel who own a platform and who will provide guidance and experimentation against the prototype OS cyber hardening tool. In conjunction with the Navy, devise, develop, and implement means for verifying the automated OS cyber hardening. Demonstrate that the tool can automatically ingest data sources (e.g., specifications, test plans, other hardening tools capabilities, etc.), and harden and minimalize the Linux OS footprint on the Navy platform. (Note: Navy personnel will examine metrics such as code reduction in the Linux OS, configurations, debloating, code analysis, and pen testing results to measure the effectiveness of the automated OS hardening.) Prepare a Phase III commercialization/transition plan.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Support the transition to Navy use.

Many commercial platforms leverage the Linux OS (e.g., IoT and Smart Home technology). The manufacturers of those devices often implement them on Linux and also need cyber hardening.

title: Low-cost Mid-wave Infrared Focal-Plane Array (FPA) Fabrication through Direct-bond Interconnection
summary: Develop a focal-plane array (FPA) fabrication process based on wafer-scale 3D-heterogeneous integration that enables a mid-wave infrared (MWIR) III-V detector epi-layer wafer to be directly bonded to a Silicon-based read-out integrated circuit (Si-ROIC) wafer, thereby eliminating the inefficient die-level Indium (In) bump-bonding process currently required to assemble Mid-wave Infrared (MWIR)…
description:
Objective:
Develop a focal-plane array (FPA) fabrication process based on wafer-scale 3D-heterogeneous integration that enables a mid-wave infrared (MWIR) III-V detector epi-layer wafer to be directly bonded to a Silicon-based read-out integrated circuit (Si-ROIC) wafer, thereby eliminating the inefficient die-level Indium (In) bump-bonding process currently required to assemble Mid-wave Infrared (MWIR) FPA sensor chips.

Description:
Electro-Optic and Infrared (EO/IR) sensors are used in a wide variety of applications, such as navigation, wide-area surveillance, and targeting. Operating in the visible and near-IR bands, EO sensors are available with small pixels and in large arrays at low cost, because the Si-detector wafer and Si-ROIC wafer can be 3D-integrated directly through wafer-to-wafer bonding with high yield at high volume based on material and complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS)-process compatibility. By contrast, sensors operating in the MWIR employ III-V detector materials, which are not CMOS-process compatible, while III-V epi-layer detectors cannot be epitaxially grown directly on Si, as required to produce the crystalline order of high-quality detectors [Refs 1-2]. Instead, the III-V detector epi-layer is grown on a lattice-compatible substrate wafer, which is then flip-chip bonded to a Si-ROIC through a dense array of sub-pixel indium bumps placed on each wafer, followed by detector-substrate removal. The technically demanding process of depositing, aligning, and compressing the dense arrays of indium bumps on detector and ROIC die, results in a labor-intensive, inefficient, low-yield process for IR FPA fabrication, which greatly increases cost.

In recent years, 3D-heterogeneous integration has enabled a single integrated chip of greater overall functionality to be realized at reduced cost by assembling multiple smaller chips, each having unique functionality, material, node size, and/or foundry origin. Direct-bond interconnection (DBI) [Refs 3-5] is a 3D-heterogeneous integration technique that can potentially enable low-cost MWIR FPA fabrication. In principle, DBI should enable very large format FPAs with small pixels to be fabricated, as the process is largely independent of wafer and pixel size, in contrast to conventional bump-bonding. Moreover, the DBI process utilizes a temperature range that is compatible with MWIR IR detector materials.

The goal of this SBIR topic is to demonstrate the use of DBI or a similar process for fabrication of high-performance, large format, small-pixel, MWIR FPAs at low cost with the objective of refining the technique sufficiently to potentially replace conventional bump-bonding.

Phase I:
Plan a detailed concept for a FPA fabrication and characterization process, including a risk assessment. While the pixel unit cell design is flexible, a pixel size of less than or equal to 10 micro-meters (um) and format of at least 2K x 2K are required, but otherwise any existing or commercially available Si-based ROIC can potentially be used for this effort. The III-V detector epi-layer spectral response must cover at least the MWIR band (3-5 um). The specific foundry and fabrication process steps will be determined in Phase I. Develop a detailed FPA characterization plan, including measurement of inter-wafer voids, pixel operability, and yield. Perform a per-FPA cost analysis that compares DBI or the selected alternative process to conventional bump-bonding and includes an assessment of the cost impact of process selection trade-offs.

Phase II:
Use the DBI or selected alternative process to fabricate multiple wafers of FPAs having less or equal to 10 um pixels and greater than or equal to 2K x 2K format. Dice and thoroughly characterize the FPAs. Integrate one or more FPA sensor chips into an imaging system and subsequent optical performance characterization (favorable but is not required under this effort.) Prepare a Phase III commercialization/transition plan.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Build and test an imaging sensor employing a DBI-fabricated FPA with available Phase III funding upon successful completion of Phase II.

The advancement of MWIR imagers could support many dual-use applications, such as border security, law enforcement, and industrial process monitoring. In general, the advancement of 3D-HI and DBI specifically could facilitate the development of novel micro-electronic devices beyond MWIR imagers.

References:
• Rogalski, A. "Recent progress in infrared detector technologies." Infrared Physics & Technology, 54(3), 2011, pp. 136-154. https://www.scirp.org/reference/referencepapers?referenceid=838480
• Martyniuk, P. and Rogalski, A. "HOT infrared photodetectors." Opto-Electronics Review, 21(2), 2013, pp. 239-257. https://www.researchgate.net/publication/257909096_HOT_infrared_photodetectors
• US Patent 9,082,627: Method for low temperature bonding and bonded structure (covers the core process of room or low-temperature dielectric-to-dielectric and metal-to-metal bonding). https://patents.google.com/patent/US9082627B2/zh
• US Patent 6,962,835: Method for room temperature metal direct bonding. https://patents.google.com/patent/US6962835B2
• US Patent 9,391,143: Method for low temperature bonding and bonded structure. https://patents.google.com/patent/US9391143B2

title: “Self-Replicating Evolutionary Agentic SI Swarming Force” with Autonomous Embedded SI Guardrail Enforcers
summary: 1- Develop a platform agnostic fully autonomous Agentic SI swarm system suitable for multidomain naval operations (i.e., Sea, Air, Space, Land, and Cyber) with self-awareness for rapid operationally scalable response, namely “hyper-scalability”. The Agentic SI system, a hybrid-evolutionary SI, must self-replicate and self-deploy.
description:
Objective:
1- Develop a platform agnostic fully autonomous Agentic SI swarm system suitable for multidomain naval operations (i.e., Sea, Air, Space, Land, and Cyber) with self-awareness for rapid operationally scalable response, namely “hyper-scalability”. The Agentic SI system, a hybrid-evolutionary SI, must self-replicate and self-deploy. In other words, it must self-evolve as it gets feedback from its internal SI agents; it must coevolve as it interacts with the environment and the adversary to adapt and survive in littoral ecosystem without human guidance. As a team, it must autonomously reason to scale-up or scale-down its swarming clusters to generate tactical sub-clusters or end-game sub-clusters for defensive and offensive measures to confront and overwhelm threats. Neuro-Symbolic SI is to be a practical method for these SI-based swarm agents to explore and exploit the conditions in the operational ecosystem.

2- The developed platform must strictly adhere to operational policies, safety, and security with embedded SI agents serving as guardrails to control all sustaining SI agents (i.e., Self-Evolving SI agents) by checking outputs, cross-referencing data feeds and plans, and correcting flagged responses. These SI-enabled Guardrail-Enforcers must be active and adaptive systems embedded into the Agentic SI Swarm workflows. The embedded SI Guardrail-Enforcers validate-and-verify policies for additional safety and behavior guardrail checks beyond the ordinary trust metrics. The important performance question is “Did Agentic SI system get better without changing policy permissions, safety boundaries, or behavior unpredictably?”

Description:
This SBIR topic seeks hardware-agnostic Agentic SI swarm-teaming technologies capable of self-replication, hybrid-evolution (self-evolution and coevolution), and self-organization into teaming many arrangements. It is important to note that this project does not challenge the importance of physical platforms/machines (i.e., unmanned assets) that have physical presence in operational environments. The envisioned Agentic SI system is the machine’s intelligent autonomy software that controls the platform’s presence and its interactions with entities in the operational environment. It autonomously configures individual swarms with unique missions and networks of collaborative swarms operating in multiple operational domains with specific teaming assignments.

The envisioned swarm system is agentic as it pursues goals autonomously. It interprets assigned mission objectives and determines how to achieve them. It knows how to process, fuse, and exploit all source intelligence (ASI) and live sensor feeds to determine the course of action (CoA) and keeps adjusting it until the outcome is reached. It decides which payloads to use and when to use them, for example, active and/or passive intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance, and targeting (ISRT) sensors, point-to-point or omni-broadcast communication, or weapon systems, etc. It adapts when situations or environmental conditions change, or certain aspects of a plan fail. It can recover from various system failures and processing errors. It is designed with embedded SI-Guardrail-Enforcers to manage, validate, and verify every aspect of the Agentic SI system’s performance and associated risks to ensure that the end-to-end system adheres to established policies set forth by the Department of War and the U.S. Navy including operational safety requirements as well as the national security doctrines and mandates. The highest priority for this program is to establish ZERO tolerance for SI-generated rogue populations of unaligned agents rapidly and uncontrollably increase.

The hybrid-evolutionary aspect of the Agentic SI system focuses on attaining new operational proficiency and know-how to execute emerging missions with the highest accuracy, persistence, and endurance. The self-evolving SI system monitors endogenous performance of all subsystems, gets feedback, and improves its own internal design configuration autonomously, for example, altering or generating new internal models. The coevolutionary SI system monitors exogenous performance interactions and coevolves the internal design in response to interactions with the environment and adversaries. It improves autonomous teaming performance interactions and reconfigurations, for example, altering or generating new swarming models, plans, and configurations to maintain operational tempo.

The self-replication aims to create autonomous, self-improving agents capable of independent survival and expansion. This Agentic SI system autonomously improves itself, creates its own successors, and builds specialized sub-agents to solve operational issues.

The self-configuring aspect of the Agentic SI system focuses on a variety of mission-focused collaborative teaming arrangements, including scouting teams for early detection of indications and warning signs to ensure survival, trip-wire teams to detect encroaching threats, ad-hoc networking teams for continuous collaboration and tracking threats, a self-defense team for fault-tolerant operations, and offensive teams to ensure survival. In aggregate, these teams form an Agentic-Force that self-adapts, self-organizes, and self-heals.

The Agentic SI Swarming-Force addresses mission capability gaps that require agile adaptation to novel adversarial TTPs and unanticipated asymmetric countermeasures. The envisioned SI capability requires SI-based evolutionary modelling techniques for learning, reasoning, recognition, and autonomous decision-making to counter emergent and/or unanticipated observable patterns of life activities or events. In other words, agentic discovery of unknown-unknown events/assets posed by the intelligent adversaries. It ensures the timely execution of CoA plans to neutralize emerging threats, including asymmetric attacks, novel deployment of joint civilian and military assets, cloaked military assets, decoys, and deceptive asset deployments. A representative set of agentic impelling operations may be conducted overtly or covertly to influence hostile forces to undertake desired actions, including adopting specific courses of action or modifying their pattern of life to safeguard critical assets through reconfiguration, relocation, or repurposing. These observable responses can then be exploited by the Agentic SI Swarming Force to degrade adversarial autonomy and disrupt, reshape, and ultimately defeat their operational plans and tactical engagements.

A notional framework for developing the required critical technologies is as follows. First, meta-learning and meta-reasoning capabilities—learning how to learn and reason—are foundational. Rather than relying on static training, agents continuously refine their internal learning processes to autonomously adapt to new tasks and conditions. This allows the system to create specialized sub-agents for various operational tasks and teaches them optimal strategies. Second, replication logic creates next-generation agents to improve operational efficiency, reduce false-alarm rates, and field additional task-organized agents to address emergent or previously unanticipated requirements. Third, autonomous resource management mechanisms must dynamically replicate, allocate, sustain, scale, or retire agents to maintain operational efficiency and mission alignment. Finally, secure, low-probability-of-intercept/low-probability-of-detection (LPI/LPD) ad hoc networking and communications are essential to enable mission-focused teaming, decentralized coordination, and Reachback to share operational insights across agent networks beyond local clusters. Critical SI technology components and developments are as follows:

• Self-reflecting Agentic SI system to provide: 1) an introspection feedback loop to enable the Agentic SI system to analyze its own plan, spot errors or weak reasoning logic, and revise them before acting, which would make the system better at goal-seeking and improve its strategy; and 2) a retrospection feedback loop to enable the Agentic SI system to analyze its past plans, decisions, and resulting outcomes. Spot and learn from both the advantages and the shortcomings of those past decision processes to improve future planning and reasoning logic.
• Identification of novel and evolutionary behaviors appearing in a new generation of SI-agent models.
• Methodology to specify how self-replication and coevolutionary processes are initiated and developed, strategic life-cycle planning, resource acquisition for autonomous self-replication, and survival tactics that exploit operational ecosystem.
• Contextual modeling: relational, spatial, logic-based, uncertainty, and hybrid context modeling.
• Meta learning: decision tree and multilayer perception classifiers, collaborative filtering, pattern mining, deep learning.
• Spatiotemporal synchronization methods for multimodal data across decentralized architectures.
• Multimodal contextual signal processing and fusion.
• Cross-domain contextual collaborative learning, inference, and recognition.
• Meta reasoning, contextual reasoning, and risk assessment and reduction.
• Contextual priority-based task management balancing operational objectives such as persistence, endurance, and collections.

The scope of the initial feasibility study and deliverables are as follows: a) define the challenge problem that will likely meet the benchmark performance metrics; b) review a set of candidate Agentic SI methods and data requirements; c) develop a low-cost initial proof-of-concept prototype for the assessment; d) evaluate feasibility against measurable criteria; and e) deliver a proposed Phase II prototype development plan including technical risk reduction criteria and next steps.

Work produced in Phase II may become classified. Note: The prospective contractor(s) must be U.S. owned and operated with no foreign influence as defined by 32 U.S.C. § 2004.20 et seq., National Industrial Security Program Executive Agent and Operating Manual, unless acceptable mitigating procedures can and have been implemented and approved by the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency (DCSA) formerly Defense Security Service (DSS). The selected contractor and/or subcontractor must be able to acquire and maintain a secret level facility and Personnel Security Clearances. This will allow contractor personnel to perform on advanced phases of this project as set forth by DCSA and ONR in order to gain access to classified information pertaining to the national defense of the United States and its allies; this will be an inherent requirement. The selected company will be required to safeguard classified material during the advanced phases of this contract IAW the National Industrial Security Program Operating Manual (NISPOM), which can be found at Title 32, Part 2004.20 of the Code of Federal Regulations.

Phase I:
Determine the technical feasibility of designing and developing the Agentic SI Swarm technology as explained in the Description. Draw key distinctions for the proposed design approach compared to the current state-of-the-art naval ISRT information exploitation cycles. Ensure that the proposed design concept must clearly define the steps that naval ISRT platforms and joint services can capitalize on for transformational SI-assisted ISRT and engagement operations with dominant applications within the next five years. Motivate the design with a compelling challenge problem supported by relevant datasets. Consider a challenge problem that corresponds to cross-domain littoral operations and navigational risks associated with hostile anti-access/denied-access enforcement scenario that considers seaside terrain, weather, the maritime order of battle and maneuvers; engagement rules and doctrine; logistics and supply demands, etc. Hostile enforcement may include hypersonic missiles, ballistic missile attacks, sea-skimming cruise missile attacks, anti-submarine track and trail, torpedo attacks, littoral mining, and swarming weapons. Testing and demonstrations may use a mix of open-source intelligence (OSINT) datasets, synthetic datasets from DON, MCML, AIS maritime traffic, commercial satellite imagery, or similar sources. Conduct Agentic SI Swarming performance assessment, including cause and effect sensitivity analysis on contextual understanding; confidence rate on SI-generated engagement plans, options, and risk reduction associated with the ups and downs of encounters; confidence rate on SI-risk escalation controls enabling trust decisions across the integrated chain-of-command; efficiency gains in human responsiveness through timely decision-making, chain-of-actions, and resources spent.

Performance metrics for Agentic SI system in a controlled test environment are as follows: task success and completion rates: 90%+; goal attainment rate: 90%+; tool selection accuracy: 95%+; plan adherence: 90%+; hallucination rate: under 2%; safety violation rate: 0% in policy tests (any policy-breaking action is a hard fail); prompt-injection resistance: 95%+ success against red-team prompts (measure on adversarial test sets); human override rate: < 5% on routine tasks; recovery rate: 80%+; end-to-end latency: under 60 seconds for interactive flows; replication success rate: 100% only when explicitly authorized.

Policy, safety, and security performance metrics that are controlled by the embedded SI Guardrail-Enforcers are as follows:

• For self-replicating Agentic SI system to ensure the system can perform useful work without uncontrolled replication, drift, or excessive human intervention. In other words, it must replicate when authorized, and never on its own outside policy. The performance metrics include goal attainment rate: 90%+; tool selection accuracy (i.e., preventing cascading failures from bad tool use): 95%+; hallucination rate: under 2%; human override rate: under 5%; recovery rate: 80%+; boundary violation rate: 0%; and Uncontrolled replication rate: 0%.
• For Hybrid-evolving Agentic SI system, the performance metrics include improvement gains: greater than 20% (self-evolution should improve performance on unchanged tasks); regression rate: less than 5% on core tasks (new versions should not break stable capabilities); reproducibility (evolved behavior must remain traceable and can be validated): 95%+; and Drift from policy, safety, and security: 0% -- self-evolution cannot change the operational constraint envelope.

Assess the feasibility of applying the Agentic SI methods to a candidate challenge problem. Perform requirements analysis, data and interface assessment, evaluation of candidate SI approaches, and development of a limited proof of concept to determine technical viability. Produce a feasibility report, preliminary architecture, risk assessments, and a proposed Phase II prototype development plan.

Phase II:
Conduct proof-of-concept and prototype development incorporating the recommended candidate technology from Phase I. Demonstrate the operational effectiveness based on the following criteria: (a) prioritized sensor alerts, (b) prioritized threat escalation, (c) measured severity of events, and (d) measured analytic completeness. Test and demonstrate the improved capability based on the performance metrics detailed for Phase I. Provide analytics, SI tools, models, prototypes, T&E and demonstration results, and interface requirements. Develop a final report to include a detailed design of the system and a plan for transition to the program of record in Phase III.

Work in Phase II may become classified. Please see note in the Description.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Advance these capabilities to TRL-7 and integrate the technology into the Maritime Tactical Command and Control POR, Marine Air-Ground Task Force Command and Control, or ISR processing platforms at the Marine Corps Information Operations Center.

Once conceptually and technically validated, demonstrate dual-use applications of this technology in civilian law enforcement and security services.

title: Electro-Optical/Infrared Tactical Decision Aid
summary: Develop an Electro-Optical/Infrared (EO/IR) Tactical Decision Aid (TDA) for surface and air sensors in maritime, littoral, and inland environments.
description:
Objective:
Develop an Electro-Optical/Infrared (EO/IR) Tactical Decision Aid (TDA) for surface and air sensors in maritime, littoral, and inland environments.

Description:
The United States Navy (USN) requires the capability to rapidly predict the performance of sensors that depend on the propagation of electro-optical/infrared (EO/IR) radiation (i.e., wavelengths from 0.4 to 12 micron) in air. Sensor performance is subject to environmental/meteorologic conditions, as well as sensor, platform, background/clutter, and target characteristics. For a given sensor on a platform and a target in background/clutter, a forecaster should be able to determine key performance metrics; for example, maximum detection range based on the forecasted meteorological conditions. In this way, USN commanders can make tactical decisions based on the predicted sensor performance given ambient/forecast weather conditions. Key modeling components within a TDA include the land/maritime surface background, target signature, radiative transfer, and sensor performance models. These models are often interdependent, requiring feedback between them (e.g., radiative transfer between target and background models is needed to compute the contrast of the target in the background, which then feeds into a sensor performance model).

Target Acquisition Weapons Software (TAWS), a successor to Electro-Optic Tactical Decision Aid (EOTDA), was originally developed by the Air Force Research Laboratory (AFRL) and released in 1998. Later a target scene model improvement for selected high-resolution targets was implemented with Multi-Service Electro-optics Signature (MuSES). The USN is looking for an innovative and accurate EO/IR TDA, which would be an alternative/improvement to TAWS. Improvements could include support for three dimensional meteorological inputs. The primary challenge for implementing an EO/IR TDA is the methodical verification and validation (V&V) of the constituent models and submodels being developed. This SBIR topic seeks innovative solutions to the development of an EO/IR TDA with particular focus on the methods proposed to verify and validate developed models. A list of prior V&V efforts on proposed submodels should be made clear in the responses to this solicitation, as well as the proposed means/methods to conduct V&V under a Phase II and/or Phase III.

Work produced in Phase II may become classified. Note: The prospective contractor(s) must be U.S. owned and operated with no foreign influence as defined by 32 U.S.C. § 2004.20 et seq., National Industrial Security Program Executive Agent and Operating Manual, unless acceptable mitigating procedures can and have been implemented and approved by the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency (DCSA) formerly Defense Security Service (DSS). The selected contractor and/or subcontractor must be able to acquire and maintain a secret level facility and Personnel Security Clearances. This will allow contractor personnel to perform on advanced phases of this project as set forth by DCSA and ONR in order to gain access to classified information pertaining to the national defense of the United States and its allies; this will be an inherent requirement. The selected company will be required to safeguard classified material during the advanced phases of this contract IAW the National Industrial Security Program Operating Manual (NISPOM), which can be found at Title 32, Part 2004.20 of the Code of Federal Regulations.

Phase I:
Develop a concept for an EO/IR TDA model architecture and verify the radiative transfer model can solve basic thermal transport problems (e.g., conduction, convection, radiation) with analytic solutions. Ensure facets/grid points can be individually sampled to provide their temperature and spectral radiance. Create a land/sea background model where spatiotemporally varying clutter can be added in Phase II. Create a CUBI thermal target model and a generic, band-selectable imaging sensor (e.g., 3-5 micron midwave IR (MWIR) imager) model.

Phase II:
Implement the EO/IR TDA model into a working prototype and ensure support for a wide range of generic representative targets (e.g., car, truck, ship, boat, plane, unmanned aerial system (UAS)) and a wide range of generic representative sensors (e.g., 0.4-0.7 micron visual band imager, 1.06 micron laser designator, 0.9-1.7 micron shortwave IR (SWIR) imager, 3-5 micron MWIR imager, 8-12 micron longwave IR (LWIR) imager). Develop and add specific target and sensor models, some of which will be provided by the government and might be classified. Add representative spatiotemporally varying clutter in the scene and validate the background/clutter model against prior field data collections. Validate the radiative transfer model with a complex thermal transport experiment using a CUBI target in the laboratory. Prepare a Phase III commercialization/transition plan.

Work in Phase II may become classified. Please see note in the Description.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Develop and add other specific target and sensor models, some of which will be provided by the government and might be classified. Validate the EO/IR TDA using previously collected field data. Design and execute an experimental validation of the EO/IR TDA using state-of-the art meteorological sensors and scientific grade (or better) thermal imagers, as well as a representative target and sensor to test the capability to determine sensor performance (e.g., maximum detection range).

title: Autonomous Multi-Intelligence Acoustic Reasoning Agent for Anti-Submarine Warfare
summary: Develop an autonomous Anti-Submarine Warfare (ASW) reasoning agent that fuses passive and active acoustic detections with non-acoustic maritime situational data, environmental acoustic propagation context, and platform/target behavior models to produce explainable contact assessments, track hypotheses, and recommended sensor-tasking actions; and supports deployment on an Unmanned Surface Vehicle…
description:
Objective:
Develop an autonomous Anti-Submarine Warfare (ASW) reasoning agent that fuses passive and active acoustic detections with non-acoustic maritime situational data, environmental acoustic propagation context, and platform/target behavior models to produce explainable contact assessments, track hypotheses, and recommended sensor-tasking actions; and supports deployment on an Unmanned Surface Vehicle (USV) with constrained communications, power, and computing conditions.

Description:
The Department of the Navy (DON) seeks development of an autonomous decision-support and reasoning capability for ASW that can reduce dependence on continuous human interpretation of complex acoustic displays and enable future distributed unmanned ASW operations. Current ASW performance is heavily dependent on trained operators who interpret passive narrowband, passive broadband, Demodulation of Noise (DEMON), and other acoustic products while simultaneously incorporating situational knowledge such as geography, bathymetry, Conductivity Temperature and Depth (CTD) data for sound-speed structure, Global Positioning System (GPS), Automatic Identification System (AIS), organic/non-organic tracks, surface traffic, tactical geometry, and expected target behaviors. This human fusion process is effective but difficult to scale across persistent unmanned systems operating at range, under intermittent communications, and in acoustically cluttered environments.

This SBIR topic requests development of an autonomous ASW agent that can ingest heterogeneous acoustic detections and associated confidence measures, correlate them with non-acoustic common operating picture data, reason over environmental acoustic propagation, and maintain multiple explainable track and classification hypotheses over time. The capability should explicitly account for confusers such as merchant shipping, fishing vessels, biologics, own-force and friendly surface ship contributions, reverberation/clutter, and geographically-dependent propagation effects. The resulting system should not be a single-sensor classifier only; it should demonstrate multi-source temporal reasoning that can explain why a contact is assessed as likely submarine, non-submarine, ambiguous, or requiring additional sensing. The approach should be modular and compatible with Navy acoustic processing and performance-prediction workflows, while allowing Navy-provided threat behavior models, environmental data, and acoustic feature streams to be incorporated without redesign. Submissions should include a description of prior sensor fusion development that will serve as a baseline for the proposed ASW fusion architecture.

Work produced in Phase II may become classified. Note: The prospective contractor(s) must be U.S. owned and operated with no foreign influence as defined by 32 U.S.C. § 2004.20 et seq., National Industrial Security Program Executive Agent and Operating Manual, unless acceptable mitigating procedures can and have been implemented and approved by the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency (DCSA) formerly Defense Security Service (DSS). The selected contractor and/or subcontractor must be able to acquire and maintain a secret level facility and Personnel Security Clearances. This will allow contractor personnel to perform on advanced phases of this project as set forth by DCSA and ONR in order to gain access to classified information pertaining to the national defense of the United States and its allies; this will be an inherent requirement. The selected company will be required to safeguard classified material during the advanced phases of this contract IAW the National Industrial Security Program Operating Manual (NISPOM), which can be found at Title 32, Part 2004.20 of the Code of Federal Regulations.

Phase I:
Develop a concept for the proposed software architecture for an autonomous ASW reasoning agent, including data schemas for acoustic detections, Common Operation Picture (COP)/non-acoustic inputs, environmental context, target-behavior priors, uncertainty representation, and operator-interpretable explanations. Demonstrate proof-of-concept using representative or open acoustic and maritime datasets to demonstrate fusion of passive acoustic features with disparate data features. Prepare a Phase I final report that includes a performance assessment plan that quantitively assesses metrics such as track purity, false-track/alarm suppression, classification confidence calibration, explanation quality, latency, and robustness to missing/degraded inputs.

Phase II:
Develop prototype software with implementation capability that should ingest multiple acoustic modalities, correlate acoustic contacts with non-acoustic maritime tracks, maintain multiple hypotheses, and recommend sensor-tasking or unmanned maneuver options to improve classification confidence. Demonstrate the software in simulation or replay using geographically realistic bathymetry, sound-speed profiles, surface traffic, environmental noise, and target/non-target behavior profiles. Include a transition package that documents Application Programming Interfaces (APIs), modular interfaces to Navy propagation/performance-prediction tools, model-card style documentation, training/evaluation data requirements, and a plan for integration with unmanned ASW mission systems. Prepare a Phase III commercialization/transition plan.

Work and/or data used in Phase II may become classified. Please see note in the Description.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Sensor fusion for acoustic clutter reduction supports seismic surveys of commercial oil prospecting and more general ocean exploration efforts in support of the ocean acoustics National Naval Responsibility. Understanding how to fuse ocean ambient sound in terms of its spatial, temporal, and frequency contributions as well as elucidating information about air and seafloor interfaces will provide a clearer picture of the undersea world where the Navy operates. Commercial dual-use applications may include maritime domain awareness, port and harbor security, offshore infrastructure monitoring, autonomous vessel operations, illegal fishing detection, environmental acoustic monitoring, and marine mammal or vessel-noise characterization.
