title: High Sensitivity Tunneling Magnetoresistive Magnetometers
summary: Modernize United States capabilities to produce ultra-low size, weight, power, and cost (SWAP-C) tunneling magnetoresistive magnetometers with industry leading sensitivities.
description:
Objective:
Modernize United States capabilities to produce ultra-low size, weight, power, and cost (SWAP-C) tunneling magnetoresistive magnetometers with industry leading sensitivities.

Description:
Many Navy systems utilize magnetometer technologies for the remote detection, localization, and classification of ferrous objects. Decades of research into different technologies including optically pumped magnetometers have provided highly sensitive technologies which meet most Navy sensitivity needs. However, higher sensitivity magnetometers also possess increased SWAP-C, which limits their applicability in many Navy applications.

Therefore, there is a direct need for highly sensitive magnetometers that are also compact, low cost, and low power to support a broader range of Navy mission requirements including one-way attack vehicles, expeditionary warfare, mine warfare, and swarming systems. Over the past 30 years, an adjacent technology known as tunneling magnetoresistance (TMR) has had drastic improvements in system sensitivities, unlocking a potential new regime of magnetometer technologies that exhibit ultra-low SWAP-C while maintaining Navy relevant sensitivities.

Design Requirements:

-Size: less than 10 mm x 10 mm per axis

-Power: less than 100 mW per axis

-Sensitivity: less than 50 pT/rt(Hz) @ 1 Hz

-Frequency Range: DC-500KHz

-Dynamic Range: -100 uT to 100 uT

-Nonlinearity over dynamic range: less than 0.1 %

-Standardized per unit electrical packaging

Phase I:
Produce a concept for single-axis TMR sensors that possess a design that satisfies the above criteria and also include a per sensor voltage-to-field calibration for confirmation by stakeholders. Provide an analysis or discussion of the potential tradeoffs in the Phase I report if the design concept cannot meet the design objectives. (Note: Justification for the prior should include comparative analysis of COTS capabilities, U.S. and International.)

Phase II:
Fabricate 6 or 9 prototype systems for evaluation and testing in a vector configuration including voltage-to-field calibration for each sensor. Demonstrate that the prototypes achieve or show potential for meeting the design requirements and intended use applications. Conduct testing in conjunction with Navy personnel. Address both cost effectiveness and manufacturability feasibility as part of the prototype test and evaluation. Consult the appropriate acquisition program office for any additional evaluation metrics needed for Phase III. Perform potential commercialization cost analysis to estimate at production cost per unit and prepare a Phase III commercialization/transition plan.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Apply the knowledge gained in Phase II to build an advanced vector TMR prototype that meets appropriate technology readiness level (TRL) metrics set by the acquisition program office. Support the Navy for test and validation of the system for certified Navy use. Develop manufacturing plans to facilitate transition to a UUV program of record.

Explore the potential to transfer these TMR sensors for potential commercial use in magnetic surveying and UXO detection.

References:
• TDK: “New Development Based on High-Sensitivity Nivia xMR Sensor: Measurement of Weak Magnetic Fields from Minute Areas.” https://product.tdk.com/en/techlibrary/developing/bio-sensor/migne-xmr-sensor.html

title: Improved Ionosphere D-region Specification for High Frequency Propagation
summary: Develop tools and/or techniques to improve characterization of the D-region ionosphere sufficient for skillful ionosphere model specification and forecast over climatology and that demonstrate the impact of improved methodology on ionosphere accuracy for use by high frequency (HF) and very low frequency (VLF) signal propagation tools.
description:
Objective:
Develop tools and/or techniques to improve characterization of the D-region ionosphere sufficient for skillful ionosphere model specification and forecast over climatology and that demonstrate the impact of improved methodology on ionosphere accuracy for use by high frequency (HF) and very low frequency (VLF) signal propagation tools.

Description:
HF and VLF skywave propagation depend on knowledge of the altitudinal structure of the ionosphere for reliable system operation. The D-region ionosphere, a region typically between 60-90 km altitude above the Earth’s surface, is particularly challenging to predict with sufficient fidelity for skywave mission planning because the region is difficult to measure with in situ measurements. Remote sensing methods provide a limited dataset from which to develop detailed physical and assimilative models that can reliably produce the regional behavior on a day-to-day basis.

Operational models like the D-Region Absorption Product (D-RAP) produce maps of outage areas as a function of radio frequency (RF) to inform HF system users of anticipated degradation or blackouts due to radiation increases. These predictions primarily address HF absorption due to solar X-ray flares at low and mid-latitudes and do not address the VLF propagation use case. While solar X-ray flares are important effects with Navy relevance, the effects of flares typically only last for a few hours and occur 10-20 times a year. For sufficient use in HF absorption and VLF propagation applications, a D-region ionosphere is required to capture seasonal, solar cycle, and day-to-day variability at all latitudes in addition to solar flare phenomenology.

The intended capability is improved D-region specification and forecast in the 60-70 km and 80-90 km altitude regions for VLF propagation and HF absorption, particularly day-to-day variability and in the high latitude regions at night.

Climatological models like the International Reference Ionosphere (IRI) produce an altitude profile at D-region altitudes. The IRI model is based on about a hundred historical rocket profiles, so it captures some of the basic day/night, latitudinal, and seasonal variations in the D-region ionosphere but the model does not capture day-to-day variations or solar X-ray flare events. The model may be sufficient for some HF propagation applications but has been shown to be severely deficient in the high latitude region and during nighttime. In addition, the observations used to create the model do not accurately capture the shape of the lower D-region, which is required for VLF propagation applications.

The Next-generation Ionospheric Model for Operations (NIMO) is an assimilative geospace model developed to address operational USN space weather needs in the ionosphere. NIMO harnesses contributions from both near real-time data and state-of-the-art implementation of ionospheric theory to provide hindcasts, nowcasts, and forecasts for operational or research purposes. NIMO is currently configured to assimilate various types of electron density measurements through the Ionospheric Data Assimilation Four-Dimensional (IDA-4D) data assimilation schema. The D-region is not included in the data assimilation process but is simply added in post processing to the bottom of the electron density grid. The D-region model includes influence from changes in the solar conditions, but uses a climatological model for the neutral atmosphere, so it does not capture the day-to-day variability that is seen in the ionosphere.

Key performance Metrics/Goals:

Techniques to improve the global specification and forecast of the D-region ionosphere is sought with particular emphasis on the low latitudes (< 30 degrees) and high latitudes (> 60 degrees). Note: Any measurement techniques should provide measurements or any model should ingest measurements of the D-region and demonstrate improvement over existing models in two key altitude regions: 60-70 km altitude and 80-90 km altitude, which are required for VLF propagation and HF absorption, respectively.

Key parameters include

• Specify electron density in the 60-70km and 80-90km regions within 10% error. Alternatively, an improvement 75% of the time over existing models is sought.
• Specification at a temporal cadence of 5-15 minutes
• Specification at a spatial resolution of 5 degrees in latitude and longitude

Technical concepts may include developing prototype concept improvements to measurement techniques and systems, developing improvements to data exploitation and modeling, or a combination of the two.

Phase I:
Develop a technical concept for improvements to D-region specification. Establish the feasibility of the concept. Provide required Phase I deliverables that include a detailed plan of operational implementation with sufficient evidence to justify claims of skill improvement.

Phase II:
Develop a prototype system that improves state-of-the-art forecasting for D-region morphology and validate the results in an operationally relevant environment. Depending on the nature of the Phase I concept demonstration, deliver a functioning prototype instrument demonstrated in an operationally relevant environment with low-latency data-feed or a functioning model software package that exploits operationally relevant data sources in near-real-time. Validate either solution using an appropriate ray-trace simulation tool that demonstrates improved performance over current state-of-the-art systems. Prepare a Phase III commercialization/transition plan.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Deliver and integrate a new D-region model concept or data exploitation methodology into the NIMO for USN operational ionosphere prediction needs. Transition new measurement systems to an appropriate operator. Note: Delivery of the measurement system will be dependent upon the intended operational mode and target environment.

References:
• Akmaev, R. A., et al. "DRAP model validation: I. Scientific report." Technical Report (2010). https://www.ngdc.noaa.gov/stp/drap/DRAP-V-Report1.pdf
• Bilitza, D., Pezzopane, M., Truhlik, V., Altadill, D., Reinisch, B. W. and Pignalberi, A. “The International Reference Ionosphere model: A review and description of an ionospheric benchmark.” Reviews of Geophysics, 60, e2022RG000792, 2022. https://doi.org/10.1029/2022RG000792
• Burrell, A. G. et al. “Next-generation Ionospheric Model for Operations – validation and demonstration for space weather and research.” Ann. Geophys., 44, 2026, pp. 303-329. https://doi.org/10.5194/angeo-44-303-2026, 2026.

title: Expeditionary Water Quality Sensors
summary: Develop simple-to-use water quality test kits or electronic sensors that require minimal training to enable personnel in the field to rapidly meet Technical Bulletin Medical 577 (TB-MED 577) requirements to certify potable water without liquid reagents.
description:
Objective:
Develop simple-to-use water quality test kits or electronic sensors that require minimal training to enable personnel in the field to rapidly meet Technical Bulletin Medical 577 (TB-MED 577) requirements to certify potable water without liquid reagents.

Description:
Expeditionary forces need updated water testing capabilities to support operations in austere, contested environments. Without proper water testing, water purified in the field are not certified potable for consumption. This creates an unacceptable logistics burden to transport water, or a health risks when consuming untested water; hindering the self-sufficiency, readiness, and lethality required for operations against a pacing challenge. Current approved state-of-the-art water quality testing kits are accurate but cumbersome, and overly complex, requiring chemical reagents, significant operator training, and for some parameters shipping to a certified lab. Present water quality testing methods are not practical for the small, distributed Stand-in Forces operating in expeditionary conditions.

In the event of detection of certain pathogens and contaminants, confirmation through certified laboratories may be required, necessitating sample transportation to CONUS, host-nation, or ally facilities—a process that can take 4-6 weeks. Delays of this magnitude are operationally unacceptable for forces in contested environments that need immediate assurance of water safety at the point of use. In addition, many critical parameters that impact water safety—including heavy metals, organic chemicals, and other contaminants—are not reliably tested with currently fielded sensors.

Force Design 2030 compels distributed forces to reduce their reliance on centralized logistics convoys; therefore, small units are increasingly required to produce and consume water at the tactical edge and at the point of need. Without a reliable and practical method to verify water quality in the field, these units face an alarming tradeoff between logistics supply certainty and warfighter health.

Therefore, the Navy needs simple, field-ready solutions to certify that expeditionary purified water conforms to TB-MED 577 short term potability military field water standards (STW MFWS) without external laboratory support. This SBIR topic seeks the development of new sensors and/or methodologies that will significantly improve existing water testing field kits. Improvements sought include but are not limited to: size and weight, more rapid testing results, simpler procedures requiring minimal training, elimination of liquid chemical reagents, and cost. Proposals can address one or more targeted improvements and can target one or more of the water parameters listed in the STP MFWS, such as physical properties, chemical properties, microbial contamination, chemical warfare agents, or radiological. Resulting improved sensors or methodologies must be integratable into future modernized water testing kits to allow squad- and platoon-level forces to verify compliance with TB MED 577 water safety standards in the field, reducing risk to personnel and decreasing reliance on vulnerable resupply chains. The expected end state of this effort is a fully developed, ruggedized, integratable sensor or set of sensors that enable rapid, automated testing of water quality in expeditionary environments in under 15 minutes (Threshold) / under 5 minutes (Objective), and/or detect all microbial threats in under 1 hour (Threshold) / under 15 minutes (Objective) without incubation or liquid reagents. Modular systems targeting specific critical parameters are equally encouraged and will be evaluated on technical merit.

Phase I:
Establish the technical feasibility of a preliminary conceptual design(s) of a new sensor or series of sensors, capable of rapidly verifying water quality in austere environments without requiring external laboratory support. Define and develop candidate concepts and sensor technologies. Conduct research that will assess the integration potential of the solution(s) into a portable kit for squad- (~13 Marines) and platoon- (40-50 Marines) level operations. Include approaches that may include modeling, simulation, and benchtop testing to evaluate detection accuracy, operational ruggedness, and ease of operation, all while referencing water safety requirements outlined in TB-MED 577. Deliver a final report documenting the technical progress; results of feasibility analyses; a breakdown of size, weight, power, and cost (SWaP-C) improvements and/or trade-offs; performance projections of candidate concepts and sensor technologies; and a defensible preliminary design concept. Ensure that the new sensor(s) should not require liquid chemical reagents, which are problematic due to a short shelf life and customs clearance. Identify anticipated technical risks, mitigation strategies, and a clear development path for Phase II prototype, fabrication, and validation in the final Phase I report.

Phase II:
Design, develop, fabricate, and test a prototype sensor or series of sensors capable of rapidly verifying water quality in simulated expeditionary environments. Ensure that the prototype integrates selected sensor technologies into a ruggedized, portable form factor appropriate for use at the squad and platoon level. Develop hardware and software interfaces, refine user interaction for minimal training burden, and ensure the sensor(s) functions across a range of environmental conditions. Demonstrate and validate the prototype through laboratory and field testing against relevant key water quality parameters such as microbial contamination, heavy metals, salinity, turbidity, and chemical pollutants. Conduct testing that should confirm performance relative to defined metrics including accuracy, test time, ease of use, and environmental durability. Provide the following required Phase II deliverables: prototype hardware, technical data documenting performance results, field evaluation in coordination with a military exercise if practicable, and a detailed plan for Phase III transition opportunities within military and commercial application.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Support transition to the Program Manager Engineer Systems (PM ES) at Marine Corps Systems Command for integration into the USMC family of water systems and direct use by small units during distributed operations.

Beyond military use, the technology has strong dual-use potential. Civilian applications include humanitarian assistance and disaster relief operations, rapid deployment by first responders in areas with compromised infrastructure, commercial water treatment facilities, and consumer safety monitoring in developing regions. The commercial pathway may include partnerships with outdoor equipment providers, municipal water authorities, and NGOs focused on clean water access.

title: Rapid Thermoplastic Patching Capability for Legacy Thermoset Airframe Sustainment
summary: Deliver a rapid, high-strength thermoplastic patching capability for legacy thermoset composite airframes by developing the necessary interfacial enabling technologies to fuse the incompatible polymer systems.
description:
Objective:
Deliver a rapid, high-strength thermoplastic patching capability for legacy thermoset composite airframes by developing the necessary interfacial enabling technologies to fuse the incompatible polymer systems.

Description:
Current composite airframe repair methodologies rely on a combination of wet-layups, B-staged epoxy prepregs, and bonded pre-cured thermoset patches. While pre-cured patches are the standard for high-quality depot repairs due to their autoclave-consolidated strength and “inspectability”, they present significant operational and logistical limitations. All these traditional methods require secondary adhesive bonding (using paste or film adhesives) to attach the repair to the airframe. This secondary bond is the inherent weak link of the repair, demanding long thermal cure cycles (often 4 to 24 hours), strict environmental controls, and burdensome cold-storage logistics (freezers) for the B-staged resins and adhesives. Furthermore, these out-of-autoclave epoxy repairs often struggle to meet the high service temperature requirements of advanced tactical aircraft.

This SBIR topic seeks to evolve the current pre-cured repair methodology by transitioning from secondary adhesive bonding to high-speed fusion welding. The objective is to develop the capability to use pre-consolidated, high-temperature thermoplastic patches (e.g., Carbon/PEEK, Carbon/PEKK) on legacy thermoset aircraft (epoxy/Bismaleimide [BMI]). By replacing the lengthy adhesive cure cycle with a rapid welding process, this technology aims to achieve flight-ready repairs in expeditionary and carrier-based environments in a fraction of the time.

Because thermoplastics melt and thermosets do not, achieving a structural weld between these dissimilar materials is the primary barrier to fielding this capability. The Department of War seeks complete thermoplastic patching solutions that incorporate the requisite chemical or mechanical interfacial enablers—such as plasma surface activation, novel chemical tie-layers, or laser-ablated mechanical interlocking. These enablers must allow the thermoplastic patch to successfully fuse with a fully cured, legacy thermoset airframe using portable ultrasonic, resistance- or -induction welding equipment. The outcome must be a deployable repair process that eliminates cold-storage logistics, restores full structural integrity, meets high service temperature demands, and drastically reduces Aircraft on Ground (AOG) time.

Phase I:
Develop a conceptual thermoplastic patching process and demonstrate the physical viability of the proposed enabling interfacial technology (e.g., tie-layers, surface functionalization). Establish the feasibility of the conceptual process. Perform coupon-level mechanical testing (such as lap-shear and peel-strength) to empirically prove that the thermoplastic-to-thermoset weld achieves a structural load transfer that is comparable to, or exceeds, baseline epoxy adhesive repairs. Deliver a detailed theoretical model explaining the fusion mechanism, an initial assessment of the repair's thermal limits (ensuring the parent thermoset is not degraded), and a conceptual workflow for field-level application that eliminates the need for depot-level infrastructure or cold-storage consumables.

Phase II:
Develop, optimize, and scale a patching capability prototype to representative legacy airframe structures, such as contoured wing skins or stiffened panels. Perform the proposed thermoplastic patch repair using field-representative heating equipment (e.g., portable induction or resistance welding). Validate the repair through rigorous structural testing, including fatigue spectrum loading, thermal cycling, and damage tolerance assessments, to prove airworthiness. Deliver a prototype repair kit and process documentation. Target metrics must include a complete return-to-flight repair cycle of under 4 hours, restoration of > 115% of the parent structure's Design Ultimate Load, and thermal isolation ensuring the thermoset parent material remains below its degradation threshold during the welding process. Prepare a Phase III commercialization/transition plan.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Transition the validated thermoplastic patching capability to Naval Air Systems Command (NAVAIR) and Air Force Life Cycle Management Center (AFLCMC) for integration into legacy platforms. Incorporate the materials, tooling, and process parameters into standardized Structural Repair Manuals (SRMs) for platforms such as the F/A-18, F-35, or V-22, providing expeditionary units with a rapid, out-of-autoclave, room-temperature-storable repair solution.

Commercial dual-use applications include rapid repair for the commercial airline industry, structural maintenance for composite wind turbine blades, and automotive crash repair for high-performance composite vehicles.

References:
• “NAVAIR 01-1A-1, General Manual for Structural Repair.” https://www.tinker.af.mil/Portals/106/Documents/Technical%20Orders/AFD-082416-1-1A-1.pdf
• Fernandes Villegas, Irene and Vizcaino Rubio, Pablo. “On avoiding thermal degradation during welding of high performance thermoplastic composites to thermoset composites, Composites Part A.” Applied Science and Manufacturing, 2015-10, Vol 77, pp. 172-180. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1359835X15002341

title: Navy Shipboard Gas Turbine Rotating Detonation Combustor Operation with Diesel Fuel
summary: Develop and demonstrate a scaled high density Rotating Detonation Combustor (RDC) that uses NATO F76 diesel fuel (MIL-DTL-16884R) and perform thermodynamic analysis on developed Navy RDC equipped shipboard gas turbine concepts to determine related performance benefits including reduction of stack up length, efficiency improvements, design limitations, and development gaps.
description:
Objective:
Develop and demonstrate a scaled high density Rotating Detonation Combustor (RDC) that uses NATO F76 diesel fuel (MIL-DTL-16884R) and perform thermodynamic analysis on developed Navy RDC equipped shipboard gas turbine concepts to determine related performance benefits including reduction of stack up length, efficiency improvements, design limitations, and development gaps.

Description:
As background, the typical arrangement used on U.S. Navy surface combatants consists of four (4) large (20+MW class – GE LM-2500) gas turbines for propulsion and three 3 smaller (3 MW class – Rolls Royce 501-K34) gas turbines for ship service electrical power generation.

Presently U.S. gas turbine powered warships use simple cycle machines. However, complex cycles with reheat and other cycle enhancements have been considered and analyzed with the potential for increased efficiency. Further examinations have been performed to evaluate improvements in maintainability/reliability, overall generator set power density/stack up length, and alternative configuration installation flexibility for use in overall electric plant designs.

RDCs are advanced power-generation and propulsion devices that operate by propagating one or more supersonic detonation waves continuously around an annular chamber. As fresh fuel and oxidizer are continuously injected into the channel, the rotating shock wave rapidly compresses and ignites the mixture, creating a self-sustaining zone of intense heat and pressure. Thermodynamically, RDCs utilize a detonation-driven pressure-gain cycle, which is most accurately modeled by the Fickett-Jacobs-Salsburg (FJS) cycle and frequently approximated as the constant-volume Humphrey cycle. Unlike conventional gas turbines that rely on the constant-pressure Brayton cycle, the FJS detonation cycle in an RDC generates a substantial net increase in total pressure across the combustor. This inherent pressure gain drastically reduces the workload required by upstream mechanical compressors and significantly boosts the overall thermal efficiency and power output of the gas turbine system. While initial government and industry investigations have centered on the use of RDCs in aerospace applications, future shipboard applications will require a greater understanding of the ability to operate with diesel fuel for long continuous operation as well as a quantification of performance benefits that can be achieved in overall shipboard electric architecture design.

While not required, discussions with Navy shipboard gas turbine Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEM) are recommended.

Phase I:
Perform an analysis of an RDC combustor ignition and continuous operation with NATO F76 fuel by the end of the Base period. Assemble and demonstrate an initial limited laboratory experiment/subscale test to verify analysis findings in coordination with Navy personnel. Complete a conceptual design for a combustor prototype and associated liquid fuel system, to include prototype design refinements, fabrication approach, and testing strategy that should include ignition and endurance operation with defined measurements in coordination with Navy personnel and within the scope of a Phase II budget. Prepare a Phase II plan.

Phase II:
Construct a combustor prototype and associated liquid fuel system. Perform startup and endurance testing for up to 500 hours as defined in Phase I utilizing F76 fuel. Based upon results generated from testing, conduct thermodynamic analyses/model of a marine gas turbine utilizing an RDC primary combustor as well as a thermodynamic analysis/models of marine gas turbine reheat cycles utilizing an RDC inter-turbine (single reheat) and intra-turbine (continuous reheat) in collaboration with Navy personnel. From this analysis, determine impact on overall efficiency, reliability, operating life, power density, and future development gaps. Prepare a Phase III commercialization/transition plan.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Demonstrate a full-scale liquid fuel combustor operating continuously for 500 hours. Based on Phase II analysis, develop a full-scale RDC-based gas turbine, either simple or complex cycle, and conduct performance testing prior to an at sea demonstration. Once complete, examine and upgrade the system for marinization requirements accounting material and maintainability improvements to successfully operate in a naval environment.

Examine and demonstrate the RDC based gas turbine in a CIPES electric plant configuration to validate ship benefits for overall operational performance and improvement in platform increases in power density. Commercial dual use application may include commercial maritime ships and offshore drilling and production platforms.

title: Rapid Imagery Creation for Navy Training
summary: Develop technology to use historic real-world satellite imagery and then rapidly (10 minutes or less) modify it to reflect a training scenario order of battle (aircraft, ships, vehicles, etc.) to allow imagery analysts to practice their tradecraft underway or ashore in support of maritime exercises.
description:
Objective:
Develop technology to use historic real-world satellite imagery and then rapidly (10 minutes or less) modify it to reflect a training scenario order of battle (aircraft, ships, vehicles, etc.) to allow imagery analysts to practice their tradecraft underway or ashore in support of maritime exercises.

Description:
Currently, imagery analysts are excluded from, or extremely limited in, participating in dynamic Navy operational and staff training such as Surface Warfare Advanced Team Trainer (SWATT), Information Warfare Advanced Team Trainer (IWATT), Fleet Synthetic Training General Commander/Joint (FST-GC/J), and Commander Training Unit Exercise (COMPTUEX).This is due to the limited ability to dynamically generate the required products for imagery analysts within a reasonable amount of time at a quality that supports training.

Currently, either summaries are provided to the training audience circumventing the imagery analysts all together or providing GRAPHPLOTS - the equivalence of stick figure drawing - to track the order of battle (OOB) made up of aircraft, ships, vehicles, etc., without any use of actual imagery or geospatial analysis.

A technology to address this shortfall would need to take real-world geo-rectified imagery as a base and then rapidly adjust/modify the image to reflect the desired OOB and in a National Imagery Transition Format (NTIF) to be provided to the training audience for imagery analysts to process.

For example, in real-life Port A, identified by Basic Encyclopedia (BE) number, is of high interest and has a collection requirement against it for satellite imagery to be collected. In reality, Port A has three Kilo-class submarines and one Luhu-class destroyer, but in the scenario things have dynamically changed such that one of those submarines is now underway and an additional Luda I-class Destroyer has arrived, requiring the rapid (less than 10 minutes) production of an NITF image depicting two Kilo-class submarines, one Luhu DD, and one Luda I DDG to provide the training audience for analysis. The same would be required for airfields depicting aircraft movement as well.

Work produced in Phase II may become classified. Note: The prospective contractor(s) must be U.S. owned and operated with no foreign influence as defined by 32 U.S.C. § 2004.20 et seq., National Industrial Security Program Executive Agent and Operating Manual, unless acceptable mitigating procedures can and have been implemented and approved by the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency (DCSA) formerly Defense Security Service (DSS). The selected contractor and/or subcontractor must be able to acquire and maintain a secret level facility and Personnel Security Clearances. This will allow contractor personnel to perform on advanced phases of this project as set forth by DCSA and ONR in order to gain access to classified information pertaining to the national defense of the United States and its allies; this will be an inherent requirement. The selected company will be required to safeguard classified material during the advanced phases of this contract IAW the National Industrial Security Program Operating Manual (NISPOM), which can be found at Title 32, Part 2004.20 of the Code of Federal Regulations.

Phase I:
Create concept formulation for electro-optical imagery, determine technical feasibility of rapidly generating an NITF image, and validation through the modification of a single image (note: format and quality are not relevant here) to change the depicted order of battle. Determine technical feasibility of infrared (IR), and Synthetic Aperture RADAR (SAR) imagery. Create demonstration standard sufficient to assess preservation of imagery characteristics necessary for realistic imagery-analysis training.

Phase II:
Develop prototype technology on the Secret Internet Protocol Router Network (SIPRnet) to effectively execute the example provided in the Description for Electro-Optical (EO) imagery. Determine a site by BE number (from a limited provided subset), outputting a near real-world NITF image of the desired OOB (from a limited inventory of platforms). Demonstrate standard sufficient to assess preservation of imagery characteristics. Prepare a Phase III commercialization/transition plan.

Work in Phase II may become classified. Please see note in Description section.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
This technology would be usable and empower any dynamic military training opportunity to support Imagery/GEOINT analysis. Possible transition to National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency, Naval Information Forces (NAVIFOR), Center for Information Warfare Training (CIWT), Carrier Strike Group FOUR and FIFTEEN (CSG-4/15), Tactical Training Group Pacific (TTGP), Tactical Training Group Atlantic (TTGL) and NSWC Corona.

This product will ideally reside on the SIPRNet as a portal for users to query on RED networks, such as NCTE-RED OPS, NMCI SIPR, SIPR TRANET, then providing the requested images.

Potential work in Phase III could include prototype refinement, testing, production, and transition support.

• “National Imagery Transmission Format Standard (NITFS) Technical Board (NTB).” https://nsgreg.nga.mil/ntb.jsp
• “National Industrial Security Program Executive Agent and Operating Manual (NISP), 32 U.S.C. § 2004.20 et seq. 1993.” https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-32/subtitle-B/chapter-XX/part-2004

title: SI-Enabled “Just-in-time” Knowledge Delivery for Naval Maintainers
summary: Develop an SI-enabled maintenance associate that delivers interactive, expert-level guidance for complex diagnostic and repair tasks at point of need, provides technicians historical context on specific vehicles or components being repaired, and curates maintenance histories into easily mineable repository for future use.
description:
Objective:
Develop an SI-enabled maintenance associate that delivers interactive, expert-level guidance for complex diagnostic and repair tasks at point of need, provides technicians historical context on specific vehicles or components being repaired, and curates maintenance histories into easily mineable repository for future use.

Description:
This effort is aimed at addressing the critical operational challenge of maintaining increasingly diverse and technologically complex arrays of systems with generalist knowledge. The solution requested in this SBIR topic is a just-in-time knowledge delivery system for Fleet maintainers that tells them what they need to know, when they need to know it. It would provide detailed procedures and technical knowledge for diagnostics, repair and maintenance procedures on demand, both ashore and at sea, where there will be limited access to remote data stores. The system will employ generative SI to analyze authoritative technical documentation and historical maintenance records, at both the Fleet and individual asset levels, and generate summarized technical guidance initiated by free-text queries or guided diagnostic dialogues. Post-task, the system will prompt the technician for repair feedback, synthesizing their insights to update the database with both general maintenance guidance and individual asset histories. Problems with current knowledge delivery are particularly acute when new systems and technology are introduced to the Fleet, such as with the introduction of unmanned systems (UxS), and when locally developed knowledge needs to be propagated across the larger maintenance community.

Operational readiness is currently bottlenecked by an inefficient maintenance paradigm: generalist maintenance technicians constantly face unfamiliar equipment without access to historical repair data, while frequent duty rotations continually erase localized (tribal) knowledge. This over-reliance on a transient pool of specialists causes extended system downtime and degrades operational readiness. These problems are particularly acute when new systems and technology are introduced to the Fleet.

While new advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) and generative SI present an opportunity to create sophisticated human-machine teaming tools for providing real-time interactive support, state-of-the-art predictive maintenance systems are not attuned to the unique challenges of the Navy’s maintenance environment. Effective solutions will need to integrate diverse approaches and overcome existing hard science problems to arrive at the desired solution. Current approaches in this domain excel at forecasting component failures and recommending procedures; however, they lack the interactive step-by-step guidance required to conduct the procedures or for dynamic on-the-job technical support to the maintainers. Existing maintenance knowledge tools operate as one-way information pipelines that fail to capture critical institutional knowledge and platform-specific maintenance histories, which prevents the continuous, enterprise-wide learning loop necessary for resilient maintenance operations.

Solutions must be able to ingest, synthesize, and appropriately structure a wide variety of data formats (e.g., technical manuals, structured databases, handwritten logs) while also integrating newly produced recurrent maintenance reports. This data should serve as a dynamically updated foundational knowledge base that is contextualized by the physical and operational situation unique to each repair, providing customized guidance to the technician. The solution should adapt its guidance to the user's specific skill level and experience to ensure interpretability across levels of expertise. Lastly, the desired Maintenance Associate solution must be capable of operating on local hardware in low-bandwidth and disconnected environments, operating on local storage and syncing fleetwide as connectivity allows.

This SBIR topic is seeking proposals that would contribute to the development of an SI-Enabled Maintenance Associate. It is expected that the initial capability would be focused on a specific technical domain and a representative set of equipment that would serve as a prototype that can be scaled up to apply to multiple domains and an array of deployed systems. One target domain of immediate interest is the maintenance and repair of unmanned systems. However, any equipment and application domain that is found within Naval systems is of interest.

The envisioned system workflow will ingest and distill technical documentation into interactive, multi-media or hard-copy repair procedures—complete with parts lists, safety warnings, and annotated tribal knowledge—delivered through a user-friendly Human-Machine Interface (HMI). The system will capture post-repair outcomes to continuously update the foundational knowledge base. Proposed solutions may address individual components of the Maintenance Associate system or work to develop a complete system.

Components of the Maintenance Associate System that may be addressed for this SBIR topic should include:

• A database management system for repair service/technical manuals and logs for distillation into maintenance procedures.
• An HMI for technician requesting support that delivers summary procedure, to include tools, parts lists, cautions, and warnings; and provides results that are appropriately annotated localized (tribal) knowledge (best practices, tips, and comments from other users).
• System products to end-users delivered as: multi-media content and/or hard copy outputs for technicians to access when performing procedures.
• An incorporated mechanism to capture results/maintenance outcomes with a data integration mechanism that feeds into the knowledge base for future reference.

Ideally, this transition effort will specifically focus on supporting the complex maintenance, diagnostics, and repair requirements of UxS hardware and platforms (e.g., Unmanned Surface Vessels, Unmanned Underwater Vehicles, Unmanned Ground Systems, and Unmanned Aerial Systems), although use cases for other Naval Applications and alternative transition customers would be acceptable. Unmanned systems and commands are nascent, and subject to wholesale platform change in short order. Operators and maintainers rely on vendor provided maintenance doctrine as they are developing historical context. Grounding for the Associate must include these documents which may be CUI or SECRET, performers must be able to operate at required classification levels. Reported technical evaluations, capability demonstrations, and success metrics will focus on the accuracy/interpretability of maintenance guidance and quality of the human-machine interaction as assessed by real-world end users and the generalizability of the technical approach across platforms and domains.

Offerors are reminded that SBIRs are expected to sufficiently develop one or more capabilities that will receive endorsement from an acquisition/development organization and who will provide matching funds for transition/acquisition during Phase II of the SBIR. Prospective agencies for potential matching funds should be identified in the Phase I proposal along with the description of the baseline capability to be delivered that the proposer believes that acquisition agency would be interested in funding during Phase II.

The proposer will need to:

1) Develop an SI-driven, maintenance task context-aware guidance prototype that functions as an on-demand technical expert and centralized intelligence hub for maintenance technicians, providing interactive support for complex diagnostic and repair tasks.

2) Incorporate a mechanism to ingest, process, and index a wide array of reference materials, including technical manuals, vendor publications, Maintenance Required Cards (MRCs), after-action reports, and historical service logs from various databases.

3) Demonstrate a workflow for capturing new experiential knowledge, observations, and "lessons learned" from maintainers post-task to ensure the system continuously learns and shares updated information across the fleet.

4) Be designed to operate effectively on simple hardware (e.g., tablets, laptops) in environments with limited or no connectivity by using a local knowledge store, with the capability to synchronize with a central cloud database when a connection is available.

5) Provide an adaptive human-machine interface that guides a user through troubleshooting and repair via natural language, tailors instructions to the technician’s skill level, and recognizes the specific system variant in use.

Work produced in Phase II may become classified. Note: The prospective contractor(s) must be U.S. owned and operated with no foreign influence as defined by 32 U.S.C. § 2004.20 et seq., National Industrial Security Program Executive Agent and Operating Manual, unless acceptable mitigating procedures can and have been implemented and approved by the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency (DCSA) formerly Defense Security Service (DSS). The selected contractor and/or subcontractor must be able to acquire and maintain a secret level facility and Personnel Security Clearances. This will allow contractor personnel to perform on advanced phases of this project as set forth by DCSA and ONR in order to gain access to classified information pertaining to the national defense of the United States and its allies; this will be an inherent requirement. The selected company will be required to safeguard classified material during the advanced phases of this contract IAW the National Industrial Security Program Operating Manual (NISPOM), which can be found at Title 32, Part 2004.20 of the Code of Federal Regulations.

Phase I:
Determine the technical feasibility of deploying a generative SI and LLM framework to support complex maintenance and diagnostic tasks in disconnected environments. Initial Phase I scoping should clearly define the domain, data sources, and commercial vendors that will inform a primary knowledge base for maintenance guidance and repair recommendations. (Note: Agent architecture and data ingest should be extensible to new domains and data types for the longer-term technical objective of applying Maintenance Associates to support both legacy platforms and novel technologies.) The system workflow will specify how newly submitted maintenance reports are ingested into the database to optimize future diagnostic guidance and dynamically tailor user assistance according to technician proficiency. Phase I success depends on selecting a use case to validate the Maintenance Associate's core methodology: generating initial repair guidance, iterating based on new inputs and evolving the knowledge base based on maintenance outcomes through an appropriate interface.

The Phase I proposal must address the following objectives:

• Identify and design a concept for the Maintenance Associate system architecture, processes through which the SI will securely ingest, process, index, and reason over heterogeneous maintenance data (e.g., technical manuals, structured databases, and unstructured historical logs).
• Analyze and classify open-source LLMs for their ability to perform consistent and accurate ingest and classification of new data sources and their capacity to generate reliable, accurate, and tailored maintenance guidance.
• Perform modeling and simulation to validate the local-to-cloud data synchronization process and the management of post-task "lessons learned" workflow, ensuring the system can continuously capture field knowledge and update the enterprise database with intermittent and/or low bandwidth connectivity.
• Define and develop a concept for operating the SI knowledge associate efficiently on tactical edge hardware (e.g., standard tablets or laptops) without relying on continuous cloud connectivity.
• Develop approaches for working prototypes for creating an adaptive human-machine interface that can dynamically tailor real-time troubleshooting guidance to the technician's specific information needs as well as address the exact equipment variant to be serviced.

Required Phase I deliverables will include:

• A technical feasibility report describing the required SI model's performance and its adequacy for employment on edge hardware with limited cloud reach back.
• A system architecture document outlining software requirements for data ingestion, local data caching, and synchronization protocols for cloud data storage and data management.
• A preliminary human-machine interface mock-up or design concept for: a) data ingestion, b) user prompting of the system to obtain maintenance procedures, c) delivering prototype output from the recommender system, and d) ingestion of results from maintenance to update the knowledge base with lessons learned and details for repairs to specific equipment.
• A detailed Phase II research and development plan that includes proposed performance metrics and a commercialization roadmap, and identifies a prospective transition target and describe customer expectations for providing matching funds as required during the Phase II development effort.

Phase II:
Develop, demonstrate, and validate a fully functional, edge-capable software prototype integrated onto representative ruggedized tactical hardware.

To the degree possible, describe the maturity of the capabilities and relevant performance metrics expected to be met in Phase II. Describe the proposed maintenance use-case(s) expected to be targeted for development and demonstration. Describe the process by which technical information will be ingested to be used by the Maintenance Associate system, and the requirements for scaling it to other application domains. Validate the system's ability to ingest a complex corpus of real-world technical manuals, proprietary vendor publications, and historical logs specific to that platform, its components, and its modular payloads. Demonstrate the bidirectional synchronization workflow, proving the prototype can capture user-generated "lessons learned" and post-task observations regarding unmanned platform anomalies at the edge, and successfully update the centralized enterprise database once connectivity is restored. Validate the human-machine interface and adaptive learning features with UxS maintenance personnel to ensure the system effectively tailors troubleshooting guidance to varying skill levels and accurately recognizes rapidly evolving unmanned equipment variants. Produce and validate a prototype of the Maintenance Associate application that successfully operates entirely disconnected from enterprise networks, simulating forward-deployed UxS maintenance hubs. Produce prototype hardware and software integrated systems (e.g., deploying the optimized LLM onto ruggedized shipboard tablets or maintenance laptops) ready for user-in-the-loop testing.

Deliver a functional, hardware-integrated prototype that demonstrates key functionality of a Maintenance Associate that can be scaled to multiple application domains. (Note: The preferred (but not required) application domain would be tailored for a maintainer of unmanned systems.); a comprehensive Test and Evaluation (T&E) report detailing the prototype's performance, utility, adequacy, and latency in delivering maintainer content using stand-alone (e.g., laptop) information technology with limited network connectivity; and a Maintenance Associate System software architecture documentation including document ingestion and end-user documentation that describes document ingestion (when required), user interaction to generate a maintenance procedure and get supporting documentation out of the system, and the mechanism by which the end user would describe the outcome of the maintenance procedure for updating the maintenance associate knowledge base.

Prepare a Phase III transition and commercialization plan detailing the path for transition to an acquisition entity or integration into a Naval Program of Record.

Work in Phase II may become classified. Please see note in the Description.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
This topic was conceived with a primary Naval transition target of Unmanned Surface Vessel Squadrons (USVRONs) and their associated maintenance hubs for UxVs. The desired system should be appropriate for use by USVRON maintenance personnel on ruggedized tactical hardware (e.g., standard issue tablets or laptops) to diagnose and repair the complex, modular systems of Unmanned Surface Vessels (USVs) and other unmanned platforms. There is a wide range of application domains, both in the commercial and military sectors that would benefit from the maintenance associate. The general purpose of this technology is intended to be a secure, deployable and scalable generative SI enabled system capable of ingesting disparate technical data, operating entirely disconnected from enterprise networks, and providing interactive maintenance and troubleshooting guidance. The desired system would integrate experiential knowledge from users to iteratively append the knowledge base with lessons learned, best practices, tips and tricks as appropriate for use by future maintainers working on the same or similar system.

Phase III work may also orient towards commercializing the core SI maintenance technology for industries that manage complex, distributed assets in commercial domains that require disconnected or remote environments (e.g., commercial maritime, aviation, or energy/infrastructure operations).

title: Collapsible Fixed-Wing Low-Cost Unmanned Aerial System for Intelligence, Surveillance, and Reconnaissance Missions
summary: Develop a collapsible, low-cost, fixed-wing Group 1 small uncrewed aerial system (sUAS) capable of autonomous intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) missions with a flight endurance of over one hour.
description:
Objective:
Develop a collapsible, low-cost, fixed-wing Group 1 small uncrewed aerial system (sUAS) capable of autonomous intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) missions with a flight endurance of over one hour.

Description:
The Navy has a growing need for a low-cost, portable, and rapidly deployable UAS to support ISR missions. Current systems are often expensive and bulky, and require significant logistical support. This SBIR topic seeks an innovative solution for a collapsible fixed-wing UAS that can be easily transported and deployed by a single operator. The UAS should be capable of autonomous flight and integration with standard flight control software (e.g., QGroundControl, Pixhawk).

Key requirements include a total cost under $5,000 for the airframe and components, a flight time exceeding one hour, a communication range of up to 10 km, and the ability to fit within a 2' x 2' x 1' case for transport. The system must support a modular nose payload, be initially equipped with an RGB camera, and have the potential to serve as a signal repeater for transmission of data. The primary technical challenge is to achieve the desired endurance and portability within the stringent cost constraints, requiring innovation in airframe design, materials, and component integration.

Phase I:
Develop a concept for a low-cost, collapsible Foldable Low-cost Expendable Wing (FLEX-Wing) sUAS. Determine the technical feasibility of the concept. Conduct trade studies for materials and components. Perform modeling and simulation to validate the aerodynamic performance, flight endurance, and structural integrity. Deliver a detailed concept design report, simulation results, field test results of the prototype, and a preliminary bill of materials demonstrating the path to achieving the cost target.

Phase II:
Design and develop a prototype through a structured, iterative engineering cycle within the appropriately distributed across the allotted Phase II timeframe to ensure feasible execution and rigorous validation. Fabricate and validate the prototype of the FLEX-Wing sUAS. Produce prototype hardware that transitions the flat-pack, off-the-shelf structural concepts into a fully integrated, flight-capable system. Deliver the physical prototype hardware (minimum of three complete kits) and associated technical data packages to the SYSCOM sponsor. (Note: The prototypes will undergo validation against the strict weight (Group 1), size, cost, and endurance metrics to verify readiness for Phase III commercialization and transition into a formal PMA-263 capability portfolio.)

The specific hardware and software to be developed and produced includes:

• The Airframe: A foldable, stackable, and bendable fixed-wing structure utilizing low-cost commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) materials (e.g., weatherproofed craft board/polymer) keeping total airframe and component costs below $5,000 per unit.
• A fully self-contained air vehicle kit that fits entirely within a compact 2 ft × 2 ft × 1 ft transit case (e.g., a Pelican case), including the folded airframe and required batteries. The Ground Control Station (GCS) may be provided separately, but must be backpack-portable (approximately laptop-sized) and capable of controlling multiple FLEX-Wing air vehicles.• Avionics & Software: Integration of a Pixhawk (or similar)-based flight controller running open-source flight software (e.g., QGroundControl).
• Payload & Communications: A modular nose-cone payload system featuring a baseline RGB camera for ISR loiter missions and an interchangeable signal repeater module. The communications suite will setup a telemetry link capable of up to 10km range.

Execution Phase Timeframe Associated Scope & Engineering Effort

• Design & Component Sourcing Months 1-6 Based on Phase I modeling, design and develop a prototype architecture. Finalize COTS component selection (e.g., Pixhawk, 5.2GHz RF modules, RGB sensors) and establish manufacturing processes for the foldable airframe materials (e.g., die-cutting, hinge reinforcement).
• Prototype Fabrication Months 7-12 Produce prototype hardware. Integrate the high-energy-density power systems required to achieve the >1 hr flight time. Assemble the modular nose payload bay and ensure the total system fits within the 2x2x1 ft storage constraint.
• Integration & Software Tuning Months 13-18 Integrate flight controller firmware with QGroundControl. Develop processes, select an application (e.g., autonomous waypoint ISR and manual FPV terminal guidance), and validate the software hand-offs in a simulated environment.
• Demonstration & Validation Months 19-24 Develop, demonstrate and validate the physical prototype in a relevant open-air test environment. Validate the up to 10km RF range, >1hr endurance, aerodynamic stability of the foldable wings, and ISR/signal-relay mission profiles.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Expected Final State of the Technology

At the conclusion of the Phase II effort, the technology will exist as a fully integrated, flight-validated Group 1 sUAS with a finalized technical data package (TDP). The final state will be a highly mature prototype characterized by a scalable, low-cost manufacturing process (e.g., die-cut stamping of the COTS airframe materials). The system will feature DoW-compliant, open-architecture avionics and a validated modular nose payload bay, consistently demonstrating the ability to meet the sub-$5,000 cost threshold and the compact 2' x 2' x 1' storage requirement.

Scale the manufacturing process for high-volume, commercial production, allowing the military to purchase the system in bulk. Tactical operators will unpack, hand-launch, and utilize the system in contested or anti-access/area denial (A2/AD) environments for beyond-line-of-sight (BLOS) ISR, target acquisition, or to establish temporary mesh network extensions. Because it is highly attritable, warfighters will employ the system aggressively without the burden of planning for asset recovery, reverse logistics, or depot-level maintenance.

Target Platform and Program of Record

The expected transition path for the Phase III technology is insertion into the Small Unit Remote Scouting System (SURSS), an Acquisition Category IV program managed by the Naval Air Systems Command, Program Manager, Air 263 (Navy and Marine Corps Small Tactical Unmanned Aircraft Systems). The FLEX-Wing will serve as a complementary, expendable platform within their broader Family of Small UAS (FoSUAS) portfolio.

Potential commercial dual-use applications include rapid damage assessment following natural disasters, environmental monitoring, agricultural and land-management surveying, infrastructure inspection, and search-and-rescue support. These applications similarly benefit from a low-cost, portable, rapidly deployable fixed-wing sUAS with extended endurance.

title: Attritable Turbine for Low-Cost Attack Systems (ATLAS)
summary: Design, develop, and prototype a low-cost, limited-life gas turbine engine producing 150-300 lbf of SLS thrust with an estimated engine life expectancy of 10-15 hours, leveraging advanced design and manufacturing techniques to significantly reduce part count, production lead time and scaling, and overall unit cost compared to traditionally manufactured engines in the same class.
description:
Objective:
Design, develop, and prototype a low-cost, limited-life gas turbine engine producing 150-300 lbf of SLS thrust with an estimated engine life expectancy of 10-15 hours, leveraging advanced design and manufacturing techniques to significantly reduce part count, production lead time and scaling, and overall unit cost compared to traditionally manufactured engines in the same class.

Description:
The Department of War has an increasing need for affordable, reliable, and rapidly producible propulsion systems to support the proliferation of attritable Unmanned Aerial Systems (UAS), loitering munitions, and stand-off strike weapons. Current small turbofan and turbojet engines in the 150-300 pounds of thrust (lbf) class often rely on traditional aerospace material and manufacturing processes, resulting in high unit costs and long supply chain lead times. These factors are prohibitive for systems intended to be employed in mass or as expendable assets.

This SBIR topic seeks innovative engineering and manufacturing approaches to design a turbofan engine that meets the thrust requirements while dramatically lowering cost per unit. Proposers should consider advanced design and manufacturing techniques to produce a low-cost engine that can leverage existing industrial base capacity to reduce risk to procurement supply chains.

Key technologies and design features to consider are:

• Additive Manufacturing: Utilizing Powder Bed Fusion, Directed Energy Deposition and Direct Metal Laser Sintering (DMLS) to consolidate part count and simplify construction.
• Industrial (Non-Aerospace) Production Capacity: Leverage non-traditional aerospace manufacturing firms to reduce cost. Consider leveraging materials, casting and production techniques found in the automotive sector. Demonstrate a manufacturing pathway that enables rapid scaling and reduces supply chain bottlenecks.
• Short Life/Expendable Components: Utilizing non-traditional lubrication systems, bearings and electronic sub-components to limit cost.
• Optimized Materials: Utilize cost-effective materials suited for limited-life/single-use engine operations rather than traditional high-lifecycle aviation materials, where appropriate.

Performance metrics of interest include specific fuel consumption (SFC), thrust-to-weight ratio, and operational reliability for mission durations typical of attritable UAS or cruise munitions.

The engine will be fully operational utilizing Navy relevant fuels and demonstrate resilience to harsh maritime storage and launch conditions without significant performance degradation. The engine is expected to demonstrate functionality when subject to storage life of 6-12 months in Maritime environments and meet minimum required performance after exposure to shore-based and shipborne launch environments.

Notional performance objectives for this SBIR topic are provided in the Tables below:

Table 1: ATLAS engine notional operational envelop and performance objectives.

Parameter Specification

Electrical Power Generation [W] 500-1500

Thrust, SLS [lbf] 150-300

SFC [lbm/lbf/hr] < 1.5

Cruise Altitude [ft] 20k

Table 2: ATLAS engine notional mass and dimensional properties objectives.

Parameter Specification

Approximate OML Diameter [in] < =10

Weight, Dry [lbm] 25-35

Length [in.] 14-24

Table 3: ATLAS engine notional storage & launch conditions.

Parameter Specification

Start Altitude Sea Level

Start Method Air Impingement

Storage Duration (Wooden Round) 6-12 months, Maritime Environment

Launch & Assist Method Rail, Catapult, or Rocket Assist

Phase I:
Conduct a feasibility study and develop a conceptual design for a 150-300 lbf. turbofan engine.

• Identify the specific advanced design and manufacturing techniques to be utilized, optimizing the finished product for cost and producibility.
• Provide preliminary conceptual design modeling and simulation data (e.g., computational fluid dynamics, structural, and thermal analysis, cycle model) to validate conceptual design.
• Develop a comparative cost analysis demonstrating the projected unit cost and production time reductions versus traditional manufacturing baselines.
• Conduct a proof-of-concept demonstration and/or test campaign of the conceptual design, components, materials and manufacturing methods utilizing component level rig testing or lab testing where applicable.
• Monitor ongoing program risk and provide status updates throughout program progression.
• Deliver a Phase II development and testing plan.

Phase II:
Refine the conceptual design based on Government feedback and develop a detailed design for a fully functional prototype engine. Transition the Phase I conceptual design into fully functioning, physical hardware and demonstrate engine operation.

• Perform detailed component and system design based on Phase I deliverables.
• Manufacture detailed design test articles (produce physical engines) utilizing low-cost supply chain suppliers.
• Build and assemble fully functioning engine test articles.
• Demonstrate a cost-effective, reliable engine start system.
• Design and integrate a cost-effective engine control solution.
• Conduct a comprehensive test and validation program including completion of the required environmental tests to demonstrate engine performance, reliability and robustness of design.
• Perform a full endurance run to operational mission profile documenting performance.
• Refine mass production cost estimates including complete cost analysis and future cost projections.
• Identify manufacturing industrial base supply chain performers.
• Monitor ongoing program risk and provide status updates throughout program progression. Prepare a Phase III commercialization/transition plan.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
• Utilize lessons learned in the Phase II outcome to perform final detailed design and design for manufacture updates to increase Manufacturing Readiness Level (MRL).
• Update and continue test campaign for finalized engine design qualification/acceptance testing.
• Deliver a comprehensive engine performance test report summarizing performance against Navy-approved ATLAS criteria.
• Provide a detailed transition plan moving from Proof of Concept (POC) to Full Rate Production (FRP),
• Monitor ongoing program risk and provide status updates throughout program progression.
• Interface with airframe producer integrate engine into a host airframe for flight testing.

title: Zero-Retrofit Robotic Ammunition Handling for the MK 45 Mod 4, 5-Inch Gun Magazine
summary: Develop a zero-retrofit robotic prototype capable of identifying, lifting, and loading 70-pound, 5-inch projectiles within the unmodified physical constraints of a DDG 51 class ships’ MK 45 Mod 4 ammunition magazine during Sea State 5 conditions.
description:
Objective:
Develop a zero-retrofit robotic prototype capable of identifying, lifting, and loading 70-pound, 5-inch projectiles within the unmodified physical constraints of a DDG 51 class ships’ MK 45 Mod 4 ammunition magazine during Sea State 5 conditions. This effort seeks a human-capable equivalent that matches the agility and operational tempo of a well-trained sailor, successfully removing human crews from the most physically exhausting and hazardous steps of the kill chain.

Description:
The tight confines of a DDG 51 5-Inch ammunition magazine present a difficult challenge for automation. Traditional robotic arms require fixed mounting and large clearance envelopes, requiring complete compartment redesigns. To avoid extensive shipyard work, the robotic prototype must adapt to the ship. The prototype must navigate narrow aisles, step over "knee-knocker" coamings, and load ammunition into the existing hoists and stowage racks alongside or in place of human sailors.

The robotic prototype must execute capture and lift of 70-pound projectiles and their propelling charges, change their orientations while captured (i.e., pivot), move ammunition between stowage racks and hoists, and safely place the projectiles into the stowage racks and hoists in the proper orientation. Furthermore, the prototype must keep kinematic stability in high sea states (up to Sea State 5) while being able to continue to complete its tasking. The prototype must be resilient to electromagnetic interference (EMI)/electromagnetic pulse (EMP), and have a power supply architecture that enables sustained fire missions without the need for recharge or obstructive cables, and ability to rapidly swap power supplies without substantial downtime.

KEY PARAMETERS FOR ZERO-RETORFIT INTEGRATION:

• Payload Capacity: Continuous capability to lift, pivot, and load 70-pound projectiles and associated propelling charges. System must meet a minimum Threshold of 6 rounds per minute, with an Objective of 12 rounds per minute.
• Form Factor: Must fit within standard 24-inch shipboard aisles and maneuver in confined magazine spaces.
• Locomotion: Able to traverse standard deck plating, step over 6-inch coamings, and brace against ship motion.
• Stability: Maintain balance and load control up to and during Sea State 5 conditions (significant pitch/roll/heave).
• Power: Minimum 2-hour continuous operational endurance with rapidly hot-swappable battery packs (changeable in under 60 seconds).
• Hardening: Built to Military Standard (MIL-STD)-461 (EMI/EMP) and MIL-S-901D (Shock) thresholds.
• Safety/Fallback: Zero-retrofit integration (i.e., no structural alteration), ensuring the space stays 100-percent operational by human fallback crews in case of robot failure.
• Explosive Safety: Must adhere to NAVSEA OP 4 protocols for the safe physical handling of ordnance (Note: meeting specific electrical power level compliance is out of scope for this effort).

Phase I:
Develop a concept for a humanoid or pseudo-humanoid robot meeting the key parameters for zero-retrofit magazine operations. Conduct kinematic and dynamic simulations modeling the robot extracting, pivoting, and loading rounds in a virtual MK 45 magazine under Sea State 5 conditions. Perform trade studies on single-arm versus multi-arm torque constraints and bipedal versus pseudo-humanoid (quadruped, tracked, or other) stability. Prepare a report on physical design, power management strategy, and a Phase II prototyping/testing plan.

Phase II:
Fabricate a functional prototype based on Phase I designs. Assess the prototype in a land-based magazine mockup. Mount the mockup on a multiaxis motion simulator to replicate Sea State 5 roll and pitch. Demonstrate the robot successfully extracting dummy 5-inch projectiles from standard horizontal racks, navigating an aisle, and vertically seating the propelling charges and projectiles into a simulated hoist. Refine grasping effectors and stabilization software. Deliver a prototype, testing data report, and a Phase III ruggedization and integration plan.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Ruggedize the Phase II prototype to meet MIL-STD shock, vibration, and EMI/EMP requirements. Integrate the system at a live testing facility (e.g., Naval Surface Warfare Center (NSWC), Dahlgren, or NSWC, Port Hueneme) alongside a fully functional MK 45 Mod 4-gun mount. Demonstrate a sustained, full-rate fire mission using the prototype as the primary loader. Finalize production designs, deliver the testing data, and mature the prototype for transition to Navy for shipboard demonstration. Primary commercial dual-use sectors for this technology include: Power Infrastructure, Offshore and Onshore Oil Rigs, Mining, and Nuclear facilities. Ultimately, this technology establishes a commercial benchmark for removing human operators from high-risk, physically grueling industrial roles. Doing so preserves human capital for critical cognitive tasks while drastically reducing injury rates in hazardous environments.
