title: Validation and Verification of Computational Modeling of Human Blast Injury on Battlefield
summary: Computational modeling and simulation of human blast injury on the battlefield has been a gap for the Department of War (DoW). DTRA Technical Reachback is tasked with supporting operational decision-making by providing advanced analytics, modeling, and simulation.
description:
Objective:
Computational modeling and simulation of human blast injury on the battlefield has been a gap for the Department of War (DoW). DTRA Technical Reachback is tasked with supporting operational decision-making by providing advanced analytics, modeling, and simulation. The Command Surgeon General Office has submitted numerous requests to estimate human blast injuries on the battlefield to inform medical planning purposes—specifically to forecast requirements for medical supplies, medical staff, and personal protective equipment (PPE). Furthermore, Combatant Commanders require assessment of casualty tolerance thresholds for specific operation environments.

To address these analytics requirements, Technical Reachback initiated and continued a human blast injury modeling effort in the past three years. As development is ongoing, it is crucial to integrate the verification and validation effort early during the data collection and model development stage to ensure sound technical approaches, data application, and expected outputs.

Description:
Blast events accounted for over 70% of casualties among service members engaged in ground combat events. The energy generated by an explosion can cause devastating physical trauma, affect multiple body systems and result in severe injuries or even fatalities (1.2). Although there has been extensive research into injury mechanisms of blast trauma, including primary overpressure effects, secondary fragmentation wounds, tertiary blunt trauma, and quaternary thermal or chemical injuries, there are no modeling & simulation (M&S) tools currently available which can provide a comprehensive view of the types and severity of injuries in the context of the uncertainties and complexities of realistic battlefield scenarios.

Existing injury modeling tools, such as Operational Requirements-based Casualty Assessment model (ORCA) developed by US Army DEVCOM, the INJURY code developed by the Medical Research and Development Command, and the AUDITORY model developed by the Joint Intermediate Force Capabilities Office (JIFCO), each model individual injuries occurring to a single person in the absence of PPE. They are not designed to address multiple, multi-modal injuries that may occur in ground combat, and they model wounds from the “skin in,” rather than accounting for the effects of clothing or PPE. These tools can only be used for research purposes and are not designed to support battlefield operation.

In contrast, the Human Injury Prediction (HIP) tool, developed by Defense Science and Technology Laboratory (DSTL) of United Kingdom, predicts injuries to multiple people from a terrorist attack. Unfortunately, this tool is limited to modeling the effects of only a single blast event caused by a terrorist weapon detonated in an urban environment. And, again, HIP models isolated injuries and cannot address multiple, multi-modal injuries.

Finally, a major challenge of leveraging these tools in DTRA Technical Reachback mission is that injuries are predicted based upon biomechanical effects, and do not address human physiology. This shortcoming becomes particularly critical with multiple injuries, where the human body response to injuries is intact and synergetic among organs/tissues.

Apart from the specific challenges of modeling injuries and the associated changes in physiology, a comprehensive battlefield blast injury M&S tool is a multidisciplinary endeavor, requiring expertise in diverse domains, to include medicine, military operations, weaponeering, synthetic population modeling, epidemiology, structures, machine learning, computational modeling, and PPE.

ASME V&V 40 serves as the gold standard for computational model credibility in biomedical applications, and DoD Instruction 5000.61 (Modeling and Simulation Verification, Validation, and Accreditation) requires human injury models to be validated before moving to support military operation (3,4,5). The modeling effort should align with the Blast Injury Research Coordinating Office (BIRCO) and the Blast Injury Prevention Standards Recommendation (BIPSR) process. The access to sensitive battle databases must be tightly controlled and limited to need-to-know personnel (6). Based on the regulation and scientific merit, the current request for proposal (RFP) will focus on validation of the on-going approach by using independent groups.

Phase I:
Phase I will focus on establishing standards to validate the current technical approach, data source, computational codes, medical definition, injury codes, environmental conditions (topography), generic weapon information and synthetic population. The offeror should thoroughly study all available injury modeling tools and provide detailed pros and cons summary for the existing methodologies (1.7,8). The contractor shall conduct a comprehensive review of pathophysiology of blast injuries and the established injury codes. Key validation methods shall be established. Due to complexity of the effort, machine learning is highly encouraged. A key requirement in this phase is delineation of where existing or synthetic data (based upon first principles modeling) may suffice, as compared to where laboratory or field testing will be required. By the end of Phase I, the offeror should deliver a preliminary approach and document all technical challenges for phase II work.

Phase II:
The validation methods proposed in Phase I should be applied in Phase II. Data sources from historical shock tube experiments, postmortem human surrogates (PMHS) testing, anthropomorphic test devices (ATDs) and computational models must be clearly identified and studied. Key challenges, such as material data gaps, incomplete injury criteria, military operational requirements and emerging weapons should be addressed in Phase II. The focus of this phase will be aggregating existing data and generating synthetic data. Test plans developed to fill in remaining gaps will be executed in Phase III.

Key deliverables include but are not limited to:

• A structured database of pre-existing data used in validation, and associated data cards.
• A list of common data elements (CDEs) associated with the database of pre-existing data. This list should be forward-looking in that if many CDEs were not collected in the historical data, they would be recommended for inclusion in future data collection efforts.
• A structured database of synthetic data and associated data cards used in validation, along with detailed documentation of assumptions to include (1) loading conditions; (2) material properties; (3) tissue/human body models; and (4) first principal codes. This information should be sufficient for a third party to replicate analyses.
• Detailed test plans with test protocols suitable for submission to IACUC/IRB authorities.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
In Phase III, the offeror will focus on the continued refinement and execution of the validation approach. This will primarily include execution of one or more test plans prepared in Phase II. In addition, the performer will have a strategy for ensuring that databases developed in Phase II are accessible to the broader DoW community, with mechanisms for integrating the latest research findings. The performer will work closely with the Blast Injury M&S team to recommend and evaluate changes to the models based upon validation findings. Finally, because new weapons or operational conditions may expand the ranges over which validation data is needed, ongoing collaboration with military medical professionals and other stakeholders is required.

References:
• Morena, A., Peroni, L., & Scapin, M. (2024). Numerical Investigation of the Blast-Induced Injuries Using an Open-Source Detailed Human Model. International Journal for Numerical Methods in Biomedical Engineering. https://doi.org/10.1002/cnm.3879
• Tan, X. G., Przekwas, A. J., & Gupta, R. K. (2017). Computational modeling of blast wave interaction with a human body and assessment of traumatic brain injury. Shock Waves, 27, 889–904. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00193-017-0740-x
• ASME V&V 40 Standard Alignment: Built core Technical Requirements around risk-risk mapping, Context of Use (COU), and quantitative credibility goals for medical modeling applications.
• DoDI 5000.61 & MIL-STD-3022 Compliance: Incorporated mandatory M&S VV&A procedures into the Statement of Work (Task 3.5) and delivery schedule (CDRL A007).
• Multi-Injury Modality Scope: Outlined validation tasks for high-risk military blast injuries: Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI), Primary Blast Lung, and Auditory damage.
• Acquisition Controls: Integrated DoD acquisition requirements including HRPO approvals, data rights, security clearances (for JTAPIC access), and ITAR restrictions.
• Liang, R., et al. (2025). Assessment model of blast injury: A narrative review. iScience, 28, 112830.
• Roberts, J.C., et al. (2012). Human head–neck computational model for assessing blast injury. Journal of Biomechanics, 45, 2899–2906.

title: Domestic Fabrication Of High-Purity Precursor Materials For Advanced Radiation Detection Scintillator Crystals
summary: DTRA seeks to establish reliable, scalable, and secure domestic sources and fabrication processes for high-purity precursor materials or pre-reacted mixes required for the growth of advanced inorganic scintillator crystals, such as LaBr₃:Ce, GGAG:Ce (GGAG), Cs₂LiYCl₆:Ce (CLYC), Cs₂LiLaBr₆:Ce (CLLB), and other materials.
description:
Objective:
DTRA seeks to establish reliable, scalable, and secure domestic sources and fabrication processes for high-purity precursor materials or pre-reacted mixes required for the growth of advanced inorganic scintillator crystals, such as LaBr₃:Ce, GGAG:Ce (GGAG), Cs₂LiYCl₆:Ce (CLYC), Cs₂LiLaBr₆:Ce (CLLB), and other materials. These materials are essential for high-resolution gamma spectroscopy and dual gamma/neutron pulse-shape discrimination (PSD) detectors used in Radiation Isotope Identification Devices (RIIDs), handheld identifiers, and other Department of War (DoW) radiation detection systems.

Description:
High-purity precursor materials are the foundational input for all high-performance inorganic scintillator crystals used in the DoW radiation detection and nuclear forensics missions. Current supply chains for key halides (e.g., LaCl₃, LaBr₃, YCl₃, LiCl, CsCl, CeCl3 etc.) and rare earth oxides (e.g., Gd2O3, CeO2, etc.) are heavily dependent on foreign sources. Several of the materials used for inorganic scintillator crystal growth are included in the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) 2025 List of Critical Minerals. This need is further reinforced by Executive Order 14415, "Securing America's Defense Supply Chains and Ensuring Domestic Acquisition of Critical Materials" (July 20, 2026), which directs the DoW to prioritize domestic sources for critical materials, restrict routine waivers for adversarial foreign suppliers effective January 1, 2027, and require supply chain mapping and mitigation plans from contractors and subcontractors.

Scaling crystal growth of these scintillators and maintaining consistent performance requires precursor materials with stringent control of purity, stoichiometry, moisture, and trace radioactive contaminants. Poor quality precursor materials often introduce variability that degrades crystal quality, light yield, energy resolution, and PSD figure-of-merit.

Desired materials typically have the following attributes, confirmed by analytical means and demonstrated by crystal growth results:

• High Chemical Purity: At least ≥4N (99.99%) anhydrous metal halides or pre-reacted mixes; sub-ppm levels of contaminants that interfere with the selected scintillator’s performance, such as transition metals (e.g., Fe, Cr, Ni, Cu) and alkali contaminants (e.g., K, Rb).
• Low Moisture / Oxygen Content: < 50 ppm (minimum) for hygroscopic materials.
• Precise Stoichiometry Control (for pre-reacted elpasolites): Precise control of multi-cation ratios to enable growth of phase-pure crystals with minimal secondary phases or compositional gradients
• Radioactive Impurity Control: Minimized 40K, 87Rb, 138La, 176Lu, and U/Th series contaminants to levels supporting low-background detector applications

This topic specifically targets the development of domestic synthesis, purification and quality-assurance processes capable of producing scintillator-grade precursor materials at laboratory, pilot, and eventually production scales. The goal is to reduce or eliminate reliance on foreign sources while enabling the next generation of compact, high-performance, ruggedized detectors for WMD detection and nuclear security applications.

The solution must meet the following minimum specifications:

• Analytical Characterization: Comprehensive analytical characterization confirming chemical purity, low moisture/oxygen content (if applicable) and stochiometric control. Appropriate methods should be used for trace-metal purity or trace moisture measurement.
• Domestic Feedstock Utilization: Primary use of U.S. or allied-nation sourced precursor materials (e.g. carbonates, oxides, chlorides) and any specialized equipment with documented traceability.
• Validation Method: Rapid feasibility screening of material performance, which may include small-scale crystal growth and measurements such as powder radioluminescence or optical transmittance.
• Production Scale: Reliable and reproducible laboratory-scale batches (e.g., 50-100 g) in Phase I; pilot-scale (e.g., 1–5 kg) in Phase II with batch-to-batch consistency. Ultimately, the focus is on material quality and potential for process scale up.
• Open market commercialization: Process development must lead to high-purity precursor materials made commercially available to the broader U.S. industrial base, rather than exclusive licenses, proprietary arrangements, or other restrictions.

Objective specifications (desired but not required for basic consideration):

• Advanced Validation Method: Produced batches must be validated through single crystal growth and complete radiation detection performance benchmarking against commercially available crystals, to include absolute light yield (photons/MeV), energy resolution at 662 keV, and PSD where applicable.
• Production Scale: Demonstration of multi-kilogram batch yields achieving or with a roadmap to achieve cost competitiveness with foreign-sourced material.
• Radiopurity: Identification of means to mitigate or minimize naturally occurring radioactive isotopes that impact detector background.
• Extensibility: Tailoring materials to be directly compatible with transparent ceramic scintillator fabrication processes (e.g. desirable particle size distribution and particle morphology).

This effort shall develop reliable domestic manufacturing processes for high-purity scintillator precursor materials while meeting the performance parameters above. Proposed work must include validation. The developed processes and materials will also be tested and validated in Phase II by delivery to DTRA or a designated partner for independent evaluation.

Phase I:
Phase I focuses on conceptualizing the approach and proof-of-principle for the fabrication process, with an emphasis on material synthesis and purity.

In Phase I, offerors shall perform a thorough assessment of current domestic and allied precursor supply chains for a select scintillator composition(s) of interest to DTRA (e.g., LaBr₃:Ce, CLYC, CLLB, GGAG, or related materials). This assessment shall consist of market research, identification of viable U.S. and/or allied material sources (including secondary chemicals and any specialized equipment), and technical risk analysis of purification and/or synthesis routes.

Following the assessment, a specific technical approach and one primary scintillator material system shall be selected for proof-of-principle. A laboratory-scale fabrication process shall be designed and demonstrated, producing at least one batch (e.g., 50-100 g total) of high-purity material. The process must demonstrate control of chemical purity, moisture, and stoichiometry. At a minimum, validation shall include rapid feasibility screening of the produced material, such as small-scale crystal growth and basic scintillation or optical properties characterization, and benchmarking against commercially-available material and/or crystals.

The Phase I final report shall include:

• Detailed supply-chain and market assessment with identified domestic precursor material sources, to include secondary chemicals and equipment used during synthesis and/or purification procedures, and any identified gaps
• Technical rationale for chosen precursor approach and compositions, supported by modeling and/or literature where applicable
• Detailed description of the developed laboratory-scale fabrication/purification process
• Analytical characterization results (e.g. chemical purity, moisture content if applicable, stoichiometry verification)
• Validation results, including test sample fabrication and characterization results.
• Yield assessment: Percentage of fabricated batches meeting target specifications and lessons learned for scale-up.
• Assessment of methods for achieving and/or improving radiopurity.

Phase II:
Phase II focuses on validating crystal growth and scintillation performance, process refinement, and scaling up the process from the laboratory-scale. The goal is a manufacturing process achieving TRL 5, with consistent batch-to-batch performance that supports reliable crystal growth yields and scintillation properties.

Validation shall include growing and characterizing test crystals (≥1 cm³). Key scintillator metrics to be characterized include but are not limited to energy resolution at 662 keV, absolute light yield (photons/MeV), and PSD if applicable. This validation may be done in-house, if the offer is capable. Offers are also encouraged to engage with a partner if this validation is outside their primary area of expertise, such as sending material to a crystal growth collaborator or sending crystals to a radiation detection characterization collaborator. Performance should be benchmarked against commercially-available crystals or crystals grown using commercially available feedstock. Crystals grown from at least one batch shall undergo independent detector fabrication/evaluation in a representative radiation detection system, which will be facilitated by DTRA.

Year 1: Focus on process optimization, reproducibility, and consistency of small batches (e.g., hundreds of grams), culminating in single crystal growth and scintillator performance validation.

Year 2: Refine the process from validation findings and scale the process to larger batch sizes (e.g., several kilograms). Perform independent evaluation of scintillation crystals produced via this process in a representative detector system, facilitated by DTRA.

The final report shall document the refined process, throughput, analytical quality control procedures, cost model, validation results, and percentage of output meeting all specifications. Grown crystals shall be delivered to DTRA. A clear pathway to Phase III commercial transition and DoW supply integration shall be provided.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Optional phase to continue scale-up, establish pilot production capability, and transition the domestic precursor materials manufacturing process to commercial or DoW-qualified production. The objective is to achieve cost-competitive, on-shore supply of scintillator-grade precursor materials that can support multiple DoW programs and commercial radiation detection markets. This phase may include qualification of the material in full-scale radiation detector systems, establishment of quality management systems (e.g., ISO or equivalent), and exploration of dual-use applications in medical imaging or homeland security.

References:
• EO 14415, “Securing America’s Defense Supply Chains and Ensuring Domestic Acquisition of Critical Materials,” July 20, 2026. Sets domestic sourcing and supply-chain mapping for defense rare earths and critical minerals; restricts waivers effective 2027.
• U.S. Geological Survey (USGS). "Final 2025 List of Critical Minerals." Federal Register, Vol. 90, No. 216, November 7, 2025.
• DTRA communications and technical exchanges (2025) documenting precursor supply disruptions for radiation detection materials and the resulting impact on crystal growth programs.

title: Domestic Scalable Growth Of Large-Format Pixelated CZT Crystals For Advanced Radiation Detection
summary: DTRA seeks to establish reliable, scalable, and secure domestic sources and fabrication processes for large-format monolithic cadmium zinc telluride (CZT) single crystals in the 44 × 44 × 15 mm form factor, optimized for pixelated electrode structures that enable high-performance room-temperature 3D position-sensitive gamma-ray imaging and spectroscopy.
description:
Objective:
DTRA seeks to establish reliable, scalable, and secure domestic sources and fabrication processes for large-format monolithic cadmium zinc telluride (CZT) single crystals in the 44 × 44 × 15 mm form factor, optimized for pixelated electrode structures that enable high-performance room-temperature 3D position-sensitive gamma-ray imaging and spectroscopy. These crystals are essential for next-generation compact radiation detection systems supporting WMD detection, nuclear forensics, and other radiation detection efforts within the Department of War (DoW).

Description:
Compact, high-resolution, room-temperature gamma imaging and spectroscopy systems are critical for a number of government agency applications (DoW, DTRA, DOE/NNSA, IAEA, DHS), in addition to a number of commercial applications (nuclear power, medical community). CZT-based 3D position-sensitive detectors provide these capabilities without cryogenic cooling, leveraging the small-pixel effect and depth-of-interaction (DOI) sensing via pixelated anodes and timing readout.

Current advanced systems rely on high-quality pixelated CZT, but most commercial modules use smaller crystals (~20–22 mm lateral dimensions). Furthermore, finished crystals with a thickness of around 5 mm are readily available for medical imaging; however, thicker crystals are often available from manufacturers by long-lead, custom order. Scaling to monolithic 44 × 44 × 15 mm crystals would significantly increase intrinsic efficiency (particularly for higher-energy gamma rays), reduce the number of crystals and interfaces per imager, improve geometrical coverage, simplify module assembly, and lower overall system complexity while maintaining or exceeding energy resolution targets of <1% FWHM at 662 keV.

High-performance spectrometer-grade CZT at this scale is currently supplied primarily by a limited number of foreign or foreign-owned sources, creating recognized supply-chain vulnerabilities for critical national security radiation detection hardware. Tellurium feedstock is heavily concentrated overseas, and domestic high-end crystal growth capacity remains limited. Zinc and Tellurium are identified in the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) 2025 List of Critical Minerals. Additionally, Executive Order 14415 "Securing America's Defense Supply Chains and Ensuring Domestic Acquisition of Critical Materials" (July 20, 2026), and related DoW supply chain initiatives, emphasize the need to strengthen domestic reliance on critical materials and components.

This topic directly addresses that gap by focusing on domestic crystal growth and machining innovation—including process improvements to the Traveling Heater Method (THM), Accelerated Crucible Rotation Technique (ACRT)-enhanced methods, alternative or hybrid growth techniques, in-situ monitoring, and stoichiometry/defect control—capable of delivering the required size, uniformity, and spectroscopic performance at scalable yield and cost. Successful development will strengthen U.S. supply chain resilience while accelerating technology transition to operational systems. A successful development under this topic should result in CZT material freely available on the commercial market rather than for exclusive or limited use by license or other restrictions. Furthermore, it is not the intent of this topic to develop detector systems utilizing CZT.

The solution must meet the following minimum specifications:

• Crystal Form Factor: Monolithic single-crystal CZT, nominal dimensions up to 44 × 44 × 15 mm (or equivalent large-format), suitable for pixelation with approximately 22 × 22 pixel anode contact matrix at ~2 mm pitch, a single cathode contact, and a guard ring contact around the edge of each.
• Material Quality: High spatial uniformity of carrier transport properties (electron μτ and adequate hole properties) across the full crystal volume; low defect density (e.g., Tellurium inclusions, grain boundaries, twins, etc.) sufficient to support high-performance spectroscopic operation; and low current leakage.
• Performance Target: Demonstrated or projected capability to achieve < 1% FWHM energy resolution at 662 keV when configured with pixelated readout and DOI sensing in a representative detector geometry.
• Domestic Production: U.S.-based growth process with clear, documented path to scalable yield, lot-to-lot reproducibility, and cost reduction; primary use of U.S. or allied-nation sourced raw materials with traceability.
• Validation: Precursor and crystal lots must be validated through non-destructive characterization (e.g., IR transmission, X-ray topography, μτ mapping) and, where feasible, proxy electrode testing or delivery to a qualified detector fabricator for performance assessment.
• Cost: Demonstrate that under high volume production cost per crystal volume is competitive with CZT commercially available from other commercial vendors.

Objective specifications (desired but not required for basic consideration):

• Larger or thicker monolithic crystals (e.g., approaching 50 × 50 × 20 mm) with maintained uniformity.
• Demonstrated full pixelated detector performance meeting or exceeding < 0.8% FWHM at 662 keV in 3D configuration.
• Production-scale batches (multiple crystals per run) with ≥ 70% single-crystal yield meeting all quality metrics.
• Cost-competitive pathway versus current foreign-sourced material at equivalent performance.
• Extensibility to related materials or detector architectures (e.g., array tiling, alternative electrode designs).

Phase I:
Conceptualizing approach and proof-of-principle fabrication process. In Phase I, offerors shall perform a thorough assessment of current domestic and allied CZT crystal growth capabilities relevant to large-format detector-grade material. This assessment shall include market research on raw material (tellurium, cadmium, zinc) sourcing, identification of viable U.S. and/or allied feedstock pathways, and an analysis of alternative growth methods capable of achieving the target 44 × 44 × 15 mm form factor with required uniformity, including a technical risk analysis for each.

Following the assessment, a specific technical approach and growth process shall be selected. A crystal growth and machining process shall be designed and demonstrated, producing at least one crystal (or multiple smaller proxy crystals demonstrating scalability) approaching the target dimensions with acceptable uniformity and performance. The process must demonstrate control of stoichiometry, defect density, and carrier transport properties.

Offerors are encouraged to seek collaborations in areas outside of their expertise if needed to reach specifications; for example, crystals may be shipped to a partner for properties characterization and validation.

The Phase I final report shall include:

• Detailed supply-chain and market assessment with identified domestic raw material sources, gaps, and risk mitigation strategies.
• Technical rationale for chosen growth method(s), supported by modeling, simulation, or literature where applicable.
• Detailed description of the developed growth and process control methodology.
• Non-destructive characterization results (e.g., IR transmission mapping, X-ray topography or equivalent, μτ property mapping) demonstrating spatial uniformity across the crystal volume.
• Proxy electrode or small-pixel test results (where feasible) or clear pathway to spectroscopic performance validation.
• Percentage of fabricated crystals (production yield) meeting target specifications, key process parameters identified for Phase II scale-up, and lessons learned.
• Analysis of potential product commercialization focusing on a commercial market at full scale production upon successful completion of the development. This should emphasis the technical and business need to reach full potential.

Phase II:
Scaling up output of crystal growth process. In Phase II, the laboratory process developed in Phase I shall be refined, optimized, and scaled to reliably produce multiple 44 × 44 × 15 mm (or equivalent) crystals with high reproducibility and yield. The goal is a manufacturing process achieving TRL 5, with consistent lot-to-lot performance that supports reliable detector fabrication and spectroscopic performance.

At least one lot of crystals (minimum three to five crystals meeting all quality metrics, or equivalent total output across validated runs) shall undergo independent characterization and, where feasible, delivery to a qualified U.S. detector fabricator, end-user partner, or academic investigator (with DTRA approval) for pixelated electrode processing and performance evaluation in a representative radiation detection configuration. The final report shall document the optimized process, throughput, analytical quality control procedures, cost model, and percentage of output meeting all specifications. A clear pathway to Phase III commercial transition and DoW supply integration shall be provided.

Phase II deliverables shall include: delivery of validated crystals to DTRA or a designated partner for independent evaluation; comprehensive process documentation suitable for technology transfer; and a detailed Phase III transition plan including potential commercial or DoW program insertion points.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Optional phase to continue scale-up, establish pilot production capability, and transition the domestic large-format CZT crystal growth process to commercial production. The objective is to achieve cost-competitive, on-shore supply of spectrometer-grade 44 × 44 × 15 mm (and larger) pixelated CZT crystals that can support multiple DoW programs and commercial radiation detection markets. This phase may include qualification of crystals in full-scale detector systems, establishment of quality management systems (e.g., ISO or equivalent), exploration of dual-use applications (medical imaging, industrial), and sustained production capacity demonstration.

References:
• EO 14415, “Securing America’s Defense Supply Chains and Ensuring Domestic Acquisition of Critical Materials,” July 20, 2026. Sets domestic sourcing and supply-chain mapping for defense rare earths and critical minerals; restricts waivers effective 2027.
• DTRA and DOE technical exchanges (2024–2026) documenting CZT supply chain constraints and the impact on advanced radiation detection system development for nonproliferation and WMD detection missions.
• Open literature on THM and ACRT enhancements for CZT growth, small-pixel effects, and 3D position-sensitive CZT detector architectures, including IEEE NSS/MIC/RTSD proceedings and related journals.
• U.S. Geological Survey (USGS). "Final 2025 List of Critical Minerals." Federal Register, Vol. 90, No. 216, November 7, 2025.

title: Biolab Mirror: Artificial Intelligence / Machine Learning (AI/ML) Digital Twin for Intent Characterization and Bio-Containment Integrity
summary: Develop a high-fidelity "Digital Twin" (The Biolab Mirror) and an advanced Artificial Intelligence / Machine Learning (AI/ML) methodology capable of continuous, non-invasive integrity verification and intent characterization of a mid-size, state-sponsored biological research facility.
description:
Objective:
Develop a high-fidelity "Digital Twin" (The Biolab Mirror) and an advanced Artificial Intelligence / Machine Learning (AI/ML) methodology capable of continuous, non-invasive integrity verification and intent characterization of a mid-size, state-sponsored biological research facility. The solution must fuse continuous physical/biological signatures (e.g., metabolic output, environmental thermodynamics, material logistics) with discrete digital telemetry (e.g., Laboratory Information Management Systems (LIMS) logs, Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) / Building Management Systems (BMS) control data). The objective is to detect clandestine biological activities, containment spoofing, and the subtle operational drift indicative of a transition from peaceful, declared research to unauthorized, non-compliant, or undeclared high-risk biological material production [1][2].

This effort bridges a critical gap between standard Information Technology (IT) network defense and biological physical reality by establishing a “Zero Trust” posture that cross-validates digital telemetry against the immutable laws of physics. Unlike current commercial cyberbiosecurity offerings that focus solely on the IT perimeter or traditional biosurveillance platforms that are purely reactive, the Biolab Mirror is proactively designed to characterize nefarious intent before unauthorized, non-compliant, or undeclared high-risk biological material production occurs.

Description:
The proliferation of dual-use biological technologies and automated, high-containment laboratories globally presents a profound challenge to arms control verification and biosurveillance [3]. A state-sponsored facility operating under a declared, peaceful mandate (e.g., vaccine development, agricultural research) possesses all the necessary infrastructure, reagents, and personnel to rapidly pivot to unauthorized, non-compliant, or undeclared high-risk biological material production [2]. Current verification methods rely heavily on periodic physical inspections, voluntary declarations, and audits of digital LIMS. However, advanced adversaries can digitally spoof BMS, manipulate LIMS records, and conceal clandestine pathogen scaling through “population ghosting” [4][5]. The Department of War (DoW) requires a “Physics-to-Mesh Zero Trust” architecture [6]. This solicitation seeks proposals for a “Biolab Mirror”—a comprehensive Digital Twin that does not inherently trust digital control logs. Instead, the Mirror must continuously cross-validate digital telemetry against the unalterable laws of physics, chemistry, and biology (Conservation of Mass, Thermodynamics, Metabolic Rates). By establishing a rigorous physical baseline (e.g., correlating total water inflow with Effluent Decontamination System (EDS) out-flow, or matching documented animal feed procurement to autoclave waste mass and vivarium Carbon Dioxide (CO2) exhaust), the AI/ML engine must automatically flag the subtle “Coherence Failures” that betray clandestine pathogen scaling, undeclared animal models, or spoofed containment boundaries.

SUPPLEMENTAL INFORMATION

• Programmatic Metrics and Data Sourcing

• Data Sourcing Strategy Synthetic Baseline Generation (Performer Sourced): The performer is responsible for generating the Phase II training and validation datasets using established biological and physical engineering standards.
• Phase I Exit Metrics Measure of Performance (MOP) 1 (Architecture Delivery): Deliver a Digital Twin architecture mapping cross-domain signatures including specialized cross-domain digital and physical validation points.

• Strategic Offshoots & Cyber-Physical Emulation

• Executive Summary: The primary objective of the Biolab Mirror SBIR/STTR is defensive: to establish a high-fidelity “Physics-to-Mesh Zero Trust” baseline to detect clandestine activity and intent. Successful completion yields a secondary strategic asset: a perfect, un-spoofed “Cyber-Terrain” map that can be ported into isolated cyber-ranges to simulate, analyze, and train against multi-domain attacks targeting critical high-containment infrastructure [10].
• The Capability Gap in Current Cyber-Ranges: Current cyber-ranges are optimized for IT network emulation and struggle to accurately emulate OT and the physical realities of a BSL-3/BSL-4 environment.
• The Biolab Mirror as the Emulation Foundation: The Biolab Mirror solves this gap. By mapping the continuous physical signatures directly to the discrete digital telemetry, the performer constructs a fully functional Cyber-Physical Sandbox.

The Attack Simulation: Authorized cybersecurity evaluation teams and system auditors can execute multi-stage simulated attacks against this virtual target (e.g., spear-phishing an academic researcher -> pivoting to the BMS network -> manipulating the Effluent Decontamination System). The Red Team must navigate the actual laws of biology and thermodynamics to succeed.

• Strategic ROI & Follow-On Potential: Authorizing the Biolab Mirror effort provides a “two-for-one” return on investment (ROI), yielding a defensive characterization engine and a foundational architecture for dedicated cybersecurity testing and critical infrastructure protection.

Phase I:
Architecture & Signature Mapping: Develop the conceptual architecture for the Biolab Mirror. The performer must comprehensively map all critical signatures of a mid-size Biosafety Level 3 (BSL-3) / Biosafety Level 4 (BSL-4) facility, categorizing them into Continuous (Physical/Biological) and Discrete (Digital/Telemetry) domains [7]. • Physics-to-Mesh Framework: Define the “Coherence Fuses” and mathematical models required to cross-validate specific digital assertions (e.g., BMS reporting “Sterilization Complete”) with physical ground truth (e.g., calculated facility equipment power utilization metrics or chemical reagent depletion). • Intent Characterization Roadmap: Develop an AI/ML roadmap demonstrating how the Mirror will analyze deviations from the established facility baseline to detect the transition from legitimate research to unauthorized, non-compliant, or undeclared high-risk biological material production. This roadmap must include not only mass-balance analysis (detecting how much is being produced) but also Procurement Vector Analysis (detecting what is being produced). • Resource Prioritization Strategy: Design a tiered sensor deployment strategy that maximizes the use of existing, zero-cost facility infrastructure while identifying the critical “Choke Points of Transduction” requiring specialized physical validation. • Final Deliverable: A comprehensive Phase I report detailing the Digital Twin conceptual architecture, the mathematical coherence models, and a preliminary design for Phase II software implementation.

Phase II:
Prototype Development: Develop, demonstrate, and validate a working software prototype of the Biolab Mirror AI/ML engine. • Synthetic Facility Ingestion: The prototype must successfully ingest and process a complex, simulated baseline dataset representing normal operations of a mid-size biological facility. • Anomaly Detection: Utilize the prototype to successfully identify simulated “Coherence Failures” introduced into the dataset. Scenarios must include: • Population Ghosting: Detecting undocumented pathogen scaling or animal models via mass balance and metabolic discrepancies [9]. • Containment Spoofing: Detecting unauthorized EDS discharges masked by manipulated operational technology telemetry [10]. • Procurement Vector Validation: Demonstrate the prototype’s capability to ingest, normalize, and categorize multi-source procurement registries. • Transition Strategy: Provide a clear transition plan detailing how the Biolab Mirror architecture can be integrated into standard government biosurveillance architectures for remote facility assessment and biological risk verification [11].

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Government Application: Integration into standard government biosurveillance architectures for remote facility assessment and biological risk verification to quickly ascertain historical facility operations. • Commercial Application: Transition to commercial pharmaceutical Quality Assurance / Quality Control (QA/QC), BSL-3/BSL-4 containment safety assurance, and insider-threat protection for proprietary genomic data and high-value biotechnology Intellectual Property (IP).

title: AI/ML Verification of Microelectronic Integrity for High-Assurance Systems
summary: Develop an innovative, Artificial Intelligence / Machine Learning (AI/ML) driven methodology and prototype architecture capable of non-destructively verifying the physical and logical integrity of Integrated Circuits (ICs). The solution must reliably detect sub-nanometer, adversarial Hardware Trojans that evade conventional functional testing.
description:
Objective:
Develop an innovative, Artificial Intelligence / Machine Learning (AI/ML) driven methodology and prototype architecture capable of non-destructively verifying the physical and logical integrity of Integrated Circuits (ICs). The solution must reliably detect sub-nanometer, adversarial Hardware Trojans that evade conventional functional testing. This ensures absolute trust in microelectronics utilized in high-assurance communications, critical infrastructure, and secure data collection systems, explicitly including protections against data-layer subversion and unauthorized RF activation. [1]

This effort bridges a critical gap between commercial supply chain illumination and physics-based national security hardware assurance. While current commercial offerings focus on firmware vulnerabilities and counterfeiting, they are blind to perfectly manufactured, sub-nanometer malicious logic such as Hardware Trojans. Furthermore, unlike existing programs such as DARPA AISS which operate in the pre-silicon design phase, this effort operates in the post-silicon verification phase assuming a "Zero Trust" posture.

Description:
The Department of War relies heavily on advanced microelectronics sourced from a globally distributed commercial supply chain. Securing this supply chain against malicious insertion is a critical national security imperative, repeatedly highlighted by the Government Accountability Office (GAO) as a high-risk area. [2]

For defense systems operating in contested environments, compromised hardware represents a catastrophic vulnerability. Advanced adversaries are capable of introducing microscopic logic alterations (e.g., dopant-level Trojans, malicious dormant circuitry) during fabrication or transit. [3] A primary use case of concern involves hardware-level Trojans engineered to bypass software encryption, forcing ultra-secure communications gear or deployable sensor packages to execute unauthorized radio frequency (RF) transmissions, thereby exposing sensitive mission telemetry to hostile forces.

Furthermore, there is a critical emerging requirement to address sophisticated vulnerabilities residing between the hardware and firmware boundaries. The DoW seeks capabilities to identify malicious logic that facilitates unauthorized data inspection within the data layer, allowing an adversary to silently monitor, filter, or alter encrypted traffic streams at the silicon level. Additionally, the solution must investigate vectors where the data layer is manipulated to trigger unintended electromagnetic emanations from legitimate components, or the covert activation of dormant RF elements, for out-of-band exfiltration. [4]

The DoW seeks proposals for an automated, AI-driven inspection capability to mitigate these threats. The desired solution should ingest a Level 3 Technical Data Package (TDP) or Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) Digital Twin to establish a definitive baseline of intended logic gate behavior. It must then utilize advanced algorithms to process data from Non-Destructive Evaluation (NDE) techniques to physically and logically interrogate the delivered hardware against that baseline, identifying deviations that could enable data-layer subversion, unauthorized emissions, or system failure. [5]

Digital Provenance Integration: This effort seeks to establish an algorithmic layer of assurance compatible with modern secure supply chain initiatives. Proposals should consider the architectural requirements necessary for the proposed engine to interface with emergent DoW digital provenance frameworks, generating unique, verifiable identifiers for individual components before they are integrated into sensitive operational packages.

Data Sourcing Strategy

• Training Dataset (Performer Sourced): Performers must leverage synthetic data (MBSE/GAN generated) and existing open-source physical benchmarks to train models.
• Validation Dataset (Performer Sourced): The performer is responsible for the independent identification, procurement, and physical acquisition of the ICs and Digital Twins required for validation. This must be accomplished without assumption of reliance on Government Furnished Information (GFI); performers may propose use of appropriate GFI if such a database is known and available. This dataset must include a significant subset of components with specific, verified Hardware Trojans to ensure objective benchmarking.

FREQUENTLY ASKED QUESTIONS (FAQs)

FAQ 1.0: Commercial Market Overlap and Capability Gaps

• Q1.1: Several commercial companies utilize AI for quality assurance, and emerging platforms offer Deep Supply Chain Illumination and Firmware Assurance. How does this SBIR/STTR effort differ from these commercial offerings, and what specific gap does it close?
• A1.1: This SBIR/STTR bridges the gap between commercial supply chain illumination/firmware analysis and physics-based national security hardware assurance.
• Market Research Summary: The current commercial market includes advanced providers specializing in Deep Supply Chain Illumination, Hardware/Firmware Assurance, and Anti-Tamper & Forensics. Separately, major Failure Analysis (FA) labs utilize tools like Focused Ion Beam (FIB) and Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) for physical defect localization. [8]
• The Commercial Blind Spot: While firmware assurance platforms excel at identifying counterfeit parts and firmware-level vulnerabilities, they are generally blind to sub-nanometer, perfectly manufactured malicious logic etched directly into the silicon (Hardware Trojans). Furthermore, commercial AI inspection models are optimized for Yield and Reliability. A Hardware Trojan is not an error; it is a Deterministic Malicious Addition. Commercial models will pass a Trojaned chip because it meets all structural tolerances, blinding the supply chain to intentional sabotage. [9][10]
• Bridging the Gap: This proposal funds the development of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) that fuse these disciplines. It seeks to train detection algorithms to find intentionally hidden, malicious logic that commercial defect scanners miss, anchoring that physical assurance to the secure supply chain.

FAQ 2.0: Programmatic Differentiation and Non-Duplication of Effort

• Q2.1: How does this proposed SBIR/STTR effort differ from the DARPA Automatic Implementation of Secure Silicon (AISS) program?
• A2.1: This proposal does not duplicate DARPA AISS. [7] AISS operates in the Pre-Silicon (Design) Phase, automating the insertion of security features into the IC blueprint. This SBIR/STTR operates in the Post-Silicon (Verification) Phase. It assumes a "Zero Trust" posture, acknowledging that adversaries may bypass AISS obfuscation during physical fabrication.

FAQ 3.0: Transition Strategy and the "Valley of Death"

• Q3.1: How does this Phase I/II proposal ensure a viable Phase III transition plan?
• A3.1: By structuring the output as a verification service capable of certifying COTS hardware, the technology becomes an enabling requirement for other acquisition programs. Primary transition targets include defense certification processes and rapid acquisition authorities.

FAQ 4.0: Data Rights and Intellectual Property (IP) Friction

• Q4.1: How will this initiative overcome the reluctance of commercial vendors to share proprietary Level 3 TDPs?
• A4.1: Performers are encouraged to design their AI/ML ingestion models using secure enclave or "zero-knowledge proof" principles to mathematically compare the physical scan against the Digital Twin without exposing human-readable schematics.

Phase I:
Conduct a feasibility study defining the proposed AI/ML architecture and the specific NDE data inputs required for high-fidelity anomaly detection. Validation Dataset Strategy: Develop a comprehensive identification and procurement strategy for a high-fidelity validation dataset. This must detail how the performer will source, verify, and curate a diverse set of IC models and physical samples—including known "clean" and strategically "poisoned" variants—without assumption of reliance on Government Furnished Information (GFI); performer may propose use of appropriate GFI if such a database is known and available. Develop a conceptual framework demonstrating the correlation of physical NDE scan data against a complex Digital Twin to identify logic-level alterations. Data-Layer & RF Activation Vectors: Define preliminary investigation routes and algorithmic models specifically tailored to detect logic anomalies within the data layer, as well as vectors allowing data-layer manipulation for unintended EM emanations or discrete RF activation. Model the system’s theoretical ability to detect distinct classes of Hardware Trojans (e.g., parametric, functional, dormant) without relying on "golden" physical reference chips. Interoperability Hook: Identify and describe the architectural requirements for the proposed engine to interface with emergent DoW digital provenance and Supply Chain Risk Management (SCRM) frameworks. Specifically, identify how the AI/ML verification attestation can be cryptographically bound to the hardware's inherent Physical Unclonable Function (PUF), creating a unique identifier suitable for integration into a Distributed Ledger-based Chain of Custody. [6] Metrics Alignment: Performers must explicitly demonstrate how their proposed research and conceptual architecture will meet or exceed the Threshold and Objective Measures of Performance (MOP) and Measures of Effectiveness (MOE) detailed in Enclosure 1: Programmatic Metrics and Data Sourcing. Deliver a comprehensive Final Report detailing the algorithmic approach, computational requirements, and a preliminary design for a Phase II software/hardware prototype. Phase I Exit Metrics

• MOP 1 (Architecture): Threshold: Deliver system architecture mapping NDE/TDP ingestion. Objective: Architecture includes a cryptographically secure "Zero-Knowledge" enclave design capable of identifying data-layer manipulation pathways.
• MOE 1 (Detection Capability): Threshold: Modeled AI demonstrates theoretical >85% detection of known functional Trojans in synthetic data. Objective: Theoretical >95% detection across multiple HT classes with simulated False Positive Rate (FPR)
• MOP 2 (Interoperability): Threshold: Define software API for cryptographic attestation output. Objective: Define methodology for securely binding the AI verification result to the hardware's PUF for DLT integration.
• MOP 4 (Data Strategy): Threshold: Complete a validated roadmap for acquiring physical and digital components for Phase II testing. Objective: Secured pre-commitments or established procurement channels for a diverse set of "poisoned" VLSI structures.

Phase II:
Develop, demonstrate, and validate a working prototype of the AI/ML verification engine. Procure and utilize the validation dataset identified in Phase I to benchmark the prototype’s detection accuracy, false-positive rate, and processing speed against the metrics outlined in Enclosure 1. Demonstrate the algorithmic capability to adapt to novel insertion methods (e.g., adaptive learning) designed to subvert secure communications or trigger unauthorized emanations. Adversarial Synthesis (GAN): Integrate a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) architecture to autonomously synthesize "Compound Trigger" Hardware Trojans. The engine must demonstrate the ability to identify theoretical insertions that rely on the correlation of a legitimate operational state (e.g., high-readiness mode) with an anomalous external input vector. Provide a clear transition plan detailing integration into existing DoW quality assurance pipelines, specifically interfacing with relevant DoW acquisition pathways and quality assurance centers. Phase II Exit Metrics (Prototype Demonstration)

• MOE 2 (Physical Detection - "Performer-Procured Validation Set"): Threshold: Prototype processes the procured validation dataset with True Positive Rate (TPR) >90%. Objective: TPR >99%, successfully identifying localized Hardware Trojans consisting of 10 or fewer manipulated logic gates within a VLSI structure.
• MOP 3 (Algorithmic Efficiency): Threshold: Prototype maintains FPR <5% on "clean" chips. Objective: Maintains FPR <1% while processing NDE data of a standard microcontroller in <60 minutes.
• MOE 3 (Adversarial Adaptability & State-Space Exploration): Threshold: Algorithmic model successfully flags a novel, previously unseen HT insertion method (provided by independent evaluation team) as an anomaly requiring human review within 72 hours of dataset ingestion. Objective: Performer's internal GAN autonomously generates and trains against a "Compound Trigger" Hardware Trojan reliant on the correlation of a defined operational state with an anomalous external input vector, unforeseen by the evaluation team.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
DoW Application: Integration into the acquisition lifecycle for systems requiring high assurance, specifically supporting deployable infrastructure, secure defense communications, and critical command and control network nodes. Commercial Application: Transition to the Quality Assurance (QA) markets for secure financial clearinghouses, medical life-support devices, and commercial autonomous systems, where hardware-level subversion presents catastrophic safety and liability risks.

References:
• Department of Defense Instruction (DoDI) 5200.44, Protection of Mission Critical Functions to Achieve Trusted Systems and Networks (TSN), (Washington, D.C.: Department of Defense, 2012, Incorporating Change 3, October 1, 2020).
• U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO), Microelectronics: DoD Has Enhanced Pandemic Coordination, but Challenges Remain in Supply Chain Risk Management, GAO-23-105658 (Washington, D.C.: January 2023).
• Mohammad Tehranipoor and Farinaz Koushanfar, "A Survey of Hardware Trojan Taxonomy and Detection," IEEE Design & Test of Computers 27, no. 1 (2010): 10-25.
• National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), Platform Firmware Resiliency Guidelines, NIST Special Publication 800-193 (Gaithersburg, MD: May 2018).
• Department of Defense, DoD Microelectronics: Vision, (Washington, D.C.: Office of the Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering, 2022).
• Department of Defense, DoD Zero Trust Strategy, (Washington, D.C.: Chief Information Officer, November 2022).
• Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA), Automatic Implementation of Secure Silicon (AISS) Program (Ongoing).
• U.S. Department of Commerce, Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), The Semiconductor Supply Chain: Assessing National Competitiveness, (Washington, D.C.: January 2022).
• Rostami, M., Koushanfar, F., and Karri, R., "A Primer on Hardware Security: Models, Methods, and Metrics," Proceedings of the IEEE 102, no. 8 (August 2014): 1283-1295.
• The MITRE Corporation, Hardware Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE), (McLean, VA: 2021).

title: Compact High Energy Density Capacitors For Pulsed Field X-Ray Generators
summary: DTRA seeks ultra-compact, high-voltage, high energy density, capacitors and related advanced dielectric materials to support the development of advanced portable X-ray radiographic imaging systems.
description:
Objective:
DTRA seeks ultra-compact, high-voltage, high energy density, capacitors and related advanced dielectric materials to support the development of advanced portable X-ray radiographic imaging systems.

Description:
High energy density capacitors and their constituent dielectrics are vital components for multiple DoW capability needs for high voltage power supplies, Marx generators, high-power microwave sources, and other pulsed-power technologies. The Missile Defense Agency, ONR, NASA and other government agencies have funded efforts into high energy density capacitors for a variety of applications.1 However, it is still very challenging to fabricate high energy density capacitors that reliably meet ultra-compact size constraints for miniaturized high voltage pulse power applications and in a ruggedized field-use system.

Recent prototype development of compact pulsed X-ray generators for portable radiographic imaging applications has underscored the difficulty of scaling capacitor technologies originally developed for larger directed energy and pulsed power systems down to the ultra-compact sizes needed for man-portable or small unmanned systems. Key challenges include preserving dielectric performance and high-voltage hold-off at reduced dimensions, achieving robust voltage reversal tolerance essential for Marx generator topologies, maintaining long operational lifetimes under pulsed conditions with repetition rates up to 100 Hz, and attaining high manufacturing yields with consistent quality for reliable field deployment. This topic specifically targets the development of reliable fabrication processes and advanced dielectric materials to overcome these miniaturization and ruggedization barriers for X-ray generator pulsed power applications.

DTRA seeks to develop reliable and efficient fabrication and production processes for compact high energy density capacitors.

The solution must meet the following minimum specifications:

• Outer Dimensions: No larger than 2 inches x 1 inch x 0.5 inch
• Voltage Rating: 100kV*
• Capacitance: ≥ 2nF
• Voltage Reversal Tolerance: 80%*
• Operating Environment: Dielectric Liquid or Pressurized Gas (e.g., such as SF6)
• Operating Temperature: Capable of meeting MIL-STD
• Ability to survive commercial requirements for shock and vibration (i.e. rough handling)
• Lifetime: Greater than 100,000 full-charge cycles
• Duty cycle: Up to 100 Hz
• Charge/Discharge time: Charging order of 10s of microseconds, discharge order of few nanoseconds

*Note: Operating voltage and voltage reversal are the highest priority specifications. DTRA may consider small deviations from the other minimum specifications (e.g. size) if the solution is capable of approaching or meeting the objective voltage and voltage reversal specifications below.

Objective specifications:

• Voltage Rating: 250kV
• Capacitance: ≥ 10nF
• Capacitance Tolerance: ±10%
• Voltage Reversal Tolerance: 100%
• Operating Temperature: Capable of meeting MIL-STD
• Vibration: Capable of meeting MIL-STD
• Lifetime greater than full-charge 1,000,000 cycles

This effort shall develop a reliable manufacturing process for high energy density capacitors while maintaining the performance parameters outlined above. The proposed effort will require that developed capacitors be tested and validated in Phase 2.

Phase I:
Conceptualizing capacitor design type and proof of principle of manufacturing process. In Phase 1 of this effort, a suitable capacitor type and design will be chosen to meet the above-listed performance parameters. This decision should be informed by extensive modeling, simulation, and market research, and guided by availability of materials needed. Preference is indicated for domestically available materials. Note that while temperature and vibration ruggedization are to meet MIL-STD ranges, formal testing and certification to the MIL-STD specifications is not required during this phase. Following the design decision, material samples will be fabricated and tested to validate performance. Evaluation of success will be weighted towards feasibility of materials to achieve the highest priority specifications: operating voltage and voltage reversal. Additionally, the offerors will define a detailed plan for a scalable prototype manufacturing process to be executed in Phase II, including equipment needs, quality control steps, and risk mitigation. The designed process should demonstrate progress towards production of capacitors that meet the defined performance criteria with particular attention to overcoming the miniaturization and reliability challenges associated with scaling from larger directed energy capacitor designs. The Phase 1 final report should include: details for chosen capacitor design along with relevant modelling, simulation, and market research results, details of the chosen manufacturing process, and test and evaluation results of the proof-of-principle capacitor performance (including but not limited to voltage reversal testing representative of Marx generator operation) and percentage of fabricated material samples that meet specifications via the initial process.

Phase II:
Manufacturing process execution, refinement, and scaling up of output. In Phase 2 of this effort, the manufacturing process designed in Phase 1 will be executed, refined, and scaled up with the goal of reliable capacitor output with high percentage of capacitors meeting performance specifications. The goal of this phase of the effort should be a manufacturing process with output and reliability of produced components that meet a TRL 5. The final report for Phase 2 will include final details of the optimized manufacturing process and throughput, output capacitor specifications, and percentage of output that meets design specifications. Capacitors will be delivered to DTRA by the end of Phase II for evaluation in a representative pulsed power system for X-ray generation, as follows: • Year 1: Fabrication of 10 prototype capacitors for testing, validation and refinement. • Year 2: Final deliverable of up to 10 fully compliant prototype capacitors to DTRA.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Optional phase that will continue scale up and output of capacitor manufacturing process. The goal of this phase 3 work will be to produce capacitors that exceed the above listed performance specification and continue to increase the output of capacitor manufacturing while maintaining high-percentage of capacitors meeting performance specifications.

References:
• NASA TechPort - Project Data (https://techport.nasa.gov/view/5114)

title: Low Cost Infrared Seeker
summary: Provide novel infrared (IR) seeker solutions that significantly reduce costs compared to the state-of-the-art onboard interceptor applications.
description:
Objective:
Provide novel infrared (IR) seeker solutions that significantly reduce costs compared to the state-of-the-art onboard interceptor applications.

Description:
Develop a cost-effective IR interceptor seeker through methods such as novel material development, advanced manufacturing and/or scalability, novel commercial-off-the-shelf (COTS) integration, or other innovations that could reduce costs and maintain acceptable seeker performance. Both full seeker solutions and novel seeker components (focal plane array, readout integrated circuit, cooling system, telescope optics, etc.) are acceptable so long as cost savings are explicitly quantified in the proposal. A "full seeker" solution should include: Cover (if applicable), telescope assembly/ optical system (lenses, mirrors, filters, etc.), the IR sensor (filter, Focal Plane Arrays (FPAs) Readout Integrated Circuit, cooling systems (if applicable, etc.), gimbal system (as applicable), signal processing electronics, and the Final seeker production cost should be less than $150,000 for objective cost or less than $250,000 for threshold. Proposed solutions should be amenable to repeatable high throughput production processes. Proposal should include a plan for demonstration of seeker performance in a ground test facility. Additionally, proposers should identify the threat type(s) (ballistic, hypersonic, cruise missile, etc.) that are relevant to the proposed technology, and any assumptions made concerning the technology or its integration into the missile defense system should be explicitly referenced.

Phase I:
Phase I-like proposals will not be evaluated and will be rejected as nonresponsive. For this topic, the Government expects the small business would have accomplished the following in a Phase I-like effort via some other means, e.g., independent research and development (IRAD) or other source, a concept for a workable prototype or design to address, at a minimum, the basic capabilities of the stated objective above. Proposal must show, as appropriate, a demonstrated technical feasibility or nascent capability. The documentation provided must substantiate the proposer’s development of a preliminary understanding of the technology to be applied in their Phase II proposal in meeting topic objectives.

Documentation should comprise all relevant information including, but not limited to, technical reports, test data, prototype designs/models, and performance goals/results. Feasibility = maturity and what have you already done/validated.

Proposers interested in participating in Direct to Phase II must include in their responses to this topic Phase I feasibility documentation that substantiates the scientific and technical merit and Phase I feasibility described in Phase I above has been met.

(i.e., the small business must have performed a proof of concept like “Phase I” component and/or other validation in a relevant environment, and/or at a much higher Technology Readiness Level (TRL) level (5 or higher) and describe the potential commercialization applications. The documentation provided must validate that the proposer has completed development of technology in previous work or research completed.)

IRAD work: Documentation should include the most relevant information including, but not limited to: technical reports, test data, prototype designs/models, and/or performance goals/results. Work submitted within the feasibility documentation must have been substantially performed by the proposer and/or the principal investigator (PI).

Phase II:
Develop a prototype low-cost IR seeker or integrated seeker component(s). Provide design specifications including size, power, weight, field of view, etc. during development. Validate concept performance in laboratory environment. Demonstrate prototype seeker performance in a ground test facility at relevant environments using an IR target source. Planning for a flight demonstration is desired, but not a requirement.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
These low-cost IR seeker technologies could be utilized in the commercial infrared camera industry.

References:
• https://aerospacedefenserd.com/modular-low-cost-cruise-missiles/
• Adrienne D. Stiff-Roberts, IEEE, “Quantum dot infrared photodetectors: Advantages, challenges, and future research directions”

title: Rapidly Deployable Aerial Interdiction Cluster
summary: Demonstrate a rapidly deployable aerial interdiction cluster to be part of the layered missile defense.
description:
Objective:
Demonstrate a rapidly deployable aerial interdiction cluster to be part of the layered missile defense.

Description:
The Missile Defense Agency seeks novel solutions for a rapidly deployable aerial interdiction cluster for close-in defense against evolving threats to national security assets, including counter-air; counter-drone; electronic warfare; and force protection. The proposed cluster should be capable of transitioning from a standby state to a deployed state and be capable of autonomous, sustained operations. Cluster should contain a number of continuously cycling elements capable of multiple modes of operation (i.e., surveillance, discrimination, electronic warfare, attack). The cluster should contain a high volume of elements that are low size, weight, power, and cost (SWaP-C). The assets should be capable of maneuvering and loitering. Assets should be able to host various sensors and/or effectors capable of interdicting various threats (i.e., hypersonic vehicles, glide vehicles, drones, low-flying aerial objects). Modular cargo bays capable of carrying payloads are desired. System should employ a resilient mesh-node architecture and utilize multiple communication pathways.

Phase I:
Phase I-like proposals will not be evaluated and will be rejected as nonresponsive. For this topic, the Government expects the small business would have accomplished the following in a Phase I-like effort via some other means, e.g., independent research and development (IRAD) or other source, a concept for a workable prototype or design to address, at a minimum, the basic capabilities of the stated objective above. Proposal must show, as appropriate, a demonstrated technical feasibility or nascent capability. The documentation provided must substantiate the proposer’s development of a preliminary understanding of the technology to be applied in their Phase II proposal in meeting topic objectives.

Documentation should comprise all relevant information including, but not limited to, technical reports, test data, prototype designs/models, and performance goals/results. Feasibility = maturity and what have you already done/validated.

Proposers interested in participating in Direct to Phase II must include in their responses to this topic Phase I feasibility documentation that substantiates the scientific and technical merit and Phase I feasibility described in Phase I above has been met.

(i.e., the small business must have performed a proof of concept like “Phase I” component and/or other validation in a relevant environment, and/or at a much higher Technology Readiness Level (TRL) level (5 or higher) and describe the potential commercialization applications. The documentation provided must validate that the proposer has completed development of technology in previous work or research completed.)

IRAD work: Documentation should include the most relevant information including, but not limited to: technical reports, test data, prototype designs/models, and/or performance goals/results. Work submitted within the feasibility documentation must have been substantially performed by the proposer and/or the principal investigator (PI).

Phase II:
Proposals would be evaluated to the degree that they deliver a solution that demonstrates the ability to become a high-volume, low cost-per-unit cluster. Evaluation would also consider to what degree cluster units could be rapidly re-deployed and what percentage of total cluster assets could remain on continuous deployment. Cluster should be capable of detection and tracking of rapidly maneuvering objects. Cluster communication capabilities should have sufficient bandwidth to process and securely relay observation data. Significant technology advancements in core capability areas (swarm autonomy and coordination, advanced sensing and fusion, resilient communications and networking, countermeasures and survivability) would be considered for evaluation. The vendor solution should culminate in a demonstration subjected to conditions to verify function and performance.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Conduct engineering and manufacturing development, test, evaluation in a realistic environment with a system level test-bed. Cluster sensitivity, performance, and communication capabilities should be verified.

References:

title: High Speed Low Size, Weight, and Power (SWaP) Radio Frequency (RF) Communications Systems for Space-to-Space and Space-to-Terrestrial Applications
summary: Provide novel and innovative space communications technologies enabling improved defensive communication capabilities.
description:
Objective:
Provide novel and innovative space communications technologies enabling improved defensive communication capabilities.

Description:
Specific to this topic, to support the Missile Defense Agency (MDA) mission of developing and deploying a layered Missile Defense System to defend the United States, its deployed forces, and friends from missile attacks in all phases of flight, the MDA seeks improved defensive communication capabilities by increasing bandwidth of new low size, weight, and power, radios and antennas to gigabyte speeds. Small form-factor (.1L) or less volume and low power (<10 W) RF radio utilizing Ku bands or higher (due to National Telecommunication and Information Administration (NTIA) restrictions) capable of transmitting data at speeds of 1.5Gbps or greater in a natural space environment is desired. Technology should also be capable of burst transmission of data through the atmosphere to flight vehicles at speeds of 1 Gbps or greater. Communications system capable of meshed (self-forming, self-healing network, high probability of delivery network) High Assurance Internet Protocol Encryptors (HAIPE) interactions for inclusion into "Zero Trust" platforms and networks. Solutions should consider frequency diversity, antenna diversification, and advanced modulation and coding schemas for security and jamming prevention. At the end of the Phase II, two flight radio payloads would be the deliverables.

title: Modeling UV/VIS/near-IR Observables of Dim Hypersonic Configurations
summary: Develop an innovative model of the ultraviolet (UV), visible (Vis), and near-infrared (near-IR) observables of hypersonic configurations at low- and high-altitudes to facilitate detection of dim, hypersonic vehicles by fast-moving observers.
description:
Objective:
Develop an innovative model of the ultraviolet (UV), visible (Vis), and near-infrared (near-IR) observables of hypersonic configurations at low- and high-altitudes to facilitate detection of dim, hypersonic vehicles by fast-moving observers.

Description:
To address dim hypersonic threats in missile defense scenarios, the government desires to enhance current physical modeling tools with the ability to simultaneously predict at-source observable properties in the ultraviolet (UV), visible (VIS), and near-infrared (near-IR) spectral regimes that are founded and built upon Navier-Stokes Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) and Direct Simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) techniques and which accounts for, but is not limited to, vehicle surface heating and ablation, Arrhenius and collisional chemically reacting flows, non-local thermodynamic equilibrium (NLTE) effects, boost and divert jet exhaust interactions with the hypersonic body flowfield, and electro-optical radiative transfer physics-based models. The modeling suite provided by the Joint Army-Navy-NASA Air Force (JANNAF) Exhaust Plume and Signatures Subcommittee (EPSS) [1-4] computes RF and certain IR observables. It is founded on CFD and DSMC flowfield codes, hardbody heating models, and radiative transfer / radar propagation techniques. However, the suite does not model all the underlying chemical and physical mechanisms needed to account for radiative emissions in the identified parts of the electromagnetic spectrum. Phenomenologies that must be enhanced within or added to the suite include, but are not limited to: characterization of thermal protection system response, development of material degradation models, detailed Arrhenius and collisional chemical kinetics models that consistently apply across the continuum and rarefied regimes, and generation of molecular band models for UV, Visible, and near-IR radiative emission. The developed models should be compatible with the JANNAF suite infrastructure. And the resulting assemblage should be able to model realistic hypersonic configurations (such as boost-glide, divert jet, and cruise missiles) under steady, unsteady, and maneuvering flight conditions lasting tens of minutes with high Mach within the atmosphere over a wide range of continuum and rarefied altitudes. The resulting capability is expected to facilitate the acquisition and tracking of dim hypersonic threats in modeling and simulation venues, such as MDA’s existing agency framework, and operational scenarios.

Focus should be on, but is not limited to, adding the capabilities specified in the Description section above. title: Low Cost / Rapidly Producible Booster Insulation Methods
summary: This topic will develop affordable, scalable, high production rate insulation technologies for solid rocket motors.
description:
Objective:
This topic will develop affordable, scalable, high production rate insulation technologies for solid rocket motors.

Description:
Solid propellant rockets use insulation to protect motor cases from the high temperature combustion gases and, in the case of composite cases, prevent egress of gases. Heritage methods for insulating motor cases utilize filled polymers with low thermal conductivities which absorb heat as they decompose. The insulation layer is typically applied through time consuming processes on custom mandrels which require significant manual labor. The Government seeks novel insulation material/processing technologies which reduce insulation processing time and/or cost compared to legacy processes for a variety of motor case geometries and sizes. The primary motor case materials of interest for this solicitation are polymer matrix composites, though applicability to metallic cases is also desirable. Proposals developing reusable or low-cost consumable mandrels which can be easily and quickly removed after insulation lay-up and winding are also of interest. The proposed insulation solution must consider stress limitations in the propellant with variations in temperature during storage and operation. The proposed insulation technology should also meet or exceed the insulating ability of the current state of the art with equal or lower inert mass with an increased production rate and/or lower per unit price.

Phase I:
Phase I-like proposals will not be evaluated and will be rejected as nonresponsive. For this topic, the Government expects the small business would have accomplished the following in a Phase I-like effort via some other means, e.g., independent research and development (IRAD) or other source, a concept for a workable prototype or design to address, at a minimum, the basic capabilities of the stated objective above.
