The documentation provided must validate that the proposer has completed development of technology in previous work or research completed.)

IRAD work: Documentation should include the most relevant information including, but not limited to: technical reports, test data, prototype designs/models, and/or performance goals/results. Work submitted within the feasibility documentation must have been substantially performed by the proposer and/or the principal investigator (PI).

Phase II:
Produce subscale insulated cases with novel, scalable insulation technology, and characterize the erosion rate compared to the current state of the art in sub-scale motor tests with relevant motor propellants. Show that the proposed insulation should meet a 20-year storage life as well as storage conditions as low as -40 °C. The proposed insulation technology must demonstrate adequate adhesion to the propellant to survive storage and operating conditions. The proposal for novel insulation technology must include thermal conductivity and other relevant material characterization. Proposals incorporating novel mandrel technologies must show that motors incorporating the technology can achieve thrust misalignment of less than 1°.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Partner with a propulsion manufacturer to insulate and static test full size motors with a variety of propellants.

title: Virtualization Bridge for Kubernetes: Enabling Complex Legacy Applications
summary: Develop a repeatable implementation pattern for running difficult-to-containerize software inside Kubernetes, beginning with legacy simulation and analysis tools and expanding to niche planning frameworks and complex “digital twins” within air-gapped, high-security environments.
description:
Objective:
Develop a repeatable implementation pattern for running difficult-to-containerize software inside Kubernetes, beginning with legacy simulation and analysis tools and expanding to niche planning frameworks and complex “digital twins” within air-gapped, high-security environments. The goal is to reduce reliance on isolated physical workstations or manually managed Virtual Machines (VMs), improve repeatability through Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC), and facilitate integration with Kubernetes-hosted services such as object storage, databases, logging, monitoring, artificial intelligence / machine learning (AI/ML), workflow engines, and secure access.

Description:
This topic proposes using a virtualization bridge to host applications that are impractical to containerize, bringing orchestration capabilities (scheduling, networking, storage, security, observability, automation, platform integration) to any workload deployed in Kubernetes.

Many mission, engineering, simulation, and analysis tools are challenging to operate as conventional containers due to dependencies on full operating system environments, desktop/Graphical User Interface (GUI) components, licensing services, specialized drivers, hardware access, or tightly coupled runtime requirements. A virtualization bridge allows virtual machines to run as Kubernetes-managed workloads, enabling VM-based applications to coexist with containerized services on the same platform.

This effort proposes using a virtualization bridge to host applications that are impractical to containerize, bringing orchestration capabilities (scheduling, networking, storage, security, observability, automation, platform integration) to any workload deployed in Kubernetes.

The starting point is an available Kubernetes environment (local clusters, hosted platforms, air-gapped environments). The virtualization bridge extends Kubernetes with VM-specific Application Programming Interfaces (APIs), centralizing workload placement, lifecycle management, access control, telemetry, and integration within the Kubernetes control plane. Compared to traditional VM hosting, this model improves operational repeatability and enables cluster-native integration with data services, Continuous Integration / Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) workflows, and AI/ML services.

This approach should be distinguished from related technologies such as container runtime isolation and enterprise virtualization layers. The core technology should be adaptable for local evaluation, deployment to hosted Kubernetes, and later for enterprise distributions or air-gapped environments.

Production-grade solutions require nodes with hardware virtualization support. For Graphics Processing Unit (GPU) or specialized device access, the virtualization bridge should support host device and GPU assignment, with integration patterns for GPU-accelerated VMs.

Phase I:
Phase I-like proposals will not be evaluated and will be rejected as nonresponsive. For this topic, the Government expects the small business would have accomplished the following in a Phase I-like effort via some other means, e.g., independent research and development (IRAD) or other source, a concept for a workable prototype or design to address, at a minimum, the basic capabilities of the stated objective above. The documentation provided must substantiate the proposer’s development of a preliminary understanding of the technology to be applied in their Phase II proposal in meeting topic objectives.

Documentation should comprise all relevant information including, but not limited to, technical reports, test data, prototype designs/models, and performance goals/results. Feasibility = maturity and what have you already done/validated.

Proposers interested in participating in Direct to Phase II must include in their responses to this topic Phase I feasibility documentation that substantiates the scientific and technical merit and Phase I feasibility described in Phase I above has been met.

(i.e., the small business must have performed a proof of concept like “Phase I” component and/or other validation in a relevant environment, and/or at a much higher Technology Readiness Level (TRL) level (5 or higher) and describe the potential commercialization applications. The documentation provided must validate that the proposer has completed development of technology in previous work or research completed.)

IRAD work: Documentation should include the most relevant information including, but not limited to: technical reports, test data, prototype designs/models, and/or performance goals/results. Work submitted within the feasibility documentation must have been substantially performed by the proposer and/or the principal investigator (PI).

Phase II:
Under the proposed solution, the contractor shall implement the virtualization bridge within a hosted or enterprise Kubernetes environment, such as Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS), Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS), or Red Hat OpenShift. The contractor shall convert the local prototype into a fully automated, reusable deployment using Infrastructure-as-Code tools (e.g., Terraform, Helm). The solution shall encompass configuration of the virtualization bridge, persistent storage integration, VM templates, golden images, namespace and Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) boundaries, secure ingress or remote desktop access, Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) / Transport Layer Security (TLS), logging, metrics, backups, and image/data import workflows. The contractor shall ensure that node selection meets hardware virtualization requirements and assess application needs for GPU passthrough, high-memory nodes, and persistent storage. The contractor shall demonstrate repeatable deployment, validated execution of legacy applications, secure user access, telemetry visibility, documented scaling constraints, and provide a baseline cost/performance comparison.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
The contractor shall scale the proposed virtualization bridge solution to support multi-user operations, defining VM profiles for various application types and utilizing Kubernetes scheduling, node pools, quotas, templates, autoscalers, and policy-driven placement. User access shall be integrated with enterprise identity management, RBAC, audit logging, session controls, and approved remote access mechanisms. The solution shall enable cluster-adjacent storage, centralized observability, AI/ML workflow integration, and advanced tooling. Compliance and security controls shall be standardized through Kubernetes-native policies, image provenance, secrets management, network policy, storage encryption, logging, and deployment pipelines. For air-gapped environments, the contractor shall deliver a deployable bundle containing all necessary artifacts and documentation, resulting in a portable, virtualization-based operating model suitable for development, integration, and secure mission deployment.

References:

• Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) – KubeVirt Project: An example of an open-source standard for building virtual machine management interfaces into Kubernetes. (https://kubevirt.io/)
• DoD Platform One / Iron Bank: Repository for hardened containers and DevSecOps standards for secure environments. (https://p1.dso.mil/)
• National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) Special Publication 800-190: Application Container Security Guide for securing container-centric enterprise architectures. (https://csrc.nist.gov/publications/detail/sp/800-190/final)

title: Configurable Operator Decision Models for Constructive Test and Evaluation Simulations
summary: Develop and demonstrate a government-configurable software capability that improves the representation, tuning, execution, and validation of human operator decision effects in constructive test and evaluation simulations.
description:
Objective:
Develop and demonstrate a government-configurable software capability that improves the representation, tuning, execution, and validation of human operator decision effects in constructive test and evaluation simulations. The capability shall enable Government analysts to instantiate credible operator behavior models across selectable conditions such as experience level, workload, decision latency, engagement posture, rules of engagement, mission priority, and information availability; execute repeatable scenario ensembles; capture decision traces and outcome metrics; and integrate with Government-owned or Government-approved constructive simulation environments used for missile defense test planning, mission engineering, wargaming, and analysis.

The desired outcome is an analyst-facing prototype that makes operator-dependent effects measurable, repeatable, explainable, and suitable for verification, validation, and accreditation (VV&A) consideration without requiring extensive scenario-specific software development.

Description:
Government problem: Missile defense test and evaluation rely on constructive simulations to examine large numbers of scenarios, explore operational concepts, evaluate system-of-systems interactions, and reduce risk before live flight events. These simulations can represent physical platforms, sensors, weapons, communications, terrain, and threat laydowns, but operator decision effects are often represented by fixed scripts, simplified timing rules, or manually coded behaviors. This can cause analysis results to overstate or understate operational performance because human choices influence detection, classification, engagement, prioritization, communication, and response timing across the kill chain.

Capability gap: The Government lacks a reusable and validated way to generate, configure, execute, and assess operator decision representations across many scenario variations and proficiency levels. Current approaches can require extensive custom programming for each model, scenario, or operator role; may not provide traceable rationale for actions taken during simulation; and may be difficult to compare across test events, analysis teams, or simulation environments. The gap affects the Government’s ability to understand sensitivity to operator behavior, evaluate alternate tactics, and support VV&A with documented evidence of intended use, assumptions, limitations, data pedigree, and risk.

Why innovative solutions are likely available: The Government believes innovative small businesses can apply advances from artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled simulation, human behavior representation, synthetic data generation, reinforcement learning, design of experiments, digital engineering, development, security, and operations, and modular simulation integration to address this problem. Related industry capabilities already demonstrate AI-assisted constructive simulation, synthetic data generation, intelligent agents, and integration of commercial simulation toolchains with Government simulation environments. This topic seeks to mature those types of innovations into a Government-purpose capability suitable for missile defense test and evaluation workflows.

Government interest: The Government is not seeking a vendor white paper, a visualization-only training game, or a single hard-coded operator model. The Government is seeking a Direct-to-Phase-II prototype capability that can be adapted to multiple missile defense analysis contexts; that can use Government-provided scenarios, models, data, and subject matter expert (SME) input; that can be evaluated against explicit measures of performance and effectiveness; and that can produce artifacts needed for future transition, reuse, and accreditation.

Desired characteristics:

• Open, modular interfaces for integration with constructive simulations and analysis workflows.
• Configurable operator roles and behavior profiles that can be reviewed and adjusted by authorized Government analysts or SMEs.
• Support for scenario ensembles, design of experiments, and repeatable Monte Carlo-style analysis.
• Decision traceability, data provenance, uncertainty characterization, and explainable outputs suitable for analyst review.

Responsible AI, cyber, data-management, and VV&A considerations incorporated from the beginning of Phase II.

Phase I:
Phase I-like proposals will not be evaluated and will be rejected as nonresponsive. For this topic, the Government expects the small business would have accomplished the following in a Phase I-like effort via some other means, e.g., independent research and development (IRAD) or other source, a concept for a workable prototype or design to address, at a minimum, the basic capabilities of the stated objective above. Proposal must show, as appropriate, a demonstrated technical feasibility or nascent capability. Phase II:
The Phase II effort shall mature, integrate, demonstrate, and document a prototype capability suitable for Government evaluation within missile defense constructive modeling, simulation, test, and evaluation workflows. The Government seeks an innovative capability that improves the representation of operator decision effects in constructive simulations, enables repeatable analysis across scenario variations, and provides evidence needed to assess credibility, limitations, and transition potential.

Offerors shall propose their own technical approach, architecture, tools, algorithms, data strategy, and integration methods. The proposed solution shall address the following Key Technical Objectives:

Key Technical Objective 1: Establish a Government-relevant use case and evaluation baseline.

The contractor shall coordinate with Government stakeholders to define at least one representative missile defense constructive simulation use case. The baseline shall include the intended use, operator roles or decision functions to be represented, data assumptions, measures of performance, measures of effectiveness, credibility considerations, and transition constraints. The use case shall be scoped to support meaningful prototype demonstration within the Phase II period.

Key Technical Objective 2: Develop a modular prototype capability for representing operator decision effects.

The contractor shall develop a prototype capability that can receive relevant simulation state information, represent operator-relevant decisions or actions, return those decisions or actions to a simulation or analysis workflow, and record the information needed for Government review. The prototype shall include well-defined interfaces, configuration controls, and logging sufficient to support repeatable analysis, technical assessment, and future integration into Government modeling and simulation environments.

Key Technical Objective 3: Provide configurable and analyzable operator behavior representations.

The contractor shall demonstrate a method for representing operator decision behavior across Government-defined conditions, such as experience level, risk posture, workload, degraded information, rules of engagement, mission priorities, or other operationally relevant factors. The capability shall allow Government users, analysts, or subject matter experts to adjust key assumptions without requiring major software redevelopment for each new scenario. The approach may use AI/ML, statistical learning, reinforcement learning, rules-based methods, hybrid methods, SME-informed models, or other innovative techniques proposed by the offeror.

Key Technical Objective 4: Enable repeatable scenario analysis, validation, and explainability.

The contractor shall provide a workflow to execute and assess repeated simulation runs across Government-defined scenario variables and operator-behavior assumptions. The prototype shall generate outputs that allow the Government to compare decision behavior, mission outcomes, and sensitivity to operator assumptions. The contractor shall provide analyst-readable decision traces, uncertainty and limitation statements, validation evidence, and documentation that supports responsible AI use, VV&A considerations, and reduction of unreviewed automation bias.

Key Technical Objective 5: Demonstrate transition-ready prototype performance and documentation.

The contractor shall conduct a mid-period technical demonstration and a final demonstration in a representative constructive simulation or analysis workflow. The final demonstration shall show configurable operator-behavior representation, repeatable scenario execution, decision/output logging, outcome analysis, and evidence generation suitable for Government evaluation. The contractor shall deliver the prototype software or executable evaluation package, architecture/interface documentation, user guidance, test plan, test report, validation evidence, cybersecurity/deployment notes, data rights assertions, and a Phase III transition plan identifying Missile Defense Agency (MDA) and non-MDA transition opportunities.

Threshold expectation: The contractor shall demonstrate a prototype capability at a relevant-environment maturity level appropriate for Direct-to-Phase-II evaluation, with sufficient integration, documentation, and test evidence for Government users to assess technical performance, credibility, limitations, cybersecurity posture, and transition risk.

Objective expectation: The contractor shall demonstrate a modular, reusable capability that can be adapted to additional constructive simulation environments, operator decision functions, missile defense mission areas, and other Government or commercial modeling and simulation applications with limited new software development.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Scale up the capability from the Phase II prototype into a mature, fieldable capability for Government modeling, simulation, test, evaluation, mission engineering, wargaming, training, and analysis workflows. Work with MDA, other Department of War organizations, Intelligence Community users, and commercial partners to integrate the technology into system-level testbeds, constructive simulation environments, and analyst workflows.

title: Multi-Fidelity Transfer Learning for Defense Applications
summary: Use new and evolving Artificial Intelligence (AI) training techniques, algorithms, and protocols to rapidly reduce the resources required to integrate AI into the Missile Defense System (MDS).
description:
Objective:
Use new and evolving Artificial Intelligence (AI) training techniques, algorithms, and protocols to rapidly reduce the resources required to integrate AI into the Missile Defense System (MDS).

Description:
Rapid Artificial Intelligence (AI) integration into the MDS is required for the United States to properly defend itself against its adversaries. The development of robust Artificial Intelligence/Machine Learning (AI/ML) agents for complex missile defense and aerospace applications is often constrained by the computational cost, limited availability, and security restrictions of high-fidelity simulation environments. Transfer learning provides a critical pathway to overcoming these barriers. By initially training agents on low-fidelity models or unclassified representations—where data is abundant and computational demands are reduced—core behaviors, strategies, and decision-making frameworks could be efficiently developed and refined. These pretrained models could then be adapted and optimized in high-fidelity and/or environments at higher classification levels, allowing the agent to leverage its foundational knowledge while rapidly acquiring the nuanced performance required for operational deployment. This staged approach significantly reduces training time, minimizes resource expenditure, and mitigates the risk of overfitting to scarce high-fidelity/classified data. Moreover, it enables iterative development cycles where low-fidelity environments serve as agile testbeds for innovation, and high-fidelity environments refine and validate for mission-readiness. Leveraging transfer learning in this manner not only accelerates capability delivery but also ensures that AI/ML systems achieve the precision, resilience, and adaptability necessary for real-world mission success.

Phase I:
Phase I-like proposals will not be evaluated and will be rejected as nonresponsive. For this topic, the Government expects the small business would have accomplished the following in a Phase I-like effort via some other means, e.g., independent research and development (IRAD) or other source, a concept for a workable prototype or design to address, at a minimum, the basic capabilities of the stated objective above. Proposal must show, as appropriate, a demonstrated technical feasibility or nascent capability. The documentation provided must substantiate the proposer’s development of a preliminary understanding of the technology to be applied in their Phase II proposal in meeting topic objectives.

Documentation should comprise all relevant information including, but not limited to, technical reports, test data, prototype designs/models, and performance goals/results. Feasibility = maturity and what have you already done/validated.

Proposers interested in participating in Direct to Phase II must include in their responses to this topic Phase I feasibility documentation that substantiates the scientific and technical merit and Phase I feasibility described in Phase I above has been met.

(i.e., the small business must have performed a proof of concept like “Phase I” component and/or other validation in a relevant environment, and/or at a much higher Technology Readiness Level (TRL) level (5 or higher) and describe the potential commercialization applications. The documentation provided must validate that the proposer has completed development of technology in previous work or research completed.)

IRAD work: Documentation should include the most relevant information including, but not limited to: technical reports, test data, prototype designs/models, and/or performance goals/results. Work submitted within the feasibility documentation must have been substantially performed by the proposer and/or the principal investigator (PI).

Phase II:
Create a full prototype capability implementing the tools and demonstrating the processes required to enable AI transfer learning for MDS applications. Design and conduct a case study using the prototype implementation with representative data and models.

Key Technical Objectives:

-Establish a low fidelity training environment based on limited data for AI agent learning applicable to MDS use cases.

-Develop, apply, and implement transfer learning methodologies to drive transfer learning.

-Develop and integrate high fidelity representations of MDS simulation environment across multiple levels of classification.

-Demonstrate resource savings of transfer learning methods versus traditional training methods.

-Design and implement a human-machine interface to seamlessly orchestrate the AI training workflows.

-Deliver prototype AI training workflows for mission relevant use cases that integrate with existing MDS agent training systems.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Scale up the capability from the prototype utilizing the new

processes and software technologies developed in Phase II into a mature, fieldable capability. Work with additional DoD or commercial organizations to integrate the technology into a system level testbed for analyst use.

title: Compact Passive Radar
summary: Develop a low-cost, small form factor, attritable passive radar sensor capable of detecting and tracking targets using external RF signals for tactical unmanned and expendable platforms.
description:
Objective:
Develop a low-cost, small form factor, attritable passive radar sensor capable of detecting and tracking targets using external RF signals for tactical unmanned and expendable platforms.

Description:
In contested A2/AD environments, active radar emissions act as beacons for adversary Electronic Warfare. To ensure survivability, the DoW requires covert sensing utilizing "illuminators of opportunity." This effort requires a 100% receive-only payload; the sensor shall not transmit any RF energy.

Current passive systems are bulky, expensive, and primarily optimized for SIGINT/ESM rather than radar functionality. They lack the tightly synchronized, multi-channel receivers necessary for direct reference signal acquisition, spatial processing, and clutter cancellation. The DoW seeks a paradigm shift toward low-cost, multi-channel "attritable" (expendable) sensors designed specifically for high-risk deployments.

This topic seeks the development of a Small Form Factor (SFF) passive X-Band radar featuring both Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) imaging and Ground Moving Target Indicator (GMTI) capabilities. Optimized for extreme Size, Weight, Power, and Cost (SWaP-C) constraints, the payload must be light enough for integration onto Group 1 or 2 UAS, loitering munitions, or unattended ground sensors.

Phase I:
The objective of Phase I is to conduct a feasibility study to determine the scientific, technical, and commercial merit of a small form factor, attritable passive radar architecture. Offerors are expected to define a comprehensive system architecture, identifying critical low-cost receiver components, antenna configurations suitable for SFF platforms, and highly efficient edge-processing hardware. The effort will include developing proof-of-concept signal processing algorithms for reference signal isolation, clutter cancellation, and target detection and/or tracking under constrained computational limits. The desired end product is a robust simulation and a basic laboratory prototype that validates the feasibility of detecting targets using signals of opportunity while strictly adhering to the SWaP-C metrics required for expendable systems.

Phase II:
Phase II culminates in the delivery of a viable hardware prototype. Offerors are expected to transition their Phase I concepts into a physical, highly miniaturized sensor prototype suitable for integration onto a small UAS or expendable ground node. The minimum required deliverable is a functional prototype that successfully demonstrates passive stationary and moving target detection, tracking, and imaging in a realistic outdoor environment utilizing RF illumination (cooperative or non-cooperative signals of opportunity) without emitting any RF energy from the passive sensor itself. The performer must characterize system performance, demonstrate real-time edge processing that outputs actionable products, and validate that the unit cost and SWaP footprint meet the criteria for a truly attritable tactical asset.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
In Phase III, the expendable passive radar sensor is expected to transition into operational military platforms and commercial markets, supported by non-SBIR/STTR funding. For DoW applications, the technology will be integrated into launched effects, loitering munitions, and distributed unattended ground sensor networks. In the commercial sector, potential applications include low-cost air traffic monitoring, counter-UAS (cUAS) surveillance for critical infrastructure, and general airspace monitoring where adding active RF spectrum clutter is undesirable or prohibited.

References:
• Melvin, W. L., & Scheer, J. A. (Eds.). (2014). Principles of Modern Radar: Radar Applications (Volume 3). SciTech Publishing / IET.
• Moo, P. W., & Ding, Z. (2015). Adaptive Radar Resource Management. Academic Press (Elsevier).

title: Monolithic Graphene–CMOS Broadband (UV-LWIR) Focal Plane Arrays for target detection in low-light conditions
summary: Develop, fabricate, and demonstrate a wafer-scale, monolithically integrated graphene-on-CMOS image sensor that provides broadband imaging from 300 nm to 10,000 nm in a compact, low-power, uncooled focal plane array.
description:
Objective:
Develop, fabricate, and demonstrate a wafer-scale, monolithically integrated graphene-on-CMOS image sensor that provides broadband imaging from 300 nm to 10,000 nm in a compact, low-power, uncooled focal plane array.

Description:
The Navy continues to field multiple seeker technologies to detect, identify and engage targets in multi-domain operations through obscurants. However, you cannot detect something you cannot see. Each wavelength range provide unique opportunity to glean information. Currently, for each wavelength range a distinct material system technology is required: AlGaN for UV, analog devices for NIR, InGaAs for short wavelength infrared (SWIR), HgCdTe (MCT) and III-V strain-layer superlattice (SLS) detectors for MWIR-LWIR. In addition, the incumbent detector technologies — for example indium gallium arsenide (InGaAs). This topic seeks to retire the principal risks that stand between these demonstrations and a fieldable naval imager: (1) graphene material quality and uniformity at the wafer scale — carrier mobility, Dirac-point control, low hysteresis, and low defect density (e.g., Raman D-to-G intensity ratio) held tight across full wafers and lot to lot; (2) repeatable, high-yield BEOL transfer, encapsulation, patterning, and contacting of graphene on CMOS read-out wafers; (3) absorber sensitization and passivation that deliver uniform, stable, low-noise broadband response; and (4) an imaging FPA meeting the noise-equivalent irradiance, dynamic range, frame rate, operability, and stability required for naval ISR. Proposers should target a substantial increase in integrated-device carrier mobility (goal approaching 10,000 cm²/V·s), tight pixel-to-pixel uniformity, and a manufacturable process flow with a clear path to pilot-scale production. photodiode arrays for SWIR are hybridized to a silicon read-out integrated circuit (ROIC) by indium-bump flip-chip bonding. This is a mature approach but constrained by high unit cost, a limited domestic foundry base, pixel pitches that are difficult to scale below roughly 15 µm, array formats limited by hybridization yield, and a spectral response that typically cuts off near 1,700 nm. These constraints limit the resolution, affordability, and proliferation of imagers across the size-, weight-, power-, and cost-constrained (SWaP-c) platforms.

Phase I:
This topic solicits Direct-to-Phase-II (DP2) proposals only; Phase I proposals will not be accepted. Offerors must document that Phase I feasibility has already been established through prior work. Acceptable feasibility evidence includes the fabrication and measured characterization of graphene phototransistor and/or graphene-on-CMOS coupon test structures exhibiting broadband (UV-through-LWIR) photoresponse; demonstration of die- or wafer-scale graphene integration with quantified device yield and uniformity. Documentation may comprise technical reports, peer-reviewed publications, measured data, and design artifacts sufficient to substantiate the scientific, technical, and commercial merit required to enter Phase II. Requirements definition for the naval use case, detailed focal-plane-array performance modeling, and pixel-architecture and back-end-of-line (BEOL) integration-flow design need not be complete at proposal; these activities are carried into the Phase II Base effort below.

Phase II:
Design, fabricate, and deliver a prototype monolithic graphene–CMOS broadband/SWIR FPA, maturing the technology from documented feasibility through a demonstrated camera. The effort is organized into a Base task that completes design and risk reduction and a prototype task that builds and characterizes the imager.Base (design and risk reduction). Define imager requirements against a representative naval ISR use case; develop and validate FPA performance models (spectral response, responsivity, noise-equivalent irradiance, dynamic range, operability); and complete the pixel-architecture and BEOL integration-flow design for a foundry CMOS ROIC. Fabricate and characterize coupon-level and small-array test structures to confirm material quality, integration yield, and broadband photoresponse, and finalize the wafer-scale process definition.

Prototype (fabrication and demonstration). Mature the wafer-scale process — graphene growth/transfer, encapsulation, patterning, contacting, and absorber sensitization — to demonstrate high device yield and pixel-to-pixel uniformity across full wafers. Build and demonstrate a functioning broadband camera (sensor plus read-out and minimal supporting electronics and optics) and characterize spectral response, responsivity, noise-equivalent irradiance, dynamic range, frame rate, operability, fixed-pattern noise, and stability against Navy-relevant targets, including passive low-light (atmospheric nightglow) imaging and imaging through obscurants such as fog and haze. Conduct an initial environmental and reliability assessment.

Deliverables. Validated performance models and final FPA design; prototype FPA(s)/camera(s); the documented wafer-scale process flow with measured yield and uniformity; a full test-and-evaluation data package; and a Phase III transition and manufacturing plan, including a path to a pilot qualification lot on the order of tens of wafers with defined yield and performance metrics.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Transition the technology to naval and joint platforms that require affordable, compact, broadband/SWIR imaging — unmanned aerial, surface, and undersea vehicles; handheld, weapon-, and helmet-mounted night-vision and threat-warning systems; shipboard situational-awareness and navigation suites; and distributed or expendable sensor nodes — and to hyperspectral and multispectral payloads for camouflage/decoy discrimination and littoral mine countermeasures. Establish and qualify a domestic, CMOS-foundry-based manufacturing capability for monolithic 2D-material FPAs. The same platform carries broad commercial dual-use value in automotive and autonomous-vehicle vision (through fog, smoke, and darkness), machine vision and semiconductor/solar-wafer inspection, agricultural and food-quality sorting, medical and biometric imaging, and environmental and industrial-process monitoring, supporting an economically sustainable supply base.

References:
• Goossens, S., Navickaite, G., Monasterio, C., et al. “Broadband image sensor array based on graphene–CMOS integration.” Nature Photonics 11, 366–371 (2017). https://doi.org/10.1038/nphoton.2017.752
• Neumaier, D., Pindl, S., Lemme, M. C. “Integrating graphene into semiconductor fabrication lines.” Nature Materials 18, 525–529 (2019). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41563-019-0359-7
• Koppens, F. H. L., Mueller, Avouris, P., et al. “Photodetectors based on graphene, other two-dimensional materials and hybrid systems.” Nature Nanotechnology 9, 780–793 (2014). https://doi.org/10.1038/nnano.2014.215

title: Smart Venues and Stadiums
summary: The objective of this Phase II effort is to design, validate, and demonstrate a secure, high-density private 5G network platform for stadiums and large venues—integrating open-source OCUDU, SD-Core, SD-RAN, and OSC components—to deliver resilient, multi-service communication alongside a 6G-ready Integrated Sensing and Communication (ISAC) architecture.
description:
Objective:
The objective of this Phase II effort is to design, validate, and demonstrate a secure, high-density private 5G network platform for stadiums and large venues—integrating open-source OCUDU, SD-Core, SD-RAN, and OSC components—to deliver resilient, multi-service communication alongside a 6G-ready Integrated Sensing and Communication (ISAC) architecture. This platform will be validated at a representative venue site to prove stable performance under extreme device congestion, enable native device localization for crowd analytics, and establish a cost-effective, vendor-neutral dual-use framework for both commercial entertainment venues and dense military installation environments.

Description:
The realistic near-to-mid-term serviceable addressable market for private 5G/6G-ready platforms among U.S. venues and stadiums is a subset of venues with acute connectivity, safety, and operational pain: major-league and collegiate stadiums, multi-purpose arenas, outdoor amphitheaters, and convention/exhibition centers that host recurring high-density events, require public-safety-grade coverage throughout bowls, concourses, tunnels, and back-of-house areas, and are increasingly asked to support fan-facing digital experiences, cashier less concessions, camera and sensor networks, and first-responder communications simultaneously on event day. Venues already invest heavily in connectivity infrastructure, yet several published industry reports indicate persistent cost and coverage pain. Distributed Antenna System (DAS) deployments in large public venues have grown from a few million dollars in early builds to routinely tens of millions of dollars. Independent of venue scale, active multi-carrier DAS hardware and installation is commonly quoted at $5–$10 per square foot, meaning even a mid-sized 300,000 sq. ft. concourse/bowl footprint implies a multi-million-dollar build before integration, spectrum, and ongoing carrier-management costs.

The United States features an extensive footprint of sports and entertainment infrastructure, spanning an estimated 2,000 to 5,000 major stadiums and arenas when accounting for all professional, collegiate, and municipal facilities, which further scales to over 15,000 total venues if relatively large localized high school stadium is included. Beyond stadiums and arenas, industry directories catalog well over 400 U.S. convention and exhibition centers, ranging from single-hall regional facilities to multi-million-square-foot complexes. Together, these figures put the large-venue addressable base at several hundred U.S. facilities, before counting mid-sized arenas, amphitheaters, and secondary convention space. Besides, localized specific large gatherings (such as fairs) add up to several thousand.

Despite this infrastructure spend, published reviews consistently cite coverage dead zones in lower bowls and concourses, congestion during peak moments (kickoff, halftime, entry/egress), and multi-year vendor lock-in as recurring pain points, and industry reporting suggests that MNO appetite to fund new DAS builds outside "Tier 1" venues (70,000+ capacity or 200+ events/year) is shrinking, leaving small and mid-sized venues with a widening connectivity gap.

This segment buys on measurable fan and operational outcomes (dropped-call rate at kickoff, POS uptime, camera uptime, incident-response time), not on global platform standardization, and its stated barriers to adopting anything other than the incumbent DAS/neutral-host model are consistent: high capex and multi-year contract terms, uncertainty about interoperability across multiple wireless carriers that must all be hosted on one system, integration complexity with legacy venue IT/OT and public-safety radio systems, and a lack of in-house RF/cellular engineering staff.

An all-open-source stack removes the structural cost and lock-in that makes proprietary DAS platforms a poor fit for this segment's economics. Because OCUDU communicates with the rest of the network over open, standardized interfaces (especially the O-RAN 7.2x split to the O-RU), the network can be assembled from whichever RU vendor and antenna form factor best fits a given venue's bowl geometry, concourse layout, and budget. Together, OCUDU, SD-Core, SD-RAN, and OSC form one integrated, fully open-source 5G stack that a systems integrator can deploy, support, and price as a right-sized, as-a-service offer for a single venue, rather than a broad, vendor-locked, multi-carrier neutral-host platform.

The trade-off of an all-open-source stack is the same one seen in other verticals: the burden of proving interoperability, stability, and security shifts from a single vendor's warranty to the integrator and the open-source community. Venue operators, who by their own account do not carry in-house cellular or RF engineering expertise, have essentially zero tolerance for connectivity failures discovered live, on a broadcast event, in front of tens of thousands of people. This is exactly the gap the on-going OCUDU Testing & Validation Plan, and its RTEC-centered extensions, are designed to close: independently witnessed, multi-vendor testing of device diversity, RU diversity, high-density/high-mobility RF performance, Core/RIC/SMO integration, and security. The proposal should leverage the current, on-going testing and evaluation activities in RTECs and associated results on this front.

Although this topic is anchored in a specific vertical to ensure a concrete deployment environment, real users, and a defensible commercialization path, proposers should recognize and are required to present the technical work in terms of the generic network performance classes it advances. Improvements made to the OCUDU O-CU/O-DU under this effort (scheduler behavior, mobility management, uplink capacity, stability under sustained load, security features) are expected to generalize across verticals and to benefit the broader community of RAN developers building on OCUDU. The Technical Volume shall include a mapping of each selected use case, and its associated Section 3.0 KPMs, to the performance class or classes it exercises, and shall identify which anticipated OCUDU code or feature enhancements correspond to each class.

Phase I:
This topic is accepting Direct to Phase II proposals ONLY. Therefore, a formal Phase I award will not be issued.

To qualify for a Phase II award, proposers must submit Feasibility Documentation (as part of their proposal package) demonstrating that they have already completed "Phase I-type" research and development. The purpose of this documentation is to prove that the underlying technology is mature, scientifically sound, and ready to transition immediately into the Phase II prototyping and testing environment.

The Government will accept a wide variety of documentation styles. Proposers do not need to have a perfect, finished product, but they must show that their core ideas have been successfully tested. One or more of the following items should be included to prove technology readiness:

• Test Data & Metrics: Real-world measurements, performance charts, or network test data from previous lab environments or early field trials.
• Technical Reports & White Papers: Written summaries explaining your previous research, system designs, or software integration efforts.
• Prototype Designs & Simulation Models: Diagrams, architectural blueprints, or computer simulation results showing how your proposed software and hardware components interact.
• Previous Project Outcomes: Success criteria, milestone reports, or commercialization results from prior private, academic, or non-SBIR federally funded work.

Phase II:
For this topic, the dominant performance classes are extreme user density, ultra-secure operation, and integrated sensing: tens of thousands of concurrent devices per venue with sharp event-day load peaks, public-safety-grade availability and access control across bowls, concourses, and back-of-house areas, and an architecture evolvable to 6G Integrated Sensing and Communication (ISAC). Research and development for this effort should address, at minimum, the following questions:

• All-Open-Source Economics: What is the fully loaded cost (integration, support, spectrum, hardware, RF design) of an OCUDU + SD-Core + SD-RAN + OSC deployment at venue scale relative to a proprietary DAS/neutral-host platform, and how should that be packaged as a CBRS-based, as-a-service offer within the price point venue operators require?
• Use-Case-First Deployment: Which of the use cases defined below deliver the fastest, most measurable ROI on the open-source stack, and what RTEC-executed interoperability tests (Device, RU, Core, RIC/SMO, and Infrastructure dimensions) are needed to validate each one end-to-end under stadium-scale, high-density loading conditions?
• 6G/ISAC Evolution Path: What architectural changes (waveform, RU capability, RIC application, and SMO orchestration) are required to evolve the platform from a 5G communications-only deployment to a 6G-ready platform capable of Integrated Sensing and Communication, and which ISAC-enabled use cases can be prototyped now using 5G-Advanced sensing features as a bridge to native 6G ISAC?
• Trust in Open Source: How does RTEC-executed testing of the full open-source stack reduce the integration risk and skills-shortage barrier venue operators most often cite, and what evidence package best converts community-maintained, no-license-fee software into a procurement-ready proof point for a buyer with no in-house cellular expertise?

Solutions leveraging artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) for crowd analytics, predictive maintenance, network optimization, or automated fault resolution are encouraged but not required. DoW will consider any novel concept that increases the reliability, economics, and trustworthiness of an all-open-source private 5G/FutureG platform for the venues and stadiums vertical.

Dual-use opportunities are expected across commercial venue operators, DoW-affiliated event and installation venues, and public-safety agencies.

Proposers must address at least two of the following four use cases in their Phase II Statement of Work and must identify which use case(s) their reference architecture and pilot deployment are designed to validate. Each use case below is defined in terms of the operational scenario it supports, the connectivity and/or sensing requirement it places on the platform. Device-Class Diversity and 5G RedCap. Each use-case set spans device classes from full-capability UEs (equipment modems, cameras, broadcast and production units) to reduced-capability IoT endpoints (sensors, wearables, tags, and trackers). Proposers shall address how the platform serves reduced-capability device classes, including 3GPP Release 17 Reduced Capability (RedCap) and Release 18 eRedCap UEs, and shall identify any OCUDU scheduler or feature enhancements required to support RedCap operation; such enhancements are strongly encouraged as upstream contributions under the common OCUDU benchmarking and enhancement work package. Where RedCap-certified devices are not commercially available for a given endpoint type at demonstration time, proposers may demonstrate with available device classes (or emulated RedCap UE profiles) and shall document the RedCap migration path.

Use Case 1: High-Density Fan Connectivity & Broadcast/Production Backhaul

Tens of thousands of fans, concession point-of-sale terminals, ticketing scanners, and broadcast/production camera and audio feeds must all operate simultaneously within a single bowl and concourse footprint, with demand spiking sharply at kickoff, halftime, and egress. Legacy DAS and Wi-Fi are commonly saturated at these peak moments, producing dropped sessions and stalled transactions. This use case requires the platform to sustain high concurrent-device density with consistent per-user throughput, plus dedicated low-latency, low-jitter uplink capacity for broadcast and production camera backhaul, across the full bowl and concourse footprint.

Use Case 2: ISAC-Enabled Crowd Analytics & Situational Awareness (6G-Ready)

Venue operators and public-safety personnel need continuous, accurate awareness of crowd density, flow, and anomalies (bottlenecks at egress, unattended objects, unauthorized drone incursion into restricted airspace above the bowl) to prevent crushing incidents/stampedes and respond quickly to emerging threats. Deploying a separate dedicated sensor network (radar, lidar, additional camera arrays) to provide this awareness is costly and adds another system to integrate. This use case requires the platform to support Integrated Sensing and Communication (ISAC). ISAC uses the same radio infrastructure and spectrum that carries communication traffic to also sense the physical environment (bistatic or monostatic sensing from gNB/O-RU hardware, correlated with RIC-hosted analytics applications), without requiring a separate sensing-only network build. [3GPP Release 19 Technical Report (TR) 22.837 identifies more than 30 ISAC use cases spanning applications such as object and intruder detection, environmental monitoring, motion sensing, and public-safety scenarios directly applicable to stadiums, arenas, and convention centers. Complementing these use cases, 3GPP TS 22.137 establishes a standardized set of ISAC performance metrics, including positioning accuracy, velocity accuracy, sensing resolution, sensing range, refresh rate, latency, and missed-detection and false-alarm probabilities, to enable consistent evaluation and deployment of sensing-enabled wireless networks.] Proposers should treat 5G-Advanced sensing features as the near-term bridge path toward native 6G ISAC.

Hybrid localization architecture. Proposers shall employ a hybrid architecture in which standardized network-native UE positioning (3GPP Release 16/17 NR positioning: UL-TDoA, multi-RTT, AoA/AoD) over the connected device population provides the primary, near-term source of crowd density, flow, and bottleneck analytics, with appropriate aggregation and anonymization for fan-facing devices and RF sensing (ISAC) is applied to non-cooperative targets that carry no connected device. Crowd-analytics KPMs may be satisfied via UE positioning in the Phase II demonstration.

Tiered scope. Sensing functions under this use case are tiered by 12-month feasibility. Tier 1 (Phase II demonstration): (a) crowd density and flow analytics derived from network-native UE positioning of connected devices (see the hybrid-localization requirement above), aggregated and anonymized; and (b) at least one non-cooperative RF-sensing bridge function achievable at 5G-Advanced maturity and deployed sensing bandwidths (for example, detection of unauthorized drone incursion exploiting Doppler and motion signatures) demonstrated in a laboratory or limited field configuration. Tier 2 (roadmap): unattended-object detection and fine-grained tracking of individuals within dense, multi-directional crowds, which are limited by achievable sensing resolution (approximately c/2B) at deployable bandwidths; these shall be addressed in the documented 6G/ISAC evolution path with quantified bandwidth, waveform, aperture, and sensor-fusion requirements rather than demonstrated in Phase II. Custom or modified waveforms are not required for Phase II. The Positioning/Velocity accuracy, Anomaly Alert, and Missed-Detection/False-Alarm KPMs in the table below apply to the Tier 1 demonstrated function(s).

Use Case 3: Public Safety & First Responder Priority Communications

First responders, venue security, and event staff require reliable, prioritized push-to-talk and data communications throughout the bowl, concourses, tunnels, loading docks, and below-grade back-of-house areas that legacy DAS and Wi-Fi frequently fail to reach or fail to prioritize during network congestion. This use case requires the platform to sustain low-latency, high-reliability, priority/preemption-capable connectivity for public-safety traffic across the full indoor venue footprint, including areas outside typical fan-facing coverage design.

Use Case 4: Venue Operations, Logistics & Outdoor Perimeter Coverage

Loading docks, outdoor plazas, parking structures, and perimeter areas surrounding a venue increasingly require connectivity for autonomous cleaning and security robots, connected cameras, RFID/asset tracking for concessions and merchandise logistics, and credentialed-access control, yet typically fall outside indoor DAS/Wi-Fi coverage entirely. This use case requires the platform to extend secure, private coverage into outdoor plaza, parking, and perimeter areas immediately adjacent to the venue, using the same OCUDU-based infrastructure rather than a separate outdoor Wi-Fi or cellular repeater buildout.

KPMs for Phase II

For Phase II, proposers should address specific, relevant, measurable, and quantifiable key performance metrics (KPMs), including, for example, concurrent-device density, sensing detection accuracy, latency, jitter, and service availability. An example KPM in context could be as follows: "The platform must sustain a session success rate greater than 99.5% for fan-facing connections at a concurrent-device density of 3,000 devices per acre in the lower bowl." Other suggested KPMs for the various use cases and system requirements are given below for reference.

The KPM values in the tables below are suggested reference values, not pass/fail contract requirements. Proposers shall propose specific, justified KPM targets in the Technical Volume, calibrated to their selected use cases, demonstration environment, spectrum plan, and channel bandwidth; deviations from the suggested values must be technically justified. Threshold values represent the intended standard of Phase II demonstration success; Objective values are stretch goals, some of which are expected to mature during Phase III or along the FutureG evolution path. Final KPM targets will be agreed with the Government at kickoff and confirmed at the Critical Design Review. Consistent with Section 4.1, partial achievement within a defined and documented scope may be considered successful.

Latency measurement definition. Latency KPMs in this document denote round-trip application-layer latency measured between the UE application interface and the local edge application endpoint served behind the on-site/edge UPF (i.e., device-to-edge through the RAN and core user plane, excluding external WAN transport). Handover time denotes user-plane interruption time at the RAN, per 3GPP definitions. For each latency KPM adopted, proposers shall specify the measurement reference points, the traffic type and packet size, and the measurement methodology (e.g., KPI definitions per 3GPP TS 28.554), and shall include in the Critical Design Document a latency budget decomposition across air interface, DU/CU processing, fronthaul and F1 transport, core user plane, and application processing.

Suggested KPMs for Use Case 1: High-Density Fan Connectivity & Broadcast/Production Backhaul

These metrics focus on the platform's ability to sustain high device density and dedicated broadcast/production bandwidth during peak event moments. Thresholds are anchored to published stadium Wi-Fi/DAS deployment data; a particular venue's own concurrent-connection and peak-throughput figures may be used instead to calibrate a proposer's specific KPM targets.

Phase II consists of an eighteen-month PoP focused on prototype production, test, and evaluation. Key milestones include:

• Month 1: Kickoff and TIM
• Monthly Status Reports (MSRs)
• Month 12: Critical Design Review (CDR)
• Month 16: Prototype demonstration
• Month 14: Final design review, demonstration, and assessment
• Month 18: Final Phase II Report

MSRs are to be presented to the OCUDU T&E Working Group as well, bringing the community up to speed on progress. Prototype demonstrations will be performed at the proposer's site, ideally an operating or representative venue/stadium environment (or a full-scale representative test bed where live-venue access is not feasible during Phase II). Partial solutions may be considered successful if effective within a defined scope. A final technical report detailing the capabilities demonstrated will be required. Extended user evaluations or additional prototypes may be pursued based on utility.

OCUDU and Open-Source Integration

The Open Centralized Unit Distributed Unit (OCUDU) software codebase is released and continuously enhanced with a 3GPP-compliant open-source Centralized Unit (CU) and Distributed Unit (DU) implementation supporting open interfaces. Proposers should integrate OCUDU together with SD-Core (5G Core), SD-RAN (Near-RT RIC), and the OSC stack (Non-RT RIC and SMO) into a single, fully open-source reference architecture, with no proprietary core, RIC, or SMO component anywhere in the stack. Proposers should additionally document, and where feasible demonstrate, the specific RAN and RIC-application changes required to bridge toward native 6G ISAC capability. The MVP demonstration, including physical RUs and UEs (and, for Use Case 2, ISAC-capable RU/sensing hardware or software-defined sensing functions), will need to occur at the venue-representative site described above. Performers should address scalability, including testing across multiple RU vendors and hardware-accelerator options, and should leverage RTEC-executed interoperability testing to address integration risks ahead of the demonstration wherever a validated reference configuration already exists.

OCUDU Baseline Benchmarking and Upstream Enhancement:

All performers under this topic shall execute the following common work package, which is a required element of the Phase II Statement of Work regardless of the use cases selected.

Task A: Baseline Benchmark. Establish a quantified performance baseline of the integrated open-source stack (OCUDU + SD-Core + SD-RAN + OSC) against the KPMs relevant to the selected use cases, including the General System and Architectural Requirements. An emulated end-to-end configuration (emulated RUs and UEs, RF channel emulation, and/or synthetic load generation) is acceptable and encouraged for the baseline, provided the benchmark methodology, tooling, configurations, and results are fully documented and reproducible. Where an RTEC-validated reference configuration already exists for the proposed RU/Core/RIC/SMO combination, the baseline shall incorporate available RTEC results rather than duplicate them. Baseline methodology and results shall be presented to the OCUDU T&E Working Group.

Task B: Code and Feature Enhancement. Identify the gaps between baseline performance and the threshold and objective values, and develop the OCUDU code improvements and features required to close them (e.g., scheduler and QoS enhancements, mobility/handover optimization, uplink capacity improvements, stability hardening, security features). All modifications to OCUDU shall be contributed upstream through the project's standard contribution and review process; enhancements that cannot be upstreamed shall be documented with rationale. Progress against each targeted KPM, and the status of each upstream contribution, shall be reported in the Monthly Status Reports presented to the OCUDU T&E Working Group.

Task C: Benchmark and Regression Harness. Deliver the emulation-based end-to-end benchmark suite developed under Task A as a repeatable, documented, open-source harness suitable for adoption by the OCUDU community and RTECs for regression testing of future OCUDU releases. This work package complements, and does not replace, the interoperability testing and the physical MVP demonstration required elsewhere in this topic. Emulated results establish the baseline and guide enhancement work; over-the-air performance with physical RUs and UEs at the RTEC and/or representative demonstration site remains the standard of evidence for final KPM achievement.

Security Requirements

Security shall be a first-class design requirement of the platform, not a demonstration afterthought. Performers shall implement and document a security architecture covering: 3GPP security per TS 33.501 (mutual authentication, air-interface encryption and integrity protection); protection of the O-RAN open interfaces (open fronthaul, E2, A1, O1) per O-RAN WG11 specifications; zero-trust principles per NIST SP 800-207, including least-privilege access and separation of management and user traffic; monitoring of Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) affecting OCUDU and its dependencies, and timely upstream patching. Security features and hardening developed for OCUDU shall be contributed upstream under the common benchmarking and enhancement work package. The security architecture shall be documented at CDR and validated in RTEC testing, and the MVP demonstration shall include at least one security capability shown live (e.g., rejection of an unauthorized device, encrypted fronthaul, or detection of a simulated intrusion).

Phase II Deliverables

Kickoff and TIM slides

• Monthly Status Reports (MSRs)
• Critical Design Document (full reference architecture: OCUDU + SD-Core + SD-RAN + OSC, including the 6G/ISAC evolution path)
• Key Performance Metrics
• MVP Demonstration Slides and Documentation, including a description of the demonstration site's fidelity to venue/stadium conditions and the KPI results achieved against Section 3.0 thresholds
• Reference Configuration Package: executables, integration documentation, and RTEC test results for the validated RU/Core/RIC/SMO combination(s) used
• Integration of the platform into an RTEC-affiliated test/evaluation network and/or a venue-representative demonstration site, demonstrating at least one of the two selected use cases.
• Integration of the platform into an RTEC-affiliated test/evaluation network and/or a factory-representative demonstration site, demonstrating at least one of the two selected use cases.
• OCUDU Baseline Benchmark Report: methodology, emulation environment description, configurations, and measured baseline results against Section 3.0 KPMs (expected by Month 3)
• Upstream Contribution Log: itemized record of OCUDU code contributions (patches/pull requests), their review status, and the KPM gap each addresses (updated in each MSR; final version in the Final Technical Report)
• Open-source benchmark and regression harness, with documentation sufficient for independent execution by RTECs and the OCUDU community
• Final Design Document
• Final Technical Report

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
The advanced private 5G and FutureG networking platform outlined in this solicitation presents significant dual-use opportunities by leveraging a single, open-source technology stack to serve both commercial venues and critical DoW operational needs.

For commercial interests, this technology offers a cost-effective and vendor-neutral alternative to proprietary systems in stadiums, arenas, and convention centers. It aims to enhance fan experiences with high-density connectivity, support broadcast backhauling, and improve venue operations through integrated sensing for crowd analytics and situational awareness.

For the DoW, the same platform provides resilient, secure, and high-density wireless coverage essential for DoW-affiliated event venues, training facilities, and large-scale installation assembly spaces. The platform's capability for Integrated Sensing and Communication (ISAC) can be adapted for enhanced situational awareness, asset tracking, and security monitoring in dynamic military environments, ensuring that advancements in commercial wireless technology directly bolster defense capabilities.
