title: Telecom Band Geometric Amplifier
summary: The primary goal of this initiative is to design, build, and test a device that uses geometric phase (also known as Berry phase) to amplify laser light in the telecom band (wavelength ~ 1,550 nm). The device will use radio-frequency modulation of linear, lossy elements to produce optical amplification that outperforms existing technologies in parameter regimes of interest to DOW
description:
Objective:
The primary goal of this initiative is to design, build, and test a device that uses geometric phase (also known as Berry phase) to amplify laser light in the telecom band (wavelength ~ 1,550 nm). The device will use radio-frequency modulation of linear, lossy elements to produce optical amplification that outperforms existing technologies in parameter regimes of interest to DOW

Description:
Present-day devices for amplifying telecom laser light mostly produce gain by incoherently pumping a medium (optically or electrically), or by coherently pumping a nonlinear medium with a laser. Both approaches are technologically mature, and offer a range of performance tradeoffs.

In contrast, geometric amplification is a gain mechanism that has only been recently proposed, and to date it has only been demonstrated in the acoustic domain [1]. However, the principle of geometric amplification can be applied to any domain. It can be realized using coupled resonators consisting only of linear, lossy components, so long as they can be modulated at a frequency comparable to the resonators’ decay rate [1].

In the telecom domain, this can be accomplished using a pair of fiber loops that include electrically tunable phase shifters that can be modulated at ~ 1 MHz. The adiabatic evolution associated with this relatively slow modulation (together with the components’ intrinsic loss) results in the accumulation of a geometric (Berry) phase [2,3] whose complex part can be engineered to provide gain [1,4,5].

Geometric gain differs existing forms of amplification in several respects, including that it achieves photon-number gain through rf modulation. This may offer practical advantages in terms of reduced device complexity, size, and power consumption.

Phase I:
Produce a complete design for a prototype telecom-band geometric amplifier based entirely on commercial off-the-shelf components. The design should be based on quantitative simulations that incorporate the components’ specifications into the mathematical model of geometric amplification.

Phase II:
Construct the device and optimize it with respect to the following performance metrics: gain, bandwidth, power consumption, added noise, and harmonic distortion. The device should exhibit > 10 dB gain with bandwidth > 100 kHz.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Collaborate with industrial and/or DOD lab partners to incorporate the lessons learned from Phase II into a commercial on-chip geometric amplifier that is superior to existing optical amplifier technologies in parameter regimes of importance to DOD.

References:
• J. R. Lane et al., Complex Berry phase and steady-state geometric amplification in non- Hermitian systems. ArXiv:2503.23197 (2025).
• M. V. Berry, Quantal phase factors accompanying adiabatic changes. Proceedings of the Royal Society of London Series A 392, 45 (1984).
• B. Simon, Holonomy, the Quantum Adiabatic Theorem, and Berry's Phase. Physical Review Letters 51, 2167 (1984).
• J. C. Garrison and E. M. Wright, Complex geometrical phases for dissipative systems., Physics Letters A 128, 177 (1988).
• K. Y. Bliokh, The appearance of a geometric-type instability in dynamic systems with adiabatically varying parameters. Journal of Physics A 32, 2551 (1991).

title: Development of Ultrafast Nonvolatile Memory Based on Sliding Ferroelectricity in Moiré Polar Homostructures
summary: Develop ultrafast, high-endurance, nonvolatile memory technology based on sliding ferroelectricity in polar moiré van der Waals homostructures.
description:
Objective:
Develop ultrafast, high-endurance, nonvolatile memory technology based on sliding ferroelectricity in polar moiré van der Waals homostructures.

Description:
Twisted stacks of van der Waals (vdW) crystals can form moiré superlattices with polar domains whose dipoles are antiferroelectrically aligned and controllable by applied electric fields [1]. Sliding ferroelectricity arises from nm-scale interlayer sliding in vdW materials, coupling in-plane atomic displacement to out-of-plane polarization switching [2]. This mechanism has been demonstrated in bilayer hexagonal boron nitride and semiconducting transition metal dichalcogenides, where polarization reversal can occur with minimal energy dissipation [3]. Recent Department of War investments through the Multidisciplinary University Research Initiative (MURI) have demonstrated advances in twisted two-dimensional heterostructures into atomically thin twistronic memory cell prototypes with potential advantages in speed, endurance, energy efficiency, and scalability [2, 3]. The advancement and prototype development requires a combined multidisciplinary expertise in the design, fabrication, measurement, and modeling of lattice dynamics in twisted moiré van der Waals structures, as well as charge transport and optoelectronics in van der Waals materials. The technical approach should exploit the atomically thin nature, low defect density, and strong in-plane bonding of vdW materials to develop sliding ferroelectric nonvolatile memory devices designed to outperform current memory technologies in speed, endurance, and scalability. Engineered nanoscale polar domains in moiré superlattices will serve as nonvolatile memory cells based on local ferroelectricity. To demonstrate the electrical and optical readouts in the designed nonvolatile memory devices, the proposal should leverage the scalability and controllability features of well-established systems, such as Graphene field-effect transistors and transition-metal-dichalcogenide-based field-effect transistors.

Phase I:
Demonstrate the feasibility of optimal moiré superlattice design for fast and durable sliding ferroelectric domain reversal, including domain wall pinning strategies and nanostructured polar moiré superlattice fabrication. Evaluate and analyze electrical and optical readout schemes using graphene field-effect transistors or transition-metal-dichalcogenide-based devices integrated with moiré polar domain structures. Perform quantitative analysis of the switching behavior, retention, readout fidelity, speed, energy efficiency, and endurance indicators under optimal device operating conditions. The success of the project will be evaluated using measurable performance indicators, including switching speed, switching energy, endurance, retention, readout fidelity, device-to-device reproducibility, and scalability beyond single-device demonstrations. During Phase I, these values will be quantified to establish appropriate performance targets for Phases II and III and to enable benchmarking against existing nonvolatile memory technologies.

Phase II:
Develop integrated sliding-ferroelectric memory-device prototypes and array-level architectures for more practical use by focusing on systematic evaluation of memory operation benchmarks including endurance, switching speed, and energy efficiency under realistic operating conditions. Particular attention must be paid to address the atomic-scale configuration of the engineered sliding ferroelectric state and the role of domain-wall pinning for controllability. Address scaling and manufacturability beyond single-device demonstrations, aiming initial demonstration of the wafer-scale patterning of local gates, partitioning of vdW structures into individual memory cells, and device packaging of memory arrays. Finally, establish quantitative comparison against competing nonvolatile memory technologies by evaluating switching energy, achievable integration density, and intrinsic fatigue resistance for long-term device operation.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Develop a high-speed memory device with low-power device operation, emphasizing energy-efficient memory for edge computing, high-density embedded memory, and robust architectures for defense-relevant electronics. Identify use cases where atomically thin, rapid, durable and low power switching will provide a demonstrable advantage over existing technology, and will describe approaches to industrial adoption and system level integration. Relatively low-power and moderate-speed operation offered by the developed technology can provide added value to the general purpose edge-computing applications. As performance metrics are established during Phases I and II, broader applications will be evaluated, including high-density embedded memory, neuromorphic and in-memory computing, reconfigurable logic, radiation-tolerant electronics, cryogenic control electronics, and memory components integrated with two-dimensional semiconductor platforms.

References:
• K. Yasuda, X. Wang, K. Watanabe, T. Taniguchi, P. Jarillo-Herrero, Science 372, 1458–1462 (2021).
• K. Ko, A. Yuk, R. Engelke, S. Carr, J. Kim, D. Park, H. Heo, H.-M. Kim, S.-G. Kim, H. Kim, T. Taniguchi, K. Watanabe, H. Park, E. Kaxiras, S. M. Yang, P. Kim, and H. Yoo, Nature Materials 22, 992–998 (2023).
• K. Yasuda, E. Zalys-Geller, X. Wang, D. Bennett, S. S. Cheema, K. Watanabe, T. Taniguchi, E. Kaxiras, P. Jarillo-Herrero, and R. Ashoori, Science 385, 53–56 (2024).

title: Design of RoomTemperature THz and Infrared Sensing Devices Using Non-Toxic, Supply-Chain Secure Material Platform
summary: Design a chip-scale oxychalcogenide film (non-toxic, supply-chain-secure material platform)-based room temperature THz and infrared sensors.
description:
Objective:
Design a chip-scale oxychalcogenide film (non-toxic, supply-chain-secure material platform)-based room temperature THz and infrared sensors.

Description:
Infrared sensing sits at an inflection point. The industry-standard HgCdTe (MCT) requires bulky cryogenic cooling and is built on toxic, supply-chain-fragile elements, while uncooled microbolometers, are limited to millisecond response times. This leaves unaddressed the regime of fast, uncooled, low-SWaP-C (Size, Weight, Power, and Cost) detection from the long-wave infrared (LWIR) through the THz, which hypersonic threat warning, proliferated drone platforms, and contested-spectrum operations now demand. Recently, new mechanisms have emerged that can fill this important technical gap. Oxychalcogenide films containing heavy elements have characteristic responses in the THz range [1-3] and can enable ms-scale detection responses in the THz and far-infrared spectral regions, e.g., hot-electron rectification/photothermoelectrics, thermally decoupled from the lattice of heavy elements [4-6]. Notably, these phenomena do not require cryogenic cooling like the MCT system because the signal is not based on an inter-band transition, and its response is orders of magnitude faster than that of room-temperature bolometers because it is driven by hot electrons decoupled from the lattice. Moreover, these materials, such as Bi2O2Se and InBiSe3, are composed of non-toxic, earth-abundant elements, and are supply-chain-secure material platforms.

Department of War’s investments through the Multidisciplinary University Research Initiative (MURI) have already enabled the development of high-mobility chalcogenide films and their characterization via optical and THz spectroscopy [1–3]. Building on this, oxychalcogenide films can serve as room-temperature detectors offering uncooled, chip-scale access to the jam-free THz and far-infrared bands — a regime current sensor technologies cannot reach without cryogenic cooling — and will directly advance Quantum and Battlefield Information Dominance. Moreover, the hot-electron mechanism is fast, which allows detection of ms transients such as laser pulses and hypersonic signatures that slow uncooled microbolometers wash out.

Phase I:
Synthesis of oxychalcogenide thin film materials with strong spin-orbit coupling that can detect THz and LWIR signals at room temperature, and demonstration of direct absorption in the Long-wavelength infrared (LWIR) and antenna-coupled rectification at THz frequencies, benchmarked by responsivity (~0.5 A/W), noise-equivalent power (~0.1 pW/ √Hz), and response speed (ms) at room temperature, is expected. These results should anchor an electromagnetic and thermal design of an integrated dual-band THz/LWIR pixel.

Phase II:
Fabricate and validate the dual-band pixels, while adding quarter-wave cavity enhancement to the LWIR channel and demonstrating simultaneous, low-crosstalk two-band readout. Refine multilayer architectures and investigate the feasibility of even higher-mobility layers and quantum wells. Scale to a small-format array (~8x8) for as high as kilohertz-rate dual-band imaging of test scenes. Deliver a SWaP-C and manufacturability assessment benchmarked against cooled MCT and microbolometer incumbents.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Terahertz (THz) and Infrared (IR) sensing devices operating at room temperature (uncooled) represent a critical dual-use technology. By eliminating the need for bulky, power-intensive cryogenic cooling systems, these sensors enable highly portable, lightweight, and low-cost systems. Features that underline a dual usage role for the developed sensing devices include:

• A fast uncooled oxychalcogenide focal plane enables short-range THz/infrared inspection of packages, vehicles, and surfaces — penetrating clothing, packaging, and dielectric coatings to reveal concealed weapons or contraband while keeping the operator at a safe standoff distance.
• The same long-wavelength response allows the sensor to see through smoke, dust, and brownout obscurants and makes a drone-borne payload effective in degraded visual environments where electro-optical and shortwave-IR imagers fail.

References:
• Romero III, Ralph, et al. "Planckian scattering and parallel conduction channels in an iron chalcogenide superconductor." Nature Physics (2026): 1-5.
• Mekonen, Sirak M., et al. "Coupled metamaterial–phonon terahertz range polaritons in a topological insulator." ACS Photonics 11.6 (2024): 2242-2246.
• Tagay, Zhenisbek, et al. "Electrodynamics of the quantum anomalous Hall state in a magnetically doped topological insulator." Physical Review B 110.24 (2024): L241106.
• Chen, et al..”Broadband Bi2O2Se photodetectors from infrared to terahertz.” Advanced Functional Materials, 31.14 (2021): 2009554.
• Chen, Hang, et al. "Broadband InBiSe3 alloy photoelectric detector from visible to terahertz." Aip Advances 14.3 (2024): 035324.
• Ding, Xiang, et al. " Bi2O2Se: A rising star for semiconductor devices." Matter 5.12 (2022): 4274-4314.

title: Scalable Processing of Large Area, Oriented 2-Dimensional Polymer Films
summary: Develop a reliable, cost-effective method to produce large area films of mechanically robust 2-dimensional polymers where the individual sheets are highly orientated perpendicular to film plane for membrane applications.
description:
Objective:
Develop a reliable, cost-effective method to produce large area films of mechanically robust 2-dimensional polymers where the individual sheets are highly orientated perpendicular to film plane for membrane applications.

Description:
2-dimensional polymers (2DPs) such as covalent organic frameworks (COFs) are an emerging class of materials which have displayed significant potential in applications ranging from catalysis, energy storage, dielectrics, nanofiltration, gas storage, and mechanically robust engineering materials. They are synthesized from geometrically pre-defined building blocks and can accommodate a wide variety of pore shapes, sizes, and functionality. Most methods used to produce 2DPs result in an insoluble microporous powder that cannot be processed into a functional form factor which limits their relevance in commercial or military applications. Despite these challenges, a variety of creative approaches have been explored to process 2DPs into films, composites, or gels. Top-down methods such as exfoliation or solution casting or bottom-up methods that form films directly from cast monomer solutions have been used to varying levels of success to access films and membranes. Interfacial polymerization has also been used to form films at the interface of two immiscible solvents. Despite this progress, many of the available techniques suffer from limitations that preclude further elaboration into industrially relevant processing techniques or lead to formation of films of poor quality. Exfoliation based approaches are low-yielding and solution casting techniques often involve appending solubilizing groups to the pore wall which can block access to the pore itself. Methods that cast directly from monomer solution can be scaled up in a roll-to-roll process but often result in films that are mechanically weak as it is difficult to control the size and orientation of the individual 2DP sheets and they often lack sufficient intermolecular interactions. More work is needed to understand the underlying kinetics and thermodynamics of the film forming processes as it relates to monomer selection, layer alignment, domain size, and formation of defects. New engineering approaches are also needed to further control film formation, thickness, functionality, and orientation during deposition and post-processing. Special focus should be given to controlling and minimizing defects that could mitigate material performance: point and stacking defects within 2D polymer crystals, stacking defects in between crystallites, pinholes, and residual solvent / reactant contaminations within the films, crystallite size distributions to name a few.

The objective of this topic is to develop a scalable, cost-effective method to produce large area 2DP ensemble films with superb control over structural evolution. Designed processes must consider monomer composition, long range structural order in lateral and parallel planes, interlayer interactions and flaw tolerance. The process should be amenable to roll-to-roll processing or a related method to produce continuous films.

Phase I:
Develop a continuous process to produce 2DP ensemble films from predefined monomer building blocks. The process should achieve a rate of 100 feet per minute of a film that is at least 1 foot wide and 1-50 microns thick. Using computational modeling and/or experimental studies, identify role of defects and flaws and quantify needed levels of domain size, layer alignments, and intermolecular interactions to achieve mechanically robust films. Using insights gained from understanding the underlying film forming mechanism, develop a framework to be implemented in Phase II to achieve required structural ordering.

Phase II:
Further develop processing approach from Phase I to increase deposition rate by 2-5X while expanding range of film width and of thickness while achieving domain sizes and orientations needed to form robust films. The method should be amenable to post-processing including annealing, tensioning, or post-polymerization modification to further increase ordering and alignment. Proxy measurement techniques may be developed to rapidly assess ordering and alignment.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Phase III efforts will further optimize the processing method and scale production to manufacturing-relevant levels and rates to achieve films with large, highly aligned domains with minimal defects. A variety of dual-use applications would benefit from an efficient production pipeline for 2DP films including nanofiltration membranes, battery separators, gas impermeable films, and critical mineral recovery.

References:
• D. W. Burke, C. Sun, I. Castano, N. C. Flanders, A. M. Evans, E. Vitaku, D. C. McLeod, R. H. Lambeth, L. X. Chen, N. C. Gianneschi, W. R. Dichtel, Angew. Chem.2020, 132, 5203. https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/ange.201913975
• Morgan G. Barnes, David C. McLeod, and Robert H. Lambeth. ACS Applied Polymer Materials. 2022 4 (3), 2017-2021. https://pubs.acs.org/doi/full/10.1021/acsapm.1c01828
• M. C. Senarathna, H. Li, S. D. Perera, J. Torres-Correas, S. D. Diwakara, S. R. Boardman, N. M. Al-Kharji, Y. Liu, R. A. Smaldone, Angew. Chem. Int. Ed.2023, 62, e202312617. https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/anie.202312617

title: Bio-inspired Underwater Teams
summary: Utilize the fundamental understanding of hydrodynamic benefits from underwater vehicles swimming in proximity to each other to develop and demonstrate a design for an underwater vehicle team optimized for range, endurance, speed and quietness.
description:
Objective:
Utilize the fundamental understanding of hydrodynamic benefits from underwater vehicles swimming in proximity to each other to develop and demonstrate a design for an underwater vehicle team optimized for range, endurance, speed and quietness. The design should be based on rigorous analysis and leverage results from recent computational and experimental fluid dynamics investigations that have shown signifcant gains in efficiency resulting from group swimming. The design should also leverage new vehicle design spaces that result from the platform being unmanned and are available that might include novel propulsors (for example, fins, tails or other bio-inspired mechanisms) that utilize unsteady propulsion, body shape and body deformation. This STTR will provide increased capabilities for UUV teams based on the technology push from the fundamental understanding we now have of how hydrodynamic benefits of underwater swimming in groups.

Description:
Bio-inspired underwater vehicles have nearly matched the speeds and efficiencies of real fish. Now, these platforms are on the cusp of operating as multiagent teams, which would further improve efficiency and unlock novel mission utility. Recent work has shown how the hydrodynamic benefits of schooling can be translated into groups of underwater vehicles. In this STTR, the use of physical models and 3D simulations of sufficient fidelity are expected to enable exploration and understanding of the effects of controlled variation of key parameters such as geometric positioning with respect to other wakes and body deformation in developing protype underwater teams. Recent progress in this area, combined with the wide availability of 3D physical and computational methods, presents a significant, new opportunity for the application of fundamental knowledge to exploit the hydrodynamic benefits that result from schooling fish. This STTR Topic will pursue the design and demonstration of innovative, bio-inspired UUV teams with capabilities well beyond the state of the art for range, endurance, speed and quietness.

The overall design objective and targeted capabilities apply to a group of untethered UUVs, each between 1-5 meters in length, and capable of operating in salt water to depths of 50 ft, to support Phase II and Phase III testing. Conventional designs and propulsors (such as propellers and jets) are not in scope for this topic. The design will be evaluated according to measurable performance criteria:

– Speed: minimum 4 meters/sec, with an objective of 6 meters/sec or higher; Cost of Transport (COT): proposed project should optimize the COT and demonstrate clear improvement over the state-of-the-art, for the chosen vehicle length and speed; Quietness: underwater acoustic energy generated by the vehicles, should be minimized by design; Power: the design shall not rely on energy harvesting from the environment but can incorporate methods of energy recovery from mechanical motion itself. It shall utilize state-of-the-art energy storage (R&D into energy storage is outside the scope of this topic); Power Transmission: the design shall use state-of-the-art means of transferring power to the propulsor. Successful proposals will explain how the proposed means of power transmission will contribute to meeting the performance objectives; Sensing and control: approaches to sensing and dynamic control that optimize hydrodynamic interactions and flow physics are in-scope for this Topic. The successful proposal will explain how these will contribute to meeting the performance objectives; Path Planning: use off-the-shelf components to provide sufficient capability for the platforms to perform the demonstrations during Phase II and Phase III, including straight line tracks and simple maneuvers sufficient to demonstrate speed, range, endurance and acoustics. R&D into path planning is outside the scope of this topic; Vehicle cost: estimated cost of scaled manufacturing is a factor in the proposal evaluations and can be used to guide material and design selection. The successful proposal will identify supply chain risks and a mitigation plan.

Phase I:
The small business shall demonstrate the feasibility of the concept in meeting Navy needs for a team of UUVs capable of meeting the desired performance objectives, via model-scale experiments, computation, previous results and data, or fabrication of components (if feasible) for any difficult-to manufacture component. This body of evidence shall support the high-risk aspects of the design. The Phase I should convincingly show that the design is sufficiently robust to undergo the testing described in Phases II and III.

Phase II:
The small business shall fabricate a prototype team of UUVs, according to the requirements stated in this Topic, and evaluate the design via in-water tests conducted at a facility arranged by the small business. These tests shall target the STTR performance objectives listed above, via untethered operations. At a minimum, the prototype testing shall consist of (1) basic operability testing, (2) speed trials, (3) range/endurance trials, and (4) acoustic testing. The small business may propose other tests as needed to demonstrate the benefits of their design. It shall also perform analyses to establish reliability, identify areas for further improvement, and analyze manufacturing scalability to transition the design to the Navy.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
The small business shall apply the knowledge gained in Phase II to build an advanced prototype UUV team. The small business shall test the advanced prototype according to the Phase II test goals. The small business shall support Government testing of the advanced prototype.

References:
• Han, T., Seyedmirzaei Sarraf, S., Mivehchi, A., & Moored, K. W. (2025) Tailoring formations of self-organizing hydrofoil schools towards high-efficiency. Journal of Fluid Mechanics. 1012, A26. doi:10.1017/jfm.2025.10239.
• J Guo, GV Lauder, R Thandiackal, H Dong, Computational analysis of fish-foil pairing and wake energy extraction in low-speed flow, Bioinspiration & Biomimetics 20(5), 056011, 2025.
• Menzer, A., Pan, Y., Lauder, G.V., Dong, H, “Fish schools in a vertical diamond formation: Effect of vertical spacing on hydrodynamic interactions,” Physical Review Fluids 10 (4), 2025.
• Guo, J. , Dong, H, “A computational Study of In-Phase and Anti-Phase Interactions of Fish in a Phalanx School,” Journal of Fluids Engineering 147 (7), 2025.
• Huang, Z., Wang, J., Dong, H., "Vortex Dynamics in Wake-Body and Wake-Fin Interactions of Tuna- Like Staggered Swimming," Bioinspiration and Biomimetics 20 (4), 2025.

title: Expeditionary Solar Refinery for Direct Synthesis of Methanol Feedstock from Water and Air
summary: Generate a minimally viable component system with solar, water, and carbon dioxide inputs which generates >66% methanol/water fuel at a rate of 0.5L/hr with a total system weight <90 lb.
description:
Objective:
Generate a minimally viable component system with solar, water, and carbon dioxide inputs which generates >66% methanol/water fuel at a rate of 0.5L/hr with a total system weight <90 lb.

Description:
Modern warfare tactics have demonstrated the need to shift toward small, specialized, dismounted tactical units which can operate free from the supply line. Systems enabling Soldier power sustainment are essential to facilitate zero-resupply operations amid increasing energy requirements on the battlefield. To accomplish this demand, we need investments to capitalize on energy sources that can be replenished in austere environments, whether to directly power devices or charge batteries. Further, this energy source needs to impart minimal cognitive load on the warfighters, acting passively until put into use. Finally, it should be invisible to modern UAS-mounted sensors (e.g., IR detection). A technology that enables continuous methanol fuel cell usage from just sunlight, water, and atmospheric gases can accomplish these goals for uninterrupted power in contested logistics environments.

The motivation for this topic has arisen from recent research that showed efficient utilization of locally available carbon resources and the selective synthesis of liquid fuels under austere conditions [5,6]. In one study, a solar-driven artificial photosynthesis platform was demonstrated that directly converts carbon dioxide and water into methanol, enabling onsite fuel generation without the high temperatures, pressures, and complex infrastructure required by conventional syngas-based processes. In a complementary effort, a pathway was developed for converting stranded natural gas and methane emissions into transportable liquid fuel using only sunlight and water, overcoming long-standing challenges associated with methane activation and overoxidation. Together, these advances establish scalable photocatalytic technologies for producing methanol from diverse carbon feedstocks, providing a foundation for expeditionary fuel manufacturing with reduced logistics burdens and enhanced energy resilience for distributed military operations.

Based on these advances, the proposed system will leverage solar (concentrated or ambient) energetic inputs along with water (potable or otherwise) and carbon dioxide (ambient or concentrated) as the only chemical inputs to generate methanol fuel capable of meeting the daily power requirements of up to 4 Soldiers. This approach will produce ≥66% methanol-in-water that is immediately available for use with direct/reformed fuel cell systems including the Honey-Badger 20/50W PEM Power Generator. The system will be operable in remote, austere locations without a direct Soldier interface, while placed on the ground, or while secured to a light tactical off-road vehicle (e.g., Flyer 60). Operation with direct access to fresh water, ambient CO2, and clear weather conditions should generate at least 0.5 L of methanol per hour, with increased efficiency if concentrated CO2 sources are available. The total system weight should not exceed 90 lb (equivalent to a typical T6 battery), nor the dimensions exceed 0.5 m3. Heat emissions from the system should be minimal such that the system remains near ambient to IR cameras.

The system will be designed with a 0.5 L (16.9 oz) input cartridge containing potable water (equivalent to a standard plastic water bottle volume) which will be converted into a 66% methanol/33% water fuel stream. Ideally, the system can also be directly powered by alternative sources (e.g., military standard generators, wind, etc.). Achieving the desired production rate while remaining lightweight and utilizing onboard vehicle power will require an innovative approach.

Phase I:
Create feasibility concepts for a methanol generation system with solar, water, and carbon dioxide inputs which generates >66% methanol/water fuel at a rate of 0.5L/hr and a total system weight <90 lb. Feasibility will be established by light harvesting toward methanol synthesis (catalytic or otherwise) and kinetics/turnover/selectivity evaluation, and analytical modeling to include engineering diagrams, heat/mass balance calculations, and computer-aided design models of possible prototype architectures. The final product is a Phase II development plan with performance goals and key technical milestones that address technical risk reduction.

Phase II:
Produce a prototype minimally viable product system for evaluation and assessment in accordance with the criteria established in this Topic. Demonstration and delivery to a DoW transition partner (e.g., DEVCOM C5ISR, DEVCOM Soldier Center, DEVCOM GVSC, etc.) is required to establish compatibility with DoW systems and direct future product iterations.

The results of the evaluation will be leveraged to generate refinement plans for the prototype to better meet DoW requirements and determine product effectiveness in an operationally relevant environment. The final products of Phase II include the prototype described above, evaluation with a DoW partner and a Phase III development plan. The technology should reach TRL 6 at the conclusion of this phase.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
The end-state of this research effort will be the introduction of an innovative strategy and prototype for producing methanol fuel in-field for use with DoW methanol fuel cell platforms. Because use of available materials represents an essential logistics benefit, the system will be designed to produce fuel from a standard 16.8 oz plastic water bottle, carbon dioxide, and direct or indirect solar energy. Such a system will permit Soldier power sustainment for mounted or dismounted teams, facilitating zero-resupply operations.

A single unit should be able to meet the daily power requirements of 4 dismounted soldiers. Multiple units should be able to link up and provide auxiliary power to a FOB. As we expand toward fuel cells for UAS and UGV, the fuel produced by the projected device will directly be able to transition to provide power for those technologies. In some military and commercial cases where methanol fuel cells are prevalent, the projected devices will be able to easily and cheaply replace solar panels and batteries.

Further, a simple, scalable method for methanol production can be directly plugged- into commercial use cases, such as industrial feedstock for other reactions (e.g., formaldehyde, hydrocarbons, olefins) for a wide array of applications (e.g., polymers). In such cases, the methanol produced by technologies driven during this STTR will enable on-site synthesis near factories and at lower temperatures (>200 °C) and energy costs than the current state-of-the-art.

title: Architected Energy Dissipation Structures with Tunable Rigid-flexible Behaviors
summary: Develop and demonstrate architected energy dissipation structures with rigid responsiveness at large tensile, compressive, and shear strains, but capable of conformability to surfaces of complex topographies and other fluid-like behaviors in response to small strains.
description:
Objective:
Develop and demonstrate architected energy dissipation structures with rigid responsiveness at large tensile, compressive, and shear strains, but capable of conformability to surfaces of complex topographies and other fluid-like behaviors in response to small strains.

Description:
The DoW requires lightweight protection materials for a variety of applications, including personal protection, vehicle safety, and shielding sensitive electronics. Most protection structures are either a) rigid materials – e.g. metals, ceramics, composites - designed to carry significant mechanical loads and/or blunt kinetic threats, or b) flexible materials – e.g. elastomers, foam structures, structures based on polymeric fibers – intended to compress and/or stretch, are conformable, and effective at reducing peak accelerations [1]. However, most protection solutions cannot provide both rigid material response and conformability which limits applications for the Warfighter.

Recently, a new family of energy dissipating structures known as “polycatenated architected materials” have been introduced that may display both solid- and fluid-like behaviors [2]. These structures, essentially “3D chainmail” and realized through additive manufacturing, derive their mechanical behaviors not through intrinsic material properties, but rather through geometric arrangement of internal solid elements, e.g. rings or cage-like particles interconnected into 3D networks (note that these materials consist entirely of solid linkages, collectively displaying “fluid-like” behaviors in response to small deformations). In response to severe loading, rigid elements may align and develop complex force chains that exhibit high strength and offer significant protection mechanisms not possible through conventional flexible options [2,3]. However, elements may also reorganize, slide, and/or rotate, which offers novel design mechanisms for dissipating energy, and new ways to enable comfort for applications related to personal protection.

The goal of this topic is to create architected structures with tunable mechanical energy dissipating behaviors that can vary spatially throughout the material. Teams will investigate element and linkage materials, geometries, and nearest neighbor spacings to design architected structures that perform optimally for various static and dynamic loading conditions, e.g. via tensile, compression, impact, and rheology characterization. Teams will then design, process, characterize, and simulate energy dissipating behaviors of materials in multiple geometrical configurations, e.g. through comparisons to legacy impact attenuating materials like foams that are used for impact protection (knee pads, elbow pads, helmet pads). Teams will be expected to work alongside Army scientists and engineers to guide the design, manufacturing, and testing of materials. If successful, this effort would enable new materials design tools for the DoW to create customized protection structures for the expeditionary Soldier.

Phase I:
Design architected structures with individual linked grains in the following approximate rectangular configuration, 82 mm x 87 mm x 19.5 mm (thickness). The given geometry approximates a commonly tested helmet pad configuration and will allow teams to make comparisons to known technologies. Architected sheets shall display conformability to various geometries to include features with radii of curvature ranging from approximately 0.5-3.0 cm. The through-thickness compression response of the material should seek to maximize energy absorption efficiency as described in Equation 1 of reference [4]. Simultaneously, the material should minimize shear stiffness in the thickness direction. Teams will use advanced processing techniques, e.g. additive manufacturing approaches, to fabricate a minimum of 10 test specimens. Teams will perform computer simulations and initial experimental mechanical characterization to estimate in-plane and out-of-plane loads required to initiate solid-to-fluid transitions in the architected materials. Teams will perform impact tests across the range of 1-50 J and use legacy foam pads as a comparison.

Phase II:
Design and demonstrate architected structures with variable energy dissipating properties with respect to spatial position. Teams may consider multi-material and/or variable grain/linkage architectures to achieve the tunable behaviors. Process a minimum of 20 specimens in the geometrical configurations provided for Phase I and develop test techniques to assess the response of the structures whose energy dissipation behaviors vary spatially. Simulate the mechanical behaviors of the architected structures in response to compressive, tensile, shear, and impact loads. Determine loads required to initiate flexible-rigid transitions at various spatial positions within the structure. Work with Army Research Laboratory (ARL) scientists to design, manufacture, and deliver test specimens for advanced dynamic mechanical testing at ARL. Develop commercial and outreach plans to market the technology for civilian and defense markets; in addition, teams shall develop plans to scale manufacturing.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
The discovery of polycatenated mechanical metamaterials has introduced a new family of structures that may display both solid- and fluid-like behaviors. The additional degrees of freedom associated with granular elements linked to nearest neighbors may enable a variety of new civilian and defense technologies, e.g. Soldier/Vehicle protection, sports equipment, law enforcement, and lightweight concepts for dissipating vibrational energy. Phase III efforts shall include outreach efforts based on market research to leverage opportunities in both civilian and defense markets. Implement plans to rapidly modify designs for specific customer needs. In addition, teams shall implement plans to scale manufacturing.

References:
• Staniszeski, J., et al., “Improved Low-Velocity Impact Performance of the Advanced Combat Helmet (ACH) at 17 ft/s through Optimization of Pad Material Response,” ARL-TR-8808 (SEP 2019).
• Zhou, W., et al., “3D polycatenated architected materials,” Science 387: 6731, pp. 269-277 (2025).
• Liu, T., et al., “3D self-locking granular metamaterial,” Science 12(15) (2026).
• Clough E, et al., “Elastomeric Microlattice Impact Attenuators,” Matter 1, 1519-1531 (2019).

title: Counter-Unmanned Aerial Systems Rapid Maturation
summary: Mature commercial and dual-use technologies that detect, track, identify, or defeat small low-flying drones (Group 1 and Group 2 unmanned aerial systems) in hostile or contested areas.
description:
Objective:
Mature commercial and dual-use technologies that detect, track, identify, or defeat small low-flying drones (Group 1 and Group 2 unmanned aerial systems) in hostile or contested areas.

Description:
Inexpensive, highly maneuverable, commercially available unmanned aerial systems (UAS) threaten tactical forces, critical infrastructure, and installations. Current defenses are limited by cost, by the operator attention they require, and by their vulnerability to countermeasures. A capability gap against Group 1 and Group 2 UAS remains.

This topic seeks mature or maturing technology at any point in the counter-UAS kill chain. The three areas below are where capability is most needed. They are examples. A proposal may address one area, more than one, or a gap not listed here.

Detection and Tracking. Detect and hold track on highly agile targets in cluttered low-altitude airspace. The proposer selects the sensing modality. Approaches that hold track when the target is not emitting are preferred. Solutions that require permanent site infrastructure or mains power, including fixed perimeter sensor installations, are out of scope for this area. The system must move with the force.

Identification and Decision Support. Classify and identify unauthorized platforms and support an engagement decision. Processing must run on tactical computing hardware carried or emplaced with the force. Proposals should describe a pathway to interoperate with existing command and control. Conformance to a named standard is not required at this stage and will not be scored.

Mitigation and Defeat. Kinetic, non-kinetic, or cyber approaches that defeat hostile UAS in remote tactical theaters and in densely populated areas. Proposals must address collateral effects.

Operating preferences. The operating environment is denied, contested, and unattended. The four conditions below are preferences, not eligibility requirements.

Every proposal must state where it stands against each one.

(a) The system does not require the target to emit radio frequency (RF) energy. Passive RF may be part of a solution; the preference is that track holds when the target is silent.

(b) The system does not radiate. The Government favors kinetic and cyber defeat over approaches that require the friendly system to emit. Jamming, active illumination, and transmission into a target's control or navigation link are in scope. A proposal that uses any of them must say so and describe the operational effect.

(c) The system does not require cloud services or reachback. Training and analytics may occur off-platform. The processing that produces the operational output should run on the platform, and the system should continue to function with all external network interfaces disabled.

(d) The system does not require a dedicated operator, meaning no person whose only task is attending it. Human judgment over the use of force is expected and is not addressed by this preference.

Out of scope: work requiring classified access or a facility clearance at the time of award, and approaches that depend on cooperative identification, including Remote ID broadcast.

Phase I:
This topic solicits Direct-to-Phase-II (DP2) proposals only. Direct to Phase II proposers shall submit documentation showing that Phase I-equivalent feasibility has already been achieved outside the SBIR/STTR program. Adequate documentation is a written record of at least one test of the proposed approach stating the conditions under which the test was conducted, the dates, the target, threat, or surrogate used, the measured result, and how it was measured.Test data, technical reports, and third-party evaluation metrics are acceptable. A system design alone is not sufficient. A self-declared technology readiness level unsupported by a documented test is not sufficient.

As required by the DoW solicitation, the feasibility documented may not rest solely upon, or logically extend from, prior or ongoing federally funded SBIR or STTR work; the proposing firm and/or the principal investigator must have substantially performed the work relied upon; and the firm must demonstrate ownership or licensure of the associated intellectual property prior to proposal submission.

Phase II:
Phase II is a major research and development effort. Performers refine the Phase I concept into an operational prototype that demonstrates real-world functionality. The primary deliverable is a functional system, software package, or physical prototype ready for test and evaluation in a militarily relevant or simulated field environment. The technology shall reach TRL 6 by the end of Phase II.

The period of performance is twelve months rather than the twenty-four the announcement allows. The intent is to move a demonstrated capability to a transition decision within one year. Proposals should be scoped to that schedule.

The Government may host a showcase about six months after award. Attendance is by invitation and is based on end user interest in the capability. It is not required of every performer. Performers shall provide operational evidence supporting a follow-on funding decision whether or not they are invited.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Commercial applications are those in which the equipment deploys with a team rather than being installed at a site: temporary airspace security for outdoor events, venues, and construction or energy sites; convoy, executive, and site-survey protection; wildfire, disaster, and critical infrastructure response; and mobile detection kits for law enforcement and allied partners. Detection, tracking, and identification technologies have a direct commercial market in these roles. Authority to mitigate or defeat unmanned aircraft in the United States is limited by statute to covered federal entities. A defeat-focused proposal is not expected to show a near-term domestic commercial market for that function.

Military applications include integration into point-defense systems for tactical units, forward operating bases, and naval vessel protection platforms, which may be funded via non-SBIR/STTR acquisition budgets.

References:
• Congressional Research Service. Department of Defense Counter Unmanned Aircraft Systems: Background and Issues for Congress. Report R48477. https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R48477
• Statement of General Michael E. Kurilla, Commander, U.S. Central Command, before the Senate Armed Services Committee on the posture of U.S. Central Command, 10 June 2025.
• U.S. Department of Defense Counter-Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Strategy (2021). https://media.defense.gov/2021/Jan/07/2002561080/-1/-1/1/DEPARTMENT-OF-DEFENSE-COUNTER-SMALL-UNMANNED-AIRCRAFT-SYSTEMS-STRATEGY.PDF

title: Real-World Applications for Prototype ISAC Demonstrations (RAPID) Small Business
summary: Design, develop and demonstrate an innovative 5G/6Gdual-use Integrated Sensing and Communications (ISAC) prototype that provides sensing capabilities without degrading communication performance.
description:
Objective:
Design, develop and demonstrate an innovative 5G/6Gdual-use Integrated Sensing and Communications (ISAC) prototype that provides sensing capabilities without degrading communication performance.

Description:
The Department of War (DoW) seeks to accelerate U.S. leadership in Integrated Sensing and Communications (ISAC), a 5G-Advanced feasibility-study area and a key technology for 3GPP 6G specifications. This project addresses the challenge of adding sensing capabilities to communication networks without degrading the primary communication link across diverse missions and environments, from established bases to remote and contested areas. The goal is to develop innovative, dual-use ISAC prototypes that leverage existing cellular infrastructure including 5G, emerging Open RAN interfaces, and AI-native networking. These solutions should offer a smaller, more cost-effective footprint than separate radar and communication systems. The effort will focus on three pathways: ISAC on fixed infrastructure, ISAC on mobile platforms, and joint AI optimization of radio resources. Success of this project will reduce barriers to market entry, enable new ISAC and AI applications, and strengthen U.S. industrial competitiveness in a field receiving substantial investment from adversaries.

The following documents are incorporated as part of this topic.

• Appendix A - ISAC KPI Framework for RAPID
• RAPID Statement of Objectives (SOO)

Phase I:
This topic solicits Direct-to-Phase-II (D2P2) proposals only; Phase I proposals will not be accepted. Offerors must document that Phase I feasibility has already been established through prior work. Acceptable feasibility evidence includes results from prior research and development performed by the small business; prototype, breadboard, model, simulation, test, demonstration, or experimental results; analytical studies, calculations, trade studies, or modeling and simulation results; data demonstrating performance against relevant technical parameters; prior relevant contract, commercial, internal research, or customer-funded work performed by the small business; and/or peer-reviewed publications, technical reports, patents, or other supporting documentation directly relevant to the SBC’s approach. Existing research publications, analytical studies, simulation results, and prototype demonstrations have already established the technical feasibility of dual-use Integrated Sensing and Communications (ISAC) systems leveraging commercial cellular infrastructure, including 5G and emerging 5G-Advanced capabilities. Industry-led standardization efforts, including ongoing ISAC work within 3GPP Release 19 and related 5G-Advanced studies, further validate the viability of the underlying concepts and technologies. As a result, the fundamental scientific and technical feasibility questions that would normally be addressed during a Phase I effort should have already been sufficiently demonstrated. The remaining challenges are focused on system integration, prototype development, performance optimization, and operational evaluation in representative environments.

Phase II:
Design, implement, and demonstrate a prototype that has potential for both military and commercial use. The prototype, whether technology, product, or service—must meet the topic objectives (Attachment 1 and Appendix A) and account for both commercial and military deployment requirements.

Prototypes shall be demonstrated in the context of military and civilian scenarios such as non-RF emitting objects, Unmanned Aerial System (UAS) detection, vehicle detection, or biometrics. The prototype should support Open-RAN interfaces (e.g., 7.2x functional split, E2 Service Model and so on) and the prototype shall be integrated or interoperable with the Open Centralized Unit/Distributed Unit (OCUDU) software baseline, as published by the Linux Foundation where applicable. The design architecture shall utilize "Secure by Design" principles and align with the Department of War's (DoW) Zero Trust Architecture (ZTA) framework.

Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) Refer to Appendix A - ISAC KPI Framework for RAPID for complete details.

Offerors, at a minimum, shall propose the below set of deliverables:

1. Program Kickoff- Format to be provided

2. Monthly Status Report- Format to be provided

3. Quarterly Technical Review- Format to be provided

4. Demonstration and Demonstration Report

5. Key Performance Indicators

6. Final implementation of the Phase 2 demonstrations

Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) Refer to Appendix A - ISAC KPI Framework for RAPID for complete details.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Smart transportation and connected infrastructure: The firm may commercialize ISAC-enabled 5G-Advanced and future 6G network products for transportation agencies, roadway operators, ports, rail systems, airports, logistics centers, and smart-city providers. These capabilities could support collision warnings, intersection safety, autonomous-vehicle infrastructure, traffic-flow optimization, perimeter monitoring, and all-weather situational awareness.

Industrial, warehouse, and critical-infrastructure monitoring:

Private 5G networks deployed in manufacturing plants, warehouses, energy facilities, mining operations, and distribution centers could use ISAC to combine reliable wireless connectivity with passive sensing. This approach could reduce the cost, complexity, and maintenance burden associated with deploying separate radar, camera, and communications systems.

Public safety, disaster response, and search-and-rescue:

ISAC-enabled portable or fixed 5G infrastructure could support first responders operating during natural disasters, infrastructure failures, and mass-casualty events. Communications nodes could simultaneously restore broadband connectivity and assist with locating vehicles, personnel, or survivors in degraded-visibility environments. Commercial transition opportunities may include emergency communications providers, public-safety agencies, temporary-network vendors, and telecommunications equipment manufacturers.

Installation protection and counter-unmanned aircraft system support:

The firm may transition ISAC technology to fixed military installations, expeditionary bases, depots, airfields, ports, and other critical sites. Existing or deployed cellular and tactical-network infrastructure could be used as a distributed sensing layer to detect, localize, and track non-RF-emitting objects, including small, unmanned aircraft systems, ground vehicles, and personnel.

Tactical edge sensing for distributed and contested operations:

Mobile ISAC solutions may support mounted and dismounted formations, unmanned systems, tactical communications relays, and mobile command posts operating where Global Positioning System access, dedicated radar coverage, or reliable backhaul is degraded or unavailable. A mobile platform could maintain command-and-control or data-backhaul connectivity while using the same radio hardware and waveforms to identify obstacles, map local terrain, detect moving objects, and support route awareness. This would reduce the need to carry, power, protect, and sustain separate sensing systems.
