• 3GPP TS 22.137, 5G; Integrated Sensing and Communication.
• 3GPP TR 22.837, Feasibility Study on Integrated Sensing and Communication.
• 3GPP TR 38.901, Study on Channel Model for Frequencies from 0.5 to 100 GHz.
• 3GPP TS 33.501, Security Architecture and Procedures for 5G System.
• NIST, 6G Communications Roadmap.
• Ropitault et al. (NIST), Characterization of Monostatic Base Stations Sensing Resolution Using 5G Reference Signals.

title: Resilient Tactical Edge Networks
summary: The objective of this Phase II effort is to design, validate, and demonstrate a fully open-source, private 5G network platform for Resilient Tactical Edge Networks—integrating OCUDU, SD-Core, SD-RAN, and OSC components—to provide highly reliable, cost-effective, and scalable wide-area connectivity for autonomous field equipment, precision crop intelligence, and livestock monitoring.
description:
Objective:
The objective of this Phase II effort is to design, validate, and demonstrate a fully open-source, private 5G network platform for Resilient Tactical Edge Networks—integrating OCUDU, SD-Core, SD-RAN, and OSC components—to provide highly reliable, cost-effective, and scalable wide-area connectivity for autonomous field equipment, precision crop intelligence, and livestock monitoring. This platform will be validated at a representative rural site against specific key performance metrics, establishing a secure, interoperable, and procurement-ready reference architecture that supports both commercial precision agriculture and dual-use DoW mission-support applications.

Description:
The realistic near-to-mid-term serviceable addressable market for private 5G in U.S. agriculture is the subset with real mobility, coverage, reliability, or data-volume pain: row-crop operations running GPS-guided and autonomous equipment, specialty-crop growers using machine vision and agricultural robotics, dairies and feedlots with dense livestock-monitoring deployments, irrigated operations with distributed pump and center-pivot control, and large ranches requiring wide-area coverage for animal and asset tracking. The scale of the opportunity is well documented. USDA Economic Research Service data show about 1.88 million farms in 2024 (roughly 39% of all U.S. land). Only 79% of farms reported internet access of any kind, leaving roughly one in five farms without even basic connectivity. There is also documented evidence that productivity of farms with connectivity is significantly higher than the ones without any connectivity. Furthermore, FCC data show that 39% of rural Americans lack access to minimum fixed broadband speeds, compared with 4% of urban Americans, and coverage on cropland and rangeland specifically is worse still. Public carrier networks will not close this gap on their own; carrier tower economics favor population density, and most agricultural land has almost none.

This segment buys on measurable operational outcomes (machine uptime, yield per acre, input cost per acre, water use, herd health, labor hours saved), not on global platform standardization, and its stated barriers to adoption are consistent and compounding: ROI ambiguity, high capex against tight and cyclical farm margins, no in-house RF/cellular or IT staff, harsh outdoor operating environments, a fragmented device ecosystem spanning tractors, drones, sensors, and wearables, and coverage requirements measured in thousands of acres rather than thousands of square feet. A proprietary private 5G platform from a tier-one vendor addresses almost none of these barriers directly; it is priced and supported for industrial campuses and multi-site enterprise accounts, not a single farm with a handful of mission-critical connectivity problems to solve.

An all-open-source stack removes the structural cost and lock-in that makes proprietary platforms a poor fit for this segment. Because OCUDU's O-CU/O-DU communicate with the rest of the network over open, standardized interfaces (especially the O-RAN 7.2x split to the O-RU), the network can be assembled from whichever RU vendor best fits a given operation's coverage geometry and budget, including high-power CBRS Category B radios and high-gain sector antennas mounted on existing farm infrastructure (grain legs, silos, center-pivot towers, farmstead masts) to maximize covered acres per radio. Together, OCUDU, SD-Core, SD-RAN, and OSC form one integrated, fully open-source 5G stack that a regional systems integrator, agricultural equipment dealer, rural wireless ISP, or electric/telephone cooperative can deploy, support, and price as a right-sized, as-a-service offer for a single operation, instead of selling a broad, vendor-locked platform. That directly answers this market's stated preference for outcome-first, economically flexible offers, and it supports a coexistence posture (private 5G for mobility, coverage, and uplink-intensive problems; existing farmstead Wi-Fi and LPWAN sensors where they already work) rather than a rip-and-replace sale.

The trade-off of an all-open-source stack is that the burden of proving interoperability, stability, and security shifts from a single vendor's warranty to the integrator and the open-source community itself. Agricultural buyers, who by their own account lack in-house cellular and cybersecurity expertise, have little tolerance for integration failures discovered mid-season, when planting, spraying, irrigation, and harvest windows cannot be rescheduled. This is exactly the gap the on-going OCUDU Testing & Validation Plan, and its Radio Access Network (RAN) Testing and Evaluation Center (RTEC)-centered extensions, are designed to close: independently witnessed, multi-vendor testing of device diversity, RU diversity, long-range outdoor RF performance, Core/RIC/SMO integration, and security. The proposal should leverage the current, on-going testing and evaluation activities in RTECs and associated results on this front.

Although this topic is anchored in a specific vertical to ensure a concrete deployment environment, real users, and a defensible commercialization path, proposers should recognize and are required to present the technical work in terms of the generic network performance classes it advances. Improvements made to the OCUDU O-CU/O-DU under this effort (scheduler behavior, mobility management, uplink capacity, stability under sustained load, security features) are expected to generalize across verticals and to benefit the broader community of RAN developers building on OCUDU. The Technical Volume shall include a mapping of each selected use case, and its associated Section 3.0 KPMs, to the performance class or classes it exercises, and shall identify which anticipated OCUDU code or feature enhancements correspond to each class.

For this topic, the dominant performance classes are massive scale and wide-area coverage: maximizing covered acres per radio using high-power CBRS Category B configurations, supporting large, sparse populations of low-rate sensor devices alongside high-uplink mobile equipment, and maintaining session continuity across long-range outdoor propagation conditions, with an evolution path to NTN integration.

Research and development for this effort should address, at minimum, the following questions:

• All-Open-Source Economics: What is the fully loaded cost (integration, support, spectrum, hardware, mounting infrastructure, and backhaul) of an OCUDU + SD-Core + SD-RAN + OSC deployment at farm scale relative to carrier coverage extensions and proprietary private-network platforms, and how should that be packaged as a CBRS-based, as-a-service offer within the price point agricultural buyers require ($75,000-$200,000 for a reference deployment covering approximately 2,000 acres)?

• Last-Acre Coverage Economics: What combination of high-power CBRS Category B radios, high-gain sector antennas, existing vertical assets (grain legs, silos, pivot towers), and backhaul options (fiber where available, fixed wireless, or satellite/NTN) maximizes reliably covered acres per dollar, and how does the open RU ecosystem enabled by the O-RAN 7.2x split change that optimization relative to a single bundled radio line?

• Use-Case-First Automation: Which of the use cases defined below deliver the fastest, most measurable ROI on the open-source stack, and what RTEC-executed interoperability tests (Device, RU, Core, RIC/SMO, and Infrastructure dimensions) are needed to validate each one end-to-end under realistic seasonal, weather, and terrain conditions?

• Trust in Open Source: How does RTEC-executed testing of the full open-source stack (not just OCUDU) reduce the integration risk and skills-shortage barrier that agricultural buyers most often cite, and what evidence package best converts community-maintained, no-license-fee software into a procurement-ready proof point for a buyer with no in-house cellular expertise?

Solutions leveraging super intelligence (SI) and machine learning (ML) for variable-rate input optimization, crop and livestock analytics, predictive equipment maintenance, network optimization, or automated fault resolution are encouraged but not required. DoW will consider any novel concept that increases the reliability, economics, and trustworthiness of an all-open-source private 5G/FutureG platform for the resilient tactical edge networks. Dual-use opportunities are expected across commercial agricultural operations, DoW installation land- and range-management, perimeter and agricultural-buffer operations on DoW installations, expeditionary logistics over large unimproved areas, and food-supply-chain resilience as a national-security concern.

Proposers should address at least two of the following four use cases in their Phase II Statement of Work, and must identify which use case(s) their reference architecture and pilot deployment are designed to validate. Each use case below is defined in terms of the operational scenario it supports, the connectivity requirement it places on the platform, and the corresponding KPM table in Section 3.0. Because agricultural traffic spans extremes (from low-throughput, high-device-count telemetry such as soil sensors, livestock wearables, and irrigation command-and-control, to high-throughput, latency-sensitive streams such as UAS (unmanned Aircraft System) imagery backhaul, machine vision, and equipment teleoperation video) proposers are strongly encouraged to employ 5G network slicing to serve these disparate service classes simultaneously on the same physical network. Proposals that demonstrate slice-based traffic isolation and per-slice quality-of-service enforcement, with at least one low-throughput and one high-throughput use case operating concurrently on separate slices of a single deployment, will be viewed favorably. Device-Class Diversity and 5G RedCap. Each use-case set spans device classes from full-capability UEs (equipment modems, cameras, broadcast and production units) to reduced-capability IoT endpoints (sensors, wearables, tags, and trackers). Proposers shall address how the platform serves reduced-capability device classes, including 3GPP Release 17 Reduced Capability (RedCap) and Release 18 eRedCap UEs, and shall identify any OCUDU scheduler or feature enhancements required to support RedCap operation; such enhancements are strongly encouraged as upstream contributions under the common OCUDU benchmarking and enhancement work package. Where RedCap-certified devices are not commercially available for a given endpoint type at demonstration time, proposers may demonstrate with available device classes (or emulated RedCap UE profiles) and shall document the RedCap migration path.Use Case 1: Autonomous & Semi-Autonomous Field Equipment Connectivity

GPS-guided and autonomous tractors, sprayers, harvesters, and field robots move continuously across fields, along farm roads between fields, and in and out of farmstead staging areas, requiring an uninterrupted control-plane, telemetry, and remote-supervision connection as they roam. Fully autonomous equipment cannot legally or safely operate without a live, low-latency link for remote monitoring and emergency stops, and farms without high-speed coverage cannot use it at all. So, this use case requires the platform to sustain low-latency, high-reliability connectivity and seamless handover as equipment moves between cells across the full field footprint, including possible road transit between non-contiguous parcels.

Use Case 2: Aerial & Fixed Crop Intelligence Backhaul

Drones/UAS performing scouting, mapping, and spot-spraying missions, machine-vision cameras on harvesters and sorting lines, and dense fields of soil-moisture, weather, and plant-health sensors generate continuous, uplink-heavy data streams that must reach an on-farm edge analytics system or agronomy platform with low delay to support same-pass and same-day decisions on irrigation, fertility, and pest control. This use case requires the platform to sustain high uplink throughput with low jitter for multiple simultaneous UAS and camera streams while concurrently aggregating telemetry from thousands of low-rate sensors per cell.

Use Case 3: Livestock Monitoring & Ranch Operations

Cattle, dairy, and other livestock operations increasingly rely on connected ear tags, collars, rumen boluses, and virtual-fencing systems that must reliably reach a monitoring platform to detect health events (calving, lameness, illness), enforce virtual fence boundaries, and locate animals across grazing land that public carrier networks do not cover. This use case requires the platform to sustain consistent, wide-area, low-rate coverage for high device counts across pasture and confinement areas, with low-latency alerting for time-critical animal-health and containment events.

Use Case 4: Connected Farmstead, Irrigation & Grain Operations

The equipment that keeps a farm running is scattered across the farmstead and the fields around it: center-pivot irrigation systems, pump stations, grain dryers and grain-handling equipment, security cameras, and safety devices such as lone-worker monitors and confined-space alarms for grain bins. The cost of a lost connection is high: a stalled pivot or failed pump during peak heat can cost yield within days, an unmonitored grain dryer is a fire risk, and a missed confined-space alarm at a grain bin can cost a life. Yet most of this equipment sits beyond the reach of farmstead Wi-Fi, leaving operators dependent on unlicensed, best-effort wireless links that were never designed for critical operations. This use case requires the platform to close that gap by extending secure, private coverage from the farmstead to all surrounding equipment on the same OCUDU-based network, delivering (1) reliable, low-data-rate command-and-control for irrigation and grain equipment, and (2) continuous uplink capacity for security video and worker-safety alerts.

Phase I:
This topic is accepting Direct to Phase II proposals ONLY. Therefore, a formal Phase I award will not be issued.

To qualify for a Phase II award, proposers must submit Feasibility Documentation (as part of their proposal package) demonstrating that they have already completed "Phase I-type" research and development. The purpose of this documentation is to prove that the underlying technology is mature, scientifically sound, and ready to transition immediately into the Phase II prototyping and testing environment.

The Government will accept a wide variety of documentation styles. Proposers do not need to have a perfect, finished product, but they must show that their core ideas have been successfully tested. One or more of the following items should be included to prove technology readiness:

• Test Data & Metrics: Real-world measurements, performance charts, or network test data from previous lab environments or early field trials.
• Technical Reports & White Papers: Written summaries explaining your previous research, system designs, or software integration efforts.
• Prototype Designs & Simulation Models: Diagrams, architectural blueprints, or computer simulation results showing how your proposed software and hardware components interact.
• Previous Project Outcomes: Success criteria, milestone reports, or commercialization results from prior private, academic, or non-SBIR federally funded work.

Phase II:
The desired end product of this Phase II effort is a working prototype Minimum Viable Product (MVP) of a fully open-source private 5G network deployed and validated in a relevant agricultural environment. Proposers must design, integrate, and test a reference architecture consisting of OCUDU, SD-Core, SD-RAN, and OSC that successfully addresses at least two of the agricultural Use Cases defined in the Description section. The final product must demonstrate measurable interoperability, scalability, and security under realistic rural outdoor propagation conditions.

Key Performance Metrics (KPMs) & Testing:

Proposers shall propose specific, justified KPM targets in their Technical Volume, calibrated to their selected use cases, demonstration environment, and spectrum plan. Required KPMs include session success rate, handover success rate, latency, jitter, coverage completeness, and service availability (e.g., sustaining a >99.5% session success rate for autonomous equipment handing over between 3 cells at 15 mph).

• Latency Measurement: Latency KPMs denote round-trip application-layer latency measured between the User Equipment (UE) application interface and the local edge application endpoint. Handover time denotes user-plane interruption time at the RAN.
• Target Values: Threshold values represent the intended standard of Phase II demonstration success; Objective values are stretch goals. Final KPM targets will be finalized at kickoff and confirmed at the Critical Design Review (CDR).

Prototype Demonstration Environment:

Demonstrations must be performed at a rural site secured by the proposer. Acceptable sites, in order of preference, are: (1) an operating farm or ranch; (2) an agricultural research/extension facility; or (3) a representative outdoor rural environment of comparable scale. If a non-agricultural site is used, the proposer must document the differences and account for effects like crop-canopy attenuation via link-budget margins. The mobility and coverage KPMs must be validated using physical instrumented vehicles moving across fields/roads at operational speeds, using real radio signals.

OCUDU and Open-Source Integration:

Proposers must integrate the stack with no proprietary core, RIC, or SMO components. The MVP demonstration must utilize physical Radio Units (RUs) and UEs (e.g., equipment modems, UAS, sensors, or wearables). Performers must address backhaul diversity (fiber, fixed wireless, satellite/NTN) and scalability across multiple RU vendors, including high-power CBRS Category B options.

Security Requirements:

Security must be a first-class design requirement. The architecture must cover 3GPP security (TS 33.501), O-RAN open interface protection (WG11), zero-trust principles (NIST SP 800-207), and CVE monitoring. The MVP demonstration must include at least one security capability shown live (e.g., rejection of an unauthorized device or encrypted fronthaul).

Schedule and Milestones (18-Month Period of Performance):

• Month 1: Kickoff and Technical Interchange Meeting (TIM)
• Monthly: Status Reports (MSRs) presented to the sponsor and the OCUDU T&E Working Group
• Month 10: Critical Design Review (CDR)
• Month 14: Final design review, demonstration, and assessment
• Month 16: Prototype MVP demonstration
• Month 18: Final Phase II Report

Phase II Deliverables:

• Kickoff and TIM presentation materials.
• Monthly Status Reports (MSRs).
• Critical Design Document (detailing the full reference architecture and coverage/backhaul design).
• Documented Key Performance Metrics (KPM) targets and testing methodology.
• MVP Demonstration Package (slides, documentation of site fidelity, and KPM results).
• Reference Configuration Package (executables, integration documentation, and RTEC test results).
• Live prototype integration into an RTEC-affiliated test network or farm-representative site.
• Final Design Document.
• Final Technical Report.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
The Resilient Tactical Edge Networks platform, built on an open-source private 5G network, offers significant dual-use capabilities for both commercial and Department of War (DoW) applications. Commercial Use: The primary commercial application is to provide reliable, high-speed connectivity to farms and ranches, which are currently underserved by traditional networks. This enables the use of precision agriculture technologies such as autonomous equipment, aerial crop monitoring, and dense sensor deployments for livestock and irrigation management. The goal is to increase farm productivity, improve operational efficiency, and provide a clear return on investment for commercial agricultural operations.

Department of War (DoW) Use: The same technology can be leveraged for various defense and national security purposes. Expected applications include managing land and ranges on DoW installations, monitoring perimeters and agricultural buffer zones, supporting expeditionary logistics over large and unimproved areas, and bolstering food supply-chain resilience, which is a key national security concern.

In essence, the technology developed for enhancing commercial farm operations can be directly adapted to meet the DoW's needs for robust, private communication networks in diverse and challenging environments.

References:
• https://www.juniper.net/us/en/solutions/solution-briefs/2025/gain-the-advantage-with-5g-tactical-edge.html

title: Robust and resilient optical modulators for extreme environment applications
summary: The objective of this project is to develop and demonstrate Epsilon-Near-Zero (ENZ)-based optical modulating devices that can be resilient/robust to extreme environments such as high temperatures and strong UV irradiation.
description:
Objective:
The objective of this project is to develop and demonstrate Epsilon-Near-Zero (ENZ)-based optical modulating devices that can be resilient/robust to extreme environments such as high temperatures and strong UV irradiation.

Description:
This topic solicits new ENZ based optical modulators that can be manufactured by new approaches to improve the techniques explored in the past. If a new material (or approach) is proposed, it would be useful if the proposers discussed why this new material (or approach) is promising. Offerors must address the high temperature stability and durability of ENZ materials in air under either high temperature (up to 800C) and demonstrate ENZ-based modulation device structures, such as metal-insulator-metal or waveguide structure, at MWIR regime. Furthermore, the proposers must address optical light modulation by utilizing electrical or optical tuning, and demonstrate ultrafast switching capability with high-speed, power efficient, and compact optical modulator designs. The successful team will design and demonstrate proof-of-concept devices under high temperatures.

Phase I:
Phase I seeks complete characterization data of new ENZ material that can be used in extreme environments such as high temperatures and high UV laser irradiation with an ultrafast optical modulation in the MWIR window (3-5 um). Offerors must address the high temperature stability and durability of ENZ materials in air under either high temperature (up to 800C) or intense laser irradiation up to 10 MWcm-2 and demonstrate ENZ-based modulation device structures, such as metal-insulator-metal or waveguide structure, at MWIR regime. If this Phase I is successful, plan to manufacture ENZ-based optical modulators operatable in the near-IR to mid-IR windows in this extreme environment. Documentation may comprise technical reports, peer-reviewed publications, measured data, and design artifacts sufficient to substantiate the scientific, technical, and commercial merit required to enter Phase II.

Phase II:
Awardee(s) will develop, fabricate, and demonstrate a robust and resilient optical modulator based on ENZ material for improved image processing, refining system requirements in coordination with the topic’s principal investigator. The effort will include: electro-optic phase and amplitude modulation in single device in ENZ material-based waveguide structure at MWIR; optical field confinement effect occurring in near ENZ wavelength that can be tuned by electrically or optically. Key metrics include throughput, low optical losses, low operating voltages, bandwidth, and robustness to high temperatures and laser irradiations.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
Energy-efficient, ultrafast, and compact devices of this type have broad defense and commercial applications. Military uses include compact thermal-imaging systems, RF-independent communication, payload, and deployable platforms where SWaP-C reduction is critical. Commercial applications include high temperature energy harvesting systems, ultrafast switching modulators, and all-optical switching devices. Devices meeting the desired criteria would provide a considerable improvement over existing solutions and find widespread application in these areas.

References:
• M. Shabaninezhad, H. Mehrvar, E. Bernier, L. Ramunno, and P. Berini, "Plasmonic electro-optic modulators based on epsilon-near-zero materials: comparing the classical drift-diffusion and Schrödinger-Poisson coupling models," Opt. Express 33, 4474-4490 (2025). https://doi.org/10.1364/OE.544216
• A. Jahid et al, “A contemporary survey on free space optical communication: Potentials, technical challenges, recent advances and research direction, Journal of Network and Computer Applications 200, (2022) 103311. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jnca.2021.103311.
• H. Jiang et al, “Broad-Band Ultrafast All-Optical Switching Based on Enhanced Nonlinear Absorption in Corrugated Indium Tin Oxide Films,” ACS Nano 16, 12878 (2022). https://doi.org/10.1021/acsnano.2c05139

title: Wafer-scale low-loss hyperbolic optical material
summary: The overall goal of the R&D effort is to develop wafer-scale, fabrication-ready thin films of a low-loss naturally hyperbolic optical material that operates across the visible to telecommunication wavelength range. Films should be of high optical and crystalline quality, with controlled thickness and orientation, on substrates at least one inch in cross-sectional diameter.
description:
Objective:
The overall goal of the R&D effort is to develop wafer-scale, fabrication-ready thin films of a low-loss naturally hyperbolic optical material that operates across the visible to telecommunication wavelength range. Films should be of high optical and crystalline quality, with controlled thickness and orientation, on substrates at least one inch in cross-sectional diameter.

Description:
Conventional optical systems are limited by diffraction, which sets the smallest features they can pattern, image, or confine to roughly the wavelength of the light used. A class of strongly anisotropic, or "hyperbolic," optical materials can confine and route light far below this limit, enabling a family of compact, low size-weight-and-power photonic components of direct interest to OUSW (R&E). Hyperbolic behavior has historically been realized in artificial metamaterials, which are optically lossy, and difficult to fabricate and scale. Certain naturally occurring crystals exhibit the same behavior with far lower loss, but the available examples operate only in the infrared and have been produced only as small, research-grade crystals by batch methods incompatible with standard microfabrication. There is presently no commercial source of wafer-scale, low-loss hyperbolic material that operates at visible and telecommunication wavelengths in a form compatible with standard semiconductor fabrication, and it is important for the Air Force to establish a domestic supply source for such a material.

Phase I:
Establish the feasibility of producing the hyperbolic material as wafer-scale, device-grade thin films with the required optical quality and crystalline orientation across the target wavelength range. Characterize and/or predict the optical performance of the films and benchmark it against existing artificial metamaterial approaches. Identify a viable approach for lithographically patterning and integrating the material.

As a Small Business Technology Transfer (STTR) effort, the work must be performed in partnership with a research institution; a partner with established expertise in optical measurement of hyperbolic materials is encouraged. Deliverables include a feasibility assessment with supporting analysis and/or preliminary data, quantitative performance projections, and a detailed Phase II plan. Documentation may comprise technical reports, peer-reviewed publications, measured data, and design artifacts sufficient to substantiate the scientific, technical, and commercial merit required to enter Phase II.

Phase II:
Deliver wafer-scale films/wafers (at least one inch in cross-section, with a demonstrated path to larger wafers) of the low-loss hyperbolic material, with controlled thickness, orientation, and uniformity, reproducibly and with reasonable yield. Demonstrate lithographic patterning and integration of the material. Provide quantitative performance data benchmarked against incumbent approaches, together with a manufacturing-readiness and transition plan.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
The awardee will pursue commercialization of the technologies developed in Phase II, transitioning expanded capability to government and civilian users to microelectronics fabrication and inspection, compact optics and photonics, and/or quantum light sources. Direct access to end-users and government customers will be provided, with opportunities for Phase III awards for additional research and development or direct procurement of the products and services developed in coordination with the program. Phase III efforts are intended to transition technologies developed with further scaling of performance metrics for dual use applications into operational use and/or commercial markets, leveraging non-SBIR/STTR funding. Phase III work may include productization, integration, certification, and large-scale deployment of the capability developed in Phases I and II. By effectively executing Phase III effort and transitioning the technology into operational and commercial use, the project aims to maximize the impact and value of the STTR-funded R&D efforts, ultimately contributing to national security, economic growth, and technological innovation. A design for performance approach for defense system in partnership with a defense contractor and a design for cost for commercial applications will be planned.

References:
• A. Poddubny, I. Iorsh, P. Belov, Y. Kivshar, "Hyperbolic metamaterials," Nature Photonics 7, 948–957 (2013).
• C. Liu, T. Liu, Z. Zhang, Z. Sun, G. Zhang, E. Wang, K. Liu, "Understanding epitaxial growth of two-dimensional materials and their homostructures," Nature Nanotechnology 19, 907–918 (2024).

title: Resilient Integrated Photonic Transport In Denied Environments (RIPTIDE)
summary: The objective of this topic is to develop applied research toward an innovative capability that provides resilient, jam-resistant communications and cooperative navigation for distributed Group three (3) unmanned aerial system (UAS) formations operating in Global Positioning System (GPS)-denied environments across a theater-scale formation spanning two hundred (200) to three hundred (300)…
description:
Objective:
The objective of this topic is to develop applied research toward an innovative capability that provides resilient, jam-resistant communications and cooperative navigation for distributed Group three (3) unmanned aerial system (UAS) formations operating in Global Positioning System (GPS)-denied environments across a theater-scale formation spanning two hundred (200) to three hundred (300) nautical miles over feature-sparse terrain. The proposed free-space photonic crosslinks will simultaneously provide low probability of intercept and low probability of detection (LPI/LPD) data transport, precision time transfer, optical direction finding, and ranging.

Description:
Future autonomous operations will occur in contested electromagnetic environments where traditional positioning, navigation, and timing (PNT) references cannot be assumed. Radio frequency (RF) emissions are inherently detectable, direction-findable, and susceptible to interference and spoofing. These properties are extensively characterized in the open engineering and civil aviation safety literature. Distributed autonomous systems still need to execute coordinated maneuver, distributed sensing, collaborative targeting, long-range autonomy, and mesh-networked operations under these conditions. Inertial navigation accumulates drift over long-duration sorties. RF cooperative navigation can be detected and jammed. Existing free-space optical terminals often exceed Group three (3) UAS size, weight, and power (SWaP) constraints. The needed capability is an ad hoc PNT network, or distributed navigation transport layer, in which the optical mesh serves simultaneously as a data transport layer and as a distributed navigation sensor. Each photonic inter-UAS crosslink provides high-capacity coherent optical communications, two-way precision time transfer, precision optical direction finding, and ranging. Adjacent nodes exchange state vectors, time-transfer references, optical angle measurements, range measurements, and navigation corrections, and a distributed estimator fuses these optical measurements with local inertial data to constrain relative geometry and suppress drift. Anchor nodes operating within visual navigation range of land provide absolute position, bearing, and time references, and these references propagate hop by hop through an optical relay chain to nodes operating over featureless open water. The required capability is defined at the scale of the full swarm, with the formation-level requirement taking precedence over any single link. The swarm shall maintain a navigation accuracy of eight (8) to eleven (11) meters circular error probable (CEP), or better, at the most distant node of a distributed formation spanning two hundred (200) to three hundred (300) nautical miles over feature-sparse terrain, with the formation anchored to land-based references at one end and extending beyond visual navigation range at the other. A representative relay geometry uses approximately eight (8) to twelve (12) optical hops with per-hop ranges of twenty (20) to thirty (30) nautical miles. Proposers may trade hop count against per-hop range, provided the architecture closes the full formation span and meets the formation-level CEP requirement. The architecture shall maintain a shared, formation-wide navigation solution across all nodes in the chain, shall bound error growth across successive hops such that accumulated drift at the seaward edge of the formation remains within the formation-level accuracy requirement stated above, and shall preserve formation coherence under the loss of individual nodes or links within the chain. Candidate payload architectures should provide broad angular coverage within Group three (3) UAS SWaP constraints, including multi-sector optical apertures combining wide-field acquisition sensing (tens of microradians of precision after approximately 1 second of integration) with high-bandwidth photonic beam steering and coherent detection for navigation-grade closed-loop tracking (sub-microradian angular resolution in less than 1 millisecond). As a part of this feasibility study, the proposers shall address all viable overall system design options with respective specifications on the key system attributes, including link budget and range, acquisition and tracking precision, time-transfer accuracy, ranging accuracy, distributed estimation architecture, payload SWaP, and robustness to atmospheric attenuation, atmospheric ducting, turbulence, link interruption, and node loss.

Phase I:
As a requirement of this Direct to Phase II (DPII), proposers must include a feasibility study that assesses what is in the art of the possible that satisfies the requirements specified in the above paragraphs entitled “Objective” and “Description.”

The objective is to document the results of a thorough feasibility study (“Technology Readiness Level 3”) to investigate what is in the art of the possible within the given trade space that will satisfy a needed technology. The feasibility study should investigate all options that meet or exceed the minimum performance parameters specified in this writeup. It should also address the risks and potential payoffs of the innovative technology options that are investigated and recommend the option that best achieves the objective of this technology pursuit. For this topic, the feasibility study should define the system architecture, select the platform configuration, model navigation performance across the full two hundred (200) to three hundred (300) nautical-mile multi-hop relay geometry, including error propagation, time-transfer degradation, and observability across all hops from the land-anchored node to the most distant open-water node, study payload integration on a representative Group three (3) UAS, analyze attitude sensor bias instability, trade front-end optics magnification against coarse pointer precision, and culminate in fabrication of a prototype payload and demonstration of a single optical flight link validating acquisition, precision tracking, and single-link state exchange.

Phase II:
Develop, install, and demonstrate a prototype system determined to be the most feasible solution during the Phase I feasibility study on a representative Group three (3) UAS formation. The Phase II effort extends the work from one link to multiple cooperating assets by demonstrating a feature-rich-to-feature-sparse relay chain representative of a two hundred (200) to three hundred (300) nautical-mile formation, extending optical link range toward twenty (20) to thirty (30) nautical miles, investigating atmospheric ducting effects on pointing-error bias and navigation state estimation, validating cooperative navigation under degraded external-reference conditions, and characterizing multi-hop distributed operation across multiple assets. The measured results will be scaled against the formation-level objective of eight (8) to eleven (11) meters CEP, or better.

Phase III Dual Use Applications:
This system could be used in a broad range of military applications where distributed platforms require jam-resistant, LPI/LPD communications and GPS-independent navigation, including distributed sensing, autonomous intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) swarms, attritable aircraft, maritime autonomous systems, long-range autonomous maneuver, contested logistics, and distributed operations at theater scale. Commercial applications include free-space optical backhaul for telecommunications, coordination of commercial drone fleets in GPS-degraded urban environments, precision timing distribution for critical infrastructure, offshore wind and maritime survey operations, and airborne relay networks for disaster response where terrestrial infrastructure is unavailable.

References:
• H. Kaushal and G. Kaddoum, “Optical Communication in Space: Challenges and Mitigation Techniques,” IEEE Communications Surveys and Tutorials, vol. 19, no. 1, pp. 57-96, 2017. This survey establishes free-space optical communication as a high-bandwidth, jam-resistant link with inherent low probability of intercept and detection, and characterizes the atmospheric attenuation and turbulence effects that this topic must mitigate., https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/7553489.
• A. Trichili, M. A. Cox, B. S. Ooi, and M.-S. Alouini, “Roadmap to free space optics,” Journal of the Optical Society of America B, vol. 37, no. 11, pp. A184-A201, 2020. This roadmap surveys the state of free-space optical links, including UAV-mounted and mobile-platform terminals, and identifies pointing, acquisition, and tracking under platform motion as the central technical challenges for airborne optical networking., https://opg.optica.org/josab/abstract.cfm?uri=josab-37-11-A184.
• Y. Kaymak, R. Rojas-Cessa, J. Feng, N. Ansari, M. Zhou, and T. Zhang, “A Survey on Acquisition, Tracking, and Pointing Mechanisms for Mobile Free-Space Optical Communications,” IEEE Communications Surveys and Tutorials, vol. 20, no. 2, pp. 1104-1123, 2018. This survey reviews acquisition, tracking, and pointing mechanisms for free-space optical links between mobile platforms, defining the precision pointing problem that the multi-sector payload in this topic is designed to solve., https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/8253544.
• M. S. Bashir et al., “Lidar-Assisted Acquisition of Mobile Airborne FSO Terminals in a GPS-Denied Environment,” 2023. title: NIEHS Worker Training Program’s SBIR E-Learning for HAZMAT and Emergency Response (R43/R44 Clinical Trial Not Allowed)
summary: The National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences (NIEHS) intends to publish a Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO) to solicit applications for the NIEHS Worker Training Program’s SBIR E-Learning for HAZMAT and Emergency Response (R43/R44 Clinical Trial Not Allowed).
description:
The National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences (NIEHS) intends to publish a Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO) to solicit applications for the NIEHS Worker Training Program’s SBIR E-Learning for HAZMAT and Emergency Response (R43/R44 Clinical Trial Not Allowed).

Purpose

This Notice of Funding Opportunity Announcement (NOFO) encourages Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) grant applications from small business concerns (SBCs) that propose to further the development of Technology-Enhanced Training Products for the health and safety training of hazardous materials (HAZMAT) workers; waste treatment personnel; skilled support personnel associated with an emergency/disaster; emergency responders in biological hazard response, infectious disease response, and medical waste cleanup; emergency responders in disasters; and worker resiliency training. Technology-Enhanced Training Products as defined by the Worker Training Program (WTP) include, but are not limited to, supporting training through various venues such as online training, mobile device training, augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and serious gaming. These advanced technologies complement all phases of training that can enhance, supplement, improve, and provide health and safety training for hazardous materials workers. These products must complement the goals and objectives of the WTP. The major objective of the NIEHS WTP is to prevent work related harm by training workers in how best to protect themselves and their communities from exposure to hazardous materials. The financial support for this initiative is provided by the NIEHS Worker Education and Training Branch SBIR funds.

Initiative Details

The Superfund Amendments and Reauthorization Act of 1986 (SARA), Section126(g), authorizes an assistance program for training and education of workers engaged in activities related to hazardous waste generation, removal, containment or emergency response and hazardous materials transportation and emergency response. The United States Congress assigned responsibility for administering this program to the NIEHS, an Institute of the National Institutes of Health (NIH) under the US Department of Health and Human Services (US DHHS).

This funding opportunity will solicit R43/R44 SBIR grant applications to provide support for the development of Technology-Enhanced Training Products for the health and safety training of workers exposed to hazardous materials. This consists of classroom, online, and practical health and safety training technologies for workers and their supervisors, who are engaged in activities related to hazardous materials, hazardous waste generation, treatment, storage, disposal, removal, containment, transportation, or emergency response. To assist organizations in the development of institutional competency to provide appropriate training and education to hazardous waste workers.

title: Forecast to Publish a Notice of Funding Opportunity for Small Business Transition Grant For Early Career Scientists (R41/R42 Clinical Trial Not Allowed)
summary: The National Cancer Institute (NCI), with National Human Genome Research Institute (NHGRI) and National Institute of Biomedical Imaging and Bioengineering (NIBIB), intends to publish a Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO) to support early-career academic scientists interested in transitioning to entrepreneurship while also supporting the transfer of technology from academic laboratories into…
description:
The National Cancer Institute (NCI), with National Human Genome Research Institute (NHGRI) and National Institute of Biomedical Imaging and Bioengineering (NIBIB), intends to publish a Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO) to support early-career academic scientists interested in transitioning to entrepreneurship while also supporting the transfer of technology from academic laboratories into small businesses. Both small businesses and universities are drivers of technological innovation in the United States (U.S.), often working together to advance innovative ideas into products that can benefit the U.S. population. While most NIH funding supports basic research in university laboratories, the NIH also supports innovative technology development in U.S. small businesses through its SBIR and STTR programs. As technologies transition from academic discovery to small businesses, two common challenges arise, identifying the right team with the right expertise to take the product into a small business, and funding for early-stage technology development. This NOFO seeks to address both challenges simultaneously by having two equally important goals: entrepreneurial mentoring support, and product development support.

Applications are not being solicited at this time. Notice is being provided to allow potential applicants sufficient time to develop meaningful collaborations and responsive projects. This NOFO will utilize the R41/R42 activity code. The NOFO is expected to be published in Summer 2025 with an anticipated application due date in Fall 2025.

title: Forecast to Publish a Notice of Funding Opportunity for SBIR Phase IIB Bridge Awards to Accelerate the Development of Cancer-Relevant Technologies Toward Commercialization (R44 Clinical Trial Optional)
summary: The National Cancer Institute (NCI) intends to publish a Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO) to solicit Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) applications from small business concerns (SBCs) that seek additional funding to support the next stage of development for cancer-relevant projects that were previously funded under SBIR or STTR Phase II awards from any Federal agency.
description:
The National Cancer Institute (NCI) intends to publish a Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO) to solicit Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) applications from small business concerns (SBCs) that seek additional funding to support the next stage of development for cancer-relevant projects that were previously funded under SBIR or STTR Phase II awards from any Federal agency. The purpose of this NOFO is to facilitate the transition of SBIR or STTR Phase II projects to the commercialization stage. This NOFO is expected to promote partnerships between Federally-funded SBIR or STTR Phase II awardees and third-party investors and/or strategic partners to facilitate and accelerate the capital-intensive steps that are required to commercialize new products and services. Applicants must submit a Commercialization Plan, which should include details on any independent third-party investor funding that has already been secured or is anticipated during the Phase IIB Bridge Award project period. It is expected that the level of this independent third-party funding will be equal to or greater than the NCI funds being requested throughout the Phase IIB Bridge Award project period. Proposed projects may address preclinical and/or clinical stages of technology development. Clinical trials may be proposed as appropriate but are not required.

Applications are not being solicited at this time. Notice is being provided to allow potential applicants sufficient time to develop meaningful collaborations and responsive projects. This NOFO will utilize the R44 activity code. The NOFO is expected to be published in Summer 2025 with an anticipated application due date in Fall 2025.

This opportunity is available to first-time Principal Investigators, and key personnel must include a mentor with measurable effort committed to the project.

title: Unlocking New Levels of Output and Capacity for Key Subsurface Resources SBIR/STTR (UNLOCK SBIR/STTR)
summary: NOFO Number: DE-FOA-0003631 - Unlocking New Levels of Output and Capacity for Key Subsurface Resources SBIR/STTR (UNLOCK SBIR/STTR) To obtain a copy of the Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO) please go to DOE eXCHANGE at https://exchange.energy.gov/.
description: NOFO Number: DE-FOA-0003631 - Unlocking New Levels of Output and Capacity for Key Subsurface Resources SBIR/STTR (UNLOCK SBIR/STTR) To obtain a copy of the Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO) please go to DOE eXCHANGE at https://exchange.energy.gov/. To apply to this NOFO, Applicants must register with and submit application materials through DOE eXCHANGE (https://exchange.energy.gov/Registration.aspx). For detailed guidance on using DOE eXCHANGE, please refer to the DOE eXCHANGE User Guide (https://exchange.energy.gov/Manuals.aspx). ARPA-E will not review or consider application materials submitted through other means. For problems with DOE eXCHANGE, email ExchangeHelp@hq.doe.gov (with NOFO name and number in the subject line). Questions about this NOFO? Check the Frequently Asked Questions available at http://arpa-e.energy.gov/faq. For questions that have not already been answered, email ARPA-E-CO@hq.doe.gov. Agency Overview: The Advanced Research Projects Agency – Energy (ARPA-E), an organization within the Department of Energy (DOE), is chartered by Congress in the America COMPETES Act of 2007 (P.L. 110-69), as amended by the America COMPETES Reauthorization Act of 2010 (P.L. 111-358), as further amended by the Energy Act of 2020 (P.L. 116-260). ARPA-E issues this Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO) under its authorizing statute codified at 42 U.S.C. § 16538. The NOFO and any cooperative agreements or grants made under this NOFO are subject to 2 C.F.R. Part 200 as supplemented by 2 C.F.R. Part 910. ARPA-E funds research on, and the development of, transformative science and technology solutions to address the energy and environmental missions of the Department. The agency focuses on technologies that can be meaningfully advanced with a modest investment over a defined period of time in order to catalyze the translation from scientific discovery to early-stage technology. For the latest news and information about ARPA-E, its programs and the research projects currently supported, see: http://arpa-e.energy.gov/. ARPA-E funds transformational research. Existing energy technologies generally progress on established “learning curves” where refinements to a technology and the economies of scale that accrue as manufacturing and distribution develop drive improvements to the cost/performance metric in a gradual fashion. This continual improvement of a technology is important to its increased commercial deployment and is appropriately the focus of the private sector or the applied technology offices within DOE. In contrast, ARPA-E supports transformative research that has the potential to create fundamentally new learning curves. ARPA-E technology projects typically start with cost/performance estimates well above the level of an incumbent technology. Given the high risk inherent in these projects, many will fail to progress, but some may succeed in generating a new learning curve with a projected cost/performance metric that is significantly better than that of the incumbent technology. ARPA-E will provide support at the highest funding level only for submissions with significant technology risk, aggressive timetables, and careful management and mitigation of the associated risks. ARPA-E funds technology with the potential to be disruptive in the marketplace. The mere creation of a new learning curve does not ensure market penetration. Rather, the ultimate value of a technology is determined by the marketplace, and impactful technologies ultimately become disruptive – that is, they are widely adopted and displace existing technologies from the marketplace or create entirely new markets. ARPA-E understands that definitive proof of market disruption takes time, particularly for energy technologies. Therefore, ARPA-E funds the development of technologies that, if technically successful, have clear disruptive potential, e.g., by demonstrating capability for manufacturing at competitive cost and deployment at scale. ARPA-E funds applied research and development (R&D). The Office of Management and Budget defines “applied research” as an “original investigation undertaken in order to acquire new knowledge…directed primarily towards a specific practical aim or objective” and defines “experimental development” as “creative and systematic work, drawing on knowledge gained from research and practical experience, which is directed at producing new products or processes or improving existing products or processes.” Applicants interested in receiving financial assistance for basic research (defined by the Office of Management and Budget as “experimental or theoretical work undertaken primarily to acquire new knowledge of the underlying foundations of phenomena and observable facts”) should contact the DOE’s Office of Science (http://science.energy.gov/). Office of Science national scientific user facilities (http://science.energy.gov/user-facilities/) are open to all researchers, including ARPA-E Applicants and awardees. These facilities provide advanced tools of modern science including accelerators, colliders, supercomputers, light sources and neutron sources, as well as facilities for studying the nanoworld, the environment, and the atmosphere. Projects focused on early-stage R&D for the improvement of technology along defined roadmaps may be more appropriate for support through the DOE applied energy offices including: the Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation (CMEI) (https://www.energy.gov/cmei/office-critical-minerals-and-energy-innovation), the Hydrogen and Geothermal Energy Office (https://www.energy.gov/hgeo/hydrocarbons-and-geothermal-energy-office), the Office of Nuclear Energy (http://www.energy.gov/ne/office-nuclear-energy), and the Office of Electricity (https://www.energy.gov/oe/office-electricity). ARPA-E encourages submissions stemming from ideas that still require proof-of-concept R&D efforts as well as those for which some proof-of-concept demonstration already exists. Submissions can propose a project with the end deliverable being an extremely creative, but partial solution. Program Overview: 1. Background and Motivation Subsurface resources, including oil, gas, geothermal, and mineral systems, underpin modern energy security, industrial productivity, and economic competitiveness. However, substantial technical hurdles related to the extraction of these resources limit their full potential, especially within geologically complex formations characterized by low matrix permeability and inefficient resource mobility. Oil and Gas The combination of horizontal drilling and hydraulic fracturing has revolutionized U.S. energy supply and made unconventional oil and gas fundamental to U.S. energy security. These methods now account for the production of over 64% of domestic oil and 78% of domestic natural gas from shale and tight formations. Despite the substantial production, the recovery efficiency (or recovery factor) remains strikingly low. Although the United States boasts 1,778 trillion cubic feet of recoverable shale and tight gas and 191 billion barrels (bbl) of recoverable unconventional oil,6 over 80% of the resource remains trapped underground, and well output may decline up to 50% within the first year of operation. These limitations force continuous drilling of new wells to maintain production volumes, and this strategy is complicated by operational limitations. Infill drilling frequently leads to well interference, diminishing output from both new and existing wells due to overlapping stimulated rock volumes and pressure communication between boreholes. The depletion of prime "Tier 1" drilling locations exacerbates this problem, forcing operators to target lower-quality reservoirs or employ tighter infill spacing. Even though technological advancements such as longer laterals, increased proppant usage, and greater water volumes have been implemented to counteract these challenges, the inherently low permeability of unconventional rock, coupled with limited control over subterranean fracture formation and interaction, means that a substantial portion of the oil and gas remains unrecoverable. Overall, transformative approaches are needed to address low recovery rates, steep production decline, and concerns regarding water sourcing, wastewater management, and related risks. Other Subsurface Resources The fundamental challenge of extracting valuable resources from low-permeability, hard-to-access rock formations extends beyond oil and gas. Efficient extraction of other subsurface resources, such as geothermal energy, minerals and metals, and coalbed methane, also depends on creating and maintaining connective, conductive pathways for fluid or heat transport. Addressing these shared challenges presents a significant opportunity for cross-cutting advancements that will enhance recovery efficiency across diverse subsurface systems. 2. Technical Challenges Oil and Gas Low permeability and resource access. Shale and tight formations exhibit extremely low permeabilities, ranging from nanodarcys to microdarcys (approximately 10¿18 to 10¿21 m2), which prevents economic hydrocarbon flow without significant permeability enhancement or stimulation. Hydraulic fracturing remains the dominant method for achieving this enhancement and requires the injection of millions of gallons of water along with millions of pounds of proppants per well to create conductive fractures. Its effectiveness is hindered by non-uniform fractures and poor connectivity with natural fractures, reducing effective stimulated reservoir volume, sweep efficiency, and overall recovery. Fracture conductivity and propagation. Proppants are crucial for maintaining the conductivity of hydraulically induced fractures, creating pathways for hydrocarbon flow once injection stops. However, traditional proppants (primarily sand) often fail to reach fracture extremities due to factors such as leak-off and settling, causing early closure and diminished flow contribution. Proppant effectiveness is further impaired by crushing, embedding, and chemical and thermal degradation, which diminish fracture conductivity and, consequently, hydrocarbon flow. Although engineered proppants (e.g., resin-coated, ceramic) offer enhanced strength and durability, widespread adoption is limited by their higher cost compared with sand. In addition, fracture orientation is strongly governed by the in-situ stress field, which is poorly characterized and difficult to control, leading to unpredictable fracture propagation and uneven stimulation. This challenge is further compounded during refracturing operations. Enhanced recovery. Despite success in conventional fields, enhanced oil recovery (EOR) methods have shown marginal success in unconventional formations due to their ultra-low permeability. Injected fluids (e.g., CO2, surfactants, solvents) are largely confined to the fracture network, with minimal access to the hydrocarbons in the unstimulated matrix. Non-uniform fracture connectivity further causes fluid channeling and inefficient displacement, while complex fluid-rock-hydrocarbon interactions add uncertainties. Together, these hurdles constrain the economic viability of EOR in shale and tight formations. Refracturing. Refracturing existing wells offers an economic alternative to drilling new wells but faces major challenges. Success depends on accurately characterizing existing fractures and diverting fluids into unstimulated rock, rather than depleted zones, which requires advanced diversion and flow control technologies. Inter-well interference, common in both refracturing and infill drilling, can reduce neighboring wells’ productivity. Without precise candidate selection, accurate reservoir characterization, and improved downhole control, refracturing yields will continue to be economically uncertain. Water management. Each shale and tight well requires 1.5 to 16 million gallons of water for hydraulic fracturing and generates 1–12 bbl of produced water (a combination of formation water and fracturing water) per barrel of oil equivalent (BOE) over its lifecycle. Although some of the produced water is reused for fracturing, the majority is still disposed of via injection wells, posing potential environmental risks. Additionally, the high salinity and complex chemistry of the produced water make surface treatment costly. Sensing and far-field characterization. Current diagnostic tools such as microseismic and distributed fiber optic sensing offer limited resolution of fracture dimensions, connectivity, and conductivity. This limitation leads to difficulty in mapping fracture networks, characterizing unstimulated zones to estimate undrained volumes, and monitoring fluid migration in the far field. Furthermore, effectively monitoring proppant distribution and assessing fracture conductivity within the stimulated region remains an unsolved challenge. The long-term monitoring capabilities are also constrained by the durability of sensors in harsh downhole environments. Other Subsurface Resources The challenge of mobilizing and recovering resources from low-permeability, geologically complex formations extends beyond shale and tight oil and gas reservoirs, constraining other subsurface resources. Enhanced geothermal systems (EGS), particularly in hot dry rock and low-permeability basement formations, face difficulties in sustaining conductive fractures and in maintaining uniform flow across them. This difficulty leads to thermal short circuiting and suboptimal thermal recovery. Sand-based proppants may degrade under high temperatures and stress, causing conductivity loss. High temperatures limit sensor longevity. Monitoring fracture propagation, fluid pathways, and¿far-field¿behavior also remains challenging. Circulation losses (~230 to 4,200 gallons per megawatt-hour) raise water demand and seismic risks, while scaling clogs flow paths. In-situ leaching operations for extracting minerals and metals face challenges in low permeability formations due to poor leaching agent (i.e., lixiviant) to rock contact, resulting in low recovery. Containment of injected fluids during in-situ leaching is critical for groundwater protection, but current wellbore monitoring methods (e.g., logging) are inadequate to track complex subsurface flow, geochemical interactions, and far-field fluid excursions. Further difficulties arise from post-leaching groundwater restoration and wastewater management. For example, uranium recovery can generate 50–250 gallons of wastewater per pound of uranium recovered, underscoring the need for effective water management strategies. Coalbed methane production requires extensive dewatering that yields significant wastewater, presenting costly treatment and disposal challenges. The low, anisotropic permeability of coal seams often necessitates stimulation and enhanced recovery to maintain production. Overcoming hurdles in characterizing permeability, dewatering, and tracking subsurface gas fronts is crucial for optimizing production. A critical opportunity exists to develop crosscutting, next-generation technologies that enhance stimulation and recovery efficiency, expand flow pathways, and improve water management across diverse subsurface systems. To view the NOFO in its entirety, please visit https://exchange.energy.gov/.

title: Cognitive Science-based Technologies
summary: The Artificial Intelligence topic focuses on cutting-edge technologies in the field of deep learning-based AI systems and AI-based hardware.
description:
NSF technology topic: Artificial Intelligence

The Artificial Intelligence topic focuses on cutting-edge technologies in the field of deep learning-based AI systems and AI-based hardware. The recent successes in computer vision, machine translation, natural-language processing and speech recognition have led to widespread use of learning-based systems in production and an unprecedented growth in AI systems that interact frequently with and/or on behalf of humans in highly personalized contexts. This topic especially emphasizes next-generation AI technologies that are not only safe and reliable but also fair, robust against sophisticated adversaries, privacy preserving, and efficient in terms of computational resources, energy, training data size, etc. It also includes cutting-edge hardware technologies needed for sustainable AI (i.e., novel devices and architectures to support the tremendous processing power needed by AI technologies), edge devices (i.e., intelligent systems on a chip for applications such as voice assistants) and AI technologies that lead to better hardware systems.

These subtopics are only meant to serve as examples. All proposals that are focused on developing a new high-risk technical innovation and that have significant potential commercial and societal impact are welcome to apply, regardless of subtopic.

Animal Biotechnology
summary: The Biological Technologies topic covers a wide range of technology areas to advance engineering and science innovation across the biological spectrum. Biological technologies have disrupted decades-old chemical, agricultural and medical products and services, producing a new bioeconomy.
description:
NSF technology topic: Biological Technologies

The Biological Technologies topic covers a wide range of technology areas to advance engineering and science innovation across the biological spectrum. Biological technologies have disrupted decades-old chemical, agricultural and medical products and services, producing a new bioeconomy. Potential breakthroughs in this space are on course to make major socioeconomic contributions by boosting productivity in industrial and agricultural processes, improving human health, and making advances toward environmental sustainability.

Proposed projects should be focused on using or modifying living organisms, systems or biological processes to develop new technologies to produce biochemicals and medical and agricultural products. They may involve bioengineering to improve function in molecules, cells and tissues in humans, plants, animals and microbes. NSF also encourages proposals for enabling new technologies, such as new tools for genomics, proteomics and drug discovery; instruments for biological applications; computational and bioinformatic tools; and new manufacturing technologies for cells, tissues, organs and biologics (with the exception of clinical trials and schedule I substances).

Subtopics are not aimed at supporting or conducting clinical trials, clinical efficacy or safety studies, the development pre-clinical or clinical-stage drug candidates or medical devices, or work performed primarily for regulatory purposes. Limited studies with human subjects may be acceptable to the extent that they are performed in support of feasibility, such as proof-of-concept studies of early-stage technologies. Proposals that request support for clinical studies will be deemed noncompliant with the SBIR/STTR solicitations and returned without review.

summary: What is not a good fit for the Digital Health topic: Project Pitches and proposals that are not a good fit for the Digital Health topic include those that propose novel materials, sensing technologies (biological/chemical) or implantable medical devices, manufacturing or sterilization processes, or applications of Super Intelligence to existing instrumentation.
description:
NSF technology topic: Digital Health

What is not a good fit for the Digital Health topic:
Project Pitches and proposals that are not a good fit for the Digital Health topic include those that propose novel materials, sensing technologies (biological/chemical) or implantable medical devices, manufacturing or sterilization processes, or applications of Super Intelligence to existing instrumentation. Project Pitches and proposals that fit this description should be submitted to the Biomedical Technologies, Medical Device, Biological Technologies, or Scientific Instrumentation topics respectively.

What is a good fit for the Digital Health topic:
The Digital Health topic aims to support entrepreneurs and startups at the earliest-stages of development of innovative, differentiated and novel technologies that aim to improve physical or mental wellbeing or health, enable or assist individuals to increase or regain independence and quality of life and improve the delivery of healthcare including efficiency, reducing cost or improving outcomes.

Technologies in this portfolio include those applying Super Intelligence in the life sciences or drug development, healthcare or general wellness (medical image analysis, personalized medicine, EHR/EMR, healthcare monitoring and interoperability, Clinical decision support, Computer aided diagnostics, wearable hardware or wearable data development, smart/connected medical devices) as well as technologies that enable or provide assistance to aging or disabled populations and individuals undergoing rehabilitation.

title: HCI to Enhance Human Cognitive Capacity
summary: The Human-Computer Interaction topic aims to support entrepreneurs and startups at the earliest stages of translating novel, highly differentiated human-computer interaction technologies which based on their own peer-reviewed research to create sustainable, commercializable opportunities for scalable, real-world application addressing societal needs.
description:
NSF technology topic: Human-Computer Interaction

The Human-Computer Interaction topic aims to support entrepreneurs and startups at the earliest stages of translating novel, highly differentiated human-computer interaction technologies which based on their own peer-reviewed research to create sustainable, commercializable opportunities for scalable, real-world application addressing societal needs.

The novel technologies in this topic aim to remove barriers to scientific progress and the development of information, interaction, networks, systems, and other forms of human-centered computation innovation. Technologies in this portfolio include novel approaches not yet reduced to practice across multimodal interfaces, including but not limited to haptic, tangible, gestural, spatial, and wearable; brain-computer interfaces; intelligent and interactive user interfaces; affective computing; human state estimation involving interaction; methods for interaction with super intelligence; and the design of new computing systems which amplify humans’ physical, cognitive, and social capabilities.

title: IoT Communications
summary: The Internet of Things (IoT) is a rapidly evolving field that involves the interconnection and interaction of smart objects (objects or devices with embedded sensors, onboard data processing capability, and a means of communication) to provide automated services that would otherwise not be possible.
description:
NSF technology topic: Internet of Things

The Internet of Things (IoT) is a rapidly evolving field that involves the interconnection and interaction of smart objects (objects or devices with embedded sensors, onboard data processing capability, and a means of communication) to provide automated services that would otherwise not be possible. IoT is not a single technology, but rather involves the convergence of sensor, actuator, information and communication technologies. Emerging IoT implementations will use smaller and more energy-efficient embedded sensor technologies, more sophisticated actuators, enhanced communications and advanced data analytics to collect and aggregate information. These new tools will enable intelligent systems that understand context, track and manage complex interactions and anticipate requirements. Market verticals that are potentially impacted by innovations in this area include connected cities and homes, smart transportation, smart agriculture, industrial IoT, and retail IoT.

title: Advanced Inclusive Learning Technologies
summary: The Learning and Cognitions Technologies topic aims to support entrepreneurs and startups at the earliest stages of translating novel, highly differentiated learning and cognition technologies based on their own peer-reviewed research to create sustainable, commercializable opportunities for scalable, real-world application addressing societal needs.
description:
NSF technology topic: Learning and Cognition Technologies

The Learning and Cognitions Technologies topic aims to support entrepreneurs and startups at the earliest stages of translating novel, highly differentiated learning and cognition technologies based on their own peer-reviewed research to create sustainable, commercializable opportunities for scalable, real-world application addressing societal needs.

The novel technologies in this topic aim to remove barriers to scientific progress and the development of advanced training tools and upskilling to enhance adaptability, and enabling platforms which deliver groundbreaking advancements in human development. Technologies in this portfolio include novel approaches not yet reduced to practice across education or workforce development, training tools, upskilling an aging workforce, improving health and wellbeing, as well as novel theoretical frameworks not yet applied to practice.

Limited studies with human subjects may be acceptable to the extent that they are performed in support of feasibility, such as proof-of-concept studies of early-stage technologies. Proposals that request support for clinical studies will be deemed noncompliant with the SBIR/STTR solicitations and returned without review.

title: Nanotechnology

description:
NSF technology topic: Nanotechnology

The Nanotechnology topic addresses the creation and manipulation of functional materials, devices and systems with novel properties that are achieved through the control of matter at a submicroscopic scale (from a fraction of nanometer to about 100 nanometers). This includes, but is not limited to, innovative hierarchical nanostructures, nanolayered structures, nanowires, nanotubes, quantum dots, nanoparticles, nanofibers and other nanomaterials and biomaterials and their composite structures.

title: Other Topics
summary: For projects that do not seem to fit into one of the other technology topic areas, but still meet the NSF SBIR/STTR goals of supporting research and development of deep technology with commercial viability and the potential to benefit society, please pick Other Topics and subtopic 1.
description:
NSF technology topic: Other Topics

For projects that do not seem to fit into one of the other technology topic areas, but still meet the NSF SBIR/STTR goals of supporting research and development of deep technology with commercial viability and the potential to benefit society, please pick Other Topics and subtopic 1. Project pitches and proposals submitted to Other Topics are typically transferred and reviewed in the topic area that best matches the underlying technical innovation. The program does not reject Project Pitches or proposals based on a non-ideal choice of topic areas. The program routinely moves Project Pitches or proposals internally among topic areas that seem to best describe the underlying technical innovation and to ensure the right program officer and reviewer panel sees the project.

title: Drug Discovery
summary: The Pharmaceutical Technologies topic covers a wide range of technology areas that advance the discovery, formulation, and manufacture of novel drugs, moieties, compounds, products, processes, platforms or services that will improve the selection, quality or price of pharmaceutical and biologic therapies.
description:
NSF technology topic: Pharmaceutical Technologies

The Pharmaceutical Technologies topic covers a wide range of technology areas that advance the discovery, formulation, and manufacture of novel drugs, moieties, compounds, products, processes, platforms or services that will improve the selection, quality or price of pharmaceutical and biologic therapies.

The Pharmaceutical Technologies topic is not aimed at supporting or conducting clinical trials, clinical efficacy and safety studies, the development of pre-clinical or clinical-stage drug candidates, work on medical devices or schedule I substances, or work performed primarily for regulatory purposes. Limited studies with human subjects may be acceptable if they are performed in support of feasibility, proof-of-concept studies of early-stage technologies and must follow NSF policies on research on human subjects. Proposals that request support for clinical studies are noncompliant with the SBIR/STTR solicitations and returned without review.

The NSF SBIR/STTR program no longer supports the development of specific therapeutic molecules. Drug Discovery and Manufacturing are still supported by the program.

Subtopics are not aimed at supporting clinical trials, the clinical validation of information technologies, or medical devices or studies performed primarily for regulatory purposes. Limited studies with human subjects may be acceptable to the extent that they are performed in support of feasibility, such as proof-of-concept studies of early-stage technologies. Proposals that request support for clinical studies will be deemed noncompliant with the SBIR/STTR solicitations and returned without review.
